en:
Asonuma Hirotsuna, also called Shirō, was a Shimotsuke warrior of the Fujiwara-descended Ashikaga clan, the fourth son of Ashikaga Aritsuna. He took the name Asonuma from his holding of Asonuma in Aso District.

When the head Ashikaga house joined the Taira in the Genpei War, Hirotsuna instead served Minamoto no Yoritomo and became a Kamakura gokenin. In 1189 he campaigned in Ōshū and was appointed jitō of Tōno manor in Hei District, Mutsu.

zh:
阿曾沼广纲，通称四郎，是下野国藤姓足利氏的武将，为足利有纲第四子，因领有安苏郡阿曾沼之地而称阿曾沼氏。

源平合战时，宗家足利氏站在平家一方，广纲却追随源赖朝，成为镰仓幕府的御家人。1189年，他参加奥州之战，获补任为陆奥国闭伊郡远野保的地头。

en: Kimisato was the fifth head of the Tōno Asonuma and a son of Kintsuna. His brother Mitsusato's descendants formed the Aki branch, while Kimisato kept the clan's lands around Tōno in Mutsu Province. His son Ujitsuna succeeded him as sixth head.

en:
Asonuma Tomotsuna was lord of the Tōno Asonuma, a warrior house of Fujiwara-descended Ashikaga stock, seated at Yokota Castle in Hei district, Mutsu province. In 1334 his title to the Tōno estate was confirmed by Kitabatake Akiie, the Southern Court's governor of Mutsu.

His second son Jirō went to Ōtsuchi to keep order on the eastern coast of Hei district and built Ōtsuchi Castle as his seat, becoming the founder of the Ōtsuchi house.

en:
Imperial Prince Atsumi (893–967), known as the Rokujō Prince, was the eighth son of Emperor Uda and a younger brother of Emperor Daigo. He reached the first imperial rank and headed the Shikibu ministry.

A gifted musician, he played flute and strings at court and led one side of the Teiji-in poetry contest of 913. He resigned in 945, took Buddhist vows as Kakushin at Ninna-ji in 950, and died there in 967 aged seventy-five. His son Minamoto no Masanobu founded the Uda Genji line.

敦实亲王（893—967），称六条宫，是宇多天皇的第八子，醍醐天皇的弟弟。他官至一品、式部卿。

敦实富有音乐才华，常吹奏笛子、演奏弦乐，并在913年的亭子院歌合中担任右方带头人。他于945年上表辞官，950年在仁和寺剃度出家，法名觉真，967年在寺中去世，终年七十五岁。其子源雅信是宇多源氏一脉的祖先。

en:
Bidatsu (538–585), the 30th emperor of Japan, was the second son of Emperor Kinmei by Princess Ishi-hime. Named crown prince in 569, he ascended in 572.

His court was dominated by the rivalry between Soga no Umako, who patronised Buddhism, and Mononobe no Moriya, who defended the native kami. Bidatsu leaned toward the traditional cults, and when plague struck in 585 he banned Buddhism; he died of it the same year. His widow, his half-sister Suiko, later reigned as empress.

zh:
敏达天皇（538—585）是日本第30代天皇，钦明天皇与石姬皇女所生的次子。569年被立为太子，572年即位。

他在位时，朝廷由苏我马子与物部守屋的对立主导：前者扶持佛教，后者维护传统神祇信仰。敏达倾向本土神道教，585年瘟疫蔓延时下令禁佛，同年染疫身亡。他的皇后、异母妹推古在他死后成为女帝。

en:
Chiba Kazutane (c. 1310–1336) was the eldest son of Sadatane, eleventh head of the Chiba clan of Shimōsa, and is counted as the clan's twelfth head, though he died before formally succeeding. In the Nanboku-chō war he served the Southern Court under Nitta Yoshisada against Ashikaga Takauji.

On the sixteenth day of the first month of 1336, at Shiga village in Tamba province, he was killed in battle by Hosokawa Jōzen of the Ashikaga army. His younger brother Ujitane eventually succeeded their father as Chiba head.

千叶一胤（约1310—1336）是下总国千叶氏第十一代当主贞胤的嫡男，被列为第十二代当主，但在正式继承家督前战死。南北朝动乱中，他加入南朝方新田义贞的军队，对抗足利尊氏。

en:
Chiba Munetane (1265–1294) was the ninth head of the Chiba clan of Shimōsa and a gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate, succeeding his father Yoritane in 1275. After the Mongol invasions he served on the Kyushu coastal guard, stationed in Ogi district, Hizen.

While Munetane was absent in Kyushu, his younger brother Tanemune, minding the home estate of Chiba-no-shō, made himself its effective master. Munetane died in 1294; his heirs fought Tanemune's line for the headship, and his second son Taneyasu founded the Kyushu Chiba.

zh:
千叶宗胤（1265—1294）是下总国千叶氏第九代当主、镰仓幕府御家人，1275年继承父亲赖胤。元寇之后，他奉命出任异国警固番役，驻扎在九州肥前国小城郡。

宗胤滞留九州期间，留守本领千叶庄的弟弟胤宗成为庄园的实际领主。1294年宗胤去世，其后人为家督之位与胤宗一系相争，次子胤泰则开创了九州千叶氏。

en:
Chiba Naritane (1155–1218) was the fifth head of the Chiba clan and held the title Chiba no suke, succeeding his father Chiba Tanemasa. In the ninth month of 1180, on the orders of his grandfather Chiba Tsunetane, he raided the pro-Taira deputy of Shimōsa at the provincial headquarters and killed him.

When the Taira-appointed governor hurried back to assault the Chiba manor, Naritane met him at Yugihama and took him prisoner. His son Chiba Tanetsuna succeeded him as clan head.

zh:
千叶成胤（1155—1218）是千叶氏第五代当主，官称千叶介，继其父千叶胤正之后继任。1180年9月，他奉祖父千叶常胤之命突袭下总国府，讨杀亲平家的下总目代。

平氏任命的下总守闻讯回师急攻千叶庄，成胤在结城浜迎战，将其擒获，即结城浜之战。其子千叶胤纲后来继任千叶氏当主。

en:
Chiba Sadatane, eleventh head of the Chiba clan, was the son of the tenth head Tanemune and took his name from the Hōjō regent Sadatoki. In 1312 he succeeded as shugo of Iga and Shimōsa. In 1333 he abandoned the Hōjō to join Nitta Yoshisada's attack on Kamakura, and from 1335 he fought his cousin Tanesada for the headship.

His heir fell in January 1336; that October Sadatane surrendered in Echizen, then defected to the Northern Court. He fought at Shijōnawate in 1348 and died in Kyoto in 1351.

千叶贞胤是千叶氏第十一代当主，第十代当主千叶胤宗之子，名字中的“贞”字得自北条执权贞时。1312年他继承家督，接任伊贺、下总两国的守护职。1333年他背弃北条氏，投奔攻打镰仓的新田义贞；1335年起又与堂兄胤贞争夺家督。

1336年1月嫡男战死，同年10月他在越前国投降，随后转投北朝方。1348年他在四条畷作战，1351年卒于京都。

en:
Chiba Tanemasa (1141–1203), fourth head of the Chiba clan, was the eldest son of Chiba Tsunetane, commonly called Shinsuke. In 1180 he and his father answered Minamoto no Yoritomo's rising, and in April 1181 he was named among the eleven warriors guarding Yoritomo's own quarters.

He fought in the Ōshū campaign of 1189 and helped crush the rebel Ōkawa Kanetō the following year. He died in 1203, traditionally aged sixty-three, and was succeeded by his son Naritane.

千叶胤正（1141—1203）是千叶氏第四代当主，千叶常胤的长子，通称新介。1180年源赖朝举兵，他与父亲一同投奔赖朝从军；1181年4月，他被选为警卫赖朝寝所的十一名武士之一。

1189年他参加奥州合战立下武功，次年又参与镇压大河兼任的叛乱。1203年去世，通说享年63岁，家督由儿子成胤继承。

en:
Chiba Tanemune (1268–1312) was the tenth head of the Chiba clan of Shimōsa and a gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate, the second son of the eighth head Yoritane. After Yoritane died in 1275, his elder brother Munetane was posted to Hizen in Kyushu on coastal guard duty, leaving Tanemune to administer Chiba-no-shō.

When Munetane died in 1294, his heir Tanesada was young and far away in Kyushu, so Tanemune made himself the tenth Chiba head. He died in 1312 and was succeeded by his son Sadatane.

千叶胤宗（1268—1312）是下总国千叶氏第十代当主、镰仓幕府御家人，第八代当主赖胤的次男。1275年父亲赖胤死后，兄长宗胤奉派前往九州肥前国担任异国警固番役，由他掌管本领千叶庄。

1294年宗胤去世，其继承人胤贞年幼且远在九州，胤宗遂成为千叶庄之主、继任千叶氏当主。1312年他去世，由其子贞胤继任。

en:
Chiba Tanetsuna (1198–1228), sixth head of the Chiba clan and a Kamakura gokenin, succeeded his father Naritane in 1218. In the seventh month of 1219 he escorted the new shōgun Fujiwara no Yoritsune down to Kamakura.

During the Jōkyū War of 1221 he marched west up the Tōkaidō with Hōjō Yasutoki against the retired emperor's forces and won distinction. He died in the fifth month of 1228, aged thirty-one.

en:
Chiba Taneyasu was a warrior of the Nanboku-chō period and the second son of Chiba Munetane, ninth head of the Chiba clan. While Munetane governed Hizen Province, his younger brother Tanemune seized the family's Chiba manor in Shimōsa, and Tanemune's son Sadatane took the headship.

In 1335 Taneyasu's elder brother Tanesada attacked Sadatane's estate, but died of disease in Mikawa in 1336. Taneyasu, established in Ogi district of Hizen, then founded the Kyushu, or Hizen, branch of the Chiba.

千叶胤泰是日本南北朝时代的武将，为千叶氏第九代当主千叶宗胤的次子。其父宗胤前往肥前国期间，叔父胤宗占据了千叶氏在下总国的本领，胤宗之子贞胤继任家督。

1335年，胤泰之兄胤贞攻打贞胤的千叶庄，1336年病死于三河。定居肥前国小城郡的胤泰由此开创九州千叶氏，又称肥前千叶氏，成为这支分家的始祖。

en:
Chiba Tokitane (1218–1241) was the seventh head of the Chiba clan, succeeding as Chiba no suke in 1228; later genealogies make him Tanetsuna's son rather than his brother. He received a character for his name from the regent Hōjō Yasutoki.

In 1236 he received an imperial edict to rebuild Katori Shrine, the chief shrine of Shimōsa. Ordered by Yasutoki to finish the work, he was kept from joining Shōgun Yoritsune's Kyoto trip in 1238, and he died in 1241 aged twenty-four with the shrine still underway, succeeded by his son Yoritane.

en:
Chiba Tsuneshige (1083–1180) was a late-Heian samurai of Shimōsa Province and the second head of the Chiba clan, son of Taira no Tsunekane. In 1124 his uncle ceded him the district of Sōma, and on his father's death in 1126 he inherited the Chiba district, uniting the two.

In 1126 he is said to have moved his seat from Ōjii in Kazusa to Chiba and built Chiba Castle. He donated the Chiba manor to Cloistered Emperor Toba in 1130, and in 1135 passed leadership to his young son Tsunetane.

Chiba Tsunetane (1118–1201), third head of the Chiba clan, raised his house to Kamakura vassal standing. Son of Chiba Tsuneshige, he fought under Minamoto no Yoshitomo in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156. He fought at Ichinotani in 1184 and commanded the Tōkaidō army in the 1189 Ōshū campaign. He died in 1201 aged eighty-four; later Chiba heads took the character tane from his name.

en:
Chiba Yoritane (1239–1275) was the eighth head of the Chiba clan of Shimōsa and a gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate. In 1241, aged three, he succeeded his father Tokitane, while the kinsman Chiba Hidetane held real power until his faction was destroyed in the Hōji conflict of 1247.

Called to the Kyushu coastal guard during the Mongol invasions, he was wounded fighting the Yuan army and died in 1275 aged thirty-seven, leaving the clan to his son Munetane.

en:
Chōsokabe Kaneyoshi was the twelfth head of the Chōsokabe clan and castellan of Okō Castle in Tosa Province, succeeding his father Nobuyoshi, who served Ashikaga Takauji on the Northern Court side. He fought under the Hosokawa, shugo of Tosa, at Higashi-Sakamoto; for this service father and son were rewarded with estate stewardships.

Around 1345 he became temple magistrate of Kyūkō-an on Mount Godai and rebuilt the temple. This office was inherited by his descendants.

en:
Chōsokabe Nobuyoshi was the eleventh head of the Chōsokabe, a warrior clan of Tosa Province in Shikoku, succeeding his father Shigemune. From his generation the clan organized the local myōshū landholders and consolidated its base as a regional lord.

In May 1333, after the fall of the Kamakura shogunate, Ashikaga Takauji ordered him and Kōsokabe Hideyori to suppress a rising of local landowners at Kera-no-shō in Tosa.

en:
Chōsokabe Yoshitoshi was the founder of the Chōsokabe clan of Tosa. At first called Hata no Yoshitoshi, he was said to descend from the Hata clan that held Sarashina district in Shinano. Chronicles relate that he fought for Retired Emperor Sutoku in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 and fled to Tosa after the defeat, settling in Sogabe in Nagaoka district.

Tradition makes him the builder of Okō castle and the first to bear the name Sogabe, later written Chōsokabe. His son was Toshimune.

en:
Chūjō Hidenaga was a commander of the Chūjō house of Musashi, a family of the Yokoyama party. In 1335, as lord of Koromo Castle in Mikawa Province, he invited the Zen monk Taiyō Gichū and founded Chōkō-ji as his family temple.

With its eighteen subtemples it was then the largest monastery in the region. Under the new Muromachi shogunate he was appointed shugo, military governor, of Owari Province, holding the post from 1336 to 1338.

Chūjō Ienaga (1165 – 26 September 1236) was a Kamakura-period warrior of the Yokoyama league in Musashi province, the eldest son of Chūjō Kanetsuna. Adopted by Hatta Tomoie, he took the surname Chūjō and claimed descent from the Michikane line of the northern Fujiwara.

He fought under Minamoto no Noriyori at Ichinotani in 1184 and in the Ōshū campaign of 1189–1190. In 1225 he joined the first Council of State, helping frame the Goseibai Shikimoku.

中条家长（1165—1236年9月26日）是镰仓时代武藏国横山党的武将，中条兼纲的长子。他被八田知家收为养子，改姓中条，自称藤原北家道兼流后裔。

1184年他随源范赖参加一之谷之战，又从军1189至1190年的奥州合战。1225年他成为幕府初代评定众之一，参与制定《御成败式目》。

en:
Chūjō Kagenaga was a warrior of the Chūjō house of Musashi Province, one of the Yokoyama party bands that had served the Kamakura shogunate. In 1290 he is recorded as shugo, or military governor, of Owari Province. In 1333 he followed Ashikaga Takauji in the campaigns that overthrew the Kamakura shogunate.

He held Koromo Castle in Mikawa Province. After his eldest son Tokinaga moved to Ōshū in 1334, his second son Nagahide succeeded him as castellan in 1354.

zh:
中条景长是武藏国中条氏的武将，该族属于效力镰仓幕府的武藏七党之一横山党。1290年，他被任为尾张国守护。1333年，他追随足利尊氏，在推翻镰仓幕府的战役中作战。

他领有三河国举母城。长子时长于1334年迁居奥州后，次子长秀于1354年继任城主。

en:
Chūjō Nagahide (d. 1384) was a Nanbokuchō-period warrior, the second son of Chūjō Kagenaga, who fought for Ashikaga Takauji against the Kamakura shogunate. In 1354 he succeeded his father as lord of Koromo Castle in Mikawa Province. He trained under Nenami Jion, founder of the Nen-ryū sword school, and was counted among the master's fourteen leading disciples before founding his own Chūjō-ryū.

He served the Muromachi shogunate as shugo of Iga and taught swordsmanship to Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. A disciple of the poet Ton'a, his verses appear in several imperial anthologies.

zh:
中条长秀（？—1384年）是日本南北朝时代武将，为追随足利尊氏攻灭镰仓幕府的中条景长之次子。1354年，他继承父亲成为三河国举母城主。他师从念流开山之祖念阿弥慈恩，位列“念流十四哲”，后综合家传武艺开创中条流平法。

他在室町幕府担任伊贺守护，并担任足利义满的剑术指南役。他又是和歌僧人顿阿的高足，作品被收入多部敕撰和歌集。

en:
Chūjō Narihiro, also recorded as Chūjō Yoshikatsu or Chūjō Kanetsuna, was a Musashi warrior of the Yokoyama league, based at Ono in Saitama district. When Minamoto no Yoritomo rose against the Taira in 1180, Narihiro answered his call and distinguished himself at the Battle of Ishibashiyama.

With his eldest son Ienaga, he fought against Fujiwara no Yasuhira in 1189 and helped suppress Ōkawa Kanetō's revolt the following year. His sons Ienaga and Yoshitoki founded the main Chūjō line and the Waga warrior house of Mutsu province.

zh:
中条成寻，史料中又记作中条义胜、中条兼纲，是武藏国埼玉郡小野地方的横山党武士。1180年源赖朝举兵讨伐平氏时，成寻响应起兵，在石桥山之战中立下战功。

1189年他与长子家长一同讨伐藤原泰衡，翌年又参与平定大河兼任之乱。他的儿子家长与义季，分别成为中条氏嫡流和陆奥国和贺氏武家的祖先。

en:
Chūjō Yoshitoki, also named Narisue and known in religion as Sainen, was a Kamakura gokenin, the second son of Chūjō Yoshikatsu. He was adopted by Wada Yoshimori, chief of the shogunate's Board of Retainers, and took the Kanmu Taira surname.

For his military service he was granted Katta district in Mutsu province. During the Jōkyū era of 1219–1222 his son Yoshiyuki entered Waga district as half-district jitō, and Yoshiyuki's line adopted the Waga clan name.

zh:
中条义季，又名成季，法名西念，是镰仓御家人、中条义胜的次子。他被镰仓幕府侍所别当和田义盛收为养子，改姓桓武平氏。

后因军功受封陆奥国刈田郡。承久年间（1219—1222年），其子义行以半郡地头的身份进入和贺郡，义行一支此后改称和贺氏，即陆奥和贺氏之祖。

en:
Emperor Chūkyō (1218–1234) was the 85th emperor of Japan, though his reign lasted barely two months in 1221. At the age of two he succeeded his father Emperor Juntoku, who abdicated to join Retired Emperor Go-Toba's rising.

When the Jōkyū Incident ended in defeat, the shogunate dethroned the infant in favour of Emperor Go-Horikawa. Long known as the Kujō Dethroned Emperor or the Half-Emperor, he was recognised as an emperor and given the posthumous name Chūkyō in 1870.

zh:
仲恭天皇（1218—1234）是日本第85代天皇，1221年在位仅约两个月。其父顺德天皇为参与后鸟羽上皇的起兵而退位，年仅两岁的怀成亲王随即继位。

承久之乱失败后，幕府废黜幼帝，另立后堀河天皇。他长期被称为九条废帝、半帝，直到1870年才被承认为天皇，获追号仲恭天皇。

en:
Emperor Daigo (884–930), personal name Atsuhito, was the 60th emperor of Japan, reigning from 897 to 930. The eldest son of Emperor Uda, he was unusual among Heian sovereigns in ruling for decades without a Fujiwara regent. In 901 his minister Sugawara no Michizane was exiled to Dazaifu.

When lightning struck the palace in 930 and killed several courtiers, it was read as Michizane's vengeance. Daigo abdicated that autumn, took Buddhist vows, and died days later at forty-six, buried at Daigo-ji.

zh:
醍醐天皇（884—930），名敦仁，是日本第60代天皇，897年至930年在位。他是宇多天皇的长子，在平安时代的天皇中颇为罕见——数十年间不设藤原氏摄政，亲理朝政。901年，大臣菅原道真被流放至大宰府。

930年雷电击中皇宫，多名朝臣毙命，时人视为道真怨灵作祟。醍醐于当年秋天退位、出家，数日后去世，终年四十六岁，葬于醍醐寺。

en:
Daihōji Nagamori, also called Mutō Nagamori, was the fifth head of the Daihōji clan of Dewa Province, son of the fourth head Akiuji. His family descended from Mutō Yorihira, a bureaucrat of the early Kamakura shogunate. In 1189 Yorihira's son Sukeyori was appointed steward of Ōizumi estate in Dewa.

During the Northern and Southern Courts period, Nagamori is said to have built a castle at Daihōji on the estate and taken its name. Morouji succeeded him as head of the clan.

en:
Mutō Ujihira was an early Kamakura-period warrior of Fujiwara descent, a son of Mutō Yorihira and the founding head of the family that later became the Daihōji of Dewa Province. As jitō of Ōizumi manor in the Shōnai region, he took the family name Ōizumi.

In 1209 the monk-soldiers of Mount Haguro brought suit against him for encroaching on the mountain temple's estates. His successors later settled at Daihōji Castle, the center of the manor, and renamed the clan Daihōji.

en:
Daijo Suemoto was head of the Daijo house of Hitachi Province, succeeding his father Tomomoto as Hitachi Daijo; in his later years he took Buddhist vows. His chosen heir, his son Mitsumoto, died young, so Suemoto had Mitsumoto's eldest son Tsunemoto named family head and acted as the boy's guardian.

Suemoto died on 27 April 1289 at the age of sixty-eight. His death at once opened a succession crisis, as the Hojo houseman Kudo Mitsuteru intervened to install his own grandson and drive Tsunemoto out.

en:
Daijo Sukemoto (died c. 1227), also called Baba Sukemoto, was a warrior and gokenin of Hitachi Province at the turn of the thirteenth century, regarded as the founder of the Daijo house. The Azuma Kagami first names him in 1190, in the vanguard when Minamoto no Yoritomo entered Kyoto. In 1193, after Taki Yoshimoto fell from power, Yoritomo granted him Yoshimoto's lands and appointed him Hitachi Daijo.

In 1214 he became jito of Hitachi-Fuchu. His heirs inherited the Daijo office, from which the family took its name.

en:
Daijō Takamoto, head of the Daijō house of Hitachi and lord of Mito Castle, was a warrior of the Nanboku-chō wars, known in religion as Jōei. In 1330 he is credited with founding Seiryō-ji in Hitachi. In 1335 he joined Hōjō Tokiyuki's Nakasendai Rebellion and fought against Ashikaga Takauji at the Sagami River.

He then sided with the Southern Court, submitted to the Northern Court in 1337, and fought in the Kannō Disturbance. Afterward he attended Kamakura kubo Ashikaga Motouji and restored his house's power, dying between 1382 and 1386.

en:
Daijo Tokimoto was a son of Daijo Mitsumoto and became head of the Daijo house of Hitachi Province while still a child named Choju. When his grandfather Suemoto died in 1289, his maternal grandfather Kudo Mitsuteru had the boy installed as family head in place of his elder brother Tsunemoto, who was driven out; after coming of age Choju took the name Tokimoto.

Tsunemoto contested the succession for more than twenty years, but Tokimoto won the final judgement in the Tokuji era of 1306 to 1308. His sons Morimoto and Takamoto succeeded him.

en:
Daijo Tomomoto was the eldest son of Daijo Sukemoto, founder of the Daijo house of Hitachi Province, and succeeded him as Hitachi Daijo. When Sukemoto died, Oda Tomoshige challenged Tomomoto's right to the post.

In 1227 the Kamakura regent Hojo Yasutoki ruled in his favour, citing Minamoto no Yoritomo's written order that the office pass from Sukemoto to his heir. The judgement confirmed the family's hereditary hold on the post, and Tomomoto was succeeded by his son Suemoto.

en:
Daijo Tsunemoto was the eldest son of Daijo Mitsumoto and briefly the head of the Daijo house of Hitachi Province. When Mitsumoto died young, Tsunemoto's grandfather Suemoto had him named heir while still a child and acted as his guardian.

After Suemoto's death in 1289, however, Kudo Mitsuteru had Tsunemoto expelled and installed his grandson Choju, later called Tokimoto, as family head. Tsunemoto carried his protest to the Kamakura shogunate, but after more than twenty years of litigation the case ended against him in the Tokuji era of 1306 to 1308.

en:
Date Masayori (1227–1301) was a mid-Kamakura gokenin and the fourth head of the Date clan, lord of Yanagawa castle in Mutsu; after taking Buddhist vows he was known as Gansai. A second son of Date Yoshihiro, he kept the clan residence in Kamakura and fathered his successor Munetsuna.

A devout Buddhist, he imitated the Five Mountains of Kyoto and Kamakura by founding five monasteries around Date, among them Tōshō-ji in 1283, which became the Date family's first ancestral temple.

政依笃信佛教，仿效京都五山与镰仓五山，在伊达一带创建五寺，合称伊达五山；其中1283年所建的东昌寺是伊达家最早的菩提寺。

政依笃信佛教，仿效京都五山与镰仓五山，在[ShowLocationName('date_loc')]一带创建五寺，合称伊达五山；其中1283年所建的东昌寺是伊达家最早的菩提寺。

en:
Date Munemura (1173–1251) was the second head of the Date clan of Mutsu, the second son of Date Tomomune by a daughter of the Yūki house. The Azuma Kagami lists him as Tameshige among the four sons who fought beside their father in the 1189 Ōshū campaign, after which the family received Date district.

Old Date genealogies even name Munemura, rather than Tomomune, as the clan's founder. He was the father of Date Yoshihiro.

zh:
伊达宗村（1173—1251）是陆奥伊达氏第二代当主、初代当主伊达朝宗的次子，母亲为结城氏之女。《吾妻镜》把他记作“为重”，列为1189年随父参加奥州合战的四个儿子之一，伊达郡即此战的恩赏。

伊达氏的古系图中，颇有以宗村而非朝宗为初代当主者。他是伊达义广之父。

en:
Date Munetō (1324–1385) was the eighth head of the Date clan of Mutsu, active in the Nanboku-chō period. From about 1380 he waged a calculated campaign against the Nagai clan, mixing alliances and surprise attacks. In 1381 he defeated the Osaki, seizing several districts, and brought Watari under his control.

In 1385 he destroyed the Nagai and secured Yonezawa for the Date. He also rebuilt the hall of the Narushima Hachiman shrine in Yonezawa.

zh:
伊达宗远（1324—1385）是陆奥伊达氏第八代当主，南北朝时代的武将。约1380年起，他软硬兼施，以一揆契约和偷袭等手段持续蚕食长井氏。1381年他与大崎氏交战，夺取数郡，将亘理郡纳入实际支配。

1385年他攻灭长井氏，为伊达氏取得米泽。他还重修了米泽成岛八幡宫的拜殿。

en:
Date Munetsuna (1254–1317) was a mid-Kamakura gokenin and the fifth head of the Date clan, the eldest son and heir of Date Masayori; he was commonly called Kai Kotarō.

His sons included his successor Date Motomune, Munemasa, and Yukitsuna, who took the Senoue name. His younger brother Munehiro left the main line to become adopted heir of Shiraishi Nagatoshi and began the Shiraishi house.

伊达宗纲（1254—1317）是镰仓时代中期的御家人、伊达氏第五代当主，伊达政依的嫡男，通称甲斐小太郎。

其子有继为当主的伊达基宗、宗昌（彦二郎），以及改称濑上氏的行纲（濑上五郎）。其弟宗弘离开宗家，出继白石长俊为养嗣子，开创白石氏。

en:
Date Tameie was the fourth son of Date Tomomune, founder of the Date clan. The Azuma Kagami names him among the sons who fought beside their father at the Battle of Ishinazaka in Minamoto no Yoritomo's 1189 Ōshū campaign, for which the family was rewarded with Date district in Mutsu.

He is regarded as ancestor of the Suruga Date line. The Date Seshin Kafu relates that his son Date Tameshige settled in Hienuki district and took the place name, beginning the Hienuki clan.

en:
Date Tomomune (1129–1199) was a late Heian warrior and the first head of the Date house. Originally called Nakamura Tarō, he administered the Nakamura estate in Haga district, Shimotsuke Province. In 1180 he joined the rising of his maternal cousin Minamoto no Yoritomo.

In the 1189 Ōshū campaign his four sons stormed the Ishinazaka fortress and captured enemy general Satō Motoharu; rewarded with Date district in Mutsu, Tomomune took the name Date. He was succeeded by his second son, Munemura.

zh:
伊达朝宗（1129—1199）是平安时代后期至镰仓初期的御家人，伊达宗家初代当主。他原称中村太郎，管理下野国芳贺郡的中村庄园。1180年源赖朝举兵时，因赖朝是他姑表兄弟，他驰赴其麾下。

1189年奥州合战中，他的四个儿子充当前锋，攻破石那坂城砦，生擒敌将佐藤基治；他以此功受领陆奥国伊达郡，遂改称伊达姓。死后由次子伊达宗村继承。

en:
Date Yoshihiro (1185–1256) was an early Kamakura gokenin and the third head of the Date clan, the second son of Date Munemura. In his generation the clan seat moved from Takakogaoka to the Kurino mansion in Kōri, Date district, and the character in his name is thought to have been granted by shogunal regent Hōjō Yoshitoki.

In the 1221 Jōkyū War he sent a retainer to fight under Yoshitoki's son Yasutoki at Uji. He took the monk name Kakubutsu; sources give his death as 1251 or 1256.

伊达义广（1185—1256）是镰仓时代前期的御家人、伊达氏第三代当主，伊达宗村的次子。他这一代把居城从伊达郡桑折乡的高子冈迁至同乡的栗野大馆；其名中的“义”字被认为得自执权北条义时。

1221年承久之乱中，他派遣家臣随义时之子北条泰时在宇治作战。他出家后法名觉佛；关于卒年，史料有1251年与1256年两说。

en:
Date Yukitomo (1291–1348), later called Yukimune, was the seventh head of the Date clan of Mutsu and a Southern Court commander in the Nanboku-chō wars. In 1331 he joined the Hōjō army sent against the Genkō rising, but after the Kamakura shogunate fell in 1333 he served under Kitabatake Akiie.

He campaigned west with Akiie in 1335 and again in 1337, and after Akiie's death held Isa Castle against Kō no Morofuyu before escaping home. He died in 1348; his verses appear in the Fūga Wakashū as Fujiwara no Tomomura.

伊达行朝（1291—1348），晚年改名行宗，是陆奥伊达氏第七代当主，南北朝时代效力南朝。1331年元弘之变时，他加入北条高时派往畿内的讨伐军；1333年镰仓幕府灭亡后，出仕北畠显家。

1335年和1337年他两度随显家西征，显家死后据守伊佐城抵御高师冬，最终突围返回本领。他于1348年去世，曾以藤原朝村之名在《风雅和歌集》中留有和歌。

en:
Sanehira Dohi (died 1191) was a Sagami warlord of the Kanmu Taira lineage, ancestor of the Dohi and, by tradition, the Kobayakawa clans. From Dohi-gō he led the Nakamura war-band, and in 1180 was among the first to join Minamoto no Yoritomo's revolt; after the defeat at Ishibashiyama he fled with Yoritomo and helped him escape to Awa.

He fought at the Fuji River, Uji and Ichinotani, leading over seven thousand cavalry on the western wing. He became military governor of the three Kibi provinces and of Nagato and Suō, and also served in the 1189 Ōshū campaign.

土肥实平（？—1191）是相模国豪族，出自桓武平氏良文流，为土肥氏之祖，相传也是小早川氏的祖先。他以土肥乡为据点统领“中村党”武士团，1180年源赖朝举兵时率先率众投奔；石桥山战败后他随赖朝逃亡，并助其渡海撤往安房国。

en:
Dohi Tōhira (died 1237) was a Kamakura shogunate retainer and heir of Dohi Sanehira. At Dohi-gō in Sagami he built a hall at Kobayakawa village, from which his descendants took their name. In 1180 he and his father joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's uprising and fought at Ishibashiyama; when Yoritomo fled to Awa, Tōhira carried word of his safety to Hōjō Masako.

After the Genpei War he was made steward of Nuta manor in Aki Province. During the Wada conflict of 1213 he stayed neutral, though his son was executed for joining the rebels.

土肥远平（？—1237）是镰仓幕府御家人、土肥实平的继承人。他领有相模国土肥乡，在小早川村筑馆，子孙后来即以小早川为姓。1180年他随父亲参加源赖朝举兵，在石桥山之战中战败；赖朝逃往安房国时，他充当使者向北条政子报告赖朝平安无恙。

en:
Doi Michimasu, called Hikokurō, was an Iyo warrior of the Kōno branch clan and eldest son of Doi Michinari. In 1321 the Kamakura shogunate gave him charge of Iyo's maritime defense. In 1333 he was among the first to rise for Emperor Go-Daigo, storming Fuchū Castle and routing Hōjō Tokinao at Ishiihama.

Under the Kenmu government he served as Bitchū no Kami, and in 1336 fought for the Southern Court with Nitta Yoshisada at Teshimagawara and Minatogawa. On 14 November 1336 he fell with his kinsmen in Shiba Takatsune's snowbound ambush at Arachi in Echizen.

en:
Emperor En'yū (959–991), personal name Morihira, was the 64th emperor of Japan, reigning from 969 to 984. The fifth son of Emperor Murakami and Reizei's younger brother, he was named heir in 967 with Fujiwara backing, and the Anna Incident of 969 ruined Minamoto no Takaakira.

He favoured his uncle Fujiwara no Kanemichi in the clan's struggle over the kampaku post, while palace fires wrecked the Sacred Mirror. En'yū abdicated in 984, took Buddhist vows as Kongō Hō in 985, and died in 991; his only son became Emperor Ichijō.

zh:
圆融天皇（959—991），名守平，是日本第64代天皇，969年至984年在位。他是村上天皇的第五子，冷泉天皇的同母弟，967年在藤原氏支持下被立为皇嗣；969年的安和之变使源高明失势。

在位期间，他在藤原氏围绕关白之位的争斗中偏袒舅父藤原兼通；皇宫屡次失火，神镜被烧毁。圆溶于984年退位，985年出家，法名金刚法，991年去世；他的独子后来成为一条天皇。

en:
En'ya Sadakiyo (died 1 May 1326) was a warrior of the late Kamakura period and shugo of Izumo Province, the son of En'ya Yoriyasu. Also called Sasaki Sadakiyo or Magojirō, he came of age between 1284 and 1311 under the ninth shikken Hōjō Sadatoki, receiving the character sada in his name, and inherited the Izumo shugo office from his father.

In the fifth month of 1325 he barred shugo officials from entering Gakuen-ji. He died on 1 May 1326, and the headship passed to his legitimate son Takasada.

en:
Enya Takasada was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts period, head of the Enya clan, a Sasaki branch that had long held the post of shugo of Izumo Province. When Emperor Go-Daigo escaped exile on Oki during the Genko War of 1333, Takasada ignored the shogunate's call to seize him and joined the emperor at Mount Senjo, afterwards becoming shugo of both Izumo and Oki.

He later sided with Ashikaga Takauji. In 1341, however, he was accused of treason and fled Kyoto, killing himself in Harima.

en:
En'ya Yoriyasu was a Kamakura shogunate gokenin and shugo of Izumo Province, founder of the Izumo En'ya clan. A son of Sasaki Yasukiyo, he came of age between 1246 and 1263 under the shikken Hōjō Tokiyori, receiving from him the character yori in his name. Around 1278 he succeeded his father as shugo of Izumo, built Ōsako Castle in Enya village and took the place name En'ya, beginning the clan.

In 1283 he funded the three-storey pagoda at Gakuen-ji. The Izumo shugo office passed through the line of his son Sadakiyo throughout the Kamakura period.

en:
Fujiwara no Akinori (1097–1152) was a court noble of the late Heian period, the son of Fujiwara no Morizane of the Northern House's Kajūji line, who rose to lesser councillor at senior fourth rank. In 1120 he was named provisional governor of Kai Province.

As his sister married Fujiwara no Tadazane and bore the minister Fujiwara no Yorinaga, Akinori served Yorinaga as a household administrator. He died suddenly in 1152 aged 54, still attending his duties the day before.

zh:
藤原显宪（1097—1152）是平安时代后期公卿，为藤原北家劝修寺流治部卿藤原盛实之子，官至正四位下少纳言。1120年他被任命为甲斐权守。

其姊妹嫁给藤原忠实并生下藤原赖长，显宪因此以舅父身份担任左大臣赖长的家司。1152年他以54岁之龄突然去世，据《本朝世纪》记载，去世前一天他仍在执行公务。

en:
Fujiwara no Akisue (1055–1123) was a nobleman and waka poet of the late Heian period, the second son of Fujiwara no Takatsune, governor of Mino Province. As his mother was Emperor Shirakawa's wet nurse, Akisue was the emperor's foster brother and trusted aide at court.

He grew wealthy through provincial governorships, and in 1104 reached Junior Third Rank, the first of his lineage at court in two centuries. Known as the Rokujō Shuri no Daibu, he founded the Rokujō Fujiwara school of poetry.

zh:
藤原显季（1055—1123）是平安时代后期的贵族与和歌歌人，为美浓守藤原隆经的次子。其母是白河天皇的乳母，显季因此作为天皇的乳兄弟深受信任，成为天皇的近臣。

他担任地方国司期间积蓄了丰厚财力，1104年升从三位，是其家族两百年来首位公卿。他号六条修理大夫，是和歌流派六条藤家之祖。

en:
Heyako no Aritsuna (?–1186), also called Ashikaga no Aritsuna, was a warrior of the Fujiwara-line Ashikaga clan of Shimotsuke Province, descended from Fujiwara no Hidesato and ancestor of the Sano and Asonuma families. As steward of the Tōdai-ji estate of Heyako-ho he built Fuma Castle. In 1180 he joined the Taira attack on Minamoto no Yorimasa at Uji, but at the Battle of Nogimiya he sided with the Minamoto alongside his sons.

In June 1186 he fought Ashikaga Yoshikane at Akamiyama. He was shot in the left eye and killed himself while fleeing.

户矢子有纲（？—1186），又称足利有纲，是下野国藤姓足利氏的武将，出自藤原秀乡一脉，为佐野氏与阿曾沼氏之祖。他担任东大寺领地户矢子保的保司，修筑不摩城。1180年宇治之战时，他随平氏攻打源赖政；后来的野木宫之战中，又与儿子们加入源氏一方。

1186年6月，他在赤见山与足利义兼交战，被箭射中左眼，败走后自尽。

en:
Fujiwara no Asayori (died c. 965) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Kanjūji branch of the northern Fujiwara, fourth son of the udaijin Fujiwara no Sadakata.

He spent his career in a string of guards and administrative posts, including lesser councillor and commander of the left middle palace guards, ending at junior fourth rank upper as head of the Audit Commissioners. Unlike his brothers Asatada and Asahira he never rose to kugyō, but his descendants prospered as the Kanjūji line.

藤原朝赖（?—约965）是日本平安时代中期的贵族，出身藤原北家劝修寺流，为右大臣藤原定方的第四子。

他历任少纳言、左兵卫督等近卫府与行政官职，最终官至从四位上勘解由长官。与兄弟朝忠、朝成不同，他终未能晋升公卿，但子孙作为劝修寺流繁衍兴旺。

en:
Fujiwara no Chikamasa was an eleventh-century Fujiwara courtier who, tradition records, was exiled to Kutsuna Island in Iyo after falling into disgrace. In 1084 he settled there as lord of the Kutsuna and Hashira island groups in the Seto Inland Sea and launched reclamation works.

In 1086 he founded Choryo-ji temple. His son Fujiwara no Chikatomo carried on the work, opening the six Kutsuna and five outer Hashira islands by about 1096. The seafaring Kutsuna clan later claimed him as its ancestor.

藤原亲贤是11世纪的藤原氏贵族。相传他因获罪被流放至伊予的忽那岛，于1084年入岛，成为忽那诸岛与柱岛群岛的领主，着手开垦各岛。

1086年，他创建长领寺。其子藤原亲朝继续经营，至约1096年陆续开垦忽那六岛与柱岛外五岛。后来称雄濑户内海的忽那水军一族忽那氏，即奉亲贤为始祖。

en:
Fujiwara no Chitsune (died 1012), also written Chizune or Tomotsune, was a military noble of the Northern Fujiwara's Uonama line and a son of Fujiwara no Hidesato. In 968 Shinano Province reported him to the court for rebellion.

After his elder brother Chiharu was exiled in the Anna Incident of 969, Chitsune became the principal heir of Hidesato's line and was named general of the chinjufu in 970. He later served as captain of the left palace guards and governor of Mino, and died in 1012.

zh:
藤原千常（？—1012），一作知常，是藤原北家鱼名流的军事贵族，为藤原秀乡之子。968年，信浓国向朝廷奏告他谋反。

969年安和之变后其兄千晴被流放，千常遂成为秀乡流的嫡子，并于970年出任镇守府将军。他后来历任左卫门尉、美浓守，1012年去世。

en:
Fujiwara no Fuhito (659–720), second son of Fujiwara no Kamatari, laid the foundations of Fujiwara power. He helped enthrone Emperor Monmu in 697, led the compilation of the Taiho Code of 701, and in 698 won his descendants exclusive right to the Fujiwara name.

He married a daughter to Monmu and another, Komyoshi, to Emperor Shomu, Japan's first non-imperial empress. His four sons founded the clan's four branches. He moved the family temple to Nara as Kofuku-ji and died in 720.

zh:
藤原不比等（659—720）是藤原镰足的次子，奠定了藤原氏权势的根基。他参与拥立文武天皇（697年），主导编纂701年的《大宝律令》，698年又为子孙争取到独用藤原姓的特权。

他把一个女儿嫁给文武天皇，女儿光明子嫁给圣武天皇——光明子是日本第一位非皇族出身的皇后。他的四个儿子开创了藤原四家，他还把氏寺迁至奈良，改称兴福寺，720年病逝。

en:
Fujiwara no Fujinari (776–822) was an early Heian noble of the Northern Fujiwara, the fifth son of Sadaijin Fujiwara no Uona. Appointed Harima suke in 811, he was tasked in 813 with civilizing Emishi captives resettled in the province.

Under Emperor Saga he served mainly as a provincial governor and ended as Ise no kami. He died in 822 aged 47, and is counted as ancestor of the warrior line of Fujiwara no Hidesato.

en:
Fujiwara no Fujitsugu (773–817) was an early Heian noble of the Northern Fujiwara, grandson of Sadaijin Fujiwara no Uona and second son of Fujiwara no Washitori. Appointed Hitachi no jō in 793, he rose rapidly under Emperor Heizei in 806.

In 809 he became Tōgū daibu, household chief to Crown Prince Takaoka, and in the 810 Kusuko Incident sided with Emperor Saga. In 812 he became Sangi and concurrently Dazai daini. He died in 817 aged 45.

en:
Fujiwara no Fuminaga was a mid-Heian military aristocrat of the Hidesato line, son of Chinjufu Shōgun Fujiwara no Chitsune and grandson of the warrior Fujiwara no Hidesato. After serving as a palace attendant and police commissioner of Shimotsuke, he was appointed Chinjufu Shōgun in 988 at an extraordinary court ceremony.

The appointment followed gifts he presented to Empress Senshi for Regent Kaneie's sixtieth year, and he then held junior fifth rank. He died in 1025.

Fujiwara no Fusasaki (681–737), second son of Fujiwara no Fuhito, founded the Fujiwara Northern House. In 709 he inspected the Tōkai and Tōsandō circuits during campaigns against the Emishi.

Fujiwara no Fusatsugu was an early Heian court noble, the son of Fujiwara no Sueshige, governor of Mimasaka. He took junior fifth rank in 811 and, after several provincial posts, became governor of Kii, in which office he died.

His daughter Sawako, a consort of Emperor Ninmyo, bore Prince Tokiyasu, who ascended as Emperor Koko in 884. Fusatsugu was posthumously raised to senior first rank and, in 885, to grand minister.

en:
Fujiwara no Fuyutsugu (775–826) was an early Heian statesman, general and poet of the Northern Fujiwara, second son of Udaijin Fujiwara no Uchimaro. A close aide to Emperor Saga from his crown-prince days, he became one of the first heads of the Kurōdo-dokoro secretariat founded by Saga in 810.

He joined the council as Sangi in 811, rose to Udaijin in 821 and was Sadaijin when he died in 826. His daughter was the mother of Emperor Montoku, who posthumously raised him to Daijō-daijin in 850.

en:
Fujiwara no Hidesato (c. 891–958), also known as Tawara Tōda, was a warrior lord of the northern Fujiwara based in Shimotsuke Province. When Taira no Masakado seized eight Kantō provinces in 939, Hidesato joined Taira no Sadamori against him, and in 940 they stormed Masakado's base in Shimōsa and killed him, ending the revolt.

Rewarded with the post of chinjufu shōgun and the governorships of Shimotsuke and Musashi, he became ancestor of numerous warrior houses, including the Ōshū Fujiwara. Legend also makes him slayer of a giant centipede in Ōmi.

en:
Fujiwara no Ienari (1107–1154) was a late Heian court noble, third son of Councillor Fujiwara no Ieyasu of the Northern House's Uona line, who became middle counsellor at senior second rank. Under Emperor Toba's cloistered rule he was the retired emperor's chief favourite and, with Bifukumon-in, led the court while amassing many estates.

In 1151 followers of Fujiwara no Yorinaga sacked his mansion, enraging Toba and setting the scene for the Hōgen Disturbance. He died in 1154, and his descendants founded the Shijō and Yamashina houses.

en:
Ashikaga no Ietsuna was a late Heian warrior and third head of the Fujiwara-surnamed Ashikaga house of Shimotsuke, adopted heir of its founder Nariyuki. A famed strongman, he entered a court sumo contest in 1111 while still under age, but was later falsely accused of treason and exiled to Anraku-ji in Dazaifu.

From 1142 to 1161 he fought Minamoto no Yoshikuni over the Yanada estate. His son Toshitsuna died after a rising in 1183; Ietsuna is last recorded in 1184.

He held a string of provincial governorships and won exceptional favour under Emperor Shirakawa's cloistered rule, rising to councillor at junior third rank in 1134.

He spent the wealth from his governorships on temples such as Shōkongō-in. After Shirakawa's death he fell from power under Emperor Toba, while his son Ienari rose.

en:
Fujiwara no Kamatari (614–669), born Nakatomi no Kamatari, was the founder of the Fujiwara clan. He refused appointment as a ritual official and plotted against the Soga regime; in 645 he joined Prince Naka no Oe in a coup that killed Soga no Iruka and forced his father Emishi to suicide, launching the Taika Reform.

As Inner Minister he helped build a Chinese-style centralized state. Shortly before his death in 669, Emperor Tenji granted him the surname Fujiwara and the highest rank Taishokan. His son Fuhito carried on the house.

Fujiwara no Kamatari (614–669), born Nakatomi no Kamatari, was the founder of the [ShowDynastyName('fujiwara_dynasty')] clan. He refused appointment as a ritual official and plotted against the [ShowDynastyName('soga_old_dynasty')] regime; in 645 he joined Prince Naka no Oe in a coup that killed Soga no Iruka and forced his father Emishi to suicide, launching the Taika Reform.

As Inner Minister he helped build a Chinese-style centralized state. Shortly before his death in 669, #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_tenji_tenno').GetID],X #L Emperor Tenji#!#! granted him the surname Fujiwara and the highest rank Taishokan. His son Fuhito carried on the house.
zh:
藤原镰足（614—669），本名中臣镰足，是藤原氏的始祖。他拒任祭官后谋划推翻苏我氏政权；645年，他与中大兄皇子发动政变，诛杀苏我入鹿，迫使其父苏我虾夷自尽，由此开启大化改新。

他作为内臣，协助建立仿唐的中央集权国家。669年临终前，天智天皇赐姓藤原，并授予最高冠位大织冠。其子不比等继承了这一家族。

en:
Fujiwara no Kanefusa (1001–1069) was a Northern Fujiwara court noble, eldest son of the chūnagon Fujiwara no Kanetaka. Appointed Right Guards captain in 1015, he became notorious for violence at court: at a 1018 palace banquet he insulted the head chamberlain Fujiwara no Sadayori and pelted his room with stones, and in 1023 he had attendants beat an official in the palace.

The regent Yorimichi expelled him, and he afterwards held only provincial posts without further promotion. He died in 1069 aged sixty-nine; his son Sōen founded the Utsunomiya line.

zh:
藤原兼房（1001—1069）是平安时代中期的贵族，藤原北家中纳言藤原兼隆的长子。1015年任右近卫少将，以在宫中行凶闹事闻名：1018年的一次内宴上，他辱骂藏人头藤原定赖并向其居室投石；1023年又指使随从在宫中殴打官员。

关白藤原赖通因此将他逐出内里，此后他历任地方官，再未升迁。1069年去世，享年69岁；其子宗圆是宇都宫氏之祖。

en:
Fujiwara no Kaneie (c. 929–990), a son of Fujiwara no Morosuke and father of three regent sons including Michinaga, was long out of favour under his ascendant brother Kanemichi. He was named minister of the right in 978.

In the Kanna Disturbance of 986 he and his son Michikane pressured Emperor Kazan into taking the tonsure, placing his seven-year-old grandson on the throne as Emperor Ichijō. He then ruled as sesshō regent, became grand minister in 989, and took Buddhist vows shortly before his death in 990.

en:
Fujiwara no Kanetaka (985–1053) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Fujiwara Hokke, the second son and heir of Regent Fujiwara no Michikane, who died weeks after taking office in 995. Unlike his cousins, he attached himself to his uncle Michinaga, becoming the youngest councillor in 1008 at twenty-four.

He rose to middle counsellor and senior second rank, though gossip blamed him for Crown Prince Atsuaki's resignation in 1017. He resigned in 1035, took vows in 1046, and died in 1053.

Fujiwara no Kinmitsu was an eleventh-century warrior of the Fujiwara's Hidesato branch, a fifth-generation grandson of Fujiwara no Hidesato and son of Shimotsuke no kami Fujiwara no Fumiyuki.

In the eleventh month of 1057, the year after the Akurigawa incident opened the Earlier Nine Years' War in the north, he followed Minamoto no Yoriyoshi against Abe no Yoritoki in Mutsu and was killed in the fighting. His son Tsunenori became ancestor of the Hatano warrior house.

en:
Fujiwara no Kinnari (999–1043) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Northern House's Kan'in line, eldest son of Middle Counsellor Fujiwara no Sanenari and maternal grandfather of Emperor Shirakawa. Adopted in childhood by his grandfather, Grand Minister Fujiwara no Kinsue, he came of age in 1011 and rose to become a councillor.

In 1043 he was promoted to provisional middle counsellor at junior second rank, but died months later aged forty-five. His daughter Shigeko, adopted by Fujiwara no Yoshinobu, married Emperor Go-Sanjō and bore Shirakawa, beginning his line's rise as imperial in-laws.

1043年他升任从二位权中纳言，但数月后便去世，享年45岁。其女茂子为藤原能信的养女，嫁给后三条天皇，生下白河天皇，开启了闲院流作为外戚的荣华。

en:
Fujiwara no Kinsada (1049–1099), known as the Takamatsu Chancellor, was a court noble of the Ononomiya branch of the Fujiwara Hokke and the eldest son of Provisional Middle Counsellor Fujiwara no Tsuneie. In 1072, after Emperor Shirakawa acceded and his brother Sanehito became crown prince, Kinsada became the prince's provisional assistant. After retired Emperor Go-Sanjō died in 1073, his appointments stalled for a time.

He became head chamberlain in 1083 and joined the kugyo as councillor in 1086. Promoted only slowly thereafter, he reached junior third rank in 1092 and senior third rank in 1097, and died in 1099 aged fifty-one.

en:
Fujiwara no Kinsue (c. 956–1029) was the eleventh son, by some accounts the twelfth, of the udaijin Fujiwara no Morosuke; his mother was Princess Yasuiko, a daughter of Emperor Daigo. After his mother died soon after his birth, his sister Empress Anshi raised him at court, where Emperor Murakami treated him much like a prince.

Named Sangi in 983, he became naidaijin in 997 after Fujiwara no Korechika fell from power, and supported Fujiwara no Michinaga's government during his long tenure. He became udaijin in 1017 and daijō daijin in 1021, and died in office in 1029. Known as the Kan'in Minister, he was the ancestor of the Kan'in Fujiwara line.

After his mother died soon after his birth, his sister Empress Anshi raised him at court, where #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_murakami_tenno').GetID],X #L Emperor Murakami#!#! treated him much like a prince.

Named Sangi in 983, he became naidaijin in 997 after Fujiwara no Korechika fell from power, and supported #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_fujiwara_michinaga').GetID],X #L Fujiwara no Michinaga#!#!'s government during his long tenure. He became udaijin in 1017 and daijō daijin in 1021, and died in office in 1029. Known as the Kan'in Minister, he was the ancestor of the Kan'in [ShowDynastyName('fujiwara_dynasty')] line.
zh:
藤原公季（约956—1029）是右大臣藤原师辅的第十一子（一说第十二子），母亲为醍醐天皇之女康子内亲王。母亲在他出生后不久去世，他由姐姐中宫安子在宫中抚养，村上天皇待他如同皇子。

他于983年任参议，997年在藤原伊周失势后接任内大臣，长期任职期间支持藤原道长的政权；1017年任右大臣，1021年升任太政大臣。1029年他在任内去世，号闲院大臣，是藤原氏闲院流之祖。

en:
Fujiwara no Kintō (966–1041), known as the Shijō Dainagon, was a Heian courtier, poet and calligrapher, the son of the regent Fujiwara no Yoritada. Admired by contemporaries including Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shōnagon, he laid the groundwork for the imperial anthology Shūi Wakashū with a draft collection made in 996–999.

He compiled the celebrated Wakan rōeishū of Chinese and Japanese verse and around 1009–1011 established the canon of the Thirty-Six Poetry Immortals. He is counted one of the Four Nagon, and his son was the poet Sadayori.

zh:
藤原公任（966—1041）是平安时代的公卿、歌人与书法家，关白藤原赖忠之子，世称四条大纳言。他深受紫式部、清少纳言等同时代人推崇，996—999年编成《拾遗抄》，为敕撰《拾遗和歌集》奠定基础。

他又编纂荟萃中日诗歌的《和汉朗咏集》，并于1009—1011年前后确立三十六歌仙的谱系，位列“四纳言”之一，其子为歌人藤原定赖。

en:
Fujiwara no Kinzane (1053–1107) was a court noble and poet of the Kan'in branch of the Fujiwara Hokke, eldest son of Major Counsellor Fujiwara no Sanesue, known as the Sanjo Major Counsellor. When his cousin Emperor Shirakawa acceded in 1072 he became a chamberlain, and rose to head chamberlain and councillor in 1080.

As maternal uncle of Emperor Toba he was made the crown prince's steward in 1103, and when Toba acceded in 1107 he claimed the regency but was rejected, dying four months later. His daughter Shoshi later bore Emperors Sutoku and Go-Shirakawa.

藤原公实（1053—1107）是平安时代后期公卿、歌人，出自藤原北家闲院流，为大纳言藤原实季的长子，人称三条大纳言。1072年从兄白河天皇即位后他出任藏人，1080年任藏人头、参议。

作为鸟羽天皇的外伯父，他于1103年兼任春宫大夫；1107年鸟羽天皇即位时他主张由自己出任摄政，却遭驳斥，四个月后去世。其女璋子后来为鸟羽天皇生下崇德、后白河两天皇。

en:
Fujiwara no Kiyofusa, also called Kanshuji Kiyofusa, was a court noble of the Kanshuji line of the Fujiwara Hokke, son of Fujiwara no Morinori. After his father and uncle were exiled in the Hogen Disturbance of 1156, the family fell, but Kiyofusa served Emperor Go-Toba and restored its standing. When the Jokyu Disturbance of 1221 brought Go-Toba's exile to Oki, Kiyofusa took the tonsure and followed him there.

In 1240 he was appointed governor of Dewa, and his second son Shigefusa, lord of the Uesugi manor in Tamba, became the founder of the Uesugi clan.

藤原清房（又称劝修寺清房）是平安时代末期至镰仓时代前期的公卿，出自藤原北家劝修寺流，为藤原盛宪之子。1156年保元之乱后，父亲与叔父都被流放，家道中落；清房近侍后鸟羽天皇，致力复兴家门。1221年承久之乱后，后鸟羽上皇被流放隐岐，他出家相随。

1240年他出任出羽守。其次子重房领有丹波国上杉庄，是上杉氏之祖。

en:
Fujiwara no Korechiyo (dates unknown) was a Heian-period noble of the southern Fujiwara house, the son of Fujiwara no Kiyoka and deputy governor of Hitachi Province. In 939 he clashed with the local magnate Fujiwara no Haruaki, who had withheld taxes and seized provincial goods, and demanded that Taira no Masakado surrender the fugitive.

Masakado refused, stormed the Hitachi headquarters with about a thousand men, routed Korechiyo's three-thousand-strong provincial force and captured him along with the provincial seal. His son Fujiwara no Tamenori later helped destroy Masakado in 940.

藤原维几（生卒年不详）是日本平安时代贵族，出身藤原南家，为藤原清夏之子，官至常陆介、从五位。939年，他与拒缴租税、夺取官物的当地豪族藤原玄明对立，要求平将门交出逃入门下的玄明。

将门不允，率约千人进攻常陆国府，击溃维几的三千国衙军队，将其俘获并夺取印玺。其子藤原为宪后来投奔藤原秀乡，于940年参与攻灭将门。

en:
Fujiwara no Korekimi (727–789), first named Kuromaro, was the eldest son of Fujiwara no Otomaro of the Fujiwara Southern House. After his father's death in 760 he held provincial governorships and rose swiftly under Empress Shōtoku, changing his name to Korekimi. Made councillor in 774, he headed the household of Crown Prince Yamabe.

When Yamabe ascended as Emperor Kanmu, he raised Korekimi to middle councillor in 781, great councillor in 782 and right minister in 783. Korekimi died in 789 aged sixty-three and was posthumously granted junior first rank.

en:
Fujiwara no Koretada (924–972) was the eldest son of Fujiwara no Morosuke and maternal uncle of Emperors Reizei and En'yū, whose mother was his sister Anshi. In 951 Emperor Murakami made him a compiler of the imperial waka anthology, and his poetry later entered the Hyakunin Isshu.

He rose to minister of the right in 970 and, after his uncle Saneyori died, became sesshō regent; in 971 he was named grand minister. He supervised En'yū's enthronement early in 972 but fell ill and died that November, aged forty-nine.

藤原伊尹（924—972）是藤原师辅的长子，其妹安子为村上天皇中宫，故他是冷泉、圆融两天皇的外伯父。951年，村上天皇命他参与敕撰和歌编纂，其和歌后来收录于《百人一首》。

他于970年任右大臣，伯父实赖去世后接任摄政，971年又任太政大臣。972年初他主持圆融天皇即位仪式，同年11月病逝，享年49岁。

en:
Fujiwara no Masanori (c. 997–1064) was a mid-Heian military commander in Kyushu, remembered as the father of Kikuchi no Noritaka, ancestor of the Kikuchi clan of Higo. Genealogies claim he was a son of Fujiwara no Takaie, though modern scholars regard this descent as a claim adopted by the Kikuchi to ennoble their line.

He served as junior assistant at Dazaifu and held the governorships of Tsushima and Hizen, and was once pursued on suspicion of murdering Fujiwara no Sadatō.

藤原政则（约997—1064）是平安时代中期在九州活动的武将，被视为肥后菊池氏始祖菊池则隆之父。各类家谱称他是藤原隆家之子，但现代学者认为，菊池氏自称出自隆家一系属于冒称。

en:
Fujiwara no Matate (715–766), first named Yatsuka, was a court noble of the Fujiwara Northern House, third son of Fujiwara no Fusasaki. A gifted poet favoured by Emperor Shōmu, he rose fast and became councillor in 748. He supported Fujiwara no Nakamaro's Chinese-style reforms and in 758 received the Tang-style name Matate.

In Nakamaro's rebellion of 764 he sided with retired Empress Kōken and commanded the imperial guards. Made great councillor in 766, he died soon after aged fifty-two and was posthumously made grand minister. His son Uchimaro continued the Northern House line.

He reached only junior fifth rank, lower grade, and died on 14 May 1038, shortly after coming of age; his grieving mother took Buddhist vows.

en:
Fujiwara no Michikane (961–995) was the third son of Fujiwara no Kaneie and a mid-Heian courtier. In 986 he played the key part in unseating Emperor Kazan: when the emperor, mourning his consort Yoshiko, was persuaded to renounce the world, Michikane escorted him secretly from the palace to take the tonsure, then left without keeping his own vow to become a monk, clearing the way for his nephew Emperor Ichijō.

He was promoted udaijin in 994 and succeeded his brother Michitaka as kampaku in 995, but died only seven days later, remembered as the Seven-Day Kampaku.

藤原道兼（961—995）是藤原兼家的第三子，平安时代中期的公卿。986年，花山天皇因宠爱的女御藤原忯子去世而悲痛厌世，道兼劝其出家，并立誓相随，趁夜将天皇秘密带出皇宫落发；天皇出家后他却借故离去，为外甥一条天皇即位扫清了道路。

994年他升任右大臣，995年继兄长道隆之后出任关白，仅七天便病死，世称“七日关白”。

en:
Fujiwara no Michinaga (966–1028) was the Heian statesman under whom Fujiwara power reached its height. After his brothers Michitaka and Michikane died in 995, he defeated his nephew Korechika in the struggle for power, rising from minister of the right to minister of the left by 996.

Though never kampaku, he ruled as the Mido Kampaku, marrying four daughters to Emperors Ichijō, Sanjō and Go-Ichijō and the future Go-Suzaku, and serving as sesshō from 1016. He yielded the regency to his son Yorimichi, took vows in 1019 and died in 1028.

藤原道长（966—1028）是把藤原氏权势推向顶峰的平安时代公卿。995年两位兄长道隆、道兼相继死后，他在与侄子伊周的权力斗争中胜出，995—996年间由右大臣升任左大臣。

他始终未任关白，却以“御堂关白”之名主宰朝政，把四个女儿分别嫁给一条、三条、后一条天皇以及后来的后朱雀天皇，并于1016年出任摄政。后来他把摄政之位让给儿子赖通，1019年出家，1028年去世。

en:
Fujiwara no Michitaka (953–995) was the eldest son of the regent Fujiwara no Kaneie and a leading courtier of the mid-Heian period. When Kaneie died in 990, Michitaka succeeded him, serving first as kampaku and then as sesshō to his nephew Emperor Ichijō. That same year he made his daughter Teishi the emperor's chūgū, creating an unprecedented four empresses.

Known as the Naka-no-Kampaku, he later fell ill and tried to hand the regency to his son Korechika, but failed; he died in 995 after barely five years in power.

en:
Fujiwara no Michito (974–1039) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Northern House, son of Major Counselor Fujiwara no Naritoki. From 996 he served Crown Prince Okisada, whose consort was his sister Seishi. When Okisada ascended as Emperor Sanjo in 1011, Michito became head chamberlain and then councilor, reaching junior third rank in 1012.

His career was checked by Fujiwara no Michinaga, who blocked his promotions and in 1017 pressured Seishi’s son, Crown Prince Atsuakira, into resigning. Michito reached senior third rank in 1023 and provisional middle counselor in 1035, dying in 1039 aged sixty-six.

藤原通任（974—1039）是平安时代中期的公卿，出自藤原北家小一条流，为大纳言藤原济时之子。996年起他侍奉皇太子居贞亲王，其姐娍子是太子之妃。1011年居贞即位为三条天皇，通任随即出任藏人头、参议，1012年升至从三位。

他的仕途受到藤原道长阻挠：道长压下他的晋升，并于1017年逼迫娍子所生的皇太子敦明亲王辞退储位。通任1023年升正三位，1035年任权中纳言，1039年去世，享年66岁。

en:
Fujiwara no Morinori was a late-Heian court noble of the Fujiwara Northern House's Kanjūji line and the eldest son of Shōnagon Fujiwara no Akinori. His aunt was Fujiwara no Yorinaga's mother, and as a maternal cousin he served Yorinaga as a close attendant. He also waited on Retired Emperor Sutoku.

In the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 he joined the Sutoku side; after the defeat he fled with Yorinaga, took the tonsure and was captured. Tortured on a sorcery charge, he was exiled to Sado Province in 1156. His grandson Shigefusa founded the Uesugi clan.

藤原盛宪是平安时代后期的公卿，出自藤原北家劝修寺流，为少纳言藤原显宪的长子。他的姑母是藤原赖长的生母，因此作为母方表亲近侍赖长，同时也是崇德上皇的殿上人。

1156年保元之乱时，他加入上皇一方；战败后随赖长逃亡，出家后仍被捕获，并因涉嫌诅咒而遭受拷问，同年流放佐渡国。其孙重房后来以上杉为苗字，是上杉氏的始祖。

Fujiwara no Morizane (died between 1107 and 1119) was a court noble of the late Heian period from the Kanjūji line of the Northern Fujiwara, the son of Fujiwara no Norisuke, minister of the palace household. His highest rank was Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade, as minister of civil administration. His daughter became Fujiwara no Tadazane's concubine and bore Fujiwara no Yorinaga.

en:
Fujiwara no Moromichi (1062–1099) was a late Heian regent, the eldest son of the kampaku Fujiwara no Morozane. In 1094 he succeeded his father as kampaku and, with Emperor Horikawa, pursued vigorous government independent of retired Emperor Shirakawa, reining in the cloister court's appointees; contemporaries praised the realm as orderly under his rule.

In 1095 he forcefully rejected Enryaku-ji monks' demands and had their armed protest driven off. He died suddenly in 1099, aged 37, and the regent house never recovered its former power against Shirakawa.

en:
Fujiwara no Morosuke (909–960), known as Kujō-dono, was the second son of the regent Fujiwara no Tadahira and a learned mid-Heian statesman. He married three daughters of Emperor Daigo in succession. Promoted to udaijin in 947, he overshadowed his elder brother Saneyori as the driving force of Emperor Murakami's Tenryaku government, aided by his daughter Anshi, the empress who bore the future emperors Reizei and En'yū.

He died in 960 aged fifty-three, having never become regent himself; under his sons Koretada and Kaneie, his Kujō line became the Fujiwara regent house.

藤原师辅（909—960），人称九条殿，是摄政藤原忠平的次子，博学多才、精通朝仪的平安时代公卿。他先后娶醍醐天皇的三位皇女为妻。947年他升任右大臣，在村上天皇的天历之治中比兄长实赖更握实权；其女安子为天皇中宫，生下后来的冷泉、圆融两位天皇。

他于960年病逝，享年53岁，生前并未出任摄关；在儿子伊尹、兼家等人手中，他的九条流成为藤原氏嫡流摄关家。

en:
Fujiwara no Morotada (920–969), fifth son of the regent Fujiwara no Tadahira, founded the clan's Koichijō lineage. He rose at court, becoming provisional middle counsellor in 948, and his daughter Yoshiko entered Emperor Murakami's harem and was named an imperial consort in 958.

After helping his brother Saneyori engineer the downfall of Minamoto no Takaakira in the Anna Incident of 969, Morotada took Takaakira's post as minister of the left, but died of illness only months later.

en:
Fujiwara no Morotsuna (died 1172) was a late Heian noble and poet of the Koichijo Fujiwara line, the eldest son of Fujiwara no Tadatoki. As a close aide of Retired Emperor Shirakawa he held several senior posts and ended at senior fourth rank, lower grade.

In 1142, while governor of Mutsu, he took a firm stand against Fujiwara no Motohira of the Oshu Fujiwara, who controlled the province, winning fame for upholding court authority. His descendants became the Anekoji house, hereditary governors of Hida.

藤原师纲（？—1172）是平安时代末期的贵族与歌人，出自小一条流藤原氏，为藤原尹时长子。他身为白河上皇的院近臣，历任多项要职，最终官至正四位下。

1142年任陆奥守期间，他对实际控制该国的奥州藤原氏当主藤原基衡采取强硬姿态，因伸张朝廷权威而声名远扬。其子孙后来成为世代担任飞驒国司的姊小路家。

en:
Fujiwara no Morozane (1042–1101), sixth son of the kampaku Fujiwara no Yorimichi, became heir to the regent's house after the sudden death of his elder brother Michifusa. He outmaneuvered his uncle Norimichi and cousin Nobunaga to become kampaku after Norimichi's death.

He then served as sessho for Emperor Horikawa, restoring the power of the Mido line. A noted poet, he placed sixteen poems in imperial anthologies and left the diary Kyogoku Kampakuki.

en:
Fujiwara no Mototsune (836–891) was the dominant statesman of the early Heian court. Third son of Fujiwara no Nagara, he was adopted by his uncle, the regent Fujiwara no Yoshifusa, becoming minister of the right in 872 and regent in 876.

After Emperor Yozei's abdication in 884 he exercised the powers later associated with the kampaku under Emperor Koko; the term appeared in an imperial edict under Emperor Uda in 887. He died in 891.

en:
Fujiwara no Muchimaro (680–737), eldest son of Fujiwara no Fuhito, founded the Fujiwara Southern House. After his father's death in 720 he became middle councillor, and in 729 led the interrogation that destroyed Prince Nagaya.

In 730 he brought his brothers into the council, establishing the rule of the four Fujiwara brothers, and became right minister in 734. He died in the smallpox epidemic of 737, receiving senior first rank and the office of left minister on his deathbed.

Fujiwara no Murao (died 932) was a noble of the Northern Fujiwara house, son of Toyosawa and father of the celebrated warrior Hidesato, known as Tawara no Tōta. He succeeded his father as senior secretary of Shimotsuke Province, rising to junior fourth rank and also governing Kawachi and Shimotsuke.

His daughter married Taira no Kunika and bore Taira no Sadamori. The office he inherited passed down among his descendants, including the Ōta and Oyama warrior clans, and he died in 932.

en:
Fujiwara no Nagaie (1005–1064) was a mid-Heian noble and waka poet, the youngest son of the regent Fujiwara no Michinaga. He advanced rapidly, joining the council in 1022 and reaching provisional senior counselor, his highest post, in 1028; his elder brothers blocked any further rise.

In 1060 he burned his carriage when his young nephew Morozane was promoted past him. He took vows during illness in 1064 and died weeks later, founding the Mikohidari house of poets, the line of Shunzei and Teika.

藤原长家（1005—1064）是平安时代中期的公卿、歌人，摄政藤原道长最小的儿子。他晋升顺利，1022年位列公卿，1028年官至权大纳言，这也是他的最高官职，此后因兄长们而再难升迁。

1060年，年轻的外甥师实官位升到自己之上，他愤而烧毁座车。1064年他在病中出家，几周后便去世，是御子左家歌人之家的始祖，俊成、定家皆出自这一流。

en:
Fujiwara no Nagara (802–856) was an early Heian statesman of the Northern House of the Fujiwara and eldest son of Minister of the Left Fujiwara no Fuyutsugu. Trusted by Emperor Ninmyo from his crown-prince years, he became councillor only in 844, ten years behind his brother Yoshifusa, and reached junior second rank in 856, dying soon after.

His daughter Takaiko bore Emperor Yozei, while his third son Mototsune, adopted by Yoshifusa, fathered the five regent houses. Nagara was posthumously made grand minister in 879.

他的女儿高子生下阳成天皇，三男基经出继良房，其后人分出五摄家。879年长良被追赠太政大臣。

en:
Fujiwara no Nakamasa was an early to mid-Heian noble, the seventh son of Councillor Fujiwara no Yamakage of the Northern Fujiwara house. He served under Emperor Daigo (r. 897–930) and Emperor Suzaku in guards and censorial posts, ending at junior fourth rank upper, and also governed Settsu Province as a zuryō.

Though never a minister, his daughter married the regent Fujiwara no Kaneie, making him maternal grandfather of Fujiwara no Michinaga and Higashi-Sanjōin, mother of Emperor Ichijō.

en:
Fujiwara no Naomichi was an early Heian noble of the Northern House Uona line, son of Kii governor Fujiwara no Fusatsugu and a maternal uncle of Emperor Koko. In 843, as a captain of the Left Military Guards, he was sent to search the Heian-kyo and Naniwa mansions of Funya no Miyatamaro, suspected of treason, for weapons.

He took junior fifth rank in 849 and thereafter held mainly provincial posts, including Mino, with brief capital interludes. He became governor of Bizen in 863.

en:
Fujiwara no Naozumi is known only through genealogies of the Ōmura and Arima warrior houses of Hizen, which called him a grandson of the rebel Fujiwara no Sumitomo. Their tradition holds that in 994 he moved from Ōzu in Iyo to Ōmura in Hizen and took that place name as his family name.

Later scholarship instead identifies him with Taira no Naozumi. He is said to have invented the Sumitomo ancestry to erase his forebears' disgrace.

Fujiwara no Naritoki (941–995) was a mid-Heian court noble, second son of Minister of the Left Fujiwara no Morotada. He became a councilor in 970, and in 977 the dying regent Kanemichi gave him the Right Imperial Guards captaincy, stripped from his rival Kaneie.

A close supporter of Regent Michitaka, he reached senior second rank in 991. He died in the 995 smallpox epidemic and was posthumously appointed minister of the right in 1012, when his daughter Seishi became Empress of Emperor Sanjō.

Fujiwara no Norisuke (died 1079) was a mid-to-late Heian noble of the Kajuji line of the Northern Fujiwara, son of Mino governor Fujiwara no Yoriaki. After serving in the Chamberlains' Office, he took junior fifth rank in 1039 and began a long career as a provincial governor.

Over twenty years across three reigns he governed provinces including Bitchū, Ōmi and Bizen, reaching senior fourth rank in 1068. He became a monk around 1077 and was known as the Bizen Novice, dying in 1079.

en:
Fujiwara no Otomaro was a Nara-period court noble of the Fujiwara Southern House, a son of Fujiwara no Muchimaro. After his father and uncles died in the 737 smallpox epidemic, a Usa Hachiman oracle in 750 brought him sudden promotion to junior third rank and governor-general of Dazaifu.

Removed in 752 and demoted to governor of Mimasaka in 757, possibly after a rift with Nakamaro, he returned as war minister in 759 and died in 760. His son was Fujiwara no Korekimi.

en:
Fujiwara no Otomo (753–811) was a court noble of the Southern Fujiwara, second son of Udaijin Fujiwara no Korekimi. Starting in 783, he rose quickly, reaching senior third rank in 804, and in 806 was made Dainagon, briefly heading the Great Council before Fujiwara no Uchimaro was promoted above him.

In the wake of the 807 Prince Iyo incident he was exiled to Iyo Province. Pardoned in 810 during the Kusuko disturbance, he died in 811 and was posthumously named Dainagon.

zh:
藤原雄友（753—811）是奈良至平安初期的公卿，出自藤原南家，为右大臣藤原是公次子。783年任美作守，此后迅速升迁，804年升至正三位，806年任大纳言，一度位居太政官首班，不久藤原内麻吕被擢为右大臣，位居其上。

807年伊予亲王之变后，他受牵连流放伊予国。810年药子之变期间获赦复位，811年去世，追赠大纳言。

en:
Fujiwara no Sadakata (873–932) was a noble and poet of the Northern Fujiwara house, second son of the naidaijin Takafuji and maternal uncle of Emperor Daigo. Named a palace page in 892, he rose through the guards, becoming a councillor in 909 and, leaping over six seniors, middle counsellor in 913.

He became dainagon in 920 and minister of the right in 924, serving alongside Fujiwara no Tadahira. He died in 932 and was posthumously granted junior first rank, known as the Sanjō minister of the right.

藤原定方（873—932）是平安时代前期至中期的贵族、歌人，属藤原北家，为内大臣藤原高藤的次子、醍醐天皇的外叔父。他于892年任内舍人，之后历任近卫府武官，909年任参议，913年越过六名上位者升任中纳言。

他920年任大纳言，924年升任右大臣，与藤原忠平并为左右大臣。他于932年去世，追赠从一位，因宅邸在三条而号三条右大臣。

en:
Fujiwara no Sadatō was a noble of the mid-to-late Heian period, of the Yamakage line of the Northern Fujiwara, whose father was Fujiwara no Tamemori, governor of Echizen. In 1020 he was admitted to the audience of Crown Prince Atsunaga, the future Emperor Go-Suzaku.

In 1040, while governor of Iga, Sugano no Atsuyori of Chikuzen asked him to exchange posts, and he may have become governor of Chikuzen. He ended at junior fourth rank upper as governor of Yamato, taking Buddhist vows in 1081 while still in office.

藤原定任是平安时代中期至后期的贵族，属藤原北家山荫流，为越前守藤原为盛之子。1020年他获准升殿春宫敦良亲王，即后来的后朱雀天皇。

en:
Fujiwara no Sadayori (995–1045) was a mid-Heian noble and poet of the Ononomiya Fujiwara line, eldest son of the poet Fujiwara no Kinto. He rose through court posts to senior second rank in 1042, though Regent Yorimichi reprimanded him in 1019 and in 1030 he was caught cheating at a palace contest.

Remembered as one of the Late Classical Thirty-Six Poets, he appears in the Ogura Hyakunin Isshu. He took vows in 1044 and died in 1045 aged fifty-one.

en:
Fujiwara no Sanenari (975–1045) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Kan'in line of the Fujiwara Hokke, eldest son of Grand Minister Kinsue. He became head chamberlain in 1004 and councillor in 1008, and rose to middle counsellor in 1023 and senior second rank in 1024.

From 1033 he headed the Dazaifu, but in 1038 he was dismissed after a retainer robbed the Anraku-ji there. Restored in 1040, he took vows and died in 1045 aged seventy-one.

en:
Fujiwara no Sanesue (1035–1092) was a court noble of the Kan'in branch of the Fujiwara Hokke, second son of Fujiwara no Kinnari. His advancement was slow until his sister Shigeko married Crown Prince Takahito, who as Emperor Go-Sanjō made him head chamberlain in 1069 and councillor in 1072.

As maternal uncle of Emperor Shirakawa he became provisional middle counsellor in 1074 and reached major counsellor in 1083. He died in 1092; after his daughter Ishi bore Emperor Toba, he was posthumously named grand minister and remembered as the Go-Kan'in posthumous grand minister.

藤原实季（1035—1092）是平安时代后期公卿，出自藤原北家闲院流，为藤原公成的次子。他早年晋升缓慢，后因妹妹茂子成为皇太子尊仁亲王之妃而得到亲信；尊仁亲王即位为后三条天皇后，他于1069年任藏人头，1072年任参议。

en:
Fujiwara no Saneyori (900–970), known as Onomiya-dono, was the eldest son of the regent Fujiwara no Tadahira. He became udaijin in 944 and sadaijin in 947, and in 949 shared the daijō-daijin's duties with his brother Morosuke.

He was named kampaku for Emperor Reizei in 967 and sesshō in 969. On his death in 970, aged seventy, his Ononomiya line never kept the regency, which passed to Morosuke's descendants.

en:
Fujiwara no Sueshige was a Nara-period noble of the Northern Fujiwara, third son of Sadaijin Fujiwara no Uona. In 777, when Emperor Kōnin visited his father's offices, he was raised three ranks, and later held military and provincial offices.

After Uona fell in 782, Sueshige was demoted to Tosa suke, and though recalled in 783 and briefly made Iyo no kami in 784, he was again exiled to Hyūga. Pardoned once more, he became Mimasaka no kami in 790.

en:
Fujiwara no Sukeie was a warrior of the late Heian period, said to descend from the Fujiwara Hokke as a grandson of the poet Fujiwara no Nagaie, sixth son of Michinaga. He is credited with destroying the bandit Iwatakemaru, who had hidden on Mount Yamizo in Mutsu.

For this exploit he received Nasu district in Shimotsuke province and settled there. Around 1125 he built Kanda Castle as his seat, and his descendants settled the land as the Nasu clan.

en:
Fujiwara no Sukemitsu, also called Nii Sukemitsu, was a fourth son of Fujiwara no Suketaka, head of the Sanuki Fujiwara, and founded the Nii warrior house. He fought in the Genpei War at the Battle of Mizushima in Bitchū in 1183 and joined Minamoto no Yoshitsune at the Battle of Yashima in 1185.

He received a letter of commendation from Minamoto no Yoritomo and was confirmed in his holdings. His son Sukemura later took the name Kōzai after the Jōkyū War of 1221.

en:
Fujiwara no Suketada (died 973) was a mid-Heian noble and waka poet of the Uonome Fujiwara, son of Fujiwara no Tsurashige. He began as a sixth-rank imperial secretary in 945 and later governed Settsu and Inaba.

In 965 he was appointed senior assistant minister of Dazaifu, serving there until recalled in 970; he ended his career as head of the Audit Commissioners. One of his poems is included in the Shūi Wakashū, and his court notes, the Suketada shiki, survive in part.

en:
Fujiwara no Sumitomo (died 941) was a Heian-period noble of the northern Fujiwara house, a son of the Dazaifu official Fujiwara no Yoshinori. Posted as an assistant governor of Iyo Province to suppress the pirates of the Seto Inland Sea, he became their leader instead.

In 939 he rose in Iyo in concert with Taira no Masakado's eastern revolt and captured Dazaifu in 941. Defeated at Hakata Bay by Ono no Yoshifuru, he was captured in Iyo and executed by Tachibana no Tōyasu.

藤原纯友（?—941）是平安时代的贵族，出自藤原北家，为太宰府官员藤原良范之子。他出任伊予国掾，起初奉命镇压濑户内海的海贼，后来却成为海贼首领。

939年，他在伊予举兵，与关东平将门的叛乱遥相呼应，并于941年攻陷太宰府。他在博多湾被小野好古击败，逃回伊予后被捕，由橘远保处死。

en:
Fujiwara no Tadahira (880–949) was a Heian-period noble, the fourth son of Fujiwara no Mototsune. After his brother Tokihira died in 909, he took charge as head of the Fujiwara clan, becoming udaijin in 914 and sadaijin in 924.

In 927 he completed the Engishiki code of rites and regulations. In 930, under the infant Emperor Suzaku, Tadahira was appointed sesshō; he became daijō-daijin in 936 and kampaku in 941, and remained in power until his death.

en:
Fujiwara no Tadazane (1078–1162) was a late-Heian regent, eldest son of the kampaku Fujiwara no Moromichi. After his father's death in 1099 he became kampaku in 1105, but a quarrel with the retired Emperor Shirakawa cost him office in 1120, and he spent ten years confined at Uji.

Restored after Shirakawa's death, he favoured Yorinaga and in 1150 disowned Tadamichi. On the losing side with the retired Emperor Sutoku and Yorinaga in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156, he was confined until his death in 1162.

藤原忠实（1078—1162）是平安时代后期的公卿，关白藤原师通的嫡男。1099年父亲去世后，他于1105年任关白；但1120年与白河上皇发生冲突而被停职，在宇治度过了十年幽禁岁月。

en:
Fujiwara no Takafuji (838–900) was a Northern Fujiwara court noble, grandson of Fuyutsugu and second son of Yoshikado. His advancement was slow until his daughter Taneko married Emperor Uda and her son was named crown prince in 893.

He reached junior third rank in 894, became councillor in 895 and dainagon in 899. In 900, as the dying maternal grandfather of Emperor Daigo, he was appointed naidaijin; he died two months later and was posthumously named grand minister.

藤原高藤（838—900）是平安时代前期公卿，属藤原北家，为藤原冬嗣之孙、藤原良门的次子。他早年升迁迟缓，直到女儿胤子嫁给宇多天皇、其子于893年被立为太子后才平步青云。

en:
Fujiwara no Takafusa (795–852) was an early Heian court noble of the Northern House of the Fujiwara, third son of Councillor Fujiwara no Fujitsugu. In 827 he took junior fifth rank and went to Mino as vice-governor, where firm yet flexible rule and his exposure of plots left the province free of bandits.

He later governed several provinces, advancing only slowly and reaching senior fifth rank in 850. He died as governor of Echizen in 852, aged fifty-eight.

Fujiwara no Takaie (979–1044) was a mid-Heian noble of the Fujiwara Hokke, fourth son of Regent Fujiwara no Michitaka. After his father died in 995 power passed to his uncle Michinaga, and in 996 Takaie and his brother Korechika were exiled for shooting arrows at Retired Emperor Kazan's party.

Pardoned in 998, he became Dazai viceroy in 1014 to treat an eye disease. In 1019 he commanded the defense of Hakata against the Jurchen Toi pirates and repelled them. He died in 1044.

en:
Fujiwara no Takanaga was a late-Heian court noble and the third son of Minister of the Left Fujiwara no Yorinaga. He rose quickly through the Palace Guards, becoming a chamberlain in 1151 and reaching senior fourth rank in 1153.

When his father was killed on Sutoku's side in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156, Takanaga was stripped of office and exiled to Izu. He never returned to the capital and died in exile; tradition holds that his grandson settled in Ōsumi and founded the Hishikari clan.

1156年保元之乱中，父亲随崇德上皇败死，隆长被解官，流放伊豆，终未返京，死于配所。相传其孙定居大隅国，成为菱刈氏之祖。

His great-grandson Fujiwara no Tamenori took the name Kudo Taifu and founded the Kudo warrior house, from which several clans, including the Ito, later branched.

en:
Fujiwara no Takatsune was a mid-Heian court noble and poet of the Uona branch of the Northern Fujiwara, the son of the Uchūben Fujiwara no Yoritō. He served crown prince Takahito, later Emperor Go-Sanjō, as Tōgū no daishin, and afterward held a string of provincial governorships.

In 1072 he rose to senior fourth rank, lower grade. He contributed three poems to the Goshūi Wakashū and seven in all to the imperial anthologies. His son was the poet Fujiwara no Akisue.

en:
Fujiwara no Tamemori (died c. 1029) was a mid-Heian noble of the Yamakage line of the Northern Fujiwara, son of the councillor Fujiwara no Yasuchika. A former sixth-rank chamberlain, he reached junior fifth rank by 1011 and had governed Kaga Province, then spent years without office.

In 1028 he was made governor of Echizen, where he lost his certificate of appointment. The court diary Shōyūki records him as dead by the leap second month of 1029. His son was Fujiwara no Sadatō.

en:
Fujiwara no Tamesuke (c. 920–986) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Kanjūji Fujiwara, eldest son of Fujiwara no Asayori and grandson of the udaijin Sadakata. He became a sixth-rank imperial secretary in 945, then served for years as governor of a series of provinces.

Appointed sangi in 975, he reached senior third rank in 984. In 986 he became provisional middle councillor and deputy viceroy of Dazaifu, but died only months later, aged sixty-seven; he was known as the Kanroji Chūnagon.

en:
Fujiwara no Tokinaga was an early Heian noble of the Northern House Uona line, son of Echizen governor Fujiwara no Takafusa. In 877, as vice-governor of Mino, he helped conduct the Yuki rites at Emperor Yozei's enthronement festival, and later became junior assistant minister of military affairs.

Fujiwara no Tootsune (835–888) was an early Heian noble of the Northern House, second son of Fujiwara no Nagara and a maternal uncle of Emperor Yozei. After guarding the palace gates he took junior fifth rank in 866.

en:
Fujiwara no Toshihito (born c. 850) was an early Heian noble and warrior of the Northern Fujiwara house, son of the minister Tokinaga. After palace guard service he held successive Bandō posts in Kōzuke, Kazusa and Musashi.

In 915 he crushed several thousand bandits who had seized tribute in Shimotsuke and was made general of the Chinjufu garrison, reaching junior fourth rank, lower grade. His second son Nobumochi founded the Saitō clan, and Toshihito became a hero of medieval warrior tales, including the imo-gruel story in the Konjaku Monogatarishū.

en:
Fujiwara no Tsuneie (1018–1068) was a mid-Heian noble of the Ononomiya line of the Northern Fujiwara, son of Fujiwara no Sadayori. After receiving junior fifth rank in 1031, he climbed the Controllers' Office, becoming head of the Chamberlains' Office in 1048 and major controller of the right in 1050.

He joined the high nobility with junior third rank in 1056, became councillor in 1061, and was appointed provisional middle counselor in 1065. He died in 1068 aged fifty-one.

en:
Fujiwara no Uchimaro (756–812) was a Northern Fujiwara noble, third son of Dainagon Fujiwara no Matate, and served Emperors Kanmu, Heizei and Saga. He became Sangi in 794 soon after the move to Heian-kyō and in 799 oversaw construction of the new capital. In 806 he was made Udaijin, head of the council.

In the 810 Kusuko Incident he backed Emperor Saga. He died in 812 aged 57 and was posthumously promoted to Daijō-daijin. His son Fuyutsugu laid the foundation of Northern Fujiwara power.

en:
Fujiwara no Uona (721–783) was a court noble of the Fujiwara Northern House, the fifth son of Fujiwara no Fusasaki. He sided with retired Empress Kōken in Nakamaro's rebellion of 764, became councillor in 768, and in 770 helped enthrone Emperor Kōnin. Rising to inner minister, he became left minister under Emperor Kanmu in 781.

In 782 he was suddenly dismissed and assigned to Dazaifu. Recalled in 783, he died soon after aged sixty-three and was posthumously restored as left minister.

en:
Fujiwara no Washitori (born c. 750) was a late-Nara noble of the Fujiwara Northern House, a son of the left minister Fujiwara no Uona. Beginning in 771 he served in Ise Province, rising to governor by 774 and junior fifth rank, upper grade, in 775.

Called to the capital, he directed palace construction and in 778 became senior assistant minister of central affairs, concurrently governor of Kōzuke in 779. His daughter Kouso became a consort of Emperor Kanmu and mother of Prince Manda.

en:
Fujiwara no Yamakage (824–888) was an early Heian court noble, third son of Echizen governor Fujiwara no Takafusa. He entered the crown prince's service in 858 and, as a trusted aide of Emperor Seiwa, held guard, secretariat and provincial posts. His promotion stalled for a decade, then quickened after Fujiwara no Yoshifusa's death in 872.

He became head of the secretariat in 875, a councillor in 879, and in 886 rose to middle counselor of junior third rank. He died in 888, aged sixty-five.

en:
Fujiwara no Yoriaki (died 1027) was a mid-Heian noble of the Kanjuji line of the Fujiwara Hokke, son of Harima governor Fujiwara no Tokitaka. A minor court official under Emperor Ichijo, he was abducted during a quarrel with the retinue of Fujiwara no Shigetada in 1000, and in 1004 won his junior fifth rank only after petitioning the grand minister who had blocked it.

In 1006 he presented two thousand volumes of texts to Fujiwara no Michinaga. He later served Grand Empress Shoshi as a senior secretary, became Mino governor in 1025, and died in office in 1027.

en:
Fujiwara no Yorimichi (992–1074), eldest son of Fujiwara no Michinaga, dominated mid-Heian court politics. He became regent for Emperor Go-Ichijo in 1017 at twenty-six, the youngest sessho ever, and as regent or kampaku led the government for some fifty years under three emperors.

He made his Uji villa into Byodo-in and its Phoenix Hall. After Emperor Go-Sanjo, with no Fujiwara mother, took the throne in 1068, he retired, took vows in 1072, and died in 1074.

en:
Fujiwara no Yorinaga (1120–1156), son of the regent Fujiwara no Tadazane, was the most formidable noble of his day. He became Minister of the Left in 1150 and was dubbed the Aku Safu for his rigid defence of the Fujiwara regency against the cloistered-court faction.

After Emperor Konoe died in 1155 he lost the succession struggle, and in 1156 he joined Retired Emperor Sutoku in the Hōgen Disturbance. Wounded when Sutoku's stronghold was stormed, he died on 1 August 1156.

en:
Fujiwara no Yoritada (924–989) was the second son of the regent Fujiwara no Saneyori and head of the Ononomiya lineage. After long court service he became minister of the right in 971 and minister of the left in 977, and later that year the dying kampaku Kanemichi made Yoritada his successor.

His daughter Junshi was named empress in 982 but bore no prince, weakening his position against Fujiwara no Kaneie. When Kaneie made the young Ichijō emperor in the Kanna Disturbance of 986, Yoritada resigned as kampaku and died in 989.

en:
Fujiwara no Yoritō (died 1030) was a mid-Heian noble, the son of Fujiwara no Tokiakira. After beginning as a literature student he served as fifth-rank chamberlain and imperial diarist, then as a police magistrate, reaching junior fifth rank in 1013.

Around 1017 he was made governor of Tamba. In 1019 its peasants protested his abuses at the Yōmeimon gate, and he sent mounted soldiers to pursue them, drawing a reprimand from Fujiwara no Michinaga. He later governed Mino and was named middle controller of the right in 1029, and died in 1030.

en:
Fujiwara no Yoshikado was an early Heian courtier of the Northern Fujiwara, the sixth son of Sadaijin Fujiwara no Fuyutsugu. Unlike his brothers he never rose above senior sixth rank, serving as an Udoneri, and he died young soon after his sons Toshimoto and Takafuji were born.

The Konjaku Monogatari recounts that Takafuji was left fatherless as a child; Takafuji only received junior fifth rank in 868. Yoshikado was ancestor of the Kajuji lineage, and Murasaki Shikibu descended from his son Toshimoto.
