en:
Fujiwara no Yoshinobu (995–1065) was a mid-Heian court noble and poet, the fourth son of Regent Fujiwara no Michinaga. He became provisional middle counsellor in 1017. In 1037 he became guardian of Prince Takahito, future Emperor Go-Sanjō, and in 1045 secured the dying Emperor Go-Suzaku's testament naming him heir.

For twenty years he was the prince's lone court supporter and married his adopted daughter Moshi to him. He died in 1065, aged seventy-one, before Takahito's accession, and in 1073 was posthumously made grand minister.

Fujiwara no Yoshinori was an early Heian noble of the Northern Fujiwara house, son of the senior court official Fujiwara no Tōtsune. He served Empress Dowager Takako in her household and received junior fifth rank in 882.

After a provincial posting in Suō, he returned to the capital in 885 as an imperial chamberlain, later serving at the Dazaifu in Kyushu. He is remembered as the father of Fujiwara no Sumitomo, who led the Seto Inland Sea pirate revolt of 939.

Fujiwara no Yoshitaka (954–974) was a mid-Heian noble and waka poet, the third son of the regent Fujiwara no Koretada. He was counted among the Late Classical Thirty-Six Poetry Immortals, and one of his poems appears in the Ogura Hyakunin Isshu.

When Koretada died in 972 he considered taking Buddhist vows, but stayed for his newborn son, the future calligrapher Fujiwara no Yukinari. In 974 he died of smallpox on the same day as his elder brother Kyoken, aged about twenty.

en:
Fujiwara no Yukinari (972–1028) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Fujiwara Hokke, the eldest son of Minor Captain Fujiwara no Yoshitaka. Orphaned in childhood, in 995 he was made head chamberlain to Emperor Ichijo on the recommendation of Minamoto no Toshikata, and he later rose to provisional major counsellor, counted among the Four Counsellors of the Kanko era.

With Ono no Michikaze and Fujiwara no Sukemasa he was one of the Sanseki, the three greatest Heian calligraphers; his style was called Gonseki, and he founded the Sesonji school of calligraphy.

en:
Emperor Fushimi (1265–1317), the 92nd emperor of Japan, was a son of Emperor Go-Fukakusa and head of the Jimyōin-tō line. He became crown prince ahead of the Daikakuji-tō and in 1287 succeeded his cousin Emperor Go-Uda, taking direct charge after Go-Fukakusa withdrew in 1290.

Naming his own son heir in 1289 deepened the rival line's hostility. He abdicated in 1298 to rule as cloistered emperor, and in 1308 the shogunate backed his fourth son's enthronement as Emperor Hanazono. He took Buddhist vows in 1313 and died in 1317.

He became crown prince ahead of the Daikakuji-tō and in 1287 succeeded his cousin #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_go_uda_tenno').GetID],X #L Emperor Go-Uda#!#!, taking direct charge after Go-Fukakusa withdrew in 1290.

He took Buddhist vows in 1313 and died in 1317.
zh:
伏见天皇（1265—1317）是日本第92代天皇，后深草天皇之子，持明院统的首领。他压过大觉寺统一脉被立为皇太子，1287年接替堂弟后宇多天皇即位，并于1290年后深草上皇停止院政后亲理政务。

1289年他立自己的儿子为嗣，加深了大觉寺统的敌意。1298年他退位实行院政，1308年在幕府支持下第四子即位为花园天皇。1313年他出家，1317年去世。

en:
Empress Genmei (660–721), Japan's fourth reigning empress, was a daughter of Emperor Tenji, consort of Crown Prince Kusakabe and mother of Emperor Monmu. When Monmu died in 707 she took the throne in trust for her young grandson Shōmu.

Copper deposits found in Musashi in 707 gave the Wadō era its name in 708, when a mint was established. In 710 she founded the new capital Heijō-kyō, now Nara, opening the Nara period; under her the Kojiki was completed in 712 and the provincial Fudoki gazetteers begun in 713. She abdicated in 715 for her daughter Empress Genshō and died in 721.

zh:
元明天皇（660—721）是日本第四位女帝，天智天皇之女、草壁皇太子之妃、文武天皇之母。707年文武天皇去世，她为年幼的孙子圣武天皇代管皇位而即位。

707年武藏国发现铜矿，708年朝廷因此改元“和铜”并设立铸币所。710年她营建新都平城京（今奈良），开创奈良时代；《古事记》于712年成书，713年又下令编纂各地《风土记》。715年她让位于女儿元正天皇，721年去世。

en:
Empress Genshō (680–748), the 44th monarch of Japan, reigned from 715 to 724. A daughter of Crown Prince Kusakabe and Empress Genmei, she took the throne when her mother abdicated, the only empress regnant in Japanese history to succeed another reigning empress, ruling as a placeholder for her young nephew Prince Obito.

During her reign the Nihon Shoki chronicle was completed in 720, and the Three-Generations Land Act was issued in 723. In 724 she abdicated in Obito's favor; he ruled as Emperor Shōmu. Genshō never married and died in 748.

zh:
元正天皇（680—748）是日本第44代天皇，715年至724年在位。她是草壁皇子与元明天皇之女，因母亲禅让而即位，是日本历史上唯一一位由女天皇传位给女天皇的君主，代年幼的侄子首亲王执掌皇位。

在位期间，《日本书纪》于720年修成，723年颁布三世一身法。724年，她让位于首亲王，即圣武天皇。元正终身未婚，于748年去世。

en:
Emperor Go-Daigo (1288–1339) was the 96th emperor of Japan and the last emperor to hold real power until 1868. Made crown prince in 1308 under the Kamakura shogunate, he took the throne in 1318. He idealized Engi-era direct rule and chose his posthumous name to match.

In 1331 his plot was betrayed; he carried the Sacred Treasures to Mount Kasagi and was exiled to the Oki Islands. He escaped in 1333 and raised an army; Ashikaga Takauji, sent against him, changed sides and took Rokuhara, while Nitta Yoshisada destroyed the Hōjō at Kamakura. Back in Kyoto he began the Kenmu Restoration.

Disputes over rewards and the samurai's exclusion from politics wore it down. After Takauji won at Minatogawa in 1336, Go-Daigo surrendered the regalia, fled in 1337, called them counterfeit and founded the Southern Court at Yoshino. In 1339 he abdicated to Prince Noriyoshi and died the next day.

zh:
后醍醐天皇（1288—1339）是日本第96代天皇，也是1868年明治维新之前最后一位掌握实权的天皇。他在镰仓幕府主导下于1308年立为皇太子，1318年即位，以醍醐天皇延喜年间的亲政为理想，生前便自定谥号与之相同。

1331年，他的倒幕计划被告密，遂带三种神器避入笠置山，城陷后被流放隐岐岛。1333年他逃出并起兵；受命讨伐的足利尊氏倒戈攻下六波罗，新田义贞则在镰仓灭亡北条氏。回到京都后，他开始推行建武新政。

封赏纠纷和武士被排除在政治秩序之外，使新政逐渐瓦解。1336年尊氏在凑川获胜后，后醍醐天皇交出神器，又于1337年潜出京都，称神器是赝品，在吉野建立南朝。1339年他让位给义良亲王，次日去世。

en:
Emperor Go-Fukakusa (1243–1304), the 89th emperor of Japan, ascended in 1246 at two years old when his father Emperor Go-Saga abdicated and kept power as cloistered emperor. In 1259 Go-Saga forced him to step down in favour of his younger brother Emperor Kameyama.

Later, negotiations with the shogunate made his son Hirohito crown prince; in 1287 Hirohito became Emperor Fushimi and Go-Fukakusa ruled as cloistered emperor until taking Buddhist vows in 1290. His descendants formed the Jimyōin-tō line, and another son, Hisaaki, became the eighth Kamakura shōgun.

zh:
后深草天皇（1243—1304）是日本第89代天皇。1246年父亲后嵯峨天皇退位，年仅两岁的久仁亲王登基，由后嵯峨上皇实行院政。1259年，后嵯峨上皇迫使他让位给弟弟龟山天皇。

后来经与幕府交涉，他的儿子熙仁被立为皇太子，1287年即位为伏见天皇，他也重开院政，直到1290年出家。他的后裔形成持明院统，另一子久明亲王则出任第八代镰仓将军。

en:
Emperor Go-Fushimi (1288–1336), the 93rd emperor of Japan, was the eldest son of Emperor Fushimi and a Jimyōin-tō prince. Named crown prince in 1289, he ascended in 1298 when his father abdicated, but in 1301 the rival Daikakuji-tō drove him from the throne for Emperor Go-Nijō.

He acted as cloistered emperor for his younger brother Emperor Hanazono from 1313 to 1318, when the shogunate sponsored a plan to alternate the throne. He petitioned Kamo Shrine for his son's elevation; in 1331 Kazuhito became Emperor Kōgon, first of the Ashikaga-backed Northern Court emperors.

zh:
后伏见天皇（1288—1336）是日本第93代天皇，伏见天皇长子，持明院统亲王。1289年被立为皇太子，1298年因父亲退位而登基，1301年被对立的大觉寺统逼迫退位，让位于后二条天皇。

en:
Emperor Go-Horikawa (1212–1234), the 86th emperor of Japan, was placed on the Chrysanthemum Throne in 1221 after the Jōkyū Incident, when the Kamakura shogunate crushed Retired Emperor Go-Toba's bid for power and barred his line from the succession.

A grandson of Emperor Takakura aged only ten, he replaced the deposed Emperor Chūkyō while his father Morisada directed the court as cloistered emperor Go-Takakura-in. In 1232 he abdicated for his infant son Emperor Shijō and ruled as retired emperor until his death two years later.

后堀河天皇（1212—1234）是日本第86代天皇。1221年承久之乱爆发，后鸟羽上皇倒幕失败，镰仓幕府将其一脉排除出皇位继承；身为高仓天皇之孙、年仅十岁的茂仁亲王取代被废的仲恭天皇登基。

en:
Emperor Go-Ichijō (1008–1036), personal name Atsuhira, was the 68th emperor of Japan. The second son of Emperor Ichijō, his mother was Fujiwara no Shōshi, daughter of Fujiwara no Michinaga; he was only eight in 1016 when Emperor Sanjō abdicated in his favour. Real power rested first with Michinaga and then with his son Yorimichi, who ruled as sesshō regent.

He married Michinaga's daughter Ishi and had two daughters but no son. On his death in 1036 at age 27 the throne passed to his younger brother, who became Emperor Go-Suzaku.

后一条天皇（1008—1036），名敦成，日本第68代天皇。他是一条天皇的次子，母亲是藤原道长之女藤原彰子，1016年三条天皇退位时年仅8岁便登基。在位期间，实权先后由任摄政的藤原道长、赖通父子掌握。

en:
Emperor Go-Murakami (1328–1368), personal name Noriyoshi, was a son of Emperor Go-Daigo and the second sovereign of the Southern Court. Named crown prince in 1338, he succeeded his father at Yoshino in 1339 and spent his reign moving between temporary palaces.

In 1348 he fled Yoshino before Kō no Moronao's attack; in 1352 Southern Court forces seized Kyōto and carried off three retired Northern emperors, only to lose the capital within weeks. A second brief occupation in 1361 also failed, and he died at Sumiyoshi in 1368 with his cause weakening.

zh:
后村上天皇（1328—1368）名义良，是后醍醐天皇之子、南朝第二代天皇。他于1338年被立为皇太子，1339年在吉野继承父位，在位期间因南北朝战乱辗转于多处临时行宫。

1348年高师直进攻吉野，他被迫出逃；1352年南朝军队一度攻入京都，裹挟三位北朝上皇退走，但不出二十天便再失京都。1361年南朝再次短暂占领京都，仍告失败。1368年他在住吉去世，南朝势力已日趋衰微。

en:
Emperor Go-Nijō (1285–1308), the 94th emperor of Japan, was the eldest son of Emperor Go-Uda, head of the Daikakuji-tō line. In 1298 he was made crown prince to the Jimyōin-tō Emperor Go-Fushimi, and in 1301 Go-Fushimi abdicated and Go-Nijō succeeded, with Go-Uda ruling as cloistered emperor.

His elevation had been secured by his grandfather Emperor Kameyama, who lobbied Kamakura on his behalf. Amid the continuing rivalry between the two imperial lines, he died of illness in 1308 at Nijō-Takakura Palace after a seven-year reign.

zh:
后二条天皇（1285—1308）是日本第94代天皇，后宇多天皇的长子，属大觉寺统。1298年，他被立为持明院统后伏见天皇的皇太子；1301年后伏见天皇退位，邦治亲王继位，由后宇多上皇实行院政。

他的继位得力于祖父龟山上皇向幕府大力奔走。在两统围绕皇位持续对立之际，他于1308年在二条高仓宫病逝，在位七年。

en:
Emperor Go-Reizei (1025–1068), personal name Chikahito, was the 70th emperor of Japan, the eldest son of Emperor Go-Suzaku and Fujiwara no Yoshiko. He succeeded on his father's abdication in 1045 and reigned 23 years, with Fujiwara no Yorimichi and later Norimichi holding the kampaku regency.

In 1051 the Abe clan rose in the north, beginning the Zenkunen War; Minamoto no Yoriyoshi was sent against them and crushed the Abe by 1062. Go-Reizei left no children at his death in 1068, so the throne went to his half-brother, Emperor Go-Sanjō.

zh:
后冷泉天皇（1025—1068），名亲仁，日本第70代天皇，后朱雀天皇与藤原道长之女嬉子所生的长子。1045年父亲退位后他随即登基，在位23年，藤原赖通、教通兄弟先后任关白。

1051年安倍氏在陆奥起兵，引发前九年之役；朝廷派源赖义前往征讨，至1062年平定安倍氏。他无子嗣，1068年去世后，皇位由异母弟尊仁亲王继承，即后三条天皇。

en:
Emperor Go-Saga (1220–1272), the 88th emperor of Japan, reigned from 1242 to 1246. A son of Emperor Tsuchimikado, he was placed on the throne after the ten-year-old Emperor Shijō died, the Kamakura shogunate rejecting a candidate from Retired Emperor Juntoku's line.

In 1246 he abdicated to his son Emperor Go-Fukakusa and ruled as cloistered emperor, forcing Go-Fukakusa aside in 1259 in favour of his younger son Emperor Kameyama. Rivalry between the two brothers' descendants produced the Jimyōin-tō and Daikakuji-tō lines and later the Northern and Southern Courts.

zh:
后嵯峨天皇（1220—1272）是日本第88代天皇，1242至1246年在位。他是土御门天皇之子，十岁的四条天皇死后被拥立为帝，镰仓幕府拒绝了顺德上皇一脉的人选。

1246年他让位给儿子后深草天皇，以上皇身份实行院政，又于1259年迫使后深草天皇退位，改立幼子龟山天皇。两兄弟的后裔彼此争夺皇位，形成持明院统与大觉寺统两大皇统，最终酿成后来的南北朝分裂。

en:
Emperor Go-Sanjō (1034–1073), personal name Takahito, was the 71st emperor of Japan. A younger son of Emperor Go-Suzaku by the imperial princess Teishi, he was the first emperor in 170 years whose mother was not a Fujiwara, and the kampaku Fujiwara no Yorimichi cold-shouldered him as crown prince.

Succeeding his half-brother Go-Reizei in 1068, he ruled in person, issuing the Enkyū Shōen Regulation Decree of 1069 to curb Fujiwara wealth. He abdicated in 1073 in favour of his son Shirakawa, took Buddhist vows, and died at 40 before his cloistered rule could begin.

后三条天皇（1034—1073），名尊仁，日本第71代天皇。他是后朱雀天皇与祯子内亲王之子，是170年来首位母亲不姓藤原的天皇，在东宫时遭到关白藤原赖通冷落。

en:
Go-Shirakawa (1127–1192), a son of Emperor Toba, took the throne in 1155 after Emperor Konoe's sudden death, bypassing retired Emperor Sutoku's heir. In 1156 he won the Hōgen Rebellion with Taira no Kiyomori and Minamoto no Yoshitomo, then abdicated in 1158 and ruled as cloistered emperor through five reigns.

After the Taira beat the Minamoto in the 1160 Heiji Disturbance, Kiyomori dominated the court and confined him after the Shishigatani plot. In the Genpei War he backed Minamoto no Yoritomo; the Taira were destroyed at Dan-no-ura in 1185.

zh:
后白河天皇（1127—1192）是鸟羽天皇之子，1155年近卫天皇骤逝后继位，越过了崇德上皇继承人的顺位。1156年，他借助平清盛与源义朝的武力赢得保元之乱，1158年让位于儿子二条天皇，以上皇身份经五帝之世执掌院政。

1160年平治之乱后源氏战败，平清盛把持朝廷，并在鹿谷阴谋后将他囚禁。源平合战中他支持源赖朝，平家于1185年在坛之浦覆灭。

en:
Emperor Go-Suzaku (1009–1045), personal name Atsunaga, was the 69th emperor of Japan and a younger son of Emperor Ichijō and Fujiwara no Shōshi. Named crown prince in 1017 after Prince Atsuakira stepped aside, he succeeded his brother Go-Ichijō in 1036 and ruled for nine years while Fujiwara no Yorimichi dominated the court as regent.

His eldest son, born of Michinaga's daughter Yoshiko, succeeded him as Emperor Go-Reizei; another son, born of the imperial princess Teishi, later became Emperor Go-Sanjō. He abdicated in 1045, took Buddhist vows, and died two days later at 37.

en:
Go-Toba (1180–1239), a son of Emperor Takakura, was enthroned at three in 1183 after the Taira fled Kyoto with Emperor Antoku and the imperial regalia, the first accession without the sacred treasures. He abdicated in 1198 and ruled as cloistered emperor through the reigns of his sons Tsuchimikado and Juntoku.

A gifted poet, he commissioned and edited the Shin Kokinshū anthology and patronized the swordsmiths who opened Japan's golden age of blades. In 1221 he rose against the Kamakura shogunate in the Jōkyū War, was defeated, and died in exile on the Oki Islands in 1239.

后鸟羽天皇（1180—1239）是高仓天皇之子，1183年平家带着安德天皇和三神器逃离京都后，年仅三岁的他即位，成为首位没有神器传承的天皇。1198年他让位给儿子土御门天皇，以上皇身份经土御门、顺德两朝实行院政。

他擅长和歌，主持编纂《新古今和歌集》，并扶持刀匠，开启日本刀剑的黄金时代。1221年他举兵讨伐镰仓幕府，史称承久之乱，兵败后被流放隐岐群岛，1239年在流放地去世。

en:
Emperor Go-Uda (1267–1324), the 91st emperor of Japan, was a son of Emperor Kameyama and head of the Daikakuji-tō line. Named crown prince under Retired Emperor Go-Saga's settlement, he succeeded in 1274 while Kameyama ruled as cloistered emperor, and his reign saw the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 repelled by the Hōjō-led shogunate.

In 1287 the rival Jimyōin-tō and the Kamakura shogunate forced him to abdicate for Emperor Fushimi. He later ran the court as cloistered emperor for his son Emperor Go-Nijō and again for his second son Emperor Go-Daigo.

zh:
后宇多天皇（1267—1324）是日本第91代天皇，龟山天皇之子，大觉寺统的首领。他依照后嵯峨上皇的安排被立为皇太子，1274年继位，由龟山上皇实行院政；在位期间，蒙古于1274和1281年两度来袭，均被北条氏主导的幕府击退。

1287年，对立的持明院统联合镰仓幕府迫使他让位给伏见天皇。后来他先后为儿子后二条天皇和次子后醍醐天皇主持院政。

en:
Gotō no Motokiyo was a Kyoto warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods. The genealogical collection Sonpi Bunmyaku makes him a son of Satō no Nakakiyo, brother of the poet-monk Saigyō, adopted by Gotō no Sanemoto. He served Minamoto no Yoritomo, fought at the Battle of Yashima in 1185, and later became shugo of Sanuki Province and of Harima.

As a western-face guard and police commissioner for the retired Emperor Go-Toba, he joined the court in the Jōkyū War of 1221; after the defeat he was beheaded on the shogunate's orders by his son Mototsuna.

后藤基清是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期的京都武将、御家人。谱系书《尊卑分脉》记载，他本为歌僧西行之兄佐藤仲清之子，被后藤实基收为养子。他出仕源赖朝，参加1185年的屋岛之战，后任赞岐国、播磨国守护。

en:
Gotō no Mototsuna (1181–1256) was a Kamakura-period gokenin and court poet, son of Gotō no Motokiyo. In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he served the Kamakura shogunate as an army commissioner and, on its orders, beheaded his father, who had fought for the retired emperor.

In 1225 he joined the newly created Council of State. Dismissed in the 1246 palace purge, he returned as a Hikitsuke-shū judge in 1252. His verses appear in imperial anthologies including the Shin Chokusen Wakashū, and some traditions name him as author of the Jikkinshō.

en:
Hanazono (1297–1348), personal name Tomihito, was the 95th emperor of Japan, reigning from 1308 to 1318. A son of Emperor Fushimi of the Jimyōin line, he succeeded his cousin Emperor Go-Nijō. The Bumpō Agreement arranged rotation between the two rival imperial lines, and in 1318 he abdicated to Go-Daigo of the Daikakuji line.

He raised his nephew Emperor Kōgon, took Zen vows in 1335 and turned his palace into Myōshin-ji temple. A waka poet of the Kyōgoku school, he left the diary Hanazono-in Minki.

花园天皇（1297—1348），名富仁，是日本第95代天皇，1308年至1318年在位。他是持明院统伏见天皇之子，在再从兄后二条天皇死后继位。文保协议安排两大皇统轮流继承皇位，1318年他让位给大觉寺统的后醍醐天皇。

他抚养了侄子光严天皇，1335年出家为禅僧，将自己的宫殿改为妙心寺。他是京极派的和歌名手，留有日记《花园院宸记》。

en:
Hata Mochi was a warrior of the Matsura confederation in Hizen Province and the second son of Matsura Hisashi, whose genealogies traced the family to the Heian warrior Watanabe no Tsuna. In 1102 he moved to the Hata district of Matsura, took the surname Hata, and built Kishidake Castle as his stronghold.

He thereby founded the Hata clan, which became the leading family among the Upper Matsura bands and held Kishidake for some four hundred years, down to the Sengoku period.

en:
Hatakeyama Iekuni was a military commander of the late Kamakura period and a member of the Hatakeyama branch of the Ashikaga clan. A son of Hatakeyama Sadakuni, he held the court rank of Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade and served as Jibu-taifu.

A daughter became the wife of Ashikaga Motouji. He later took Buddhist orders under the name Sairen and died in 1335; his descendants grew into the house that supplied kanrei deputies to the Muromachi shogunate.

en:
Hatakeyama Kunikiyo (d. 1362 or 1364), clerical name Dōsei, was a son of Hatakeyama Iekuni and a leading general of the early Ashikaga bakufu. After fighting at Tatarahama in 1336 he was made shugo of Izumi, later holding Kii and Kawachi. In 1353 he became the first Kantō kanrei, adviser to Kamakura kubo Ashikaga Motouji, and in 1358 arranged the murder of Nitta Yoshioki.

Ousted in 1361, he rebelled in Izu, surrendered at Shuzenji Castle, and died soon after. He is regarded as the founder of the Kawachi Hatakeyama line.

畠山国清（1362或1364年卒），法名道誓，是畠山家国之子、室町幕府初期的重要武将。1336年在多多良滨之战立功，被任命为和泉守护，后来历任纪伊、河内守护。1353年他成为首任关东管领，辅佐镰仓公方足利基氏，1358年策划谋杀新田义兴。

1361年他被罢免，在伊豆举兵反叛，最终在修禅寺城投降，不久死去。他被视为河内畠山氏的实际始祖。

en:
Hatakeyama Kuniuji was a Nanboku-chō warrior and the heir of Hatakeyama Takakuni. Appointed Ōshū kanrei in 1345, he joined his father at Taga in Mutsu to subdue Southern Court forces.

He later clashed with Kira Sadaie, an ally of Ashikaga Tadayoshi, siding with Takauji in the Kannō Disturbance. In 1351 Sadaie's troops besieged Iwakiri Castle, and Kuniuji and his father took their own lives. His son Kuniakira became ancestor of the Nihonmatsu clan.

en:
Hatakeyama Tadaaki (d. after 1358), first named Yoshiaki, was a warrior of the Ashikaga-related Hatakeyama clan, a son of Hatakeyama Muneyoshi. After Ashikaga Takauji's victory at Tatarahama, Tadaaki was sent to Hyūga to subdue Southern Court forces in Kyushu, bringing local lords to submission by 1339. In 1345 he was appointed shugo of Hyūga.

During the Kannō Disturbance he sided with Ashikaga Tadayoshi, but defeat at Shibushi Castle in 1357 by the Shimazu and by Kikuchi Takemitsu shattered his power; he fled to Bungo in 1358.

en:
Hatakeyama Tadamune was a warrior of the Mino branch of the Hatakeyama clan, son of Hatakeyama Munekuni and nephew of Hyūga shugo Hatakeyama Tadaaki. He became a close aide to Ashikaga Tadayoshi, receiving the character tada of his name from him.

In 1349 he and Uesugi Shigeyoshi secured the dismissal of Tadayoshi's rival Kō no Moronao, then plotted his murder; the plan leaked, Tadamune was exiled to Echizen, and that year Moronao's agents forced him to kill himself, the opening bloodshed of the Kannō Disturbance.

Hatakeyama Takakuni (1305–1351) was a Northern and Southern Courts era warrior, son of Hatakeyama Tokikuni and head of the main Hatakeyama line. He fought for Ashikaga Takauji at Kyoto in 1336 and became shugo of Ise, but lost the post in 1338 after failing to stop Kitabatake Akiie's march.

en:
Hatakeyama Tokikuni was a Kamakura-period warrior, possibly the renamed Kuniuji, eldest son of Hatakeyama Yasukuni, and jitō of the Nakakita manor in Mino. In the Kenchō era of 1249 to 1256 he and Yasukuni served the bakufu only as ordinary gokenin, and never entered the regime's inner circle.

The house in Tokikuni's time nonetheless ranked with the heads of Hōjō branch families. His eldest son Takakuni founded the Ōshū Hatakeyama line and his second son Sadakuni the Kawachi Hatakeyama, later one of the three Kanrei houses.

en:
Hatakeyama Yasukuni was an early Kamakura gokenin of the Ashikaga-related Hatakeyama clan, the third son of Ashikaga Yoshizumi. His mother was a daughter of Hōjō Tokimasa and widow of Hatakeyama Shigetada, through whom he inherited the Hatakeyama legacy, and he was the first of the line to bear the Hatakeyama name.

His name character came from his cousin Hōjō Yasutoki. He held lands in Mino and served the bakufu with his son Kuniuji in the Kenchō era (1249–1256), and was afterwards succeeded by Kuniuji.

名字中的“泰”字得自表兄#TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_houjou_yasutoki').GetID],X #L 北条泰时#!#!的偏讳。他领有[ShowLocationName('mino')]国的领地，建长年间（1249—1256年）仍与子国氏一同出仕幕府，后由国氏继承家督。

en:
Hatakeyama Yoshifuka (1331–1379) was the sixth head of the Hatakeyama clan and younger brother of the Kantō kanrei Hatakeyama Kunikiyo. He fought for the Northern Court, facing Southern Court troops at Ryūmonzan in 1359. Joining his brother's revolt in 1361, he surrendered with him.

Pardoned in 1366, he was made shugo of Echizen and overthrew Shiba Takatsune in the Jōji Incident. He later held several more shugo posts and died in 1379.

zh:
畠山义深（1331—1379）是畠山氏第六代当主、关东管领畠山国清之弟。他为北朝作战，1359年在龙门山迎战南朝军队。1361年他参与兄长国清举兵，随兄投降。

1366年他获幕府赦免，被任命为越前守护，在贞治之变中击败斯波高经，此后又历任数国守护，1379年去世。

en:
Hatakeyama Yoshizumi (1174–1210), born Ashikaga Yoshizumi, was the eldest son of Ashikaga Yoshikane, raised at Nitta manor in Kōzuke by his great-uncle Nitta Yoshishige.

In 1205, after the Hōjō destroyed Hatakeyama Shigetada, Hōjō Yoshitoki married Yoshizumi to Shigetada's widow, a daughter of Hōjō Tokimasa, and had him succeed to the Hatakeyama name. He is counted the ancestor of the Minamoto-line Hatakeyama clan, and Hatakeyama Yasukuni was his son. He died in 1210, aged thirty-seven.

畠山义纯（1174—1210），原名足利义纯，是足利义兼的长子，由大伯父新田义重在新田庄养大。

1205年北条氏攻灭畠山重忠后，北条义时将重忠的遗孀、北条时政之女嫁给他，令其继承畠山的名号，由此被视为足利一门中源姓畠山氏之祖，畠山泰国即其子。1210年去世，终年37岁。

en:
Hirosawa no Sanekata, born of the Hatano clan of Sagami, was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods and ancestor of the Hirosawa house. In 1155 he fought under Minamoto no Yoshihira at the Battle of Ōkura, and the next year received lands at Hirosawa in Musashi Province, from which he took his name.

He served Minamoto no Yoritomo in the Genpei War, winning merit at Fujito in 1184, and in 1192 was granted twelve estates in Bingo Province.

广泽实方出身相模波多野氏，是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期的武士、广泽氏之祖。1155年，他随源义平参加大藏合战，翌年受赐武藏国广泽之地，遂以广泽为姓。

治承·寿永之乱中他追随源赖朝，1184年在藤户之战立功，1192年获赐备后国十二乡。

en:
Hirosawa Sanetaka was a warrior of the Hatano clan of Sagami, son of Hirosawa Sanekata. In 1211 he went down to the family's lands in Bingo province to crush a bandit rising.

During the Wada War of 1213, Wada Yoshimori requisitioned a hundred arrowheads from him in the shōgun's name; after the revolt Sanetaka was slandered as a Wada ally until his Hatano kinsmen cleared him in Kamakura.

en:
Hatano no Tōyoshi was a late-Heian warrior of Sagami Province and the fourth head of the Hatano clan, ruling Hatano manor in Yurugi District, an estate of the Fujiwara regents' house. He combined local lordship with court service, belonging to Emperor Sutoku's secretariat and in 1124 attending the Ise princess Shushi's first purification.

His sons, led by his second son Yoshimichi, who inherited Hatano manor, followed Minamoto no Yoshitomo and Yoritomo, and the Kawamura and Ōtomo houses traced their descent to him.

波多野远义是平安时代后期相模国的武士、波多野氏第四代当主，本领为余绫郡的波多野庄，即藤原摄关家的领地。他一边在地经营，一边出仕朝廷，曾任崇德天皇藏人所众，1124年参与伊势斋宫守子女王的初次禊仪。

en:
Saeki no Tsunenori, also known as Hatano no Tsunenori, was a mid-Heian warrior of Sagami Province and the recorded founder of the Hatano clan. Genealogies name him a son of the Sagami governor Fujiwara no Kinmitsu, descended from Fujiwara no Hidesato.

He held Hatano manor in Yurugi District, from which his house took its name, served Minamoto no Yoriyoshi of the Kawachi Minamoto, and fought in the Earlier Nine Years' War of 1051–1062.

en:
Hatano no Yoshimichi (1108–1169) was a late-Heian commander and fifth head of the Sagami Hatano, based at Hatano manor in Sagami Province. Son of Tōyoshi, he served Minamoto no Yoshitomo from the latter's youth in the east, and his sister became Yoshitomo's concubine.

He fought for Yoshitomo in the 1156 Hōgen Disturbance, but fell out with him and left Kyoto in 1158, then joined him again in the 1159 Heiji Disturbance. He died in 1169; his son Yoshitsune opposed Yoritomo's 1180 uprising and took his own life.

zh:
波多野义通（1108—1169）是平安时代末期的武将、相模波多野氏第五代当主，本据为相模国波多野庄。他是远义之子，自在东国的源义朝少年时便近身侍奉，其妹后为义朝侧室。

1156年保元之乱中他随义朝从军，1158年与义朝不和、离开京都，1159年平治之乱中再度追随义朝。1169年去世；其子义常与1180年举兵的源赖朝敌对，最终自尽。

en:
Hatano no Yoshitsune, also Matsuda Yoshitsune, was a late-Heian warrior and sixth head of the Sagami Hatano, son of Hatano no Yoshimichi. After 1159 he served in Kyoto as a Right Stables officer and became a leading Sagami magnate.

But when Yoritomo rose against the Taira in 1180, Yoshitsune refused the call. Yoritomo sent troops against him, and before they reached Matsuda manor Yoshitsune killed himself in the tenth month of 1180. His heir Aritsune was pardoned in 1188 and founded the Matsuda house.

His heir Aritsune was pardoned in 1188 and founded the [ShowDynastyName('matsuda_dynasty')] house.
zh:
波多野义常，亦称松田义常，是平安时代末期的武士、相模波多野氏第六代当主，波多野义通之子。1159年平治之乱后，他在京都出仕，任右马允，成为相模国有力武士。

但1180年赖朝举兵讨伐平氏时，义常拒绝参阵。赖朝派兵前来诛伐，军队尚未抵达松田乡，义常便在1180年十月先行自害。其嫡子有常于1188年获赦，是松田氏之祖。

en:
Oda Haruhisa (1300–1353), eighth head of the Oda family of Hitachi, a Hatta branch, was the son of the seventh head Sadamune. First named Takatomo, he fought in his father's place in 1327 to crush the Ando rebellion. After the Kamakura shogunate fell in 1333 he served Emperor Go-Daigo, taking the name Haruhisa from him.

In 1336 he joined the Southern Court, fighting the Northern Court Satake and sheltering Kitabatake Chikafusa at Oda Castle, until submitting to Ashikaga rule in 1341. He died in 1353 and his son Takatomo succeeded him.

zh:
小田治久（1300—1353）是常陆小田氏第八代当主。小田氏出自八田氏，他是第七代当主小田贞宗之子，初名高知。1327年，他代父出征，平定安藤氏之乱。1333年镰仓幕府灭亡后，他出仕后醍醐天皇，受天皇名讳中的一字改名治久。

1336年他加入南朝，与北朝的佐竹氏作战，并将北畠亲房迎入小田城，直至1341年归降足利方。1353年去世，由其子孝朝继嗣。

en:
Oda Sadamune (1283–1335), also called Sadatomo, was the seventh head of the Oda warrior family of Hitachi, a branch of the Hatta clan. A character in his name was granted by the Hōjō regent Sadatoki.

In 1327, when the Kamakura bakufu ordered the Andō rebellion in Mutsu crushed, he sent his heir Haruhisa to lead the family's men. After the bakufu fell in 1333, Haruhisa entered Emperor Go-Daigo's service, and Sadamune died in 1335.

小田贞宗（1283—1335），又名贞知，是常陆国武将小田氏（八田氏分支）的第七代当主，名字中的一字得自北条执权贞时的偏讳。

1327年镰仓幕府下令平定陆奥国安藤氏之乱时，他派嫡子治久代己出征。1333年幕府灭亡后，治久出仕后醍醐天皇。贞宗于1335年去世。

en:
Oda Tokitomo was a Kamakura-period head of the Oda family of Hitachi, the main line of the Hatta clan, succeeding his father Yasutomo. A character in his name came from the Hōjō regent Tsunetoki or Tokiyori.

After the Hōji conflict of 1247 destroyed the Miura clan, his family's Miura ties cost it the Hitachi shugo post and part of its lands; he was still a minor in 1252. He was succeeded by his son Munetomo.

en:
Hatta Tomoie (1142–c. 1225) was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods, son of Utsunomiya Munetsuna, based at Hatta in Hitachi. After joining Minamoto no Yoritomo in 1180, he helped crush Shida Yoshihiro at Nogi in 1183 and commanded the Tōkaidō army in the Ōshū campaign of 1189.

As shugo of Hitachi he brought down the rival Daijō faction in 1193, and in 1199 joined the Council of Thirteen advising Shōgun Yoriie. He founded the Oda clan and built Oda Castle.

zh:
八田知家（1142—约1225）是平安末期至镰仓前期的武士，宇都宫宗纲之子，以常陆国八田为据点。1180年起追随源赖朝，1183年在野木宫之战中击溃志田义广，1189年奥州合战时担任东海道军大将。

任常陆国守护期间，他于1193年扳倒敌对的大掾氏，1199年又成为辅佐将军源赖家的十三人合议制成员。他是小田氏的始祖，主持修筑了小田城。

en:
Oda Tomoshige, also called Hatta Tomoshige, was a Kamakura warrior, son of Hatta Tomoie, whose shugo post in Hitachi he inherited. In 1181 Minamoto no Yoritomo named him one of eleven archery masters guarding his bedchamber, and he fought beside his father in the Ōshū campaign of 1189.

In 1213 he warned Ōe no Hiromoto of Wada Yoshimori's troop build-up, opening the Wada battle. In 1228 the bakufu rebuked his scheme to seize the hereditary Daijō office in Hitachi.

小田知重（一称八田知重）是镰仓幕府御家人，八田知家之子，后来继承了常陆国守护之职。1181年，源赖朝把他选为担任寝所警卫的十一名弓术达人之一；1189年他随父亲参加奥州合战。

1213年，他察觉和田义盛聚集兵马，随即报告大江广元，揭开和田合战的序幕。1228年，他图谋夺取常陆大掾的世袭职位，被幕府斥为非分之想。

en:
Oda Yasutomo was a mid-Kamakura warrior, the legitimate son of Oda Tomoshige and grandson of Hatta Tomoie, and the third shugo of Hitachi in his line. He died in 1245 at thirty-five, leaving a young heir, Tokitomo.

The office passed to Yasutomo's cousin Shishido Iechika, possibly because Tokitomo was young or because his mother was of the Miura clan, destroyed in the Hōji conflict of 1247. Another account, conflicting with his death date, claims he fought for the Miura and lost office and lands.

小田泰知是镰仓时代中期的武士，小田知重的嫡男、八田知家之孙，继父亲之后担任常陆国守护，是家族中第三代出任此职者。他于1245年去世，年三十五岁，留下年幼的嫡子时知。

守护之职改由泰知的堂弟宍户家周继任，原因可能是时知年幼，或是其生母出自1247年宝治合战中覆灭的三浦氏。另有一说称泰知加入三浦方作战而失去职位和部分领地，此说与他的卒年相矛盾。

en:
Hei no Chikamitsu was a warrior of the Hei clan of Mutsu province and a son of Hei no Mitsuyori. After the Kamakura shogunate fell in 1333, he took service with Kitabatake Akiie, governor of Mutsu, who confirmed the family's holdings in Hei district.

The clan then marched south in Akiie's Oshu army on the Southern Court side, routing Ashikaga Takauji's forces at Aonogahara before defeat at Ishizu, both in 1338.

闭伊亲光是陆奥国闭伊氏的武士，闭伊光赖之子。1333年镰仓幕府灭亡后，他追随陆奥国司北畠显家，闭伊郡的家族所领得到安堵。

en:
Hei no Mitsuyori was a Kamakura-period gokenin of the Hei clan, a warrior family of Hei district in Mutsu province. Between the Shōō and Gen'ō eras (1288–1319), he and his kinsman Hei no Kazutsura disputed the lands left by Hei no Mitsukazu, and the regent Hōjō Takatoki judged the case himself at Kamakura.

Mitsuyori kept the estates along the Hei River, including Takusari and Akimae, while Kazutsura received Kuwasaki and Kasama. His son was Chikamitsu.

闭伊光赖是镰仓时代陆奥国闭伊郡武家闭伊氏的御家人。正应至元应年间（1288—1319），他与同族闭伊员连围绕先代闭伊光员留下的领地发生继承纠纷，官司打到镰仓，由执权北条高时亲自裁决。

en:
Hei no Yorimoto was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods, remembered as founder of the Hei clan of Hei district in Mutsu. Late Edo genealogies claim he was the third son of Minamoto no Tametomo, who escaped exile in Izu and reached the Sanriku coast.

Said to have met Yoritomo in the 1189 Oshu campaign, he took the name Sasaki Juro Yukimitsu, received Hei and Kesen districts after the Northern Fujiwara fell, and then called himself Hei no Yorimoto. No contemporary source supports his claimed Genji birth.

zh:
闭伊赖基是平安时代末期至镰仓时代前期的武将，被尊为陆奥国闭伊郡闭伊氏的始祖。江户时代后期的诸家谱称，他是源为朝的三子，逃出配流之地伊豆，漂流至三陆海岸。

相传他在1189年奥州合战时谒见源赖朝，改名佐佐木十郎行光，奥州藤原氏灭亡后受命统治闭伊、气仙两郡，随后取领地之名改称闭伊赖基。其源氏出身并无同时代史料佐证，后世多认为属于冒称。

en:
Emperor Heizei (774–824) was the 51st emperor of Japan, reigning from 806 to 809. The eldest son of Emperor Kanmu, he succeeded his father in 806. During his brief reign he reorganized the imperial bodyguards, appointing Sakanoue no Tamuramaro senior commander of the right.

In 809, seriously ill, he abdicated in favor of his younger brother Emperor Saga and retired to Nara. In 810 his consort Fujiwara no Kusuko and her brother Nakanari raised a failed revolt in his name, the Kusuko Incident; Heizei then took Buddhist vows and died in 824.

zh:
平城天皇（774—824）是日本第51代天皇，806年至809年在位。他是桓武天皇长子，806年继位。在位时间不长，曾改组近卫府，任命坂上田村麻吕为右近卫大将。

809年他因病重，让位于同母弟嵯峨天皇，退居奈良。810年，其宠妃藤原药子与药子之兄仲成借他的名义起兵失败，史称药子之变；事败后平城出家为僧，于824年去世。

Tameshige Hienuki was the traditional founder of the Hienuki clan. The Date clan genealogy names him as a son of Date Tameie.

In 1197 he went to Hienuki district in Mutsu province, entered Osegawa Castle, and took the district name as his family name. Tradition holds that he served Minamoto no Yoritomo and was granted the lands along the Kitakami River after the Ōshū campaign. His son Mitsuie succeeded him.

Hiraga no Koreyasu, also called Matsuba no Koreyasu, was the son of Sukemune, founder of the Aki Hiraga clan. In his generation the family settled on its estate in Hiraka district of Dewa Province and took the place name as its family name, styling itself Hiraka, later written Hiraga.

He came of age at the Kamakura mansion of Hojo Yasutoki, the shogunal regent. Yasutoki gave him the character yasu from his own name.

en:
Hiraga Naomune was a warrior of the Hiraga clan and its sōryō, the head of the main family line. Around 1274 a clansman went from Dewa to Takaya in Aki Province after the Mongol invasion; Naomune's illegitimate elder brother Tomokane later held Takaya and served Ashikaga Takauji when the Kamakura shogunate fell in 1333.

The brothers then fought over the succession; Naomune won, took up residence at Takaya and ruled the district himself. Under him Takaya became the Hiraga clan's permanent base, while its ancestral lands in Dewa were gradually lost.

平贺直宗是平贺氏的武士，也是宗家的总领。约1274年，族人因元军入侵自出羽下向安艺国高屋保；后来直宗的庶长兄共兼领有该地，并在1333年镰仓幕府灭亡时追随足利尊氏。

此后兄弟二人为家督继承相争，直宗获胜，亲自下向高屋保实施统治。在他治下，高屋保成为平贺氏的永久本据，而出羽的祖领则逐渐丧失。

en:
Hiraga no Sukemune, first called Matsuba no Sukemune, was the founder of the Aki Hiraga clan. A late-Heian warrior, he backed Minamoto no Yoritomo in the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 and won repeated distinction.

He was rewarded with estates in four provinces, including Hiraka district in Dewa. His descendants later settled at Hiraka and took its name as Hiraga, and the clan claimed descent from the great minister Fujiwara no Yoshifusa.

en:
Hirosawa Yoshizane (c. 1165–c. 1240), also written Yata Yoshizane, was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods, the son of Ashikaga Yoshikiyo, who fell at the Battle of Mizushima in 1183. He was known as Hirosawa Hangandai after the Hirosawa village where he lived.

After the Jōkyū War of 1221 his sons settled in Mikawa: Sanekuni's descendants became the Niki clan and Yoshisue's the Hosokawa clan.

Fujiwara no Shigetae, later known as Hishikari Shigetae, was by tradition a grandson of Fujiwara no Takanaga, exiled to Izu after the Hōgen War of 1156.

en:
Hongō Suketada was a Nanboku-chō-period warrior and first head of the Hongō branch of the Satsuma Shimazu. He was the sixth son of the fourth Shimazu head, Shimazu Tadamune; the eldest brother inherited the main house while the other six each founded a cadet house.

From 1336 he campaigned for his eldest brother Sadahisa, commanding a wing at the siege of Kaseda castle in Ōsumi. In 1351 he served the Northern Court in Chikuzen, and in 1352 he received part of Hongō in Hyūga.

Tradition says he entered Satsumasako that winter and took the Hongō name, though the date of his entry is uncertain. He died in 1359 or 1365.

1336年起，他随长兄贞久转战，在攻打大隅加濑田城时担任搦手大将。1351年他在筑前为北朝作战，1352年获授日向北乡的部分土地。

相传他于同年冬进入萨摩迫，以乡名为氏，称北乡氏，但确切入部时间不详。他于1359年或1365年去世。

en:
Honkōin (born c. 1306) was the wife of Ashikaga Tadayoshi, co-director of the early Muromachi shogunate. A daughter of Shibukawa Sadayori, her secular name is unrecorded. In 1347, at about forty, she bore him a son, Nyoimaru.

During the Kannō Disturbance of 1350–1352 she lost both husband and son. She inherited his Akatsuka estate in Musashi, took the tonsure and prayed for their souls; one account places her death around 1363, and she was dead by 1383.

Honma Tadaie was an early Kamakura-period warrior and the eldest son of Honma Yoshitada, holder of Echi in Sagami. In 1219 he was among the palanquin attendants when Fujiwara no Yoritsune traveled to Kamakura.

In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he served in Hōjō Tokifusa's army, fought at Seta and Uji, and helped capture Kōji Yoritsune at Kibune. Remaining in Kyoto with the Rokuhara deputies, he later led troops against disorderly monks at Onjō-ji and Kōya-san, and became shugodai of Ise Province.

Emperor Horikawa (1079–1107) was the 73rd emperor of Japan. The son of Emperor Shirakawa, he was only seven when his father abdicated in 1087 and placed him on the throne.

A regent handled administration while Shirakawa ruled through his new cloistered government, so Horikawa's reign was largely ceremonial; he devoted himself to scholarship, poetry and music. His son Prince Munehito succeeded him as Emperor Toba, and Horikawa died in 1107 aged 28.

摄政处理政务，白河上皇则通过首创的院政总揽大权，堀河天皇在位期间因而多居象征性地位，本人潜心于学问、和歌与音乐。皇子宗仁后来继位为鸟羽天皇。堀河天皇于1107年病逝，年仅28岁。

Hosokawa Akiharu (1330–c. 1367) was a warrior of the Northern and Southern Courts era and founder of the Hosokawa Awa shugo house. A son of Hosokawa Yoriharu, he was known as Kuro in childhood and took the name Akiharu through a character granted by Shogun Ashikaga Yoshiakira.

He followed his elder brother Yoriyuki into Awa Province, and tradition credits him with building Shozui Castle in 1363. He died young around 1367, and his son Yoshiyuki succeeded him.

en:
Hosokawa Akiuji (died 1352), second head of the Hosokawa Oshu branch, was a Northern Court general, the son of Hosokawa Yorisada of Mikawa. From the Genko War he served Ashikaga Takauji, and in 1336 crossed to Shikoku to win its warriors for him. He became shugo of Sanuki, Tosa and other provinces, but in 1347 was routed by Kusunoki Masatsura and lost his offices.

In the Kanno Disturbance he first backed Ashikaga Tadayoshi, then returned to Takauji. In 1352 he led Northern troops against a Southern Court drive on Kyoto, dying that July.

细川显氏（？—1352）是细川奥州家第二代当主、北朝武将，为出身三河国的细川赖贞之子。自元弘之乱起他便追随足利尊氏，1336年渡海前往四国，争取岛上的武士归附足利方。他先后受任赞岐、土佐等国守护，但1347年被楠木正行击败而遭解职。

en:
Hosokawa Jozen (born c. 1320) was a son of Hosokawa Yorisada of Mikawa and younger brother of Akiuji. Originally a betto administrator at the Tsurugaoka Wakamiya shrine, he served Ashikaga Takauji with his brother and won distinction in the Nakasendai War of 1335.

Sent to rally the warriors of Shikoku, in January 1336 he struck at Kyoto, and that May fought at the Minato River. He kept campaigning against Southern Court forces around the capital until the autumn of 1339, when records of him cease.

细川定禅（约1320年生）是三河细川赖贞之子、显氏之弟。他原为鹤冈若宫的别当，后与兄长显氏一同出仕足利尊氏，在1335年的中先代之乱中立功。

en:
Hosokawa Kazuuji (1296–1342), fourth head of the Hosokawa clan, was a Mikawa-born warrior serving Ashikaga Takauji. After the Genkō War he helped Takauji overthrow the Kamakura shogunate and became governor of Awa. In 1335 he helped crush the Nakasendai rebellion, then fought the imperial court for Takauji.

In 1336 he and his cousin Akiuji secured Shikoku for the Ashikaga. He later headed the Boards of Inquiry and Retainers, then retired to Akizuki in Awa, where he invited Musō Soseki to found Fudaiji and died in 1342.

zh:
细川和氏（1296—1342）是细川氏第四代当主、出身三河国的武将，效力于足利尊氏。元弘之乱后，他参加尊氏推翻镰仓幕府的行动，随后受任阿波守。1335年他参与镇压中先代之乱，随尊氏与朝廷官军作战。

1336年与堂兄弟细川显氏一同争取四国归附足利方。幕府开创后，他历任引付头人、侍所头人，后隐居阿波秋月，延请梦窗疎石开创补陀寺，1342年去世。

en:
Hosokawa Kimiyori was a gokenin of the late Kamakura period and the third head of the Hosokawa clan, eldest son of Hosokawa Toshiuji, commonly called Hachirōtarō.

He kept his seat at Hosokawa-gō in Mikawa Province and later took Buddhist orders under the name Raibutsu, also styled Keitokuin. His sons Kazuuji, Yoriharu and Morouji became ancestors of the clan's principal branch houses.

en:
Hosokawa Kiyouji (c. 1325–1362), fifth head of the Hosokawa and Kazuuji's son, fought for Takauji in the Kanno Disturbance and became shugo of Ise. In 1353 he shielded Emperor Go-Kogon during a Southern raid on Kyoto, carrying him on his back over the mountains to Omi.

In 1358 Yoshiakira made him steward, but rivals drove him out in 1361 and he defected south. In 1362 his cousin Yoriyuki cornered him in Sanuki; the Taiheiki says Yoriyuki's feint split his army and he died alone.

细川清氏（约1325—1362）是细川氏第五代当主、和氏的嫡子，观应之扰乱中率四国军队为足利尊氏作战，后受任伊势守护。1353年南朝军进攻京都时他护卫后光严天皇，曾背负天皇翻越山岭撤至近江。

1358年，足利义诠任命他为执事；但他于1361年被政敌逐出幕府，投奔南朝。1362年，堂弟赖之在赞岐将他逼入绝境，《太平记》称赖之以诱敌之计分散其兵力，清氏随后单骑战死。

en:
Hosokawa Kokai (born c. 1323) was a monk-general of the Hosokawa, a son of Yorisada and younger brother of Akiuji, holding the clerical title Sanmi Ajari. Formerly betto of Tsurugaoka Hachiman shrine, he followed Ashikaga Takauji against the Southern Court.

In the third month of 1337 he fought on Kutsuna Island in Iyo, then campaigned in Kii, subduing its northern districts by late 1338. He served as shugo of Tosa from 1339 to the end of 1340, when the sources lose sight of him.

en:
Hosokawa Morouji (1305–1348), first head of the Hosokawa Awaji line, was a son of Hosokawa Kimiyori of Mikawa. In the Genko War he followed Ashikaga Takauji against the Kamakura shogunate, then served under Tadayoshi in Kamakura and fought the Nakasendai War of 1335.

As shugo of Awaji, he crushed the Southern Court Uhara clan at Tachikawase. In 1347 he reduced Shodo Island, forcing its Southern Court defenders to submit. He died in June 1348, and his descendants held Awaji as their shugo province.

细川繁氏（约1325—1359）是细川奥州家第三代当主、北朝武将，为细川显氏之子。他随父亲为足利尊氏作战，1352年父亲去世后，他继承家督，出任赞岐、土佐守护。

1355年起他在土佐与南朝势力作战。《太平记》记载，1359年他在赞岐为筹划大规模远征而侵夺崇德上皇的院领以充军资，当年夏天暴病而亡，史书将其死归于崇德院的咒诅。

en:
Hosokawa no Toshiuji was a gokenin of the Kamakura period (1185–1333) and the second head of the Hosokawa clan. The son of Yoshitoshi, who died young, he and his brothers were adopted by their grandfather Yoshisue, who made Toshiuji his heir.

He took Buddhist vows under the name Raisai and seems to have kept his base at Hosokawa-go in Mikawa. His tomb stands at Rinsho-ji in Toyota beside those of Yoshisue and his son Kimiyori.

他出家后法号赖西，似乎一直以三河国细川乡为据点。其墓与祖父义季、其子公赖之墓一同存于丰田市的邻松寺。

en:
Hosokawa Ujiharu (c. 1325–1387), second head of the Hosokawa Awaji line, succeeded his father as shugo of Awaji in 1348. In 1361 his kinsman Kiyouji defected to the Southern Court, and Ujiharu followed him, helping seize Kyoto.

He crossed to Sanuki in 1362, and after Kiyouji was killed there by their cousin Yoriyuki, Ujiharu surrendered and was restored as Awaji shugo. He served the Muromachi regime thereafter and died in 1387, succeeded by his son Mitsuharu.

1362年他渡海至赞岐，清氏在当地被堂弟赖之攻杀后，氏春归降幕府，重新受任淡路守护。此后他仕于室町幕府，1387年去世，由子满春继任。

en:
Hosokawa Yoriari (1332–1391), son of Hosokawa Yoriharu, was a warrior of the Northern and Southern Courts era and first head of the Hosokawa Izumi-kami shugo house. After his father's death in 1352 he led Sanuki troops at the Battle of Otokoyama beside his brother Yoriyuki.

After Yoriyuki became kanrei, Yoriari governed Awa as his deputy. When Yoriyuki fell in the 1379 Koryaku coup, Yoriari stood by him. He yielded the headship to his son Yorinaga in 1387 and died in 1391.

en:
Hosokawa Yoriharu (c. 1304–1352) was a Northern Court general, son of Hosokawa Kimiyori of Mikawa and ancestor of the Hosokawa kanrei line. In 1333 he and his brother Kazuuji joined Ashikaga Takauji's rising and guarded the child Senju-o, the future shogun Yoshiakira.

He fought at the Minato River in 1336 and went on to hold four shugo posts. In 1348 he helped destroy Kusunoki Masatsura at Shijo Nawate, and in 1352 fell defending Yoshiakira.

en:
Hosokawa Yorisada was a warrior of the late Kamakura period and founder of the Hosokawa Oshu house. Born at Hosokawa-gō in Mikawa, he was by tradition adopted in childhood by his great-grandfather Yoshisue.

During the Nakasendai War of July 1335 his son Akiuji's army was routed. The bedridden Yorisada refused to be a burden: the Taiheiki says he disembowelled himself facing the enemy, while other accounts place his death at Kawamurayama in Sagami.

en:
Hosokawa Yoriyuki (1329–1392), son of Yoriharu, was the leading statesman of the early Ashikaga shogunate. He campaigned in Shikoku and in 1362 destroyed his defected cousin Kiyouji at Sanuki's Shiramine Castle. In 1367 Yoshiakira named him kanrei to the young Yoshimitsu.

As kanrei he issued the 1368 half-tax law protecting court and temple estates and set the office to rotate among the Hosokawa, Shiba and Hatakeyama. Ousted in the 1379 Koryaku coup and pardoned in 1389, he died in 1392.

细川赖之（1329—1392）是室町幕府初期最重要的政治家，为细川赖春之子。他在四国征战，1362年在赞岐白峰城攻灭叛投南朝的堂兄清氏。1367年，足利义诠任命他为管领，辅佐年幼的义满。

任内他颁布1368年的半济令，保护公家与寺社领地，并确立管领由细川、斯波、畠山三家轮任的制度。1379年他在康历政变中被逐，1389年获赦，1392年去世。

en:
Hosokawa no Yoshisue was a Kamakura-period gokenin and founder of the Hosokawa clan. The second son of Hirosawa no Yoshizane of the Ashikaga line, he moved from Hirosawa in Kozuke to the Hosokawa manor in Nukata district of Mikawa. His elder brother Sanekuni founded the Niki clan and his younger brother Yoshimune the Togasaki clan.

His grandson Toshiuji, son of Yoshitoshi, became his heir. His tomb lies at Rensho-in Jokyu-ji, said to have been built by his descendant Yoriyuki in 1392.

en:
Hosokawa no Yoshitoshi was a warrior of the Kamakura period (1185–1333) and a son of Yoshisue, founder of the Hosokawa clan of Mikawa. Because Yoshisue adopted Yoshitoshi's own sons, including the future heir Toshiuji, historians infer that Yoshitoshi died young, before his father.

The Hosokawa were then only minor gokenin in Mikawa. The Enshu and Toichi Hosokawa branches, later shugodai of Tosa Province, descended from his son Muneyoshi.

en:
Hōjō Hisatoki (1272–1307), also called Akahashi Hisatoki, was a late-Kamakura Hōjō clansman and son of Hōjō Yoshimune. In 1280 Shikken Tokimune made him shugo of five provinces.

From 1293 to 1297 he was northern Rokuhara tandai, the shogunate's deputy in Kyoto. Returning to Kamakura, he held senior council and judicial posts before taking vows in 1307, the year he died aged 36. His son Moritoki became the last Hōjō shikken, and his daughter married Ashikaga Takauji.

en:
Hōjō Moritoki (1295–1333), also called Akahashi Moritoki, was the sixteenth and last shikken of the Kamakura shogunate, son of Hōjō Hisatoki. He took office in 1326 after the Karyaku disturbance, though power lay with the retired tokusō Takatoki and the Nagasaki family.

In 1333 his brother-in-law Ashikaga Takauji rebelled and destroyed the Rokuhara tandai. Moritoki led the vanguard against Nitta Yoshisada at the Kobusagoe pass and, overwhelmed, killed himself at Suzaki in June 1333, aged 39; his son Masutoki died with him.

en:
Hōjō Muneyori (died 1279) was a mid-Kamakura commander of the Hōjō tokusō line, fourth son of Shikken Tokiyori and half-brother of Shikken Tokimune. He died in 1279.

In 1276, with another Mongol attack expected, the shogunate created the Nagato tandai post to guard the west, and Muneyori became its first holder in Nagato province. His son Munekata became Tokimune's adopted son.

en:
Hōjō Nagatoki (1230–1264), also called Akahashi Nagatoki, was the heir of Shigetoki. He grew up in Kyoto and in 1247 succeeded his father as Rokuhara tandai.

In 1256 the tonsured Tokiyori made him the sixth shikken as caretaker for the young Tokimune, keeping real power himself. Nagatoki held office until illness forced him to resign and take the tonsure in 1264; he died weeks later aged thirty-five. Twelve of his waka entered the imperial anthologies.

en:
Hōjō Sadatoki (1272–1311), the ninth Kamakura shikken, was Tokimune's eldest son. He succeeded in 1284 aged twelve. The 1285 Shimotsuki Disturbance destroyed his mother's Adachi clan and left Taira no Yoritsuna in control; in 1293 Sadatoki had Yoritsuna killed in the Heizenmon purge.

He strengthened tokusō rule, created the Chinzei tandai in 1296 and issued the Einin edict of 1297. He took vows in 1301 and passed the regency to Hōjō Morotoki but kept power until his death; his son was Hōjō Takatoki.

en:
Hōjō Shigetoki (1198–1261) was the third son of the shikken Yoshitoki. In 1230 he was appointed Rokuhara tandai in Kyoto, overseeing the court and western Japan for seventeen years.

Recalled after the Miura were destroyed in 1247, he became rensho, or co-shikken, to his son-in-law Tokiyori and helped stabilize Hōjō rule. He took the tonsure in 1256 and retired to Gokuraku-ji, and is also known for the warrior house-precepts Rokuhara-dono Gokun. He died in 1261.

en:
Hōjō Takatoki (1304–1333), son of Sadatoki, was the last Hōjō tokusō and became the fourteenth shikken in 1316, with the Nagasaki family long dominating the government. In 1326 he fell ill, resigned and took vows; the Karyaku succession feud left Akahashi Moritoki as shikken while Takatoki stayed supreme.

His regime foiled Emperor Go-Daigo's 1324 plot and exiled him to Oki in 1332. In 1333 Go-Daigo escaped, Ashikaga Takauji defected and Nitta Yoshisada stormed Kamakura, and Takatoki killed himself at Tōshō-ji with his clan, ending the Hōjō regime; his son Tokiyuki survived.

en:
Hōjō Tokimasa (1138–1215) was an Izu magnate who guarded the exiled Minamoto no Yoritomo and gave him his daughter Masako. He backed Yoritomo's 1180 uprising against the Taira and helped found the Kamakura shogunate.

After Yoritomo's death he rose to power, and in 1203 became the first Hōjō shikken, crushing the Hiki family. In 1205 his plot to replace Shōgun Sanetomo failed; Masako and Yoshitoki forced him to take the tonsure and retire to Izu, where he died in 1215.

en:
Hōjō Tokimune (1251–1284), eighth shikken of the Kamakura shogunate, held Japan against Kublai Khan's invasions. Second son of the shikken Hōjō Tokiyori, he was made heir ahead of an elder concubine-born half-brother. He became family head in 1263 and shikken in 1268, when a Korean envoy brought Kublai's demand for submission.

Tokimune never answered the Mongol letters, ordered western Japan's vassals to arm, and had Kublai's envoys executed in 1275 and 1279. At home he banished the monk Nichiren in 1271 and crushed the February Disturbance of 1272, in which his half-brother Tokisuke died. After the 1274 landing he walled Hakata Bay; the invasion of 1281 was wrecked by a typhoon and a Japanese assault.

A Zen patron, he founded Engaku-ji in 1282 for the Mongol war dead. He took the tonsure on 4 April 1284 and died the same day, aged thirty-two, leaving the war's veterans unrewarded.

zh:
北条时宗（1251—1284）是镰仓幕府第八代执权，顶住忽必烈入侵、守住日本。他是执权北条时赖的次男，因异母兄长为侧室所生而成为继承人；1263年他成为家主，1268年就任执权，同年高丽使节带来忽必烈要求臣服的国书。

时宗始终不回复蒙古国书，命西国御家人备战，于1275年和1279年两度处死忽必烈的使节。对内也强硬：1271年流放僧人日莲，1272年镇压二月骚动，异母兄时辅在其中被杀。1274年蒙古首次登陆后，他在博多湾修筑石垒；1281年的第二次入侵被台风和日军摧毁。

他崇信禅宗，1282年创建圆觉寺，纪念抗击蒙古而死的人。1284年4月4日他出家当天去世，年仅三十二岁，身后留下参战御家人的赏赐难题。

en:
Hōjō Tokiuji (1203–1230) was the eldest son of the shikken Yasutoki. At eighteen he fought in the Jōkyū War of 1221, distinguishing himself by fording the Uji River under court-army fire in the battle that opened Kyoto to the bakufu. In 1224 he was appointed Rokuhara tandai and became shugo of Wakasa in 1228.

A quarrel between his retainer and Enryaku-ji monks in 1229 led to his recall. He died in Kamakura in 1230, aged twenty-eight, before his father; his sons Tsunetoki and Tokiyori later became shikken.

A quarrel between his retainer and Enryaku-ji monks in 1229 led to his recall. He died in [ShowLocationName('kamakura')] in 1230, aged twenty-eight, before his father; his sons Tsunetoki and Tokiyori later became shikken.
zh:
北条时氏（1203—1230）是执权泰时的长子。1221年承久之乱时，年仅十八岁的他在宇治川之战中冒着朝廷军的箭雨强渡，为幕府军打开入京之路。1224年他就任六波罗探题北方，1228年兼任若狭守护。

1229年，其家臣与延历寺僧侣发生冲突，他因此被召还。1230年他在镰仓病逝，年仅二十八岁，先于父亲而亡；其子经时、时赖后来都成为执权。

en:
Hōjō Tokiyori (1227–1263), fifth Hōjō shikken, was the second son of Tokiuji, raised by his grandfather Yasutoki. He succeeded his brother Tsunetoki in 1246, crushed the Nagoe plot and sent Yoritsune back to Kyoto, and in 1247 destroyed the Miura clan in the Hōji Battle.

In 1249 he created the Hikitsuke courts, and in 1252 replaced Shōgun Yoritsugu with Prince Munetaka, the first imperial prince shōgun. Tonsured in 1256, he handed the shikken post to Nagatoki but kept real power until his death in 1263.

zh:
北条时赖（1227—1263）是镰仓幕府第五代执权，时氏的次男，由祖父泰时抚养长大。1246年他接替兄长经时就任执权，镇压名越光时拥兵之变（宫骚动），将前将军赖经遣送回京都；1247年在宝治合战中诛灭三浦泰村一族。

1249年他新设引付，审理御家人诉讼；1252年废黜将军赖嗣，改立宗尊亲王，首开亲王将军之例。1256年他因病出家，把执权之位让给长时，但仍掌握实权，直至1263年去世。

en:
Hōjō Tokiyuki (died 1353), second son of the last Kamakura tokusō Hōjō Takatoki, led the Hōjō attempt to restore the fallen shogunate. He escaped Kamakura's fall in 1333 with Suwa retainers, who in 1335 placed him at the head of the Nakasendai rising. His army defeated Ashikaga Tadayoshi and retook Kamakura, only to be driven out by Ashikaga Takauji.

Pardoned by Emperor Go-Daigo, he served the Southern Court and retook Kamakura twice, in 1337 and 1352. Captured in 1353, he was executed at Tatsunokuchi.

北条时行（？—1353）是镰仓幕府末代得宗北条高时的次子，力图复兴灭亡的幕府。1333年镰仓失陷时，他靠诹访氏家臣救出；1335年，诹访氏奉他为首举兵，即“中先代之乱”。他的军队击败足利直义，夺回镰仓，但又被足利尊氏逐走。

en:
Hōjō Yasutoki (1183–1242), third Hōjō shikken, was Yoshitoki's eldest son. In 1221 he commanded the bakufu army that won the Jōkyū War, forcing the Uji River and taking Kyoto.

He succeeded as shikken in 1224 and set up the Hyōjōshū council. In 1232 he enacted the Goseibai Shikimoku, Japan's first warrior law code. In 1242 he forced through Emperor Go-Saga's enthronement and died later that year.

en:
Hōjō Yoshimune (1253–1277), also called Akahashi Yoshimune, was a Hōjō clansman of the Kamakura period and the eldest son of Nagatoki, the sixth shikken. As second head of the Akahashi branch, he was appointed northern Rokuhara tandai, the shogunate's deputy in Kyoto, in 1271.

On Shikken Tokimune's orders, he led the troops that hunted down and killed Tokimune's half-brother Hōjō Tokisuke during the February Disturbance of 1272. Recalled to Kamakura in 1276, he joined the hyōjōshū council in 1277 but died the same year, aged 25. His son was Hōjō Hisatoki.

en:
Hōjō Yoshitoki (1163–1224), second Hōjō shikken, was a son of Tokimasa and younger brother of Masako. In 1203 he helped destroy the Hiki clan and enthrone Sanetomo; in 1205 he and Masako ousted their father, making him the shogunate's strongest man.

After Sanetomo's assassination in 1219 he ruled outright. When Retired Emperor Go-Toba ordered his overthrow in 1221, bakufu forces took Kyoto in the Jōkyū War and exiled three retired emperors. Yoshitoki died suddenly in 1224.

en:
Emperor Ichijō (980–1011), personal name Kanehito, was the only son of Emperor En'yū and the sixty-sixth sovereign of Japan. He ascended in 986 at age six after Emperor Kazan's abdication, with Fujiwara regents ruling until Michinaga held power from 995 through the office of nairan.

His reign marked the apex of Fujiwara power and Heian court culture: his empresses Teishi and Shōshi kept salons served by Sei Shōnagon and Murasaki Shikibu. A lover of letters and music, he abdicated in 1011 and died days later. His sons Atsunari and Atsunaga both became emperors.

一条天皇（980—1011）名怀仁，是圆融天皇的独子、日本第六十六代天皇。花山天皇退位后，他于986年六岁即位，初由藤原氏摄政，995年起道长以内览掌握朝政。

他的治世是藤原氏权势与平安朝宫廷文化的顶峰：皇后定子与道长之女彰子各开文化沙龙，清少纳言与紫式部分别侍奉左右。他雅好文学与音乐，1011年退位，数日后去世，其子敦成、敦良后来都登上皇位。

en:
Ii Tomoyasu (1010–1093) was the founder and first head of the Ii clan of Iinoya in Tōtōmi Province. Clan tradition relates that on New Year's Day 1010 the priest of the Iinoya Hachiman shrine found him as a newborn abandoned beside a sacred well; so precocious was he that at seven he was adopted by Fujiwara no Tomosuke, governor of Tōtōmi, whose daughter he married.

In 1032 he succeeded to the estate, built his residence at Iinoya, and took the name Ii. He died in 1093 and was buried at Jizō-ji.

zh:
井伊共保（1010—1093）是远江国井伊谷井伊氏的初代当主。相传1010年正月元旦，井伊谷八幡宫神主在御手洗井旁发现一名弃婴；孩子天资聪颖，七岁时被远江国司藤原共资收为养子，并娶其女为妻。

1032年，他继承家业，在井伊谷修筑居馆，号称井伊氏。1093年去世，葬于地藏寺。

en:
Ii Yukinao was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Southern and Northern Courts period, the ninth head of the Ii clan of Iinoya in Tōtōmi and a son of Ii Yasunao. He took the Southern Court side and welcomed Emperor Go-Daigo's son Prince Muneyoshi into his stronghold of Mitsutake Castle.

In 1337 he fought the Northern Court commander Imagawa Norikuni at Mikatagahara. From 1339 Northern Court forces captured his satellite castles; Mitsutake fell in 1340 and Ōhira later that year, when he surrendered.

zh:
井伊行直是镰仓末期至南北朝时代的武将，远江国井伊谷井伊氏第九代当主，井伊泰直之子。他站在南朝一边，将后醍醐天皇之子宗良亲王迎入本城三岳城。

1337年，他在三方原与北朝武将今川范国交战。1339年起北朝军队逐一攻陷其支城，1340年三岳城失守，大平城随后陷落，行直遂降。

en:
Ijūin Tadakuni (fl. 1337–1351), son of Tadachika, was a Satsuma warrior and fifth head of the Ijūin clan, a Shimazu branch. He at first served the Northern Court with Shimazu Sadahisa, but in 1337, after a Southern Court envoy reached Satsuma, he alone of the Shimazu kindred rose for the South at Ichiuji Castle.

For years he warred with the main Shimazu house across Satsuma and Ōsumi, taking Matsuo Castle in Kōriyama in 1350. Later reconciling with the clan, he married his daughter to Shimazu Ujihisa.

zh:
伊集院忠国（活跃于1337—1351年）是萨摩武将，岛津氏支流伊集院氏的第五代当主，忠亲之子。他起初随岛津贞久从属北朝，1337年南朝使臣抵达萨摩后，他在岛津一族中唯一据一宇治城举兵投奔南朝。

此后数年，他在萨摩、大隅与宗家交战，1350年攻下郡山松尾城。后来他与宗家和解，女儿嫁给岛津氏久。

en:
The Settsu Ikeda genealogy names Ikeda no Korezane as the second son of the Heian noble, Confucian scholar and poet Ki no Yoshimochi, who died in 919, and of a daughter of the local magnate Ikeda no Koremasa.

As steward of the Ikeda manor in Settsu Province, Koremasa granted the estate to Korezane, who thereupon took the Ikeda name. He is counted the ancestor of the Ki line of the Settsu Ikeda clan.

en:
Ikeda no Noriyori was a local magnate of the Teshima district of Settsu Province who, around 1334, built Ikeda Castle at the foot of Mount Satsuki. The clan genealogy calls him a ninth-generation descendant of the Minamoto warrior Yasumasa.

He married a daughter of Naito Mitsuyuki, widow of Kusunoki Masatsura; after Masatsura fell in battle in 1348 she wed Noriyori, later giving rise to a claim that her son Norimasa was Masatsura's child.

池田教依是摄津国丰岛郡的土著豪族，约于1334年在五月山南麓修筑池田城。池田氏系图称他是源氏武士源泰政的九世孙。

他娶内藤满之之女为妻，此女先前已嫁楠木正行；1348年正行战死后她改嫁教依，后来因此产生教依之子教正实为正行之子的说法。

en:
Ikeda no Yasutsugu was a warrior of the Settsu Ikeda clan and, in the clan genealogy, a son of Ikeda no Yasunaga and grandson of Ikeda no Yasumitsu. After the Genpei War, Yasumitsu placed him in charge of the Ikeda district of Mino Province, where he founded the Mino branch of the Ikeda.

By the Kenmu Restoration of 1334 the district had become the direct holding of the Toki shugo, whom they then served. One tradition traces the later daimyo Ikeda house to his line.

en:
Imagawa Kuniuji (1243–1282) was a Kamakura-period warrior and the founder of the Imagawa clan. The second son of Kira Osauji and grandson of Ashikaga Yoshiuji, he inherited Imagawa Manor in Hazu District, Mikawa Province, served as its land steward, and took the name Imagawa from the estate.

In his day the family ruled little more than three villages. He took Buddhist vows in 1281 and died in 1282, aged about forty, and his eldest son Motouji succeeded him.

en:
Imagawa Motouji (1259–1323) was the second head of the Imagawa clan and heir of its founder Kuniuji. He inherited Imagawa Manor in Mikawa and later settled at Hikuma Manor in Tōtōmi. Genealogies credit the Hikuma grant to service in the Shimotsuki Disturbance of 1285, but as Kuniuji had died before it, the recipient is identified as Motouji.

The move to Tōtōmi opened the way for the clan's later rise as shugo lords of Suruga and Tōtōmi. He died in 1323 aged sixty-three, and his youngest son Norikuni succeeded him.

en:
Imagawa Nakaaki (fl. 1368–1412) was a son of Imagawa Norikuni adopted by his elder brother Imagawa Sadayo. In 1368 he became head of the Board of Retainers and constable of Yamashiro.

From 1371 he fought under Sadayo in Kyūshū against the Southern Court, defeating Kikuchi Takemasa in 1372 and killing Shōni Fuyusuke at the Mizushima incident of 1375. Appointed constable of Tōtōmi in 1388, he took Buddhist vows in 1395, and in 1412 Sadayo gave him the house code Imagawa-jō.

en:
Imagawa Norikuni (1295–1384) was a Nanboku-chō shugo daimyō and the first head of the Suruga Imagawa clan, the fifth son of Imagawa Motouji. After the Kamakura shogunate fell he joined Ashikaga Takauji, and in 1336 received the shugo posts of Tōtōmi and Suruga.

In 1353 he retired, passing the headship to his son Noriuji. A master of waka and court precedent, he guided Ashikaga ceremonial and died in 1384.

zh:
今川范国（1295—1384）是南北朝时代的守护大名，骏河今川氏初代当主，今川基氏第五子。镰仓幕府灭亡后，他追随足利尊氏，1336年先后获得远江、骏河守护之职。

1353年，他把家督让给嫡子范氏后隐居。他精通和歌与有职故实，曾指导足利将军家的典礼，1384年去世。

en:
Imagawa Noriuji (c. 1316–1365) was the second head of the Suruga Imagawa clan and a Nanboku-chō shugo daimyō. In 1353 he inherited the headship and the shugo posts of Suruga and Tōtōmi from his father Norikuni, but remained overshadowed by his father and his gifted younger brother Sadayo.

He died in 1365. His eldest son Ujiie was named shugo by Ashikaga Yoshiakira but soon died, whereupon his second son Yasunori left holy orders to succeed him.

今川范氏（约1316—1365）是骏河今川氏第二代当主、南北朝时代的守护大名。1353年，他从父亲范国手中接管家督以及骏河、远江的守护之职，但因父亲健在、弟弟贞世更具将才，存在感一直淡薄。

1365年他去世。长男氏家被足利义诠任命为守护，不久后死去，曾为僧人的次男泰范于是还俗继任。

en:
Imagawa Sadayo (1326–1420), known in religion as Ryōshun, was a poet and a son of Imagawa Norikuni, constable of Suruga and Tōtōmi. He had taken Buddhist vows when the Ashikaga bakufu named him tandai of Kyūshū in 1371 to crush Prince Kaneyoshi's Southern Court revolt.

He secured northern Kyūshū by 1375. Recalled in 1395 on suspicion of disloyalty and stripped of his posts in 1400, he spent his last years on religion and poetry.

zh:
今川贞世（1326—1420），法号了俊，是骏河、远江两国守护今川范国之子，也是歌人。他已出家受戒，1371年室町幕府任命他为九州探题，前往镇压怀良亲王的南朝势力。

至1375年他平定北九州。1395年他因涉嫌不忠被召回，1400年遭夺官职，晚年潜心佛法与和歌。

en:
Imagawa Ujiie (born before 1334, died c. 1369) was a mid-fourteenth-century constable of Suruga, the eldest son of Imagawa Noriuji and elder brother of Imagawa Yasunori. When his father died in 1365, his grandfather Norikuni sought to pass the constableship to Sadayo, but Sadayo declined, and the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiakira confirmed Ujiie in the post.

In 1366 he received full judicial powers over Suruga. He died without issue before 1369, by which time Yasunori already held the post.

zh:
今川氏家（生于1334年以前，约1369年去世）是14世纪中期的骏河守护，今川范氏长子、今川泰范之兄。1365年父亲范氏去世后，祖父范国本想让贞世继任守护，因贞世推辞，由足利义诠任命氏家出任该职。

1366年他获准执掌骏河检断权。氏家没有子嗣，于1369年以前去世，届时泰范已经继任守护之职。

en:
Imagawa Ujikane (c. 1329–c. 1398), later called Naoyo, was the third son of Imagawa Norikuni and a younger brother of Imagawa Sadayo. In 1370 he served under the kanrei Hosokawa Yoriyuki in Kawachi and was appointed deputy constable of Echigo.

He then joined Sadayo's Kyūshū campaign against the Southern Court's Kikuchi forces, returning to Kyoto in 1374. He took the name Naoyo in 1396 and died around 1398 at Kambara, ancestor of the Kambara clan.

zh:
今川氏兼（约1329—约1398），后改名直世，是今川范国第三子、今川贞世之弟。1370年，他随管领细川赖之出征河内，被任命为越后守护代。

此后他随贞世前往九州，与南朝方的菊池势力作战，1374年返回京都。1396年他改名直世，约1398年在蒲原去世，为蒲原氏之祖。

en:
Imagawa Yasunori (1334–1409), third head of the Suruga Imagawa, was the second son of Imagawa Noriuji and brother of Imagawa Ujiie. A novice monk at Kamakura's Kenchō-ji, he left holy orders at his uncle Sadayo's bidding and inherited the family after his father died in 1365 and his brother soon after.

In 1378 Ashikaga Yoshimitsu made him head of the Board of Retainers, and he fought for the bakufu in the Meitoku War of 1391 and the Ōei War of 1399. He died in 1409, succeeded by his son Norimasa.

今川泰范（1334—1409）是骏河今川氏第三代当主，今川范氏次子、今川氏家之弟。他本在镰仓建长寺出家为僧，1365年父亲去世、兄长随后亦故，他遂奉叔父贞世之命还俗，继承家督。

1378年，足利义满任命他为侍所头人，他在1391年明德之乱和1399年应永之乱中均加入幕府军。1409年他去世，由嫡子今川范政继任。

en:
Tsunetsura Inawashiro was an early Kamakura-period warrior who founded the Inawashiro house of Aizu. The eldest son of Moritsura Sahara, of a warrior line claiming Kanmu Heike and Miura descent, he is said to have held Inawashiro in the Yama district after his grandfather Yoshitsura Sahara was enfeoffed with the four Aizu districts for his part in the Ōshū campaign of 1189.

Local records place his fort at Yadeyama, later called Kamega-jō, in 1191; the Date family genealogy instead says that in 1248, while serving Shogun Fujiwara no Yoritsugu, he received the Asaya estate and took the name Inawashiro.

猪苗代经连是镰仓时代前期武将，会津猪苗代氏的始祖，佐原盛连的长子，家族出自桓武平氏三浦氏一脉。相传其祖父佐原义连因1189年奥州合战的军功获赐会津四郡，经连遂领有耶麻郡猪苗代之地。

《会津温故拾要抄》等地方志称他于1191年在当地修筑八手山馆，即后来的龟城；《伊达世臣家谱》则记载，他在1248年出仕征夷大将军藤原赖嗣，获赐麻谷庄，这才改称猪苗代氏。

en:
Isa Tamemune was an early Kamakura-period warrior of Hitachi Province and the eldest son of Date Tomomune. In 1189 he joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's Ōshū campaign; at the battle of Ishinazaka he stormed the enemy stronghold and took the head of Satō Motoharu with seventeen others.

The feat won his family the district of Date, where his kinsmen founded the Date clan while Tamemune kept the ancestral Isa estate. In 1221 he was killed fighting for the shogunate at the Uji River in the Jōkyū War.

zh:
伊佐为宗是镰仓时代初期常陆国的御家人，伊达朝宗的长子。1189年，他随源赖朝参加奥州合战，在石那坂之战中攻破敌军城寨，斩下佐藤基治等18人的首级。

凭此战功，其家族获封伊达郡，族人在彼地开创伊达氏，为宗则留在本领伊佐郡。1221年承久之乱中，他追随北条泰时，在宇治川战死。

en:
Ise Sadatsugu was a warrior of the Kamakura and Muromachi periods who served the Ashikaga shoguns Takauji, Yoshiakira and Yoshimitsu. By 1361 he had taken Buddhist vows as Shōzen while remaining Yoshiakira's mōshitsugi usher.

After the Kōryaku coup of 1379 he became shitsuji of the shogunate's Mandokoro, holding the office until his death in 1391 and beginning the Ise family's hereditary hold on it. Yoshimitsu was born at his residence.

伊势贞继是镰仓末期至室町时代的武将，先后侍奉足利尊氏、足利义诠、足利义满三代将军。1361年之前他已出家，法号照禅，仍担任义诠的申次。

1379年康历政变后，他出任室町幕府政所执事，一直任职到1391年去世，开启了伊势氏世袭该职的先例。足利义满就出生在贞继的宅邸。

en:
Ishidō Yorifusa (1321–1413), second son of Ishidō Yoshifusa, was the third head of that Ashikaga branch house. In 1349 he was appointed shugo of Ise and Shima. In the Kannō Disturbance he sided with Ashikaga Tadayoshi against Takauji, raising troops in 1350 and routing Takauji's army in Harima.

He later repeatedly raided Kamakura and Kyoto and in 1361 helped drive Ashikaga Yoshiakira from the capital. He surrendered around 1364, took Buddhist vows, and died in 1413 aged ninety-three.

zh:
石塔赖房（1321—1413）是足利氏支族石塔氏第三代当主、石塔义房的次子。1349年他被任命为伊势、志摩两国守护。观应之乱中他追随足利直义与尊氏为敌，1350年举兵，在播磨击败尊氏军。

此后他屡次进攻镰仓与京都，1361年曾协助把足利义诠逐出京都。约1364年他投降后出家，1413年去世，享年93岁。

en:
Ishidō Yorishige was a mid-Kamakura-period warrior, known as Ishidō Shirō. Genealogies variously make him a son of the fourth Ashikaga family head, Ashikaga Yasuuji, or a grandson whom Yasuuji adopted.

He took the name Ishidō from an estate granted to him and became the founder of the Ishidō, a cadet branch of the Ashikaga clan. He was the father of Yoshifusa; another son, Kuniaki, is said to have become the Ji-sect preacher Kokua Shōnin.

en:
Ishidō Yoshifusa was a warrior of an Ashikaga branch house in the Nanboku-chō wars. In 1334 he became shugodai of Suruga and Izu under Ashikaga Takauji, and in 1336 was appointed shugo of both provinces. The following year he went to Mutsu as Ōshū commander, campaigning there against Southern Court forces until 1345.

In the Kannō Disturbance he sided with Ashikaga Tadayoshi and fought at Satta Pass in 1351, later joining Ashikaga Tadafuyu. He vanishes from the records after Takauji took Kyoto in 1355.

石塔义房是南北朝时代足利氏支族石塔氏的武将。1334年，他担任足利尊氏治下骏河、伊豆两国的守护代，1336年就任两国守护。次年他被派往陆奥，任奥州总大将，至1345年一直在奥羽与南朝势力作战。

en:
Ishidō Yoshimoto, third son of Ishidō Yoshifusa, was a Nanboku-chō warrior. In 1335 he took arms for the Ashikaga with his father, whom he accompanied to Mutsu in 1337 as Ōshū commander, remaining in Ōu until 1346. He joined Ashikaga Tadayoshi in the Kannō Disturbance and later renamed himself Ishidō Yoshinori.

In 1354 he took Taga Castle in Mutsu and was named Ōshū governor by Ashikaga Tadafuyu, only to be reportedly defeated and killed by Shiba Iekane at Mount Shiei late that year.

石塔义基是石塔义房的三子，南北朝时代武将。1335年他随父亲为足利氏举兵，1337年父亲出任奥州总大将时随行前往陆奥，至1346年一直滞留奥羽。观应之乱中他追随足利直义，后来改名石塔义宪。

1354年他夺取陆奥多贺城，被足利直冬任命为奥州管领，但相传同年末即在志荣山被斯波家兼击败战死。

en:
Ishikawa Akimochi (died 1351), fifteenth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa clan, was the eldest son of Ishikawa Yoshimitsu. Adopted by his childless predecessor Sadamitsu, he succeeded as clan head in 1339.

In the tenth month of 1351 he went up to Kyoto, where Shogun Ashikaga Yoshiakira granted him the character that formed his new name, Akimochi. He died of illness at Kamakura on the fourth day of the twelfth month that same year, leaving a son, Mitsumochi.

en:
Minamoto no Arimitsu (1037–1086), second son of Minamoto no Yoritoo and second head of the Mutsu Ishikawa, was born at Monotsu manor in Settsu. He campaigned in Mutsu with his father under Minamoto no Yoriyoshi from 1051, and when Yoritoo fell at the Kuriyagawa stockade in 1062 took command. His merit won him Junior Fifth Rank Lower as Aki no kami and Ishikawa lands.

He built several castles before moving, by tradition, to Mitsuashi Castle; he then took the name Ishikawa and installed Iwashimizu Hachiman as the clan's tutelary deity.

zh:
源有光（1037—1086）是源赖远次子、陆奥石川氏第二代当主，出生于摄津国物津庄。1051年起，他随父亲跟从源赖义出征陆奥；1062年赖远战死厨川栅后，有光接掌军队，以军功任从五位下安艺守，受赐石川之地。

他修筑数座城馆后，相传移居三芦城，此后改称石川氏，又迎来石清水八幡宫的分灵作为一族氏神。

en:
Ishikawa Hirosue (died 1248), second son of Ishikawa Motomitsu, was the seventh head of the Mutsu Ishikawa, chosen over a sickly elder brother. In 1183 he sent troops to join Minamoto no Yoritomo after he rose against the Taira in Izu.

Bedridden when Yoritomo marched against the Ōshū Fujiwara in 1189, he sent a kinsman as deputy to join the campaign, and Yoritomo later granted the clan shrine lands in Shida district. After visiting Kamakura in 1197 he became Daizen no daibu; his son Mitsusada succeeded him in 1248.

石川广季（？—1248）是石川基光次子、陆奥石川氏第七代当主，因兄长体弱多病而被选中继承。1183年，他派兵投奔在伊豆举兵讨伐平家的源赖朝。

1189年赖朝讨伐奥州藤原氏时，广季卧病在床，派同族代他领兵从征；赖朝后来向氏神神社寄进志田郡的领地。1197年广季赴镰仓谒见赖朝，随后被任为大膳大夫。1248年他去世，子光贞继任。

en:
Iemitsu Ishikawa (died 1330) was a Kamakura-period warrior and the twelfth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa clan in southern Ōshū, the eldest son of Moriyoshi Ishikawa. In 1318 he visited Kamakura, met the regent Hōjō Takatoki and was presented to Shogun Prince Morikuni, after which the Kyoto court appointed him Governor of Suruga at junior fifth rank.

Returning to Kyoto in 1325, he rose to junior fourth rank as Governor of Settsu. He married a daughter of Yoshinari Tatara and died in 1330.

en:
Mitsunaga Ishikawa (died 1291) was a Kamakura-period warrior and the ninth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa, the eldest son of Mitsusada Ishikawa. After coming of age he was appointed Governor of Yamato at junior fifth rank.

When the Mongol invasion was reported in 1281, he led his men into the Rokuhara army guarding Kyoto, then went west to join the defense of Dazaifu. Rewarded for his service, he became Left Head of the Stables at junior fourth rank, and died in early 1291.

en:
Mitsusada Ishikawa (died 1269) was a Kamakura-period warrior and the eighth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa, a warrior house claiming descent from the Yamato Genji. The eldest son of Hirosue Ishikawa, he married a daughter of the regent Hōjō Yasutoki and served as Governor of Suruga at junior fifth rank.

In 1263 he paid homage to Shogun Prince Munetaka at Kamakura and then traveled up to Kyoto, where he was appointed Left Head of the Stables at junior fourth rank. He died in 1269.

en:
Ishikawa Motomitsu (1058–1099), third son of Minamoto no Arimitsu, was the third head of the Mutsu Ishikawa, rising to Junior Fourth Rank Upper as Daizen no daibu. He briefly changed the characters of his given name before resuming Motomitsu when he succeeded his retired father.

In 1087 he joined Minamoto no Yoshiie's campaign in the Later Three Years' War, fought at the Kanazawa stockade, and received Tagawa district for his merit. In 1095 he went up to Kyoto with his kinsmen to receive court rank and office.

Ishikawa Motomitsu (died 1199), whose name was written 基光, was the sixth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa, second son of Yoshisue, distinct from the third head Motomitsu.

In 1179 he went to Kyoto and was appointed Junior Fifth Rank Lower, Yamato no kami. In 1181 he reburied Arimitsu's remains at Ganpō-ji and raised a three-story pagoda, and in the same year took Buddhist vows as Ryōzen. He died in the fourth month of 1199 and was succeeded by his son Hirosue.

en:
Motomori Ishikawa (died 1307) was a Kamakura-period warrior and the tenth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa clan in southern Ōshū, second son of Mitsunaga Ishikawa.

In 1291 the regent Hōjō Sadatoki presented him to Shogun Prince Hisaaki at Kamakura. He then went to Kyoto, entered court service, and was appointed Governor of Yamato at junior fifth rank. His son Moriyoshi carried on the house, and Motomori died in 1307.

石川元盛（？—1307）是镰仓时代武将，陆奥石川氏第十代当主，石川光长的次子。

1291年，执权北条贞时引他在镰仓拜谒征夷大将军久明亲王。其后他上洛入朝，出任从五位下大和守。其子盛义继承家名，元盛于1307年去世。

en:
Ishikawa Sadamitsu (died 1341) was the fourteenth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa clan, based at Shirakawa. During his minority his uncle Tokimitsu held the headship; at his coming-of-age he took a character from the regent Hōjō Sadatoki's name.

In 1335 he defeated Kitabatake Akiie's officer Hirohashi Tsuneyasu at Bababara, and again in 1336 before Yumoto Castle. Having no son of his own, he adopted Yoshimitsu's sons and named the eldest, Akimochi, his heir. He died in 1341.

石川贞光（？—1341）是陆奥石川氏第十四代当主，据点在白河。他幼年由伯父石川时光暂掌家督，元服时取执权北条贞时名字中的一字。

1335年，他在马场原击败北畠显家的部将广桥经泰，1336年又在汤本城下再破经泰。贞光没有亲生子嗣，便收义光诸子为养子，立长子诠持为继承人，1341年去世。

en:
Tokimitsu Ishikawa (died 1335) was a late Kamakura-period warrior and the thirteenth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa clan, fourth son of Moriyoshi Ishikawa. First named Mitsunori, he took the name Tokimitsu from a character granted by Hōjō Tokimune. When his brother Iemitsu died in 1330 leaving a young heir, Mitsuhide, Tokimitsu took over and raised him.

In 1333 his son Yoshimitsu joined Nitta Yoshisada's campaign against the Kamakura shogunate; Tokimitsu then led troops to Kyoto and was appointed Kunai no Taifu at junior fifth rank, rising to junior fourth rank in 1334. He died the next year.

en:
Minamoto no Yoritoo (1007–1062) was a mid-Heian Yamato Genji warrior, third son of Minamoto no Yorichika, and held Junior Fifth Rank Lower as Ise no kami. He sat out his father's fatal clash with Kōfuku-ji monks and so escaped Yorichika's exile.

In 1051 he followed Minamoto no Yoriyoshi against the Abe in the Earlier Nine Years' War, and fell in 1062 storming their Kuriyagawa stockade in Mutsu. His son Arimitsu took over the army; Yoritoo is revered as ancestor of the Mutsu Ishikawa.

源赖远（1007—1062）是平安时代中期的大和源氏武将、源赖亲第三子，官至从五位下伊势守。父亲与兴福寺僧人交战败死，他因没有参战而免于流放。

en:
Ishikawa Yoshimitsu was a Mutsu warrior of the Ishikawa clan's Ōshima branch. In 1333 he joined Nitta Yoshisada's army and fought at Inamuragasaki, helping overthrow the Kamakura shogunate, after which the Kenmu government gave him court rank and office.

In 1335 he went over to Ashikaga Takauji, followed him to Kyushu and fought at the Minatogawa River. He was killed in battle before the Jizō hall on Mount Hiei in the sixth month of 1336. His son Akimochi was adopted by Ishikawa Sadamitsu.

石川义光是陆奥国武士，出身石川氏庶流大岛氏。1333年他加入新田义贞的军队，参加攻灭镰仓幕府的稻村崎之战，建武新政成立后获任官职。

en:
Ishikawa Yoshisue (died 1177), eldest son of Ishikawa Mitsuyoshi, was the fifth head of the Mutsu Ishikawa. In 1157 he went to Kyoto and was appointed Junior Fourth Rank Lower, Yamato no kami, the office his father had held.

In the generations from Arimitsu to Yoshisue the clan's cadet branches were established across the Ishikawa manor. He died on August 1, 1177, and his second son Motomitsu succeeded him.

en:
Prince Isobe was a Nara-period imperial prince, grandson of Prince Nagaya and son of Prince Kuwata. Probably still an infant when his grandfather and father perished in the Nagaya Incident of 729, he survived the ruin of his house.

In 767 he received junior fifth rank, and later served as governor of Mikawa Province and head of the Takumi artisans' bureau. Through his son Prince Iwami he was an ancestor of the Takashina clan.

矶部王是奈良时代的皇族，长屋王之孙、桑田王之子。729年长屋王之变中祖父与父亲遇害，他推测尚在襁褓，得以幸免于难。

en:
Isshiki Kimifuka (1263–1330) was a Kamakura-period warrior and founder of the Isshiki clan. The seventh son of Ashikaga Yasuuji, he first lived at Isshiki in the Kira manor of Mikawa Province, from which he took the family name.

In 1319 he moved to the Tamiya manor in Shimōsa, where he is said to have built Satte Castle. He held the title Sakyo no daibu, later took Buddhist vows as the Isshiki Ajari, and left sons Yoriyuki and Noriuji. He died in 1330.

en:
Isshiki Naouji, fourth head of the Isshiki clan, went to Kyushu in 1346 and later succeeded his father Noriuji as the Muromachi bakufu's second Kyushu tandai. In the Kannō Disturbance he backed Takauji.

In 1353 Kikuchi Takemitsu's Southern army crushed him at Harizurihara, and in 1355 he fled to Nagato. Sent back to Kyushu, another defeat at Mount Asō drove him to Kyoto in 1358. His later life is unknown; his brother Norimitsu succeeded him.

en:
Isshiki Norimitsu (1325–1388), fifth head of the Isshiki clan and a shugo daimyo, fought alongside his father Noriuji and brother Naouji against the Southern Court in Kyushu, becoming Hizen shugo in 1353, until defeat by the Kikuchi drove him back to Kyoto in 1359.

He kept the trust of Shoguns Yoshiakira and Yoshimitsu, receiving Wakasa in 1366. From 1369 to 1371 he crushed the Wakasa kokujin ikki, securing the clan's place among the Four Offices. Later ordained, he died in 1388 aged 64.

en:
Isshiki Noriuji (1300–1369) was the third head of the Isshiki clan and a retainer of Ashikaga Takauji. After victory over Kikuchi Taketoshi at Tatarahama in 1336, he became the bakufu's first Kyushu tandai, charged with subduing the great shugo houses. In 1346 his eldest son Naouji joined him there.

During the Kannō Disturbance he backed Takauji, but repeated defeats by Kikuchi Takemitsu, climaxing at Harizurihara in 1353, forced him to abandon Hakata in 1355 and retire to Kyoto, where he died in 1369.

en:
Isshiki Yoriyuki (died 1337) was the second head of the Isshiki clan and a retainer of Ashikaga Takauji. He followed Takauji's break with the Kenmu government and retreat to Kyushu. In 1336 he held Nangō Castle, where Southern Court forces killed his steward.

In the fourth month of 1337 he advanced into Higo with his half-brother Noriuji, the new Kyushu tandai, and fell at the Battle of Inuzukabaru. He left a son, Yukiyoshi, but Noriuji succeeded him.

en:
Itō Sukemune (1266–1349) was a warrior of the late Kamakura period and the fourth head of the Hyūga Itō clan in Kyushu. When his father died, his kinsman Kiwaki Sukeyori took the headship as his self-styled guardian, but with his mother's backing Sukemune eventually succeeded as clan head.

He and his retainers fought in the opening battles of the Genkō War, including the Battle of Akasaka Castle in 1331. He died in 1349.

en:
Suketoki Itō (1185–1252) was an early Kamakura-period warrior and gokenin, remembered as the founder of the Hyūga Itō clan. As a small child called Inufusamaru, he lost his father Suketsune Kudō when the Soga brothers killed him in their famous revenge of 1193; although some sought to spare the captured Soga Tokimune, his tearful pleas led to Tokimune being handed over to the family and executed.

He served the shogunate thereafter, joined its Tōkaidō army during the Jōkyū War of 1221, and in 1235 became Governor of Yamato. He died in 1252, aged 68.
