en:
Empress Jitō (645–703), born Princess Uno-no-sarara, was Emperor Tenji's daughter and empress to her uncle Emperor Tenmu. After Tenmu's death in 686 she ran the court, and when her son Crown Prince Kusakabe died in 689 she upheld the claim of her young grandson Karu.

Enthroned in 690 as Japan's third empress regnant, she carried on Tenmu's centralising reforms. In 697 she abdicated for her grandson Emperor Monmu, becoming the first daijō-tennō, and ruled on in retirement until her death in 703.

en:
Emperor Jomei (593–641), formerly Prince Tamura, became Japan's 34th sovereign in 629 after the death of his great-aunt Empress Suiko. The Soga leader Soga no Emishi backed him against the rival Prince Yamashiro, and the Soga family dominated politics throughout his reign.

His empress was Princess Takara, later Empress Kōgyoku, and their sons became Emperors Tenji and Tenmu. He died in 641 without naming an heir. A poem in which he climbs Mount Kagu and surveys the land is preserved in the Man'yōshū.

en:
Emperor Junna (786–840), a son of Emperor Kanmu, was Japan's 53rd emperor, reigning from 823 to 833. Made crown prince in 810 after the Kusuko Incident, he succeeded Emperor Saga in 823.

He promoted able officials and oversaw the legal commentary Ryō no Gige and the court chronicle Nihon Kōki. In 833 he abdicated in favor of his nephew Emperor Ninmyō and retired to the Junna-in villa. He died in 840, leaving orders for a simple burial; the disputed succession after his death sparked the Jōwa Incident.

en:
Emperor Junnin (733–765) was the 47th emperor of Japan, reigning from 758 to 764. A son of Prince Toneri and grandson of Emperor Tenmu, he was named crown prince by Empress Kōken in 757 and enthroned on her abdication, though only as a figurehead.

In 764, during Fujiwara no Nakamaro's Rebellion, the former empress reclaimed the throne as Empress Shōtoku and forced him to abdicate. He died in exile on Awaji in 765, possibly by assassination, and was not included on the official imperial list until 1870.

en:
Juntoku (1197–1242), a son of Emperor Go-Toba, became crown prince in 1200 and succeeded his brother Tsuchimikado in 1210 when Go-Toba forced the abdication. Real power stayed with Go-Toba as cloistered emperor. In 1221 he abdicated for his infant son Chūkyō and backed Go-Toba's rising against the Kamakura shogunate, the Jōkyū War.

The court's forces were crushed within weeks; Juntoku was exiled to Sado Island and lived there twenty-one years, dying in 1242. A pupil of Fujiwara no Teika, he left a poem in the Ogura Hyakunin Isshu.

顺德天皇（1197—1242）是后鸟羽天皇之子，1200年立为太子，1210年后鸟羽逼迫土御门天皇退位，他接替兄长即位，实权仍由后鸟羽上皇以院政掌握。1221年，他让位给幼子仲恭天皇，支持父亲起兵讨伐镰仓幕府，即承久之乱。

朝廷军队数周内即被击溃，顺德被流放佐渡岛，在岛上度过二十一年，1242年去世。他师从藤原定家，有一首和歌收入《小仓百人一首》。

en:
Kagami Tomitsu (1143–1230) was a Kai Genji warrior and founder of the Kagami clan, holding the Kagami estate in Kai Province. Tradition records that in 1171, as a takiguchi guardsman, he performed the bow-sounding rite to quiet a haunting at Emperor Takakura's palace and was rewarded with an image of Fudo Myoo.

He and his son Ogasawara Nagakiyo fought in the Genpei War, and in 1185 Minamoto no Yoritomo named him governor of Shinano. His sons founded the Ogasawara and Nanbu clans, and he died in 1230.

en:
Fujiwara no Tsunehira was, by Kajiki family tradition, the third son of the Fujiwara kampaku Fujiwara no Yoritada (924–989). In the mid-Heian period Ōkura no Yoshinaga, head of the local Ōkura clan of Kajiki in Ōsumi Province, had no male heir and adopted Tsunehira as a son-in-law.

Tsunehira settled on the estate and took the place name as his family name, becoming ancestor of the Kajiki warrior house, whose descendants served the Kamakura shogunate as gokenin and helped repel the Mongol invasions.

en:
Emperor Kameyama (1249–1305), the 90th emperor of Japan and younger brother of Emperor Go-Fukakusa, reigned from 1260 to 1274. In 1265 a mission from Kublai Khan reached Japan demanding submission; the court favoured compromise, but the Kamakura shogunate sent the envoys away.

He abdicated in 1274 to his son Emperor Go-Uda and ruled as cloistered emperor, praying at Ise Shrine during the second Mongol invasion of 1281. Distrusted by the shogunate, he lost power in 1287, took Zen vows in 1289, and helped found Kyoto's Nanzen-ji in 1291. His descendants made up the Daikakuji-tō line.

龟山天皇（1249—1305）是日本第90代天皇，后深草天皇之弟，1260至1274年在位。1265年，忽必烈派遣的使节抵达日本要求称臣，朝廷主张妥协，镰仓幕府却将使节遣返。

en:
Kaneko Iehiro (d. 1385) was a local lord of the Kaneko clan based at Kaneko in Iruma District of Musashi Province, an offshoot of the Murayama warrior party. In 1368 he joined the Musashi Heiikki rising, but the Kanto kubo Ashikaga Ujimitsu and Uesugi Noriaki crushed it.

Iehiro then submitted and served the Uesugi, deputies of the Kanto region. In 1382 he campaigned in Shimotsuke Province against Oyama Yoshimasa's rebellion. He died in 1385, leaving a son, Ieshige.

en:
Kaneko no Ietada (1138–1216) was a Musashi Province samurai of the Murayama band, son of Kaneko no Ienori. At nineteen he won his first fame in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156, serving Minamoto no Yoshitomo and killing the famed Takama brothers in single combat, a feat celebrated in the Hōgen Monogatari.

In 1180 he fought for the Taira at Kinugasa Castle, holding his ground after taking twenty-one arrows before another under the jaw forced his retreat. He then submitted to Minamoto no Yoritomo and joined the chase of the Taira, and was made steward of estates in three provinces.

In 1180 he fought for the Taira at Kinugasa Castle, holding his ground after taking twenty-one arrows before another under the jaw forced his retreat. He then submitted to Minamoto no Yoritomo and joined the chase of the Taira, and was made steward of estates in three provinces.
zh:
金子家忠（1138—1216）是武藏国村山党的武士，金子家范之子。1156年保元之乱时，十九岁的他初次上阵，追随源义朝，在单挑中斩杀以勇武闻名的高间兄弟，其事为《保元物语》所传颂。

1180年衣笠城之战中，他站在平家一方，身中二十一箭仍坚守阵地，直到下颚再中一箭才退却。他后来归降源赖朝，加入追讨平氏的大军，因功成为三地庄园的地头。

en:
Prince Kaneyoshi (c. 1329–c. 1381) was a son of Emperor Go-Daigo and the Southern Court's chief commander in Kyushu. In 1336 Go-Daigo named him Seisei Shogun and sent him west; in 1348 he entered the Kikuchi stronghold of Waifu Castle in Higo and built his Chinzei government there.

By 1365 he controlled all of Kyushu, and Ming envoys addressed him as King of Japan. Ashikaga forces landed in Ōita in 1371 and broke his northern Kyushu base, after which he withdrew to the Chikugo plain and died around 1381.

怀良亲王（约1329—约1381）是后醍醐天皇之子、南朝在九州的最高统帅，人称征西将军宫。1336年后醍醐天皇封他为征西大将军，派往西方；1348年他进入肥后菊池氏的隈府城，建立征西府。

到1365年，他已控制整个九州，明朝使臣更以“日本国王”相称。1371年足利一方的军队在大分登陆，摧毁他在北九州的基业，他退往筑后川一带，约1381年去世。

en:
Emperor Kanmu (737–806), eldest son of Emperor Kōnin, was Japan's 50th emperor, reigning from 781 to 806. In 784 he moved the capital from Nara to Nagaoka-kyō, and again in 794 to Heian-kyō, opening the Heian period.

His armies, led by Ōtomo no Otomaro and Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, campaigned against the Emishi of northern Honshū, and in 794 Ōtomo became the first commander bearing the title sei-i taishōgun. Kanmu also sponsored the monks Saichō and Kūkai on their journeys to Tang China, after which they founded the Tendai and Shingon schools in Japan.

桓武天皇（737—806）是光仁天皇长子、日本第50代天皇，781年至806年在位。784年他将都城从奈良迁至长冈京，794年再迁平安京，开启了平安时代。

他以大伴弟麻吕和坂上田村麻吕为将征讨本州北部的虾夷，794年大伴弟麻吕成为首任征夷大将军。桓武还资助最澄与空海入唐求法，二人归国后分别创立天台宗与真言宗。

en:
Kasai Kiyoshige (1161–1238) was a late Heian and early Kamakura warrior and founder of the Kasai clan, a Toshima cadet line. Third son of Toshima Kiyomoto, he inherited the Kasai manor in Shimōsa and joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's uprising in 1180, fighting in the Genpei War and the 1189 Ōshū campaign.

Yoritomo made him first Ōshū sōbugyō, entrusting him with Mutsu's government. A trusted Hōjō elder, he later took vows and died a monk under Shinran.

Kasai Munekiyo, also called Kiyomune, was a busho of the late Kamakura and early Nanboku-chō periods and the fifth, or by another count sixth, head of the Kasai clan in Mutsu Province. The mune in his name is said to derive from the regent Hōjō Tokimune.

The genealogy accounts differ over his parentage, making him either a son or grandson of Kasai Tokikiyo. In 1335 he and his son Sadakiyo joined Kitabatake Akiie's army marching west from Oshu against Ashikaga Takauji.

Kasai Sadakiyo was a late Kamakura and early Nanboku-chō busho of the Kasai clan in Mutsu, son of Kasai Munekiyo. The sada of his name was granted by the Hōjō regent Sadatoki.

In 1335 he and his father joined Kitabatake Akiie's western campaign against Ashikaga Takauji; in 1337 he followed Akiie to Ryozen Castle for the renewed campaign. After Akiie fell in 1338 he returned to Oshu and fought the Northern Court alongside Kitabatake Chikafusa, dying in 1350.

In the Genkō War of 1331 the Kamakura shogunate sent him with a punitive army to the capital; he is thought to be the Kasai Saburō Hyōe-no-jō on its rolls. He died on 17 April 1365, aged 54.

en:
Kasai Tokikiyo, also called Kiyotoki, was a mid-Kamakura-period warrior and gokenin, counted as the third or fourth head of the Kasai clan. Born at Hiraizumi in Ōshū, he is variously named the son of Kasai Kiyochika or of the founder Kiyoshige; the ‘toki’ in his name was probably granted by the regent Hōjō Yasutoki.

Few of his deeds are recorded, but documents of 1234–1247 show him attending the shogun Fujiwara no Yoritsune as the head of a leading gokenin house.

Katō Kagekado (1156–1221) was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods and a leading Kamakura gokenin. A second son of Katō Kagekazu of Ise, he settled in Izu and in 1180 joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's uprising against the Taira.

He fought at Ishibashiyama and in the 1189 Ōshū campaign, and in 1203 killed Nitta Tadatsune on Hōjō orders during the Hiki incident. He took the tonsure after Shōgun Sanetomo's murder in 1219 and died in 1221.

He fought at Ishibashiyama and in the 1189 Ōshū campaign, and in 1203 killed Nitta Tadatsune on Hōjō orders during the [ShowLocationName('hiki')] incident. He took the tonsure after Shōgun Sanetomo's murder in 1219 and died in 1221.
zh:
加藤景廉（1156—1221）是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期的武将，镰仓幕府的有力御家人。他是伊势国加藤景员的次子，随父亲移居伊豆；1180年源赖朝举兵讨伐平氏时，他加入赖朝麾下。

他参加石桥山之战和1189年的奥州合战，1203年又在比企能员之变中奉北条氏之命诛杀仁田忠常。将军源实朝于1219年遇刺后，他出家为僧，1221年去世。

en:
Katō Kagekazu (dates unknown) was a late-Heian warrior from Ise province, the son of Katō Kagekiyo and father of Kagekado. After killing a Taira retainer in Ise he fled to Izu, sheltering with the Kudō family.

In 1180 he and his sons joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's uprising and fought at Ishibashiyama; old and fearing to be a hindrance, he sent his sons on through the Hakone mountains and took Buddhist vows. Yoritomo confirmed his lands that October.

en:
Katō Kagemichi, recorded as Fujiwara no Kagemichi, was a mid-Heian warrior of the northern Fujiwara Toshihito line, son of Fujiwara no Masashige and ancestor of the Katō clan. With his son Kagesue he served Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie.

In the Earlier Nine Years' War of 1051–1062 he fought Abe no Sadatō in Mutsu under Yoriyoshi and was ranked first of the seven mounted warriors for his merit. Kagesue fell in the campaign, but Kagemichi's descendants prospered as the Katō.

加藤景通，朝廷系谱中记作藤原景通，是平安时代中期的武将，出自藤原北家利仁流，藤原正重之子，被尊为加藤氏之祖。他与儿子景季一同侍奉源赖义、源义家父子。

en:
Kawakami Yorihisa was a Nanboku-chō warrior and founder of the Kawakami branch of the Shimazu of Satsuma. Eldest son of Shimazu Sadahisa, he was born of a concubine and never inherited the headship.

In 1335 he joined Ashikaga Takauji with his father, and in 1336 he led Satsuma troops at the siege of Nitta Yoshisada's Kanagasaki castle in Echizen. Sent home in 1337 to crush a Southern Court rising in Satsuma, he fought there until in 1352 he received the stewardship of half the Kaseda Beppu estate and took the name Kawakami.

川上赖久是南北朝时代的武将，萨摩岛津氏分家川上氏的初代当主。他是第五代当主岛津贞久的长子，因是庶出而未能继承宗家。

1335年他随父亲投奔足利尊氏，1336年率领萨摩军队参加攻打新田义贞据守的越前金崎城之战。1337年萨摩的南朝势力举兵，他奉命回国镇压，1352年获封加世田别府半分的地头职，自此以川上为氏。

en:
Kawano Michiari (1250–1311), head of the Kawano clan of Iyo Province, was a Kamakura gokenin who led the Iyo navy against the Mongols. In 1272 the shogunate mediated the settlement of the succession feud with his uncle Michitoki.

In 1281 he moored his warships on the Hakata beach with the stone wall behind his force; his resolve became known as Kawano's rear wall. At Shikanoshima he boarded a Yuan ship, was wounded by a crossbow bolt, and took a Mongol general alive. Grants restored the clan's lost estates, and he is remembered as the Kawano restorer.

en:
Kawano Michihisa headed the Kawano clan of Iyo Province in the early Kamakura period, a son of Kawano Michinobu and reputedly of a daughter of Hōjō Tokimasa. During the Jōkyū War of 1221 his father and most of the clan joined the imperial court, but Michihisa alone took the Kamakura shogunate's side through his mother's kin.

After the defeat he became clan head, his relatives killed or exiled, and received the jitō post of Tonda manor in Awa. In 1267 he disinherited his eldest son Michitoki and named Michitsugu heir.

en:
Kawano no Michikiyo was a late-Heian warrior chieftain of the Kawano clan in Kazahaya District, Iyo Province, and a son of Chikakiyo. When Minamoto no Yoritomo rose against the Taira in 1180, Michikiyo raised troops, drove out Taira no Koremori's provincial deputy and brought Iyo under his control.

In 1181 a Taira army under Taguchi Shigeyoshi and Nuka Nyūdō Saijaku invaded; Michikiyo held Takanawayama Castle until betrayed from within, then charged out and died fighting.

en:
Kōno Michimori (died 1364) was a warrior lord of Iyo Province and the seventh son of Kōno Michiari. In the Genkō War of 1333 he fought for the Rokuhara deputies, then surrendered and took the tonsure. He joined Ashikaga Takauji in 1336 and was appointed shugo of Iyo.

During the Kannō Disturbance he sided with Takauji and rebuilt Kōno power, retiring in 1363 in favour of his son Michitomo. When Hosokawa Yoriyuki invaded Iyo in 1364, Michitomo was killed and Michimori died of illness weeks later.

en:
Kawano no Michinobu (c. 1155–1223) was an Iyo Province warrior and commander of the Iyo naval forces, son of Michikiyo and grandfather of the preacher Ippen. After his father fell at Takanawayama in 1181, he harried the Taira from the Takanawa Peninsula, and in 1185 brought his warships to Minamoto no Yoshitsune and fought at Dannoura.

He became a Kamakura vassal, but in the Jōkyū War of 1221 backed the retired emperor Go-Toba; defeat brought exile to Mutsu, where he died in 1223.

After his father fell at Takanawayama in 1181, he harried the Taira from the Takanawa Peninsula, and in 1185 brought his warships to Minamoto no Yoshitsune and fought at Dannoura.

He became a [ShowLocationName('kamakura')] vassal, but in the Jōkyū War of 1221 backed the retired emperor Go-Toba; defeat brought exile to Mutsu, where he died in 1223.
zh:
河野通信（约1155—1223）是伊予国武将、伊予水军将领，河野通清之子，也是时宗祖师一遍的祖父。1181年父亲战死于高绳山城后，他在高绳半岛以游击战继续抗击平氏；1185年率战船投奔源义经，参加坛之浦海战。

战后他成为镰仓幕府御家人，但在1221年承久之乱中站在后鸟羽上皇一方，兵败后被流放陆奥国，1223年死于流放地。

en:
Kawano Michitomo (died 1364) was a commander, the son of Kōno Michimori and father of Kōno Michitaka. He fought for the Northern Court and became governor of Tōtōmi through Ashikaga Yoshiakira's recommendation. In 1363 he succeeded to the Kōno headship on his father's retirement.

The next year Hosokawa Yoriyuki invaded Iyo and in the ninth month besieged Michitomo in Setayama Castle. After two months the castle fell and Michitomo was killed on the sixth day of the eleventh month, 1364.

en:
Kawano Michitsugu was a warrior of Iyo Province in the mid-Kamakura period who succeeded his father Kawano Michihisa as head of the Kawano clan. In 1237 his father granted him part of Ishii manor in Iyo, and in 1267 passed him the clan headship and the whole manor after the elder son Michitoki had been disinherited.

Michitoki sued him at the Kamakura shogunate, claiming Michitsugu was the one who had had the affair behind the family breach. Settlement came only in 1272, after Michitsugu's death, in a compromise with his son Michiari.

Kawanobe Jiro was the son of Kawanobe Sukeshige, head of the Kawanobe clan of Hitachi Province. In 1335 he rose with his father for the Southern Court, fought at Mikanohara against Northern Court forces, and marched on Kyoto with Kitabatake Akiie.

After the Kawanobe were crushed at Urizura in 1336, he took service under Kikuchi Takenao in Kyushu and won distinction, but later fell in battle at Yoshino. His son Michiyasu went on fighting for the Southern Court in Hitachi.

en:
Kawanobe Sukeshige was head of the Kawanobe, a Fujiwara-descent warrior clan of Hitachi Province. In 1335 he and his son Jiro rose for Emperor Go-Daigo's Southern Court, defeated Hitachi governor Satake Sadayoshi at Mikanohara, and marched on Kyoto with Kitabatake Akiie; Go-Daigo granted the clan the chrysanthemum badge.

In 1336 he fought around Urizura Castle under Kusunoki Masaie. There Kimura Yoshimasa defeated him at Dokushōhō, and most of the clan perished.

川野边资镇是常陆国武家川野边氏的总领，该族自称出自藤原氏。1335年，他与儿子次郎一同为后醍醐天皇的南朝举兵，在瓮之原击败常陆守护佐竹贞义，又随北畠显家上洛，蒙后醍醐天皇赐下菊纹。

en:
Emperor Kazan (968–1008), personal name Morosada, was the eldest son of Emperor Reizei and the sixty-fifth sovereign of Japan, reigning from 984 to 986. He commissioned the imperial waka anthology Shūi Wakashū, but his short rule was dominated by the Fujiwara regents.

In 986 Fujiwara no Kaneie tricked the nineteen-year-old emperor into believing the imperial regalia had already passed to Prince Kanehito, and Kazan abdicated at Gangyō-ji and took Buddhist orders. In later life he re-established the Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage of thirty-three temples.

花山天皇（968—1008）名师贞，是冷泉天皇的长子、日本第六十五代天皇，984年至986年在位。他曾下诏编纂敕撰和歌集《拾遗和歌集》，但短暂的统治始终受制于藤原氏摄关。

986年，藤原兼家哄骗十九岁的花山天皇，说神器已转交怀仁亲王，花山天皇遂在元庆寺退位出家。晚年他重新整备了由三十三处寺院组成的西国观音灵场。

en:
Prince Kazurawara (786–853), third son of Emperor Kanmu, was a Japanese imperial prince and the ancestor of the Kanmu Taira clan. After coming of age in 798, he held senior court posts including minister of the treasury and minister of ceremonial, and in 812 was also appointed governor-general of the Dazaifu.

In 825 his petition to demote his son to commoner status with the surname Taira was approved, beginning the clan's history. He later received the highest princely rank, first grade, and died in 853.

en:
Keitai (c. 450–531), the 26th emperor of Japan, reigned from 507. Before his accession he ruled in Echizen as Prince Ōdo, a fifth-generation descendant of Emperor Ōjin. When Emperor Buretsu died without an heir in 506, the minister Ōtomo no Kanamura secured the distant kinsman's elevation, and Keitai married Buretsu's sister.

His title long disputed, he entered the Yamato heartland only around 526. In 527 the Iwai Rebellion erupted in Kyushu; he sent Mononobe no Arakabi, who suppressed it. Three of his sons reigned in turn: Ankan, Senka and Kinmei.

继体天皇（约450—531）是日本第26代天皇，507年即位。即位前他称男大迹王，是应神天皇的五世孙，在越前一带为王。506年武烈天皇无嗣而终，权臣大伴金村主导迎立这位远支王族，他遂娶武烈之妹为皇后。

其继承权长期存在争议，约526年才进入大和的政治中心。527年九州爆发磐井之乱，他派大连物部麁鹿火将其平定。他死后有三子相继即位，即安闲、宣化、钦明天皇。

en:
Utsunomiya Fuyutsuna, also known as Kii Fuyutsuna, was a Southern and Northern Courts commander and the seventh head of the Kii clan. Adopted by Utsunomiya Yorifusa, he first called himself Takafusa after receiving a character from Hōjō Takatoki. He fought for Ashikaga Takauji's Northern Court and became shugo of Chikugo and Buzen in 1352.

In 1355 he surrendered to the Southern Court and took the name Fuyutsuna, but soon rejoined the North. In 1359 he fought Kikuchi Takemitsu at the Battle of the Chikugo River; defeat there began the Kii clan's rapid decline.

宇都宫冬纲，又称城井冬纲，是南北朝时代武将，城井氏第七代当主。他被宇都宫赖房收为养子，初名高房，得名于北条高时的偏讳。他初为足利尊氏的北朝而战，1352年成为筑后、丰前两国守护。

en:
Utsunomiya Michifusa, also called Kii Michifusa, was a mid-Kamakura warrior of the Buzen-Utsunomiya clan. His house had become a direct vassal of the Hojo tokuso, and during the Mongol invasions he went down to Kyushu as a Hojo deputy.

In 1286 he was made a head of the new Chinzei Council, hearing suits of Kyushu vassals. He later served as Chikugo shugo and as Hojo Sadatoki's deputy in Higo, and in 1290 received the stewardship of Sada manor in Buzen, where his descendants settled as the Chinzei-Utsunomiya.

zh:
宇都宫通房，亦称城井通房，是镰仓时代中期丰前宇都宫氏的武将。其家已成为北条得宗的被官，元寇袭来时他下向九州，担任北条氏的代官。

1286年镇西谈议所设立，他被任为头人之一，审理九州御家人的诉讼；其后历任筑后守护、北条贞时的肥后守护代。1290年他得到丰前国佐田庄的地头职，子孙在当地定居，称镇西宇都宫氏。

en:
Utsunomiya no Nobufusa (1156–1234) was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods, the eldest son of Nakahara no Munefusa and founder of the Buzen Utsunomiya, later called the Kii clan. In 1180 he rode from Shimotsuke to join Minamoto no Yoritomo's rising, and in 1183 won distinction suppressing a revolt.

As Chinzei commissioner he campaigned against Taira remnants on Kikaigashima in 1187, and in 1192 Yoritomo granted him estates in Bungo and Hyūga. He died in 1234.

zh:
宇都宫信房（1156—1234）是平安时代末期至镰仓时代前期的武将，中原宗房的长子，被奉为丰前宇都宫氏（后来的城井氏）之祖。1180年，他从下野国驰赴源赖朝举兵；1183年在讨伐叛乱时立下战功。

1187年，他以镇西奉行的身份征伐鬼界岛的平氏残党，1192年获赖朝赐予丰后、日向两国的领地。他于1234年去世。

en:
Utsunomiya Toyofusa (1293–1369) was the founder of the Iyo Utsunomiya clan and a son of Utsunomiya Yorifusa, sixth head of the Buzen Utsunomiya clan. In 1330 he was appointed shugo of Iyo, and the next year he entered Ōzu and built Jizōgatake Castle, later Ōzu Castle.

He founded Jōgan-ji as the family temple. With no son of his own, he adopted Utsunomiya Muneyasu of the Chikugo Utsunomiya as his heir, and died on 19 September 1369.

zh:
宇都宫丰房（1293—1369）是伊予宇都宫氏的初代当主，丰前宇都宫氏第六代当主宇都宫赖房之子。1330年他被任为伊予国守护，次年进入大洲，在地藏岳筑城，即后来的大洲城。

他又建城愿寺为菩提寺。因无亲生儿子，他收筑后宇都宫氏的宇都宫宗泰为养子继任，于1369年9月19日去世。

en:
Kikkawa Sanetsune (fl. 1331–1363) was a warrior of the Aki Kikkawa clan, son of Tsunenaga, and fought as the main strength of the clan's weak head house in the Nanboku-chō wars.

He changed sides with the times: in 1335 he helped the Ashikaga-aligned Takeda Ujinobu storm Yano Castle, but in 1336 he took Nitta Yoshisada's order and joined the Southern Court, later returning to the Northern side. In 1352 he captured Kotosaki Castle from Mōri Motoharu, who surrendered the following month.

In 1363 he granted land to his son Kogumamaru, who died young. Sanetsune eventually adopted Tsunemi of the rising Iwami branch.

zh:
吉川实经（活动于1331—1363年）是安艺国国人吉川氏一门，吉川经长之子。宗家当主势力软弱，石见分家日益坐大，实经作为宗家的主力在南北朝动乱中东征西战。

他在南北朝之间几度改换阵营：1335年配合从属足利的武田氏信攻陷矢野城，1336年又奉新田义贞的御教书加入南朝，后来复归北朝。1352年他从毛利元春手中攻下琴崎城，元春次月投降。

1363年他将所领让给儿子虎熊丸。虎熊丸夭折后，他最终收势力日盛的石见分家经见为养子。

en:
Kikkawa Tomokane (1159–1200) was the second head of the Kikkawa clan and a Kamakura gokenin. He fought under Minamoto no Yoritomo in the Ōshū campaign of 1189, earning recognition for his bravery, and stood guard at the Fuji no Makigari hunt of 1193 during the Soga brothers' revenge.

In 1200, in the revolt against Kajiwara Kagetoki, he detected Kagetoki's party in Suruga and joined local warriors in attacking them. He slew Kagetoki's third son Kagemochi, famed for his courage, but died of his own wounds. His son Tomotsune was rewarded with the jitō post of Fukui Manor in Harima.

吉川友兼（1159—1200）是吉川氏第二代当主、镰仓幕府御家人。1189年随源赖朝出征奥州合战，武勇受到赏识；1193年在富士卷狩时担任警护，经历曾我兄弟复仇的骚动。

1200年梶原景时之变中，他在骏河国察觉景时一行的异动，联合当地武士袭击，斩杀其三子、以豪勇闻名的梶原景茂，自己也因伤重而死。其子朝经因此受赏，被任为播磨国福井庄的地头。

en:
Kikkawa Tomotsune (1182–1240) was the third head of the Kikkawa clan and a Kamakura gokenin. In the purge of Kajiwara Kagetoki in 1200 his father Tomokane was killed fighting in Suruga; Tomotsune was rewarded for his own and his father's service with added lands and the jitō post of Fukui Manor in Harima.

He died in 1240; his heir Tsunemitsu may already have succeeded him as clan head before then. As their recorded birth years are only ten years apart, Tsunemitsu may have been adopted from a kinsman.

en:
Kikkawa Tsuneaki was the seventh head of the Aki Kikkawa clan, based at Surugamaru Castle. In 1350 he succeeded his father Tsunemori while the clan followed the Ashikaga Northern Court.

He could not hold the family together: the Iwami branch joined the Southern Court and grew powerful under Tsunekane and Tsunemi. Having no son, Tsuneaki married his daughter Mitoku to Tsunemi and made him his adopted heir. He died in 1383.

吉川经秋是安艺国国人吉川氏第七代当主，驻骏河丸城。1350年，他从父亲吉川经盛手中继承家督，当时吉川氏追随足利的北朝一方。

en:
Kikkawa Tsunehide was the second head of the Iwami branch of the Kikkawa clan and the second son of Tsuneshige, founder of the Iwami line; his sister married the Aki clan head Tsunemori. In the Kenmu and Engen years he fought for Ashikaga Takauji and was appointed governor of Shinano.

After succeeding his father, he quarrelled with his mother Magayasha in 1349; his younger brother Tsunekane sided against him, and Tsunehide was disinherited. Tsunekane then took the Iwami headship.

吉川经任是吉川氏庶流石见吉川氏的第二代当主，石见吉川氏开创者经茂的次子，姊妹嫁给安芸宗家当主经盛。建武、延元年间，他为足利尊氏作战，被任为信浓守。

en:
Kikkawa Tsunekane was a warrior of the early Nanboku-chō period and the third head of the Iwami branch of the Kikkawa clan. In 1349 he took his mother Ryōkai's side in her quarrel with his elder brother Tsunetō, drove Tsunetō out, and succeeded to the family.

In the Kannō Disturbance he backed Ashikaga Tadayoshi and Tadafuyu, campaigning in Aki and Nagato. In 1358 the Southern Court emperor Go-Murakami appointed him acting governor of Suruga, and in 1368 Tadafuyu granted him the stewardship of Ōasa-no-shinshō.

Kikkawa Tsunemitsu (1192–1267) was the fourth head of the Kikkawa clan and a mid-Kamakura gokenin. He fought for the Kamakura shogunate in the Jōkyū War of 1221 and won distinction at the Battle of Uji Bridge outside Kyoto.

Besides his family's Kikkawa Manor in Suruga and Fukui Manor in Harima, he was appointed jitō of Ōasa Honjō in Aki Province, the foothold in which the clan later settled. His sons founded the Aki, Iwami and other branches of the Kikkawa.

除本家的骏河国吉河庄与播磨国福井庄外，他又被任命为安艺国大朝本庄地头，吉川氏后来便以此为据点在当地定居。他的诸子开创了安艺、石见等吉川氏支流。

en:
Kikkawa Tsunemori (died 1358) was the sixth head of the Kikkawa clan of Aki Province and lord of Surugamaru Castle. He succeeded his father Tsunetaka in 1319.

During the Nanboku-chō wars he backed the Ashikaga: in 1335, under the Aki shugo Takeda Nobutake, he attacked the Southern Court garrison at Yano Castle, and later campaigned for Ashikaga Tadayoshi in Iwami. His cousin Tsunekane and younger brother Tsunenaga both joined the Southern Court. Troubled by this split, he passed the headship to his son Tsuneaki in 1350 and died in 1358.

en:
Kikkawa Tsuneshige was a warrior of the late Kamakura period and the founder of the Iwami branch of the Kikkawa clan. A son of Kikkawa Tsunemitsu, he married the daughter of a local lord of Iwami Province and probably settled on her estate there to manage her household.

In 1313 he probably administered the clan's holding at Ōasa in Aki Province before his elder brother Tsunetaka moved there. The brother later granted him the stewardship of Tsufuchi-no-shō in Iwami, making him first head of the Iwami line.

en:
Kikkawa Tsunetaka (1234–1319) was the fifth head of the Kikkawa clan and a late-Kamakura gokenin, remembered as the real founder of the Aki Kikkawa. He succeeded his father Tsunemitsu in 1267.

After clan lands in Aki and Harima were seized, he won their restoration from the Kamakura shogunate in 1313 and, nearing eighty, left the family's old base in Suruga for Ōasa Manor in Aki, where he built Surugamaru Castle. In 1319 he retired in favour of his eldest son Tsunemori and died the same year.

en:
Kikkawa Tsuneyoshi (1132–1193), first known as Irie Tsuneyoshi, was a warrior of Suruga Province and great-great-grandson of Irie no Korekiyo. He was a gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate.

In 1183, after entering the service of Minamoto no Yoritomo, he received Kikkawa Manor in Suruga and took its place name as his family name, founding the Kikkawa clan. He died in 1193, and his son Tomokane succeeded him.

Kikuchi Noritaka (1029–1101), also recorded as Fujiwara no Noritaka, was the founder of the Kikuchi clan of Higo Province. The genealogies name him a son of Fujiwara no Masanori and a grandson of the chūnagon Fujiwara no Takaie.

Takaie was famed for leading the defense of Dazaifu against the Toi raid of 1019. Noritaka died on 15 March 1101.

en:
Kikuchi Takanao (1146–1188) was the sixth head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo Province. Resenting Taira control of the trade with Song China, in 1180 he raised the Chinzei Rebellion. Pardoned and then condemned, he submitted to Taira no Sadayoshi in 1182.

He fought for the Taira at Dannoura in 1185 and surrendered to Minamoto no Yoshitsune, who handed him to his rival Ogata Koreyoshi. The Heike Monogatari places his beheading in that year, clan genealogies in 1188.

Kikuchi Takefusa (1245–1298), third son of the ninth head Takayasu, was the tenth head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo. In the 1274 Mongol invasion he fought Yuan troops at Akasaka, hurling them back to Sohara in a scene depicted in the Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba.

In the 1281 invasion he served at Hakata, but received only armor and no bakufu reward, turning him against the Hōjō. His eldest son Takamori predeceased him, so his grandson Tokitaka succeeded him in 1298.

en:
Kikuchi Takehito (1321–1352) was the fourteenth head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo and the twelfth son of Taketoki. When his brother Takeshige, the thirteenth head, died in 1341, Takehito succeeded him over his older brothers because his mother was of high birth.

He proved a weak leader: in 1343 the Ōtomo invaded Higo and the clan was sustained only by his brothers. His rule so dissatisfied the clan that his elder brother Takemitsu deposed him, after which Takehito took Buddhist vows. He died in 1352.

菊池武士（1321—1352）是肥后菊池氏第十四代当主，菊池武时的第十二子。1341年第十三代当主、次兄武重去世后，他因母亲出身高贵，越过诸位兄长继任当主。

但他生性柔弱，缺乏当主才干：1343年大友氏入侵肥后，全靠兄长们辅佐才勉强支撑家势。他最终被十兄武光废去家督之位，出家为僧，1352年去世。

en:
Kikuchi Takemitsu (c. 1321–1373) became the fifteenth head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo after displacing his ineffective brother Takehito. As the leading Southern Court general in Kyushu serving Prince Kanenaga, he defeated the tandai Isshiki Noriuji at Harisuruhara in 1353, crushed the Shōni at the Chikugo River in 1359 and occupied Dazaifu in 1361.

His eastward campaign of 1368 was blocked near Shimonoseki by the Ōuchi, and in 1372 the new tandai Imagawa Sadayo stormed Dazaifu. Takemitsu withdrew with the prince to Kōra-san in Chikugo and died in 1373.

zh:
菊池武光（约1321—1373）废黜柔弱的弟弟武士后，成为肥后菊池氏第十五代当主。作为南朝在九州的主将，他辅佐怀良亲王：1353年在针摺原击败北朝九州探题一色范氏，1359年在筑后川大破少贰氏，1361年攻取大宰府。

1368年他的东征在下关附近被大内氏阻挡；1372年新任探题今川贞世攻陷大宰府，武光随怀良亲王退据筑后高良山，于1373年去世。

en:
Kikuchi Takeshige (died August 1341) was the 13th head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo Province and a son of Kikuchi Taketoki. In 1333 he joined his father's attack on the Kamakura shogunate's Chinzei tandai Hōjō Hidetoki at Hakata; Ōtomo Sadamune and Shōni Sadatsune instead counterattacked, Taketoki was killed, and Takeshige fled home to succeed him.

Under the Kenmu Restoration he was made governor of Higo for his father's merit. In 1335 he served under Nitta Yoshisada against Ashikaga Takauji, and from 1337 led Southern Court armies in Kyushu, winning at Inuzuka and Ishigakiyama.

zh:
菊池武重（?—1341年）是肥后国菊池氏第十三代家督，菊池武时之子。1333年，他随父亲进攻身在博多的镰仓幕府镇西探题北条英时；大友贞宗、少贰贞经倒戈反击，武时战死，武重逃回本国继任家督。

建武新政中，朝廷以其父之功封他为肥后守。1335年他隶属新田义贞麾下与足利尊氏作战；1337年起率领九州的南朝军队，在犬冢原、石垣山击败北朝军。

en:
Kikuchi Taketoki (1292–1333) was the twelfth head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo. He succeeded as a child after his brother Tokitaka and their uncle killed each other in a family feud.

In 1333, answering Emperor Go-Daigo's call against the Kamakura shogunate, he plotted to attack the Chinzei tandai at Hakata. When the plan leaked and his allies held back, he attacked anyway in the third month and fell with two hundred clansmen. His rising opened Kyūshū's anti-shogunate revolt; the tandai fell two months later.

zh:
菊池武时（1292—1333）是肥后国菊池氏的第十二代当主。其兄时隆与叔父武本在家族争斗中同归于尽后，他幼年继任家督。

1333年，他响应后醍醐天皇推翻镰仓幕府的号召，合谋进攻博多的镇西探题。计划泄露、盟友按兵不动，武时仍于三月举兵，与约二百名族人一同战死。他这次举兵揭开了九州倒幕运动的序幕，两个月后镇西探题便告覆灭。

en:
Kikuchi Taketoshi (died 1357), ninth son of Kikuchi Taketoki, was a Kyushu warrior of the Southern Court in the Nanboku-chō wars. For his father's service to Emperor Go-Daigo he was made Kamon-no-suke. In 1335 he rose in Higo against Ashikaga Takauji and defeated Shōni Sadatsune.

At Tatara-no-hama in 1336 Takauji defeated Taketoshi's larger army; his allies Aso Korenao and Kamachi Takehisa fell, and he fled alone into the hills. He died in Usa, Buzen, in 1357.

zh:
菊池武敏（？—1357）是菊池氏第十二代当主菊池武时的第九子，日本南北朝时期效力南朝的九州武将，通称菊池九郎。因父亲为后醍醐天皇效忠之功，他被任为扫部助。1335年他在肥后举兵反对足利尊氏，击败少贰贞经。

1336年多多良滨之战中，尊氏大破武敏的军队，同盟阿苏惟直、蒲池武久战死，他仅以身免逃入山中。1357年他死于丰前国宇佐郡。

en:
Kikuchi Takeyoshi (died 1377), also called Fukagawa Takeyoshi, was a son of the twelfth Kikuchi clan head Taketoki and a younger brother of Takemitsu, the fifteenth head. A warrior of noted bravery, he served the Southern Court in Kyushu and defeated an attack by the tandai Shiba Ujitsune.

After Takemitsu and his heir Takemasa died, Takeyoshi and his nephew Takeyasu supported the twelve-year-old new head Taketomo. In 1377 he was killed fighting the tandai Imagawa Sadayo's army in Hizen.

菊池武义（？—1377），一作深川武义，是菊池氏第十二代当主菊池武时之子、第十五代当主武光之弟，以勇武著称，为南朝效力于九州。他击退了九州探题斯波氏经的进攻。

武光及其继承人武政相继死后，他与侄子武安辅佐年仅十二岁的新当主武朝，苦撑南朝方的局势。1377年，他在肥前蜷打之战中迎战探题今川贞世，兵败战死。

Kikuchi Tokitaka (1287–1304), childhood name Jirō, was the eleventh head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo and eldest son of Kikuchi Takamori. With his father already dead, he succeeded his grandfather Takefusa.

One account says that in 1304 he and his uncle Takemoto killed each other after the Kamakura bakufu ruled in Tokitaka's favor in a land dispute; another says he died of illness. His younger brother Taketoki succeeded as the twelfth head.

菊池时隆（1287—1304），幼名次郎，是肥后国菊池氏第十一代当主，菊池隆盛的长子。因父亲早逝，他继承祖父武房的家督。

en:
Kikuchi Tsunetaka (1053–1105), also called Fujiwara no Tsunetaka, was the second head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo and the third son of its founder Noritaka, whom he succeeded.

During the Kanji era (1087–1094) he is credited with inviting the deities of the Akita Suwa and Hachiman shrines of Dewa to branch shrines in Kikuchi. He died on 28 June 1105; a grave was later said to stand at Ideda Wakamiya Shrine, though no gravestone remains.

菊池经隆（1053—1105），一作藤原经隆，是肥后菊池氏初代当主则隆第三子，继承父业成为第二代当主。

en:
Kikuchi Yoshitaka (1201–1258), known as Yajirō, was the eighth head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo Province and a Kamakura bakufu vassal. His father Tsunetsugu died in 1204, leaving him heir to his grandfather Takasada.

en:
Kimotsuki Kaneshige (d. 1349), second son of the Kimotsuki clan's sixth head Kanefuji, became its eighth head after managing the family lands as deputy for his brother Kanehisa. From late 1335 he held Takajō in Hyūga for the Southern Court, campaigning with the Kikuchi against the Shimazu and Hatakeyama Noriaki.

He repulsed Noriaki's attack on Takajō, but the fortress fell in 1339 and Kimotsuki power in Hyūga declined. He died of illness in 1349 shortly after attacking Ishii Shigenobu, and was succeeded by his son Arikane.

Kimotsuki Kanetoshi was the first head of the Kimotsuki clan of Ōsumi Province. The eldest son of Tomo no Kanesada, an official of Kimotsuki district, he settled at Takayama in the district and took the clan name Kimotsuki from it.

His younger brothers founded branch houses with holdings across Satsuma, Ōsumi and Hyūga provinces. From Takayama the Kimotsuki grew into the greatest warrior house of southern Kyushu. His son Kanetsune succeeded him.

en:
Kinmei (509–571), the 29th emperor, reigned from 539 and is often regarded as the first historically verifiable Yamato sovereign. A son of Emperor Keitai, he succeeded his half-brother Senka and ruled with Soga no Iname and Mononobe no Okoshi as chief counselors.

In 552 King Seong of Baekje sent a Buddha image and scriptures, marking Buddhism's official arrival in Japan and opening the Soga–Mononobe feud. Silla overran Japan's Korean foothold of Mimana, and his expeditions failed to retake it. Four of his children later became sovereigns.

钦明天皇（509—571）是日本第29代天皇，539—571年在位，常被视为第一位可由史料证实的大和王权君主。他是继体天皇之子，继异母兄宣化天皇即位，以苏我稻目、物部尾舆为大臣、大连。

552年百济圣明王向他赠送佛像与经论，标志佛教正式传入日本，也开启了苏我氏与物部氏的对立。其间新罗攻灭日本在朝鲜半岛的据点任那，他多次出兵均未能收复。他的四名子女先后成为君主。

en:
Kira Mitsuie was the second Ōshū kanrei and eldest son of Kira Sadaie. When his father took up the northern post in 1345, his family moved to Mutsu and based themselves at Taga Castle. In the Kannō Disturbance Mitsuie backed Ashikaga Tadayoshi and helped destroy his co-kanrei Hatakeyama Kuniuji, becoming sole Ōshū kanrei.

He retook Taga Castle from a Southern Court army in 1352 and captured Utsumine in 1353. Driven out in 1354, he fled to the Date clan and recovered the castle that July. His last surviving documents date to 1356.

吉良满家是第二代奥州管领、吉良贞家的嫡子。1345年其父就任奥州管领后，全族迁往陆奥，以多贺城为据点。观应之乱中，满家支持足利直义，参与攻灭同为奥州管领的畠山国氏，成为独任管领。

en:
Kira Mitsusada (died 1384) was lord of Saijō Castle in Mikawa Province, eldest son of Kira Mitsuyoshi and founder of the Saijō Kira branch. He joined Ashikaga Takauji's rising with his father, and in the Kannō Disturbance fought for Ashikaga Tadayoshi; after Tadayoshi's death he allied with the Southern Court and briefly seized Kyoto.

In 1360 he blocked Hatakeyama Kunikiyo's retreat at Yahagi in Mikawa, but submitted to the shogunate in 1361. From 1363 he served 21 years as a hikitsuke headman, and he died in 1384.

en:
Kira Mitsuuji was a late-Kamakura warrior and gokenin, lord of Saijō in Mikawa and heir of Kira Osauji. He held Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade. The Azuma Kagami first records him in 1252 escorting Shōgun Prince Munetaka to Kamakura, and he returned to Kira Manor in 1263 after guard service. In 1271 he invited the Zen monk Enni to found Jissō-ji.

After the first Mongol invasion he became shugo of Echizen, the only Ashikaga branch head with such a post. He took vows around 1284 and was killed in the Shimotsuki incident of 1285.

zh:
吉良满氏是镰仓时代后期武将、御家人，三河国西条领主、吉良长氏的嫡子，位至从五位下。《吾妻镜》中他最早于1252年随将军宗尊亲王进入镰仓时出现，担任番役后于1263年回到吉良庄。1271年，他请来禅僧圆尔创建实相寺。

文永之役后，他出任越前国守护，是足利庶流中唯一担任守护者。他约于1284年出家，1285年在霜月骚乱中被杀。

en:
Kira Mitsuyoshi (died 1356) was lord of Saijō Castle in Mikawa Province and a Northern and Southern Courts era warrior. He took part in Ashikaga Takauji's assault on the Rokuhara Tandai in the Genkō War, fought at the Battle of Aonogahara in Mino in 1338 and served as shugo of Shinano Province around 1340.

He later assisted Ashikaga Tadayoshi's administration in Kyoto. In the Kannō Disturbance he sided with Tadayoshi before returning to the Northern Court, and in 1355 he guarded Emperor Go-Kōgon. He died in 1356.

zh:
吉良满义（？—1356）是三河国西条城城主、南北朝时代武将。元弘之乱中，他随足利尊氏进攻六波罗探题，1338年参加美浓国青野原之战，约1340年就任信浓国守护。

其后他在京都辅佐足利直义处理政务。观应之乱中他站在直义一方，后来归顺北朝；1355年奉命警卫后光严天皇，1356年去世。

en:
Kira Osauji (1211–1290) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and gokenin, the eldest son of Ashikaga Yoshiuji and founder of the Kira clan. Born to a low-ranking mother, he could not inherit the main line and took Kira Manor in Mikawa as his fief and name.

First named in 1228 escorting Shōgun Fujiwara no Yoritsune, he served until 1241 and then returned to Kira Manor. In 1251 he built Tsurugasaki Tenmangū. After his heir Mitsuuji died in the Shimotsuki incident of 1285, he adopted his grandson Sadayoshi, and died in 1290 aged eighty.

吉良长氏（1211—1290）是镰仓时代中期的武将、御家人，足利义氏的庶长子，吉良氏之祖。因生母身份低微，他不能继承足利宗家，领有三河国吉良庄，遂以吉良为姓。

他最早于1228年以将军藤原赖经随兵的身份出现，承役至1241年后回到吉良庄。1251年，他营造鹤崎天满宫。1285年继承人满氏在霜月骚乱中死去，他收孙子贞义为养子，于1290年去世，享年八十岁。

en:
Kira Sadaie (died c. 1354) was a Northern and Southern Courts era warrior and the first Ōshū kanrei, the Muromachi shogunate's northern deputy. Eldest son of Kira Tsuneie of the Tōjō Kira branch in Mikawa, he fought at Hakone-Takenoshita in 1335 and across Owari and Mikawa in 1336.

In 1345 he was appointed Ōshū kanrei jointly with Hatakeyama Kuniuji. During the Kannō Disturbance he destroyed the Hatakeyama in 1351, retook Taga Castle in 1352 and stormed the Southern Court base of Utsumine in 1353, after which he disappears from the records.

吉良贞家（？—约1354）是南北朝时代武将、初代奥州管领，即室町幕府统辖北方诸州的代表。他是三河东条吉良氏吉良经家的嫡子，1335年参加箱根·竹之下之战，1336年转战尾张与三河。

1345年他与畠山国氏同任奥州管领。观应之乱中他于1351年攻灭畠山氏，1352年夺回多贺城，1353年攻陷南朝据点宇津峰城，此后便不见于史料。

en:
Kira Sadatsune (fl. 1335–1367) was a warrior of the Tōjō Kira branch in Mikawa and younger brother of the Ōshū kanrei Kira Sadaie. When his brother marched east in 1336, Sadatsune stayed to hold Kira Manor and is the likely commander who defeated Nitta's Southern Court army there.

During the Kannō Disturbance he alone of the Kira backed Takauji and Kō no Moronao. From 1352 he fought in Mutsu, helping retake Taga Castle and storm Utsumine. After 1367 he vanishes from the records amid a feud within the clan.

en:
Kira Sadayoshi (died 1343), also called Ashikaga Sadayoshi, was lord of Saijō Castle in Mikawa Province and a Kamakura vassal. During the Kōan invasion of 1281 he is said to have gone down to Iwami Province. After his father Mitsuuji was killed in the Shimotsuki Disturbance of 1285, he became heir to his grandfather Nagauji.

In 1333 at Yatsuhashi he encouraged Ashikaga Takauji's decision to rebel against the Hōjō, and he went on to fight in the Nakasendai War of 1335. He died in 1343.

en:
Kira Tsuneie was a warrior of the Kamakura period (1185–1333) and the third head of the Oshu, or Musashi, branch of the Kira clan, the early Tojo Kira. A note in the Sonpi Bunmyaku gives him the style Fujitani; he is said to have held the Fujitani estate in Adachi district of Mutsu province and taken the Fujitani name.

Tradition also credits him with building Yotsuhongamatsu Castle there, but the estate's location is unknown and the story is unconfirmed, perhaps confused with his son Sadaie, the powerful Oshu kanrei.

吉良经家是镰仓时代（1185—1333年）的武将，吉良氏奥州（武藏）家，即前期东条吉良氏的第三代当主。《尊卑分脉》注其“号藤谷”；另有说法称他领有陆奥国安达郡的藤谷庄，并以藤谷为氏。

相传他还在当地修筑四本松城，但藤谷庄的位置至今不明，此说并无确证，可能是与其子、权势显赫的奥州管领贞家的事迹混淆而来。

en:
Kira Tsuneuji was a warrior of the Kamakura period (1185–1333) and the second head of the Oshu, or Musashi, branch of the Kira clan, the early Tojo Kira.

He is usually called a son of Kira Yoshitsugu, but other accounts make him the natural son of Kira Mitsuuji of the Saijo Kira, or Yoshitsugu's son adopted by Mitsuuji after Yoshitsugu took vows in China. The Sonpi Bunmyaku first attaches the Kira name to his line, suggesting his may have been the first generation to hold Tojo.

en:
Kitabatake Akiie (1318–1338) was the eldest son of Kitabatake Chikafusa and a Southern Court general in the Nanboku-chō wars. In 1333 he accompanied his father and Prince Noriyoshi to Taga Castle in Mutsu and rallied the Date, Yūki and Nambu warrior houses of the northeast to the court, later becoming chinjufu shōgun. In 1336 he marched west and helped Nitta Yoshisada drive Ashikaga Takauji from Kyoto.

Campaigning south again in 1338 he captured Kamakura, but was overwhelmed and killed by Kō no Moronao at the Battle of Ishizu in Izumi, aged twenty.

zh:
北畠显家（1318—1338）是北畠亲房的长子，南北朝时代的南朝武将。1333年，他随父亲护卫义良亲王进驻陆奥国多贺城，号召伊达、结城、南部等东北武士家族为朝廷效力，后来出任镇守府将军。1336年建武之乱中，他西上勤王，与新田义贞等合力将足利尊氏逐出京都。

1338年他再度南下，攻陷镰仓，却在和泉国石津之战中被高师直的军队围攻击杀，年仅20岁。

en:
Kitabatake Akinari (c. 1335–1386) was a Southern Court noble in Japan's Nanboku-chō era and the legitimate son of Kitabatake Akiie, who died fighting for Emperor Go-Daigo in 1338. He first appears in court records in 1352 with junior fourth rank, and in 1378 was made provisional major counselor of junior second rank.

Later traditions make him a co-author of the Taiheiki under the clerical name Gyōi, a follower of Prince Kanenaga in Kyushu, and ancestor of the Namioka Kitabatake family.

北畠显成（约1335—1386）是日本南北朝时代南朝的公卿，为1338年追随后醍醐天皇战死的北畠显家的嫡男。他于1352年（正平七年）首见记载，叙从四位上，1378年叙任从二位权大纳言。

en:
Kitabatake Akinobu (1320–c. 1380) was the second son of Kitabatake Chikafusa and a Southern Court court noble of the Nanboku-chō wars, called the Kasuga Shōshō. In 1336 he raised troops in Ise for Emperor Go-Daigo and became Ise governor.

After his brother Akiie fell in 1338 he succeeded him as chinjufu shōgun and fought on in Mutsu, holding Ryōzen Castle until 1347. In 1351 he routed a Northern Court army at the Hirose River and retook Taga Castle, but Kira Sadaie drove him out in 1352.

He moved to Utsumine Castle and, after its fall in 1353, reportedly withdrew to Dewa. He died around 1380; his daughter became empress to Emperor Go-Kameyama.

北畠显信（1320—约1380）是北畠亲房的次子、北畠显家之弟，南北朝时代的南朝公卿，通称春日少将。1336年他在伊势国起兵援助后醍醐天皇，就任伊势国司。

1338年兄长显家战死后，他继任镇守府将军，在陆奥坚持抵抗，据守灵山城直至1347年落城。1351年，他在广濑川击溃北朝军队、夺回多贺城，但于1352年被吉良贞家逐出。

他转往宇津峰城，据传1353年城陷后退往出羽。他约于1380年去世，其女后来成为后龟山天皇的中宫。

en:
Kitabatake Akiyoshi (c. 1326–c. 1383), third son of Kitabatake Chikafusa, founded the Ise Kitabatake house. He went to Ise Province in 1336, built Tamamaru Castle and was apparently appointed governor around 1338; after the castle fell in 1342 he held Taki as the Southern Court's bulwark.

In 1352 he led three thousand cavalry into Kyoto, routed Hosokawa Akiuji and drove Ashikaga Yoshiakira into Ōmi to briefly restore Southern rule; defeated at Otokoyama, he escorted the emperor to Anō. His verses appear in the Shin'yō Wakashū, and war chronicles say he died at Taki in 1383.

北畠显能（约1326—约1383）是北畠亲房的第三子，伊势北畠氏的始祖。1336年他前往伊势国，修筑玉丸城，约于1338年受任伊势守；1342年玉丸城陷落后，他以多气为据点，充当南朝在伊势的屏障。

1352年，他率骑兵三千攻入京都，击败细川显氏，将足利义诠驱往近江，一度恢复南朝对京都的统治；男山战败后，他护送天皇退往贺名生。其和歌收录于《新叶和歌集》，军记称他于1383年在多气去世。

en:
Kitabatake Chikafusa (1293–1354) was a Murakami Genji court noble and a chief advisor to Emperor Go-Daigo in the Kenmu restoration of 1333. That year he accompanied his son Akiie and Prince Noriyoshi, the future Emperor Go-Murakami, to Taga Castle in Mutsu.

After Ashikaga Takauji revolted he joined the Southern Court at Yoshino, and in 1339, from Oda Castle in Hitachi, wrote the Jinnō Shōtōki in defence of the Southern imperial line. From 1344 he led the court under Go-Murakami, briefly retook Kyoto during the Kannō Disturbance, and died at Anō in 1354.

北畠亲房（1293—1354）出身村上源氏，是后醍醐天皇建武新政的核心谋臣。1333年，他随儿子显家，护卫后来成为后村上天皇的义良亲王前往陆奥国多贺城。

足利尊氏反叛后，他加入南朝；1339年前后在常陆国小田城时，撰写《神皇正统记》，论证南朝皇统的正统。1344年返回吉野后，他辅佐后村上天皇总揽南朝政务，在观应之乱期间一度收复京都，1354年在贺名生去世。

en:
Kitabatake Masaie (1215–1275) was a court noble of the early to mid-Kamakura period and the founder of the Kitabatake house. He was born the second son of Senior Counselor Minamoto no Michikata, but was treated as a non-heir son while his younger brother Michishige carried on the main line.

Masaie built his residence at Kitabatake north of Kyoto and adopted that place name as his family name. He died in 1275; the house he founded rose to prominence only under his great-grandson Chikafusa.

北畠雅家（1215—1275）是镰仓时代前期至中期的公卿、北畠家之祖。他是大纳言源通方的次男，被作为庶子对待，由弟弟通成继承嫡系。

雅家在京都北郊的北畠营建宅邸，遂以地名为家名，开创北畠家。他于1275年去世，北畠家直到其曾孙亲房一代才登上历史舞台。

Kitabatake Morochika (1241–1315) was a court noble of the middle and late Kamakura period, the son of Kitabatake Masaie, founder of the Kitabatake house. He was the father of Moroshige and the grandfather of the later court statesman Chikafusa.

In the ninth month of 1289, when the Retired Emperor Kameyama took Buddhist vows as a cloistered emperor, Morochika entered religion alongside him. He died in the tenth month of 1315, at the age of seventy-five.

en:
Kitabatake Moroshige (1271–1322) was a court noble of the late Kamakura period, son of the councillor Morochika and father of Chikafusa. A trusted attendant of the Retired Emperor Go-Uda, he rose through provincial and guards posts to Junior Third Rank in 1291 and became Provisional Major Counselor in 1303.

He resigned in 1305, and in 1307 took Buddhist vows under the name Kyōgaku when Go-Uda became a monk. After fifteen years in retreat he died in 1322, aged fifty-three. Seven of his poems enter imperial anthologies.

en:
Uesugi Kiyoko (1270–1343) was the mother of Ashikaga Takauji and Tadayoshi, founders of the Muromachi shogunate. A daughter of Uesugi Yorishige, she became a concubine of Ashikaga Sadauji and bore Takauji in 1305.

After her husband's death she sustained the Ashikaga house and stayed with her sons through the wars overthrowing the Kamakura shogunate, then advanced the Uesugi. Known as the Nun Ōkata, also a waka poet, she died on 20 January 1343.

en:
Kobayakawa no Kagehira was an early Kamakura-period warrior, a shogunal gokenin ruling the Numata estate in Aki Province. Born the fifth son of Hiraga Yoshinobu, he was adopted by Dohi Tōhira, jitō of Numata, and took the Kobayakawa name.

In 1206 he divided Numata between his eldest son Shigehira and second son Suehira, founding the Numata and Takehara branches, and secured shogunal confirmation in 1207.

After his adoptive brother Korehira was executed for backing Wada Yoshimori in the Wada disturbance of 1213, he inherited the Dohi main line. He died on 18 August 1244.

小早川景平是镰仓时代初期的武将、统治安艺国沼田庄的镰仓幕府御家人。他本是平贺义信第五子，被沼田庄地头土肥远平收为养子，改称小早川。

1206年，他将领地沼田庄分给嫡子茂平与次子季平，分别开创沼田小早川氏和竹原小早川氏两支，并于1207年获得幕府承认。

1213年和田合战时，养父的嫡子土肥维平因追随和田义盛被处死，他于是又继承土肥氏嫡流。1244年8月18日去世。

en:
Kobayakawa no Nobuhira was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts period who headed the Numata-Kobayakawa clan of Aki Province, succeeding his father Tomohira.

He distributed the Numata estate lands among his several sons, one taking newly opened fields in 1341, with branch houses including the Ikuguchi and Ura families founded in the process. Under him the clan expanded into the Geiyo Islands of the Seto Inland Sea, laying the base of the Kobayakawa navy.

小早川宣平是镰仓末期至南北朝时代的武将，继父亲朝平之后担任安艺国沼田小早川氏当主。

他把沼田庄的领地分给诸子，其中一子于1341年分得新垦田地，衍生出生口氏、浦氏等分家。在他这一代，小早川氏开始向濑户内海的艺予群岛扩张，为小早川水军奠定基础。

en:
Kobayakawa no Sadahira was head of the Numata-Kobayakawa clan of Aki Province, active from the late Kamakura through the Northern and Southern Courts period. In 1333, aged about sixteen, he fought for the Kamakura shogunate in the Genkō War, following the Rokuhara tandai's fleeing followers to their mass suicide at Renge-ji in Ōmi before escaping to his Numata estate.

He received junior fifth rank and the office of Bingo no Kami in 1337, inherited Yasunao lands from his father Nobuhira in 1341, and in 1351 was appointed shugo of Aki.

zh:
小早川贞平是安艺国沼田小早川氏当主，活跃于镰仓末期至南北朝时代。1333年元弘之乱时，他年约十六岁，作为镰仓幕府一方出阵，追随六波罗探题败走的族人到近江国莲华寺，目睹集体自刃后脱身，逃回本领沼田庄。

他于1337年获封从五位下、备后守，1341年继承父亲宣平的安直领地，1351年被任命为安艺国守护。

en:
Kobayakawa no Shigehira (died 1264) was a Kamakura-period warrior and gokenin who held the Numata estate in Aki Province. In 1206 he and his younger brother Suehira divided their father Kagehira's lands, and Shigehira built Takayama Castle, later seat of the Numata-Kobayakawa.

He won distinction on the shogunate side in the Jōkyū War of 1221, receiving the stewardship of the Tsū-Takehara estate in Aki. From 1247 to 1257 he guarded Kyoto and the Rokuhara tandai. He later enfeoffed his younger sons and left the main Numata lands to his heir Masahira.

zh:
小早川茂平（1264年卒）是镰仓时代中期的武将，作为镰仓幕府御家人领有安艺国沼田庄。1206年，他与弟弟季平分割父亲景平的领地，并修筑高山城，此地后来成为沼田小早川氏的本据。

1221年承久之乱中，他加入幕府一方立下军功，获封安艺国都宇竹原庄的地头职。1247至1257年间，他驻留京都，负责洛中警备并护卫六波罗探题。晚年他将领地分封给诸子，沼田本庄大部传给嫡子雅平。

en:
Kobayakawa no Tomohira was head of the Numata-Kobayakawa clan of Aki Province and a powerful gokenin vassal of the Kamakura shogunate. He enforced shogunate orders against Seto Inland Sea pirates, capturing the Iyo pirate Yagorō Iehide in 1319.

During the Genkō War of 1333 he sent his grandson Sadahira to Kyoto on the shogunate's side. After its defeat the Kenmu regime seized the Numata estate, until the Takehara branch won a pardon; the clan then served the Ashikaga.

en:
Kondō Kunihira (dates unknown) was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods whose family had held lands in Izu Province since his grandfather's day. He joined Minamoto no Yoritomo at the start of the Jishō-Juei War in 1180 and served as a Kamakura vassal.

In 1185 he went up to Kyoto as Yoritomo's deputy to suppress lawless warriors around the capital, and later performed the same duty in Kyushu. In 1199 he was appointed shugo of Sanuki Province; the Sanuki-based Ōhira house claimed him as ancestor.

近藤国平（生卒年不详）是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期的武将，其家族自祖父一代起便在伊豆国拥有地盘。1180年治承·寿永之乱爆发时，他在源赖朝举兵之初便加入麾下，成为镰仓御家人。

1185年，他作为赖朝的代官上洛，负责平定在畿内近国趁乱为非作歹的武士，随后又奉命前往镇西执行同样任务。1199年，他被任命为赞岐国守护；以赞岐为本据的大平氏自称是他的后裔。

en:
Kondō Yoshishige was a warrior of the late Heian period and the biological father of Ōtomo Yoshinao, founder of the Ōtomo clan. Of Fujiwara-descended stock, he served as gōji headman of Furusho-gō in Sagami Province and joined Minamoto no Yoritomo during the Jishō-Juei War.

In 1182 monks of Kongōji accused him at Kamakura of seizing temple lands, and Yoritomo ordered the abuses stopped. He married a daughter of Ōtomo Tsuneie; their son Yoshinao was raised as a son by Nakahara Chikayoshi and inherited his Kyushu estates.

en:
Konoe (1139–1155), son of Emperor Toba, was named heir at birth and enthroned in 1141 at age three when Toba forced Emperor Sutoku to abdicate. His father ruled as cloistered emperor throughout, with Fujiwara no Tadamichi as regent until 1150.

In 1150 he married two Fujiwara consorts from the rival camps of Tadamichi and Yorinaga. He died in 1155 at seventeen without an heir; the ensuing succession dispute brought his brother Go-Shirakawa to the throne and set the stage for the Hōgen Rebellion.

zh:
近卫天皇（1139—1155）是鸟羽天皇之子，出生即被立为储君，1141年鸟羽逼迫崇德天皇退位后，年仅三岁的他登基。在位期间由父亲实行院政，藤原忠通担任摄政至1150年。

1150年，他迎娶的两位藤原氏后妃分别出自忠通与政敌赖长两派。1155年他以十七岁早逝且无子嗣，随之而来的继位之争使兄长后白河天皇登位，并为保元之乱埋下伏笔。

en:
Kotō Takefuji was a younger son of the Nagato warlord Kotō Takezane and younger brother of Takemura. During the Kannō Disturbance the clan split over allegiance: its heads Takenao and Yoshitake backed the Muromachi shogunate and Isshiki Noriuji.

Takefuji instead sided with Ashikaga Tadafuyu, Takauji's disaffected son, and the Southern Court. In 1352 Tadafuyu was defeated by Isshiki at Dazaifu and withdrew to Nagato, where Takefuji's branch held sway.

en:
Kotō Takekage was the eighth head of the Kotō clan, a Mononobe-descended warrior family of Nagato, and the son of Takemitsu. As district magistrate of Kotō, he inherited from his father the post of shugo, or military governor, of the province.

Under him the clan entered the service of the Kamakura shogunate. He died in Kamakura during the Jōkyū era of 1219–1222, leaving the headship to his son Takeyoshi; his Buddhist name was Jakuson.

en:
Kotō Takemitsu was the seventh head of the Kotō, a Nagato warrior clan of Asa District, and its leader in the Genpei War. Before the war he held the posts of shugo and police chief.

He first fought for the Taira at Ichinotani in 1184, but switched to the Minamoto as the Taira collapsed, and at Dannoura in 1185 furnished boatmen from Kushizaki for their fleet. He took Buddhist orders as Nensai and built Shimofuri Castle at Tanoi.

en:
Kotō Takemura was the fifteenth head of the Kotō warrior clan of Nagato Province and son of Takezane. In 1333 he and his father turned against the Hōjō and attacked the Nagato tandai, and the next year he was enfeoffed with Kikuna District in Buzen Province for his service.

In 1335 he served in Nitta Yoshisada's army against Ashikaga Takauji and fought at Hakone-Takeshita. He succeeded his father as shugo of Nagato in 1348, taking the style Suruga no Kami, and died in 1351.

en:
Kotō Takezane (died 1348) was the fourteenth head of the Kotō, a warrior clan of Asa District in Nagato Province. In the Genkō War he served the Nagato tandai Hōjō Tokinao, but in 1333 turned against him and helped drive him from Nagato, after which the Kenmu government made him shugo of Nagato in 1334.

When Takauji rebelled, Takezane joined him in Kyushu in 1336 and fought the Southern Court, keeping the post under the Muromachi shogunate. After the 1348 fighting at Shijōnawate he fell ill, passed the office to his son Takemura, and died in Kyoto that November.

Kotō Takezane (died 1348) was the fourteenth head of the Kotō, a warrior clan of Asa District in Nagato Province. In the Genkō War he served the Nagato tandai Hōjō Tokinao, but in 1333 turned against him and helped drive him from Nagato, after which the Kenmu government made him shugo of Nagato in 1334.

When Takauji rebelled, Takezane joined him in Kyushu in 1336 and fought the Southern Court, keeping the post under the Muromachi shogunate. After the 1348 fighting at Shijōnawate he fell ill, passed the office to his son Takemura, and died in Kyoto that November.
zh:
厚东武实（？—1348）是以长门国厚狭郡为根据地的厚东氏第十四代当主。元弘之乱中他本是长门探题北条时直的部下，1333年倒戈，参与将时直逐出长门，1334年被建武政权任命为长门守护。

足利尊氏举兵后，武实于1336年在九州加入尊氏一方与南朝作战，在室町幕府下继续担任长门守护。1348年四条畷之战后他病倒，将守护职让给儿子武村，同年11月在京都病没。

en:
Kō no Koremasa was a son of Kō no Koreyori and a retainer of Minamoto no Yoshiie (1039–1106). He followed Yoshiie's third son Minamoto no Yoshikuni east to Ashikaga Manor in Shimotsuke and settled there, planting the Kō clan in the Ashikaga lands.

From his generation the Kō served the Minamoto-line Ashikaga as senior vassals, fighting the rival Fujiwara-line Ashikaga. His descendants included the Ashikaga stewards Kō no Shigeuji and Kō no Moronao.

en:
Kō no Koreyori was an eleventh-century warrior from whom the Kō clan of Shimotsuke traced its line. Later genealogies, including the Sonpi Bunmyaku, name him as the fourth son of Minamoto no Yoshiie (1039–1106), given in infancy to Takashina no Koreaki to raise and styled Ōdaka no Tayū.

Around Koreyori's time the Takashina house shortened its name to Kō, became warriors, and entered Yoshiie's service in the east, the beginning of the clan's martial identity.

en:
Kō no Moroaki was a Nanboku-chō commander, the son of Kō no Moroyuki and cousin of the powerful steward Kō no Moronao. He served Ashikaga Takauji's brother Tadayoshi, becoming shugo of Ise in 1338 and taking Kamiyama Castle from the Southern Court.

In the Kannō Disturbance he and his son Moroari sided with Tadayoshi against Moronao, one grievance being Moronao's killing of his wife's brother. When Tadayoshi fled to Hokuriku in 1351 Moroaki followed, and his son Moroari later entered the service of the Kamakura kubō Ashikaga Motouji.

en:
Kō no Moroakira was a warrior of the Northern and Southern Courts era and a son of Kō no Moronao, steward to Shogun Ashikaga Takauji. When his father and much of the Kō clan were killed during the Kannō Disturbance in 1351, Moroakira escaped and was made the clan's successor. Around 1352 he was named shugo of Tango and, in 1353, of Tajima, to watch the wavering Yamana Tokiuji.

When Yamana rebelled for the Southern Court in 1353, Moroakira led the warriors of three provinces against him, was defeated at Nishiyama Yoshimine and took his own life.

en:
Kō no Moroari (died 1364) was a Nanboku-chō commander, the son of Kō no Moroaki. During the Kannō Disturbance he and his father sided with Ashikaga Tadayoshi against the rest of the Kō clan. After Tadayoshi's downfall at Kamakura in 1352 he entered the service of the Kamakura kubō Ashikaga Motouji.

In 1362, when the Kantō steward was driven from office for opposing Motouji, Moroari was named his successor. His last issued document dates to 1363, and he died in the second month of 1364, the last Kantō steward chosen from outside the Uesugi clan.

en:
Kō no Morofuyu (died 1351) was a Nanboku-chō commander, shugo lord and waka poet, adopted heir of Kō no Moronao. He helped defeat the Southern Court general Kitabatake Akiie in 1338 and, as Kantō steward from 1339, subdued it by 1343, becoming shugo of Musashi and Iga.

In 1349 he was assigned to counsel the young Kamakura kubō Ashikaga Motouji. During the Kannō Disturbance he fled Kamakura in late 1350 and, besieged at Sunzawa Castle in Kai, killed himself in early 1351.

en:
Kō no Moronao (died 1351), son of Moroshige, was the chief retainer of Ashikaga Takauji and the first steward of the Muromachi bakufu. He fought for Takauji at the Minatogawa River in 1336 and slew the Southern Court general Kitabatake Akiie in 1338. In 1348 he destroyed Kusunoki Masatsura's army at Shijōnawate and burned the Southern Court base at Yoshino.

His feud with Takauji's brother Tadayoshi ignited the Kannō Disturbance; after his defeat at Uchidehama in 1351 he took the tonsure, only to be killed with his brother Moroyasu on the Mukogawa River by Tadayoshi's men.

en:
Kō no Moroshige was a retainer of the Ashikaga house from the late Kamakura into the Nanboku-chō period and the father of Kō no Moronao. Succeeding his father Morouji, he served Ashikaga Sadauji and Takauji as steward, first recorded in that office in 1301, and also judged disputes among Ashikaga vassals.

By 1333 he had passed the family headship to his son Moronao, alienating his nephew Moroaki, who took Tadayoshi's side in the Kannō Disturbance. The diary Jōraku-ki records his death in the fifth month of 1343.

en:
Kō no Morouji was a Kamakura-period warrior of the Kō clan in Shimotsuke and the grandfather of Kō no Moronao. He succeeded his father Shigeuji as steward, or shitsuji, to the Ashikaga, serving Ashikaga Ietoki and the young Sadauji. When Ietoki committed suicide in 1284, he entrusted Morouji with his last affairs in a letter.

In 1286 Morouji issued a steward's writ concerning a Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine appointment without his lord's sleeve signature, a mark of his standing among the Ashikaga retainers. He remained steward until his death in 1301, when his son Moroshige succeeded him.

en:
Kō no Moroyasu (died 1351) was a commander under Ashikaga Takauji and brother of Kō no Moronao. He fought in the 1333 rising against the Hōjō and helped put down the 1335 Nakasendai War, then fought at Minatogawa in 1336 as Tadayoshi's vice-general and against Kitabatake Akiie in 1338.

As shugo of Kawachi he helped crush Kusunoki Masatsura and burn Yoshino in 1348. Leading his brother's faction against Ashikaga Tadayoshi, he was defeated at Uchidehama in 1351, took the tonsure, and was killed with Moronao and his son Moroyo on the Mukogawa River.

高师泰（？—1351）是足利尊氏麾下武将，高师直之弟。1333年他参加推翻北条氏的举兵，1335年协助平定中先代之乱；1336年以足利直义副将身份在凑川作战，1338年又参与讨伐北畠显家。

en:
Kō no Moroyo (died 1351) was a Nanboku-chō commander of the Kō clan, the son of Kō no Moroyasu and nephew of the steward Moronao. When Moronao briefly resigned the stewardship amid his feud with Ashikaga Tadayoshi, Takauji appointed Moroyo to succeed him, though Moronao soon reclaimed the office.

In the Kannō Disturbance he fought under his father and uncle for Takauji against Tadayoshi, and after the defeat at Uchidehama in 1351 he took the tonsure. While being escorted to Kyoto he was cut down at the Mukogawa River with Moronao, Moroyasu and their kinsmen.

en:
Kō no Shigemochi was a Nanboku-chō commander and waka poet, younger brother of the steward Kō no Moronao. He served Ashikaga Takauji from the 1333 rising, fighting at Tatarahama and the Minatogawa River in 1336. In 1337 he was appointed shugo of Musashi and guarded the young Ashikaga Yoshiakira at Kamakura, but was removed after defeats by Kitabatake Akiie.

He later headed the bakufu's Hikitsuke court, served as Kantō steward, and presented waka at Kōyasan in 1344. He survived the killing of his brothers in 1351 and resumed office under Yoshiakira; by 1352 he had become a monk.

en:
Kō no Shigeuji was a mid-Kamakura warrior and steward, or shitsuji, to the Ashikaga lords Yoriuji and Ietoki in Shimotsuke Province; he was the great-grandfather of Kō no Moronao. A writ he issued in the eleventh month of 1281 is the oldest surviving evidence of a Kō heading the Ashikaga household, by which point the stewardship had become hereditary.

He had died by 1284, when his son Morouji received Ashikaga Ietoki's farewell letter at his suicide. Shigeuji also took part in the Utsunomiya waka circle as a poet.

en:
Prince Ōtomo (648–672), posthumously called Emperor Kōbun, was Emperor Tenji's son by a concubine. In 671 his father named him the first Daijō-daijin. When Tenji died he took power at Ōmi, but his uncle Prince Ōama challenged the succession, fled Yoshino and raised the eastern provinces.

The Jinshin War of 672 ended within a month: Ōama's eastern armies destroyed the Ōmi forces and Ōtomo killed himself in the mountains. No early source counts him an emperor; the title Kōbun was confirmed only in 1870.

en:
Kōgon (1313–1364), personal name Kazuhito, was the first emperor of Japan's Northern Court, reigning from 1331 to 1333. A son of Emperor Go-Fushimi of the Jimyōin line, he was made heir to Emperor Go-Daigo in 1326 under the throne-alternation agreement. After Go-Daigo's rising against the Kamakura shogunate in 1331, the Hōjō exiled Go-Daigo to Oki and enthroned Kōgon.

Go-Daigo returned and deposed him in 1333. In 1336 Ashikaga Takauji placed Kōgon's brother Kōmyō on the Northern throne. Southern forces seized him at Kyoto in 1352 amid the Kan'ō Disturbance and kept him captive until his death in 1364.

光严天皇（1313—1364），名量仁，是日本北朝第一代天皇，1331年至1333年在位。他是持明院统后伏见天皇之子，1326年依照两统迭立的约定被立为后醍醐天皇的皇太子。1331年后醍醐天皇倒幕失败被流放隐岐，光严随即被拥立为帝。

en:
Empress Kōgyoku (594–661), born Princess Takara, ruled Japan twice: as the 35th sovereign, Kōgyoku, and from 655 as the 37th, Saimei. She ascended in 642 amid Soga clan domination. In 645 her son Prince Naka no Ōe killed Soga no Iruka in the Isshi incident, after which she abdicated for her brother Emperor Kōtoku.

Her Saimei reign saw large building works at Asuka. After Paekche fell in 660 she marched to its aid but died in Kyūshū the next year before the expedition sailed.

en:
Empress Kōken (718–770), personal name Abe, was the 46th and 48th monarch of Japan, its only twice-reigning empress. A daughter of Emperor Shōmu, she succeeded her father in 749 and later abdicated for Junnin.

After crushing Fujiwara no Nakamaro's rebellion in 764, she deposed Junnin and retook the throne as Empress Shōtoku. Her second reign was dominated by the monk Dōkyō, whom she made Buddhist king; the 769 Usa oracle claiming Hachiman wanted him emperor was challenged by Wake no Kiyomaro. She died in 770.

孝谦天皇（718—770）名阿倍，是日本第46代和第48代君主，也是唯一两度登基的女天皇。她是圣武天皇之女，749年受父禅让即位，后让位于淳仁天皇。

764年平定藤原仲麻吕之乱后，她废黜淳仁，重祚称称德天皇。第二次在位期间，僧人道镜专权，被她封为法王；769年宇佐神托宣称八幡神有意让道镜即皇位，遭和气清麻吕驳斥。770年她去世。

en:
Emperor Kōkō (830–887) was the 58th emperor of Japan, reigning from 884 to 887. The third son of Emperor Ninmyō, he was placed on the throne in 884 by the kampaku Fujiwara no Mototsune after Emperor Yōzei's deposition, and Kōkō entrusted him with government.

On his enthronement he demoted all his children to commoner rank, but on his deathbed in 887 he restored his son Minamoto no Sadami to imperial status as crown prince; Sadami succeeded him as Emperor Uda that same day.

光孝天皇（830—887）是日本第58代天皇，884年至887年在位。他是仁明天皇第三子。884年阳成天皇被废后，关白藤原基经将他拥上皇位，光孝也把政务托付给基经。

en:
Kōmyō (1322–1380), personal name Yutahito, was the second Northern Court emperor and the first backed by Ashikaga Takauji, reigning from 1336 to 1348. A younger son of Emperor Go-Fushimi and Kōgon's brother, he was enthroned at Kyoto after Takauji drove Go-Daigo from Kyoto in 1336, without the sacred imperial treasures; Go-Daigo then founded the Southern Court at Yoshino.

In 1348 Kōmyō abdicated to his nephew Sukō. Southern forces took Kyoto in 1352 and carried him off with Kōgon and Sukō; held in Yamato until 1355, he returned to Kyoto and took monastic vows, and died in 1380.

光明天皇（1322—1380），名丰仁，是日本北朝第二代天皇，也是第一位得到足利尊氏支持的北朝天皇，1336年至1348年在位。他是后伏见天皇较年幼的儿子、光严天皇之弟。1336年足利尊氏将后醍醐天皇逐出京都后，他在没有三神器的情况下于京都即位；后醍醐天皇随后在吉野建立南朝。

en:
Emperor Kōnin (708–782), personal name Shirakabe, was the 49th emperor of Japan and a grandson of Emperor Tenji. He is said to have feigned a love of drink to survive the purges of the 760s and won credit for suppressing the Fujiwara no Nakamaro rebellion of 764. When Empress Shōtoku died without an heir in 770, ministers placed the sixty-two-year-old Shirakabe on the throne.

In 772 he deposed Empress Inoe and Crown Prince Osabe, later named his son Yamabe heir, and abdicated to him in 781; Yamabe ruled as Emperor Kanmu.

en:
Emperor Kōtoku (596–654), personal name Karu, was Japan's 36th sovereign (r. 645–654) and Empress Kōgyoku's younger brother. Enthroned after the Isshi incident broke Soga power, he let his nephew Crown Prince Naka no Ōe direct policy. He proclaimed Taika, Japan's first era name, and the 646 Reform Edict launched the Taika reforms of centralised administration.

The court moved to Naniwa palace, where a white pheasant tribute in 650 brought the Hakuchi era. In 653 the crown prince led the court back to Asuka; Kōtoku stayed behind and died at Naniwa in 654.

zh:
孝德天皇（596—654）名轻，是日本第36代天皇，645—654年在位，皇极天皇的弟弟。乙巳之变削弱苏我氏势力后，他被拥立为帝，实权则掌握在侄子皇太子中大兄皇子手中。他下诏启用日本第一个年号“大化”，646年颁布《改新之诏》，推行中央集权的大化改新。

朝廷迁至难波宫；650年进献白雉，改元“白雉”。653年，皇太子率朝廷迁回飞鸟，孝德留在难波，于654年去世。

en:
Kōzai Sukemura (1183–1235) was a Kamakura-period warrior, founder of the Kōzai clan of Sanuki Province, and a son of Nii no Sukemitsu. Fighting for the shogunate in the Jōkyū War of 1221, he won distinction and became district magistrate of Aya and Kagawa districts.

He set up his steward's residence at Saryō in Kasai, Kagawa District, from which he took the name Kōzai, and he also built Katsuga Castle on Mount Shōga. He died in 1235, aged fifty-three.

Kōzai Sukemura (1183–1235) was a Kamakura-period warrior, founder of the [ShowDynastyName('kouzai_dynasty')] clan of Sanuki Province, and a son of Nii no Sukemitsu. Fighting for the shogunate in the Jōkyū War of 1221, he won distinction and became district magistrate of [ShowLocationName('aya')] and Kagawa districts.

He set up his steward's residence at Saryō in Kasai, Kagawa District, from which he took the name Kōzai, and he also built Katsuga Castle on Mount Shōga. He died in 1235, aged fifty-three.
zh:
香西资村（1183—1235）是镰仓时代武将、赞岐国香西氏的始祖，新居资光之子。1221年承久之乱中，他为镰仓幕府方作战立功，被任命为阿野、香川两郡的郡司。

他在香川郡笠居乡的佐料修建地头屋敷，并由“笠居”的读音改称香西，又在胜贺山上修筑胜贺城。1235年去世，享年五十三岁。

en:
Kudō Kagemitsu was a twelfth-century warrior of the Kudō clan active in Kai and Izu Provinces. He backed Minamoto no Yoritomo's 1180 rising and helped rout a Taira force at the Battle of Hashidayama. In the 1189 Ōshū campaign he and his son Yukimitsu served with distinction; Yukimitsu received lands in Iwate District, founding the Kuriyagawa Kudō line.

At Yoritomo's 1193 Fuji hunt, Kagemitsu three times missed a great deer, declared it the mountain god's mount and his own death near, and fell ill that night.

工藤景光是12世纪活动于甲斐、伊豆两国的工藤氏武士。1180年源赖朝举兵，他起兵响应，在波志田山合战中协助击溃平家军队。1189年奥州合战时，他与儿子工藤行光率一族从军立功；行光受封岩手郡领地，开创厨川工藤氏一脉。

1193年赖朝举行富士卷狩，景光三射大鹿不中，称此鹿乃山神坐骑、自己命数将尽，当夜便病倒。

en:
Kudō no Korekage was an eleventh-century warrior of the Kudō clan, listed in clan genealogies as a grandson of the clan's founder Fujiwara no Tamenori and son of Kudō Tokisato, with the title Suruga no kami.

Genealogies and local tradition record that he settled at the Kanō manor in Izu around 1050 and took its place name, becoming the ancestor of the Kanō warrior house, from which the painters of the Kanō school later claimed descent. His son Koremoto is recorded as ōryōshi, military chief of Izu.

en:
Kudō Sadasuke was a late-Kamakura inner retainer of the Hōjō Tokusō, the son of Kudō Tokimitsu. He received the character sada from Hōjō Sadatoki at his coming of age and served both Sadatoki and Hōjō Takatoki.

From 1308 to 1331 he superintended the rebuilding of Tada-in in Settsu, and from 1309 to 1324 he was deputy shugo of Wakasa. In 1326 he took the field against the Andō rebellion in Ōshū and captured Andō Suenaga.

en:
Kudō Sadayuki was a warrior of Tsugaru in the late Kamakura and Nanboku-chō periods. A Hōjō retainer, he entered Inaka district and fought for Kamakura when the Andō rebelled in 1322. After the shogunate fell in 1333, he joined the imperial army under Kitabatake Akiie and fought at the Battle of Daikōji against Hōjō remnants.

In 1335 he received Kudō Sadasuke's former estates. With no legitimate son, he left them to his daughter, wife of Nambu lord Nobumasa; the lands became the Nambu base in Tsugaru.

工藤贞行是津轻的武将，活跃于镰仓时代末期至南北朝时代。身为北条氏的御内人，他进入津轻田舍郡赴任，1322年安东氏之乱时为镰仓方作战。1333年镰仓幕府灭亡后，他加入北畠显家的朝廷军，在大光寺合战中征讨北条残党。

1335年他获赐工藤贞祐的旧领。因无嫡子，他把所领让给嫁给南部氏信政的女儿，这些领地日后成为南部氏进出津轻的据点。

en:
Kudō Sukenaga was an early-Kamakura warrior and gokenin, the third son of Kudō Suketsune. When his father was killed by the Soga brothers during the Fuji hunt in 1193, he was appointed jitō of Nagano in Ise Province, receiving the districts of Anō and Aki to subdue the remaining Taira followers.

His son Sukemasa settled at Nagano and took its name, founding the Nagano Kudō family, which grew into a powerful local warrior house in Ise.

其子工藤祐政移居长野并以地名为姓，开创长野工藤氏，后来成为伊势国有力的国人家族。

en:
Kudō Suketaka was the sixth head of the Kudō clan and the lord who developed Kusumi Manor in Izu Province. He gave the clan's old Kanō Manor to his fourth son Shigemitsu, founder of the Kanō clan, and settled at Kusumi, where he founded the Itō clan.

After his heir Sukeie died early, Suketaka divided his Kusumi lands between his son Suketsugu and his grandson Itō Sukechika. The disputed inheritance drew the Kudō, Itō and Kawazu lines into a blood feud that ended with the Revenge of the Soga Brothers in 1193.

工藤祐隆是工藤氏第六代当主、伊豆国久须美庄的开发领主。他把一族旧领狩野庄交给四子茂光，茂光为狩野氏之祖；自己则移居久须美，开创伊东氏。

嫡子祐家早逝后，祐隆将久须美的领地分给儿子祐继与孙子伊东祐亲。这场继承纠纷把工藤、伊东、河津三家卷入仇杀，最终酿成1193年的曾我兄弟复仇事件。

en:
Kudō Suketsugu (1120–1162) was a warrior of the Kudō clan in Izu Province in the late Heian period. An adopted son of Kudō Suketaka, he was not meant to be heir, but after Itō Sukeie died young he received the Itō Manor and succeeded as family head.

Before dying he arranged for his son Suketsune to marry Mangō Gozen, daughter of Itō Sukechika, after coming of age, and Sukechika became the boy's guardian. After Suketsugu's death in 1162 Sukechika seized Suketsune's lands, opening the feud that ended with the Revenge of the Soga Brothers.

en:
Kudō Suketsune (1147–1193) was a late-Heian warrior of the Fujiwara Nanke line, heir of Kudō Suketsugu in Izu Province. While he served Taira no Shigemori in Kyoto, his guardian Itō Sukechika seized his estate and wife, and in 1176 Suketsune's men ambushed Sukechika and killed his son Kawazu Sukeyasu.

After Minamoto no Yoritomo rose in 1180, Suketsune became his Kamakura attendant, valued for court music and knowledge of the capital, and joined the 1184 Taira campaign. In 1193, at Yoritomo's Fuji hunt, Sukeyasu's sons the Soga brothers slew him in revenge.

工藤祐经（1147—1193）是平安时代末期武士，出身藤原南家，为伊豆国工藤祐继的嫡子。他在京都侍奉平重盛期间，后见人伊东祐亲夺取了他的领地与妻子；1176年，祐经派郎党伏击祐亲，未能得手，却射杀其嫡子河津祐泰。

1180年源赖朝举兵后，祐经前往镰仓臣从，以通晓都中风物与歌舞音乐成为赖朝的近侍，并参加1184年讨伐平氏的战役。1193年，在赖朝于富士山麓举行的卷狩中，祐泰之子曾我兄弟为报父仇将他刺杀。

en:
Kudō Takamitsu was a powerful inner retainer of the Hōjō Tokusō in the late Kamakura period. When Daijō Takamoto, head of the Hitachi Daijō house, died in 1289, Takamitsu intervened in its succession, securing the expulsion of the heir Tsunemoto and installing his own grandson Chōju, later called Tokimoto, as family head.

The brothers' lawsuit ran for more than twenty years and ended in Tokimoto's favour. Genealogies make Takamitsu the son of Kudō Shigemitsu and the father of Kudō Tokimitsu.

工藤高光是镰仓时代后期北条得宗家权势颇重的御内人。1289年，常陆国大掾氏当主大掾孝幹去世，高光出面干预其家督继承，使原定继承人经幹遭到放逐，改立自己的外孙长寿（后名时幹）为大掾氏当主。

en:
Fujiwara no Tamenori was a mid-Heian noble and warrior of the Fujiwara Southern House, son of Hitachi governor Fujiwara no Korechika and cousin of Taira no Masakado. Defeated by Masakado in 939, he fled to his kinsman Taira no Sadamori.

In the second month of 940, as an imperial commander with Sadamori and Fujiwara no Hidesato, he helped destroy Masakado and freed his father. Rewarded with junior fifth rank and the office of moku no suke, he took the title Kudō Taifu, becoming ancestor of the Kudō clan, and later held provisional governorships in several provinces.

en:
Kudō Tokimitsu was a late-Kamakura warrior and inner retainer of the Hōjō Tokusō, a member of the Ōshū Kudō lineage; the Southern House Itō Fujiwara genealogy identifies him as the son of Kudō Takamitsu. After taking the tonsure he was called the lay monk Jirōuemon Nyūdō.

en:
Kudō no Yukitō was a Heian-period courtier of the Kudō clan, a Southern Fujiwara branch, who held Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade; the Nikaidō genealogy names him governor of Tōtōmi.

The Sonpi Bunmyaku makes him the son of Kudō no Koreyuki who, in the Hōen era (1135–1141), killed the provincial governor and was exiled to Owari, taking the byname Shirao Saburō. He married a daughter of Fujiwara no Suekane, and his son Nikaidō Yukimasa became the Kamakura shogunate's Mandokoro chief and one of its thirteen councillors.

en:
Prince Kusakabe (662–689) was the son of Emperor Tenmu and Empress Jitō and crown prince from 681. When Tenmu fell ill in 686 he and the empress were entrusted with the government; after the emperor's death Kusakabe led the funeral rites but was never enthroned.

He married Princess Abe, later Empress Genmei; their children included Emperor Monmu and Empress Genshō. He died suddenly in 689 aged 28, before his coronation, and was posthumously honoured as Emperor Okanomiyagyou. The throne passed instead to his mother Jitō, who held it for his young heirs.

草壁皇子（662—689）是天武天皇与持统天皇之子，681年被立为皇太子。686年天武天皇病重，把政务托付给他与皇后；天武天皇去世后，草壁主持了葬礼，却始终没有即位。

en:
Kusunoki Masanori (c. 1333–c. 1390) was the third son of Kusunoki Masashige. After his brothers Masatsura and Masatoki fell at Shijōnawate in 1348, he became the Southern Court's foremost general and retook Kyoto from the Northern Court four times between 1352 and 1369, while leading its peace faction.

When peace negotiations failed he defected to the Ashikaga shogunate and served Yoshimitsu, and in 1373 he led the storming of the Southern capital at Amano. After 1379 he returned to the Southern Court and died shortly before the 1392 reunification.

楠木正仪（约1333—约1390）是楠木正成的第三子。1348年兄长正行、正时在四条畷战死后，他成为南朝的首席大将，于1352至1369年间四度从北朝手中夺回京都，同时主持南朝的和平派。

en:
Kusunoki Masashige (1294–1336) was a samurai commander of Kawachi Province, later called Dai Nankō, who became Japan's model of the loyal warrior. He answered Emperor Go-Daigo's call to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate in 1331. He held Akasaka Castle against a shogunal army, pouring down logs, stones and boiling water, then burned the fort so the enemy believed him dead.

In 1332 he retook the castle by smuggling men in among rice bales, and built Chihaya Castle on Mount Kongō, where from February 1333 he pinned down the shogunal host until Rokuhara fell on 7 May.

In 1336 he urged Go-Daigo to make peace with Ashikaga Takauji, but the courtiers refused. Ordered against Takauji at Hyōgo, he killed himself with his brother Masasue at Minatogawa; the Taiheiki says his brother wished to be born seven times to destroy the court's enemies. His son Masatsura took up the loyalist cause.

zh:
楠木正成（1294—1336）是河内国的武士将领，后世称“大楠公”，被视为日本忠义武士的典范。1331年，他响应后醍醐天皇推翻镰仓幕府的号召而起兵。他据守赤坂城，抵挡幕府大军，向攻城者投下圆木、石块，浇下滚水，随后烧毁城寨，幕府以为他已死而撤兵。

1332年，他把士兵藏入米包潜入，夺回此城；又在金刚山上筑起千早城，自1333年2月起牵制幕府大军，直至5月7日六波罗陷落。

1336年，他曾劝后醍醐天皇与足利尊氏讲和，被公卿拒绝。他奉命在兵库迎战尊氏，在凑川与弟弟正季一同自尽；《太平记》说，他的弟弟临终愿七世转生，消灭朝廷之敌。其子正行继起效忠朝廷。

en:
Kusunoki Masasue, commonly called Shichirō, was a warrior of the late Kamakura period and the Kemmu government, remembered as Kusunoki Masashige's younger brother. In the Genkō War he fought at Tennō-ji in 1333 and helped defend Kami-Akasaka castle, contributing to the overthrow of the Kamakura shogunate.

The Taiheiki presents him as Masashige's right arm and recounts that he took his own life beside his brother at the battle of Minatogawa in 1336, vowing to destroy the court's foes in seven lives.
