Kusunoki Masatoki (died 1348), commonly called Jirō, was a Southern Court warrior of the Nanbokuchō wars, the second son of Kusunoki Masashige and a younger brother of Kusunoki Masatsura.

On 4 February 1348 he served as deputy commander of the Southern army at the Battle of Shijōnawate, fighting beside Masatsura against the shogunal host of Kō no Moronao. When the Southerners were overwhelmed he was killed together with his brother.

en:
Kusunoki Masatoo was an akutō, a provincial outlaw chief, of Kawachi Province in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, traditionally remembered as the father of Kusunoki Masashige and Masasue. His name appears in no contemporary record and rests only on the Tachibana genealogy preserved in the Sonpi Bunmyaku.

Some scholars identify him with Kawachi no Kusunoki Nyūdō, a tonsured strongman and former steward of the Ōbe estate in Harima whom its peasants denounced to Tōdai-ji in 1295. He is thought to have died around 1320.

en:
Kusunoki Masatsura (c. 1326–1348) was the eldest son of Kusunoki Masashige and succeeded him as head of the Kusunoki family in the service of the Southern Court. From 1340 he administered Kawachi Province, and in 1347 he campaigned in Kii, rallied Southern Court supporters across several provinces and defeated a Northern Court army under Hosokawa Akiuji at Sakainoura.

In 1348 the shogunal general Kō no Moronao overwhelmed his outnumbered force at the Battle of Shijōnawate, where Masatsura and his brother Masatoki killed themselves. He was later revered as the Little Nankō.

en:

When Takauji marched from Kyushu in 1336, Shigekiyo defected to the Ashikaga and fought in Kyoto, Iyo and Aki. In his later years he was overshadowed by his Southern Court brother Yoshinori.

Kutsuna Yoshinori was a naval commander of the Kutsuna clan who held Kōura Castle on Kutsuna Island in Iyo Province. Unlike his brother Shigekiyo, he served the Southern Court throughout and led the clan after his brother's death.

en:
Sasaki Dōyō (1296–1373), lay name Takauji, was a warrior lord of the Kyogoku branch of the Sasaki clan in Omi province. He served the Hojo regent Takatoki and later helped build the Muromachi shogunate, becoming governor of six provinces. Under Shogun Yoshiakira he was the shogunate's most powerful figure, engineering Shiba Takatsune's fall in 1366.

He was famed for his extravagant basara style and renga linked verse, contributing 81 poems to the Tsukubashu anthology, and died in 1373.

佐佐木道誉（1296—1373），俗名高氏，是近江国佐佐木氏京极分家的武将大名。他原仕于北条高时，后来参与建立室町幕府，历任六国守护；在将军义诠时代，他是幕府最有权势的人物，于1366年扳倒斯波高经。

en:
Sasaki Hidetsuna (died 1353), eldest son of Sasaki Doyo, was a Northern Court warrior who became head of the Board of Retainers and military governor of Kazusa province.

In 1338 he helped block Kitabatake Akiie's advance on Kyoto, and in 1340 he and his father were briefly exiled to Kazusa after setting fire to a cloister. He fought at the 1348 Battle of Shijonawate and in 1351 joined Ashikaga Takauji against Tadayoshi alongside his father, being appointed governor of Kazusa that year.

In 1353 he was guarding the fugitive Emperor Go-Kogon near Katada in Omi when a Southern Court force under Horiguchi Sadayasu attacked at Mano-ura and killed him.

en:
Sasaki Muneuji (1269–1329), also called Kyōgoku Muneuji, was the fourth head of the Kyōgoku clan. Born the legitimate son of the gokenin Sasaki Mitsunobu, he succeeded his cousin Sadamune, the third head, when Sadamune died without a male heir in 1305.

A devoted lover of waka poetry, he had poems included in the Shoku-Senzai Wakashū and Shin-Senzai Wakashū imperial anthologies. He died in 1329 aged 61, and the headship passed to his son Takauji, better known as Sasaki Dōyo.

佐佐木宗氏（1269—1329），又称京极宗氏，是京极氏第四代当主。他是御家人佐佐木满信的嫡子，1305年第三代当主堂兄贞宗无嗣而亡，由他继承家督。

他酷爱和歌，作品收入敕撰和歌集《续千载和歌集》与《新千载和歌集》。1329年去世，享年61岁，家督由其子高氏继承——高氏即佐佐木道誉。

en:
Sasaki Sadamune (1287–1305), also called Kyōgoku Sadamune, was the third head of the Kyōgoku clan. A son of Sasaki Munetsuna, he received the character sada in his given name from the Kamakura regent Hōjō Sadatoki and succeeded his father in 1297.

He died in 1305 at the age of 19, killed in the Kagen disturbance while campaigning against Hōjō Munekata. He left only a daughter, so the headship passed through his cousin Muneuji to his adopted nephew Takauji, later Sasaki Dōyo.

佐佐木贞宗（1287—1305），又称京极贞宗，是京极氏第三代当主，佐佐木宗纲之子。他从镰仓幕府执权北条贞时的名字中受赐偏讳，取名贞宗，1297年继承父亲的家督。

1305年去世，年仅19岁，在嘉元之乱中随讨伐北条宗方的军队作战时阵亡。他只留下一个女儿，家督于是经堂兄宗氏，传给养子外甥高氏，即后来的佐佐木道誉。

en:
Sasaki Sadauji (died 1355), also called Kagami Sadauji, was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts era and a son of Sasaki Muneuji, fourth head of the Kyogoku clan. He took the Kagami family name and became a monk in 1335.

In 1341, on Ashikaga Tadayoshi's orders, he attacked a priest in Yamato, and in 1347 Ashikaga Takauji granted him a shrine stewardship in Omi. He died in 1355, and his sons afterwards founded several branch houses.

en:
Sasaki Takahide (1328–1391) was a shugo daimyō and the third son of Sasaki Doyo. He became the Kyogoku heir after his brothers fell in battle in 1348 and 1353, and after succeeding his father in 1373 ruled as military governor of Izumo, Hida and Oki.

In the 1379 Koryaku Disturbance he raised troops in Omi to force the kanrei Hosokawa Yoriyuki from office, but lost all his domains, recovering only Hida in 1381. He campaigned against a rebel in 1390, died in 1391, and his third son Takahisa founded the Amago clan of Izumo.

佐佐木高秀（1328—1391）是南北朝时代的守护大名，佐佐木道誉的三子。两位兄长先后于1348年、1353年战死，他因而成为京极氏嗣子，1373年继承家督，历任出云、飞驒、隐岐三国守护。

1379年康历政变中，他在近江举兵，迫使管领细川赖之下台，却被没收全部领地，1381年仅领回飞驒一国。1390年他出兵讨伐叛军，翌年去世；其三子高久后来成为出云尼子氏的始祖。

en:
Sasaki Ujinobu (1220–1295), also called Kyōgoku Ujinobu, was a mid-Kamakura warrior and the founder of the Kyōgoku branch of the Sasaki clan. The fourth son of Sasaki Nobutsuna, governor of Ōmi, on his father's death in 1242 he inherited six districts of northern Ōmi and the clan mansion at Kyōgoku-Takatsuji in Kyoto, from which his descendants took their name.

He joined the Hikitsukeshu and Hyōjōshū, became governor of Ōmi in 1283, and founded Seiryōji, later the Tokugen-in temple. He died in 1295 aged 76.

zh:
佐佐木氏信（1220—1295），又称京极氏信，是镰仓时代中期的武将，佐佐木氏分支京极氏的始祖。他是近江守护佐佐木信纲的第四子，1242年父亲死后，继承北近江六郡以及京都的京极高辻宅邸，子孙由此得名京极氏。

他先后加入引付众与评定众，1283年任近江守，并创建日后成为京极氏菩提寺的清泷寺（后改称德源院），1295年去世，享年76岁。

en:
Mashiko no Masashige was an early Kamakura-period warrior and head of the Mashiko family, holders of Saimyōji Castle in Haga District, Shimotsuke Province, and retainers of the Utsunomiya.

In 1189, when Minamoto no Yoritomo marched against the Northern Fujiwara of Ōshū, Masashige led the clan's Ki-tō warrior band under Utsunomiya Tomotsuna and fought with distinction alongside the Haga clan's Sei-tō. Yoritomo rewarded the Mashiko and the Haga each with a Minamoto white banner, an honour long treasured by the family.

益子正重是镰仓时代初期的武将、益子氏当主，一族领有下野国芳贺郡的西明寺城，为宇都宫氏的郎党。

1189年源赖朝举兵讨伐奥州藤原氏，正重率领本族的纪党武士团追随宇都宫朝纲从军，与芳贺氏的清党并立战功。赖朝将源氏的白旗各赐一面给益子氏与芳贺氏，这份武勋成为益子氏长久相传的荣誉。

en:
The Mashiko clan genealogies name Mashiko no Masataka, second son of Ki no Sadataka, as the founding head of the Mashiko family of Mashiko village in Haga District, Shimotsuke Province.

He is called Ki Gon-no-kami, and the provincial gazetteer Shimotsuke-kokushi records that he built the clan's Saimyōji Castle during the Kōhei era of 1058–1065. His daughter married Fujiwara no Sōen, regarded as the founder of the Utsunomiya lords, binding the two houses together.

en:
Mashiko Masatsuna (c. 1250–1302) was a warrior of the late Kamakura period. Born the fourth son of Utsunomiya Yoritsuna of Shimotsuke Province, he married a daughter of Mashiko Munetomo and succeeded as head of the Mashiko clan, whose holdings lay around Mashiko in Haga district.

During the Mongol invasion of 1281, the Kōan campaign, he took the field under his kinsman Utsunomiya Sadatsuna. He died in the second month of 1302.

en:
Mashiko Sadamasa was a Nanboku-chō warrior and the eleventh head of the Mashiko clan, retainers of the Utsunomiya of Shimotsuke Province. The second son of Mashiko Sadashige, he held Saimyōji Castle in Haga District. Following Utsunomiya Ujitsuna, he switched from the Southern to the Northern Court and fought Southern Court armies in Hitachi.

In 1339 a force sent by Kitabatake Chikafusa seized his castles, including Saimyōji. In 1351, during the Kannō Disturbance, he led over seven hundred horse in Ujitsuna's rout of Momonoi Naotsune's far larger army, an episode recorded in the Taiheiki.

1339年，北畠亲房派遣军队来攻，他的西明寺城等城池一度失守。1351年观应之扰乱中，他追随氏纲，率七百余骑击溃兵力数倍于己的桃井直常大军，事见《太平记》。

en:
Masuda Kanemi was a kokujin lord of the Masuda clan, based at Masuda in Iwami Province on the Sea of Japan. In 1366 he cooperated with the army of Ōuchi Hiroyo, newly appointed shugo of Iwami, at a castle siege and helped subdue the province.

During the Ōuchi civil war of 1380 to 1381 he sided with Ōuchi Mitsuhiro against his elder brother Yoshihiro, helping pin down Yoshihiro's supporters. After Yoshihiro prevailed, Kanemi was confirmed in his hereditary lands and won over to the victor's side.

益田兼见是日本海沿岸石见国益田地方的国人领主，出自益田氏。1366年，他配合新任石见守护大内弘世的军队参与攻城，协助平定石见国。

1380至1381年大内氏爆发家督之争，他站在大内满弘一边、与其兄大内义弘为敌，协助牵制义弘的支持者。义弘获胜后，承认他对祖传领地的所有权，将他争取到胜利者一方。

en:
Kanetaka Masuda was a warrior of Iwami Province from the late Heian to the early Kamakura period, the fourth head of the Mikamoto house, later called Masuda, and eldest son of Mikamoto Kaneharu. In the Genpei War he was the only Iwami lord to answer Minamoto no Yoritomo's call, fighting at Ichinotani in 1184.

Appointed Iwami's oryoshi that year, he went on to fight at Dannoura, where he took twenty-five enemy ships, and secured his family's twenty-two estates. In 1192 he moved to Masuda in Mino District and took the Masuda name, beginning Nanao Castle the next year. His son Kanesue succeeded him.

益田兼高是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期石见国的武将，御神本氏（后称益田氏）第四代当主，第三代当主御神本兼荣的长子。源平合战时，他是石见唯一响应源赖朝号召的豪族，1184年参加一之谷之战。

同年他被补任为石见国押领使，后来在坛之浦之战中缴获二十五艘敌船，并确立了家族二十二处领地的所有权。1192年他迁居美浓郡益田并改称益田氏，翌年着手修建七尾城。其子兼季继位。

en:
Aritsune Matsuda, also called Hatano Aritsune, was a late Heian and early Kamakura warrior in Sagami and the founder of the Matsuda clan. His father Hatano Yoshitsune opposed Minamoto no Yoritomo's rising in 1180 and was driven to suicide, so the boy was entrusted to his maternal uncle.

In 1188 his mounted archery at the yabusame before Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine so pleased Yoritomo that he was granted Matsuda-gō in Ashigara, the finest village of his father's old lands; he took the name Matsuda Jirō and became a Kamakura gokenin.

en:
Matsura no Hisashi (1064–1148) was a late-Heian samurai and the ancestor of the Matsura clan of Hizen Province. Said to descend from the warrior Watanabe no Tsuna, in 1069 he became steward of the Uno imperial estate in Matsura District and settled at Kajitani.

He held roughly 2230 chō of fields across Matsura and Sonogi districts and Iki Province, took the name Matsura, and was made kebiishi at junior fifth rank. Calling himself Gendayū Hōgan, he ruled these lands and began the Hizen Matsura warrior band.

他领有松浦郡、彼杵郡和壹岐国约2230町田地，遂以松浦为姓，后任检非违使，叙从五位。他自称源太夫判官，治理上述地区，肥前松浦党的历史由此开端。

en: Matsuura no Sunao was a son of Matsura no Hisashi, founder of the Matsura clan of Hizen Province, and is named in genealogies as the ancestor of the Lower Matsura warrior party. His sons founded branch houses including the Arita and Yamashiro families.
en_rich: Matsuura no Sunao was a son of #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_matsura_hisashi').GetID],X #L Matsura no Hisashi#!#!, founder of the [ShowDynastyName('matsura_dynasty')] clan of Hizen Province, and is named in genealogies as the ancestor of the Lower Matsura warrior party. His sons founded branch houses including the Arita and [ShowDynastyName('yamashiro_dynasty')] families.
zh: 松浦直是肥前国松浦氏之祖松浦久之子，家谱中被记为下松浦党武士团的始祖。他的儿子们分出有田氏、山代氏等若干松浦党支族。

en: Migita Hirohide, a late-Kamakura head of the Suo warrior house, was the first of his line to call himself Migita and is counted as its founder. Called Hachiro, he was ordained under the Zen master Issan Kokushi with the clerical name Jodo, and fathered Shigetoshi.

zh: 右田弘俊是镰仓时代后期周防国武家右田家的当主，初代自称右田，被奉为右田氏之祖。他通称八郎，师从禅僧一山国师出家，法名净道，生子重俊。

en: Morinaga was the younger brother of Ouchi Morifusa, a provincial official of Suō in late Heian Japan, and founded the Migita branch of the Ouchi clan through his holding at Migita in Saba District.

en: Mikamoto no Kaneharu was the third head of the Mikamoto house of Iwami, succeeding his father Kanezane; in his generation and his son Kanetaka's, the family grew into a powerful warrior band in Iwami, and Kanetaka moved its residence to Masuda and adopted that name.

en:
Fujiwara no Kunikane, later Mikamoto no Kunikane, was a noble counted as the ninth-generation descendant of Fujiwara no Tadahira and ancestor of the Masuda clan of Iwami Province. Appointed governor of Iwami, he journeyed west to take office in 1114.

He stayed on after his term ended in 1118, built his residence at Mikamoto in Hamada and adopted the name Mikamoto. His family is thought to have taken root among the local elite through marriage with powerful families.

藤原国兼，后称御神本国兼，相传为藤原忠平的九世孙，出任石见守，是石见国益田氏的初代当主。1114年，他西下石见赴任。

en:
Minami Munetsugu was a commander and administrator of the late Kamakura and early Nanboku-cho periods, head of the Minami clan of Ashikaga in Shimotsuke Province. After the Nakasendai rebellion of 1335 he accompanied Ashikaga Takauji east and served the Muromachi bakufu as head of the Samurai-dokoro and as a provincial shugo.

During the Kanno Disturbance he fought for Takauji and Ko no Moronao against Ashikaga Tadayoshi, and after Moronao's murder in 1351 became one of Takauji's closest aides. He founded a temple in Ashikaga in 1357 and died in 1371.

zh:
南宗继是镰仓时代末期至南北朝时代初期的武将与官僚，为下野国足利庄南氏的栋梁。1335年中先代之乱爆发后，他追随足利尊氏东进，出仕室町幕府，历任侍所头人及诸国守护。

观应之乱中，他站在高师直与尊氏一方与足利直义作战；1351年师直被杀后，他成为尊氏最倚重的亲信之一。1357年他在足利创建寺院，1371年去世。

en:
Minamoto no Akifusa (1037–1094) was a late-Heian court noble and poet of the Murakami Genji, the second son of right minister Minamoto no Morofusa. After his daughter Kenshi, adopted into the regent house, was made empress to Emperor Shirakawa in 1074, he was appointed right minister in 1083.

When Kenshi's son ascended as Emperor Horikawa in 1087, Akifusa became the emperor's maternal grandfather. He took junior first rank and died in 1094, aged fifty-eight.

zh:
源显房（1037—1094）是平安时代后期的公卿、歌人，村上源氏右大臣源师房的次子。其女贤子被摄关家收为养女，于1074年册立为白河天皇的中宫，显房遂于1083年任右大臣。

1087年，贤子所生的善仁亲王即位为堀河天皇，显房成为天皇的外祖父。他于1094年叙从一位，同年去世，终年58岁。

en:
Minamoto no Akimichi (1081–1122) was a late-Heian court noble of the Murakami Genji, eldest son of grand minister Minamoto no Masazane. He rose steadily through court office, joining the senior nobles as a councillor in 1100.

Made provisional major counselor early in 1122, he died of a chest illness a few months later, aged forty-two, holding senior second rank, and was remembered as the Koga Major Counselor. His son Masamichi carried on the family line.

en:
Minamoto no Yoshikiyo, known as Yata no Hangandai (c. 1145–1183), was a late Heian warrior, the eldest son of Ashikaga Yoshiyasu by a concubine and ancestor of the Niki and Hosokawa clans.

After Prince Mochihito's rising in 1180 he joined Kiso Yoshinaka and entered Kyoto with him in 1183. Sent west as Yoshinaka's deputy to pursue the Taira, he met their fleet off Mizushima in Bitchū, where his army was routed and he was killed amid a storm of arrows.

zh:
源义清，通称矢田判官代（约1145—1183），是平安时代后期武将、足利义康的庶长子，仁木氏和细川氏的始祖。

1180年以仁王举兵后，他投奔木曾义仲，1183年随义仲进入京都。此后他作为义仲的代官率军西追平氏，在备中国水岛附近与平氏水军遭遇，所部在海战中大败，义清在箭雨中力战而死。

en:
Minamoto no Atsuru (933-953) was a mid-Heian warrior of the Saga Genji, great-grandson of the sadaijin Minamoto no Toru and son of the Musashi governor Minamoto no Tsuko. Born at Mita in Adachi District of Musashi, his father's posting, he was known as Mita Genji. He married a daughter of Minamoto no Mitsunaka and died in 953 at only twenty-one.

Watanabe no Tsuna, said to have been his son though his parentage is disputed, is thought to have been born in the same year. The Konjaku Monogatari preserves a tale of his single combat with Taira no Yoshifumi, governor of Mutsu.

zh:
源宛（933—953，名字又作充）是平安中期武士，嵯峨源氏左大臣源融的曾孙、武藏守源仕之子。他生于父亲任地武藏国足立郡箕田村，号箕田源二，娶源满仲之女为妻，953年仅21岁便去世。

相传渡边纲是他的儿子，父系归属另有异说，纲生于同年。《今昔物语集》载有他与陆奥守平良文一骑讨的逸话。

en:
Minamoto no Han'en was an early Kamakura Buddhist monk, the second son of Minamoto no Noriyori, who held Yoshimi in Musashi Province.

When his father was exiled to Izu on suspicion of treason in 1193, Han'en and his brother were spared through the plea of their great-grandmother, the nun Hiki-ama, and both took the tonsure. He later received the Yoshimi estate in Musashi, and his son Tameyori adopted the name Yoshimi, founding the Yoshimi house.

zh:
源范圆是镰仓时代初期的僧人，源范赖的次子。父亲领有武藏国吉见。

1193年父亲被疑谋反、流放伊豆时，他与弟弟因外曾祖母比企尼求情而得免一死，兄弟二人都出家为僧。他后来受领武藏国吉见庄，其子吉见为赖以吉见为苗字，开创镰仓御家人吉见氏。

en:
Minamoto no Kiyomitsu (1110–1168), also called Kuro Genta and Henmi Kiyomitsu, was third head of the Kai Genji and son of Minamoto no Yoshikiyo. He was born at Takeda-gō in Hitachi.

Exiled with his father to Kai after a 1130 boundary feud, he later settled below Mount Yatsugatake and took the name Henmi. He stayed out of both the Hōgen and Heiji disturbances and built his power within Kai; his son Takeda Nobuyoshi founded the Takeda clan. He died in 1168 at 59.

zh:
源清光（1110—1168），通称黑源太，又称逸见清光，是平安时代末期武将，甲斐源氏第三代、源义清之子。他出生于常陆国武田乡。

1130年因庄园边界争斗，他与父亲一同被流放甲斐，其后在八岳山南麓定居，以逸见为号。保元之乱、平治之乱他都没有参与，专心在甲斐扩张势力。其子武田信义是武田氏之祖。1168年他去世，得年59岁。

en:
Minamoto no Kunifusa (died 1119), also called Toki Kunifusa, was a Heian warrior, the sixth son of Minamoto no Yorikuni and ancestor of the Mino branch of the Seiwa Genji. In 1064 he clashed in Mino with Minamoto no Yoshiie, whose men raided his mansion over a retainers' quarrel.

In 1079 his private war with a fellow Minamoto in Tagi District brought confinement in Kyoto. He later governed Shinano and, from 1096, Izu, reaching junior fifth rank in 1099.

源国房（卒于1119年），又称土岐国房，是平安时代武将、源赖国第六子，清和源氏美浓源氏之祖。1064年，他在美浓国与源义家发生冲突，义家因双方郎党之争突袭了他的宅邸。

1079年，他因在多芸郡与人私斗被召至京都拘禁。他后来历任信浓守，1096年起任伊豆守，1099年叙从五位。

en:
Minamoto no Masamichi (1118–1175) was a late Heian court noble and poet of the Murakami Genji's Koga line, the second son of Minamoto no Akimichi. Losing his father young, he became the adopted heir of his uncle Minamoto no Masasada, and in 1155 was raised to junior third rank.

He eventually rose to senior second rank and naidaijin. Ill after 1169, he died at his Koga villa in 1175 aged 58; ten of his waka entered imperial anthologies.

en:
Minamoto no Masanobu (920–993) was a court noble of mid-Heian times, the third son of Imperial Prince Atsumi and ancestor of the Uda Genji. In 936 he left the imperial family and took the Minamoto name, and he rose to minister of the left.

Trusted by Emperors Enyū and Kazan, he ran the Council of State as ichinokami, balancing the Fujiwara regents. His daughter Rinshi married Fujiwara no Michinaga and bore Yorimichi and Empress Shōshi.

en:
Minamoto no Masazane (1059–1127) was a late-Heian noble of the Murakami Genji, eldest son of right minister Minamoto no Akifusa and maternal uncle of Emperor Horikawa. He became a councillor at nineteen in 1077, inner minister in 1100 and right minister in 1115.

In 1122 he was made grand minister of state, the first Minamoto to hold the highest court office. Illness led him to take Buddhist vows in 1124, and he died in 1127; his descendants founded the Koga family.

en:
Minamoto no Michichika (1149–1202) was a Murakami Genji noble and statesman of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods. He joined the kugyō as sangi in 1180, and in 1198 secured the enthronement of his adopted daughter's son as Emperor Tsuchimikado, dominating the court as the emperor's maternal grandfather and rising to naidaijin.

Serving seven emperors, he brought the Murakami Genji to the height of their power. He died in 1202. A waka poet, he helped plan the Shin Kokin Wakashū.

源通亲（1149—1202）是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期的村上源氏公卿、政治家。他1180年任参议，跻身公卿；1198年拥立养女之子为土御门天皇，以天皇外祖父的身份主宰朝政，官至内大臣。

他历仕七代天皇，将村上源氏推向权势的顶峰。1202年去世。他擅长和歌，曾参与《新古今和歌集》的编纂筹备。

en:
Minamoto no Mitsukuni (1063–1148), also recorded as Toki Mitsukuni, was a late-Heian warrior and the eldest son of Minamoto no Kunifusa, ancestor of the Mino Genji. He served Retired Emperor Shirakawa as a guards officer and kebiishi.

Appointed governor of Dewa, he joined the 1109 campaign against Minamoto no Yoshitsuna's family, but in 1110 he illegally entered the regent's Sagae estate and abandoned his post. In 1113 he helped defend Kyoto against the mass protest by Enryaku-ji and Kōfuku-ji monks.

他后任出羽守，1109年参与追讨源义纲一族；但1110年他滥入摄关家领有的寒河江庄，又擅自弃官。1113年延历寺与兴福寺发起大规模强诉时，他参与了京都的防卫。

en:
Minamoto no Mitsukuni was a mid-Heian warrior, the eldest son of Minamoto no Mitsuyoshi and a nephew of Mitsunaka. Around 987 he built the Emi-no-yakata hall in Settsu Province and made it his residence.

While governor of Tōtōmi, he was exiled to Mikawa for defying an imperial order; at Karijuku he is said to have founded a temple and shrine to pray for his late mother. His heir Tamemitsu married a daughter of Minamoto no Yorinobu, tying the line to the Kawachi Genji.

en:
Minamoto no Mitsunaga (died 1184), also called Toki Mitsunaga, was a Mino Genji warrior and head of the Toki clan, a police commissioner in Kyoto under the Taira. In 1180 he led troops to arrest Prince Mochihito, and in 1181 joined a revolt against the Taira; defeated and exiled to Izu, he there met Minamoto no Yoritomo.

In 1183 he entered Kyoto with Kiso Yoshinaka, then died defending Retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa at the Battle of Hōjūji in January 1184.

en:
Minamoto no Mitsunaka (912–997) was a Heian-period samurai and court official, son of Tsunemoto, who built the Seiwa Genji into a military power. He tied the clan to the Fujiwara regents.

In 969 he accused Minamoto no Tsura and others of plotting to depose the crown prince, an affair that brought down Minamoto no Takaakira, and in 986 he helped Fujiwara no Kaneie force Emperor Kazan to abdicate. As acting governor of ten provinces, above all Settsu, he was one of the wealthiest courtiers, his warriors the Fujiwara's 'teeth and claws'. He took Buddhist vows in 987 and died at his Tada manor, and his sons included Yorimitsu and Yorinobu.

源满仲（912—997）是平安时代的武士与朝廷官员，源经基之子，奠定清和源氏武力根基的人物。他把源氏绑定在藤原摄关家。

969年他密告源连等人谋废皇太子，此事导致源高明失势；986年又协助藤原兼家迫使花山天皇退位。他历任十国国司，以摄津国为根本，是当时最富有的公卿之一，麾下武士被称为藤原家的“爪牙”。987年他出家，法名满庆，最终在摄津多田庄去世，其子有源赖光、源赖信等。

en:
Minamoto no Mitsunobu (c. 1093–1145), also called Toki Mitsunobu and the Tosa Lieutenant, was a late Heian warrior and eldest son of Dewa governor Minamoto no Mitsukuni. He served retired emperors Shirakawa and Toba as Northern Guardsman and Kebiishi, counted among the Four Warriors of Toba's court.

In 1130 two men posing as the dead Minamoto no Yoshichika fought outside his Kyoto mansion; Mitsunobu raided ex-regent Fujiwara no Tadazane's residence and killed one, for which he was exiled to Tosa. Pardoned in 1143, he died in 1145.

源光信（约1093—1145），一作土岐光信，通称土佐判官，是平安时代末期武将，出羽守源光国的长男。他侍奉白河、鸟羽两上皇，历任北面武士、检非违使，列为鸟羽院四天王之一。

1130年，两名冒充已故源义亲之人在他京都宅邸前相斗，光信袭击前关白藤原忠实的邸宅，杀死其中一人，因此被流放土佐。1143年获赦，1145年去世。

en:
Minamoto no Morofusa (1008–1077) was a Heian noble, ancestor of the Nakanoin line of the Murakami Genji. The eldest son of Imperial Prince Tomohira, he received the Minamoto surname in 1020 and became a foster son of Regent Fujiwara no Yorimichi. In 1024 he married Sonshi, a daughter of Fujiwara no Michinaga, whose only non-imperial son-in-law he was.

Named inner minister in 1065, he was the first Minamoto minister in seventy years, then right minister in 1069. He died in 1077 after taking the tonsure.

en:
Minamoto no Nakamasa (born c. 1050), also called Baba no Nakamasa, was a late-Heian warrior and poet, the second son of Settsu Genji leader Minamoto no Yoritsuna. In 1095 he and his elder brother were named chamberlains to Emperor Horikawa through Shirakawa's favor, and he later served the Shirakawa and Toba courts as kebiishi.

Around 1118–1124 he captured an impostor claiming to be Minamoto no Yoshichika. Fifteen of his poems entered imperial anthologies, and between 1135 and 1142 he passed the family headship to his son Yorimasa.

Minamoto no Noboru (848-918) was a Saga Genji noble, the second son of the sadaijin Minamoto no Toru. He held a string of guards posts before entering Emperor Uda's inner circle as head chamberlain in 893 and becoming a councilor in 895, the year his father died and he inherited the famous Kawara-no-in villa.

He later rose to major counselor and senior third rank, and died in 918 aged seventy-one, known as the Kawara Major Counselor.

en:
Minamoto no Noriyori (1150–1193), called Kaba no Kaja, was Yoshitomo's sixth son and a half-brother of Yoritomo and Yoshitsune. Raised in Totomi Province after his father's overthrow, he joined Yoritomo's uprising.

In 1184 he led an army west as Yoritomo's deputy against Kiso Yoshinaka and the Taira while Yoshitsune destroyed the Taira at Dannoura. After the Soga brothers' vendetta of 1193, a careless word to Hojo Masako made Yoritomo suspect him; exiled to Izu, later accounts say he was killed there that September.

en:
Minamoto no Sukenori (951–998) was a mid-Heian court noble of the Uda Genji, the fourth son of the Sadaijin Minamoto no Masanobu. Unlike most aristocratic heirs, he studied at the State Academy, becoming a literary scholar in 975 and a palace secretary in 977.

After provincial governorships he served Emperor Ichijō, heading the imperial secretariat in 991 and joining the council as Sangi in 994. His eldest son Nariyori was the ancestor of the Sasaki clan of Ōmi Province.

en:
Minamoto no Tametomo (1139–1170), called Chinzei Hachiro, was the eighth son of Minamoto no Tameyoshi and uncle of Yoritomo. The Hogen Monogatari relates that he was banished to Kyushu in his youth and subdued the region, taking the name Chinzei Hachiro.

In the Hogen Disturbance of 1156 he fought for Retired Emperor Sutoku against his brother Yoshitomo; the tale says that after the defeat his bow arm was crippled and he was exiled to Oshima. The tale also relates that he mastered the Izu Islands and killed himself when a punitive force arrived in 1170, in an early account of seppuku.

en:
Minamoto no Tametomo (1005–1075) was a late-Heian warrior of the Seiwa Genji, son of Kai governor Minamoto no Tamemitsu. Tradition records that he became governor of Shinano and settled in Ina District, where his descendants grew into local lords.

He is counted the ancestor of the Shinano Genji and Ina Genji, and the Kaminohira fort in northern Ina is said to be his work. He died in 1075, aged seventy-one.

Minamoto no Tameyoshi (1096–1156), also called Mutsu Shirō, was head of the Kawachi Genji. The son of Minamoto no Yoshichika and grandson of Minamoto no Yoshiie, the court favoured Taira no Tadamori over him.

Around 1113 he is said to have scattered brawling warrior-monks in Kyoto with a handful of mounted samurai. In 1156 he backed Retired Emperor Sutoku in the Hōgen Disturbance; defeated, he took the vows and was handed to his son Yoshitomo, who beheaded him on 17 August 1156.

en:
Minamoto no Toru (822-895), a son of Emperor Saga, received the Minamoto surname in 838 and founded the Toru line of the Saga Genji. He rose to sadaijin in 872, though Fujiwara no Mototsune held the real power; after 876 Toru largely withdrew to his Kyoto villa.

His Kawara-no-in mansion, whose garden imitated the Shiogama scenery, and his Kokinshu poems made him famous; the Hyakunin Isshu calls him the Kawara Minister, and he is a leading candidate for the model of Hikaru Genji.

en:
Minamoto no Tsuko (891-942) was a mid-Heian military aristocrat of the Saga Genji, second son of the major counselor Minamoto no Noboru and grandson of the sadaijin Minamoto no Toru. Holding junior fifth rank, he served as governor of Musashi and went east to the Kanto.

The Fuso Ryakki records that in 919 the former provisional vice-governor of Musashi seized official stores and attacked the provincial headquarters against Governor Takamuko no Toshiharu; no punishment is recorded. His descendants flourished as the Mita Genji.

en:
Minamoto no Tsunemoto (894–961) was a Heian-period warrior and founder of the Seiwa Genji line of the Minamoto clan. A son of Prince Sadazumi and grandson of Emperor Seiwa, he became vice-governor of Musashi Province in 938.

After a clash with local magnates he fled to Kyoto and accused Taira no Masakado of plotting revolt; when Masakado rose in 939–940, Tsunemoto was sent against him but returned on learning he had already been defeated. His son was Mitsunaka.

en:
Minamoto no Yorichika (966–1057) was a mid-Heian warrior, second son of Mitsunaka and ancestor of the Yamato Genji. Serving Fujiwara no Michinaga, in 994 he was named among the warriors sent against bandits.

Denied the governorship of Settsu, he built his power in Yamato as its three-term governor, fighting Kōfuku-ji over land. In 1017 he lost his posts for ordering the killing of Kiyohara no Motonobu, and in 1049 his son Yorifusa's clash with Kōfuku-ji brought him exile to Tosa. His subsequent fate is unknown.

en:
Minamoto no Yorikuni (died 1058) was a mid-Heian warrior and court official, eldest son of Yorimitsu. He made his career as a middle-ranking officer in the capital, long serving Michinaga's daughter Shōshi.

More man of letters than soldier, he attended Michinaga's Chinese poetry gathering in 1007 and married his daughters to high nobles including the regent Fujiwara no Morozane. His real deeds were police work, like arresting an assailant in 1019, though legend sends him with his father against Shuten-dōji.

en:
Minamoto no Yorimitsu (948–1021) was a Heian-period warrior, eldest son of Mitsunaka and third head of the Seiwa Genji. He inherited his father's Tada manor, and his descendants were called the Settsu Genji.

Serving the Fujiwara regents, he attached himself to Fujiwara no Michinaga from about 990 and held several governorships. Later legend made him the slayer of the oni chief Shuten-dōji of Ōeyama, with his Four Retainers. He died in 1021, leaving his heir Yorikuni.

en:
Minamoto no Yorinobu (968–1048) was a Heian-period commander, son of Mitsunaka, progenitor of the Kawachi Genji and holder of the chinjufu shōgun title. With his brother Yorimitsu he served Fujiwara no Michinaga, who counted him among his four warrior favourites.

Yorinobu governed several provinces, and in 1030 was sent against Taira no Tadatsune of Kazusa, who had rebelled in 1028 and surrendered without resistance in 1031; the victory drew the warriors of the Bandō eastlands into Minamoto service. His son Yoriyoshi and grandson Yoshiie led the Kawachi Genji after him. He died in 1048, dharma name Renshin.

en:
Minamoto no Yoritsuna (1025–1097), also known as Tada no Yoritsuna, was a late Heian warrior and waka poet, fifth son of Minamoto no Yorikuni and heir to the main Settsu Genji line. He served Regent Fujiwara no Morozane and rose to Mikawa governor and junior fourth rank. In 1079 he helped defend Kyoto against the Enryaku-ji monks' protest.

He joined six contests and placed eight poems in imperial anthologies. He took vows in 1096 and died the next year.

en:
Minamoto no Yoriyoshi (988–1075), head of the Kawachi Genji and chinjufu shōgun, was the son of Yorinobu. As governor of Mutsu from 1051 he fought the Abe clan in the twelve-year Zenkunen War.

Crushingly defeated at the Battle of Kinomi in 1057, he won Kiyohara aid from Dewa and in 1062 stormed the Abe stronghold of Kuriyagawa, slaying Abe no Sadato and ending the war; his son Yoshiie fought beside him in the campaign. In 1063 he founded Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine in Kamakura. Ordained in 1065, Yoriyoshi died in 1075.

en:
Minamoto no Yoriyuki (d. 1157), also called Oguni Yoriyuki, was a late Heian warrior, second son of Minamoto no Nakamasa and a younger brother of Minamoto no Yorimasa. He served as a palace chamberlain and is recorded as governor of Tango Province.

In 1157, after the Hōgen Disturbance, the court exiled him to Aki for unlawfully mustering soldiers. On 23 August, while escorted out of Kyoto, he killed his Kebiishi guard Nobuzumi at Nishi-Shichijō and committed seppuku. His sons were adopted by Yorimasa, and his descendants became the Oguni clan of Echigo.

Minamoto no Yoshichika (died March 1108) was a late-Heian warrior, the second son and heir of the celebrated Minamoto no Yoshiie. Appointed governor of Tsushima, he was accused in 1101 by the Dazaifu authority Ōe no Masafusa of seizing tribute and killing people.

After slaying more officials he was exiled to Oki in 1102, but he stayed in Izumo Province and again attacked officers. The court charged Taira no Masamori with his suppression; Masamori defeated and killed him in 1108 in the Yoshichika disturbance. His son was Minamoto no Tameyoshi.

en:
Minamoto no Yoshiie (1039–1106), known as Hachimantarō, was the foremost late-Heian warrior and third-generation head of the Kawachi Genji, eldest son of Minamoto no Yoriyoshi. He fought beside his father against the Abe clan in the Earlier Nine Years' War.

From 1083 he led the suppression of the Kiyohara in the Later Three Years' War, storming the Kanazawa stockade in 1087 with his brother Yoshimitsu. Retired Emperor Shirakawa called him the mightiest warrior in the land, and legend made him a son of the war god Hachiman. He died in 1106.

1083年起他率军在后三年之役中平定清原氏，1087年与弟弟源义光合力攻陷金泽栅。白河法皇称他为天下第一武勇之士，相传他是战神八幡神之子。1106年去世。

en:
Minamoto no Yoshikiyo (c. 1075–1145) was a late Heian warrior and second head of the Kai Genji, son of its founder Minamoto no Yoshimitsu. Enfeoffed at Takeda-gō in Hitachi by his father, he called himself Takeda Kaja. In 1130 his son Kiyomitsu clashed with the local Daijō family over a boundary, and father and son were exiled in 1131 to Ichikawa manor in Kai.

Yoshikiyo became its steward around 1133 and died at Ichikawa in 1145. His descendants, led by the Takeda, became the Kai Genji houses.

约1133年义清出任市河庄司，1145年卒于市河庄。其子孙以武田氏为首，形成甲斐源氏诸家。

en:
Minamoto no Yoshikuni (c. 1082–1155) was a Kawachi Genji warrior, third son of Minamoto no Yoshiie and ancestor of the Nitta and Ashikaga clans. He inherited the Hachiman manor in Kōzuke Province.

In 1106 he fought his uncle Minamoto no Yoshimitsu in Hitachi and incurred imperial censure. He built up holdings in neighbouring Shimotsuke and in 1142 donated his Ashikaga lands to Anrakuju-in to form Ashikaga manor. His sons founded the Nitta and Ashikaga houses. He took vows in 1154 and died at Nitta the next year.

en:
Minamoto no Yoshimitsu (1045–1127), known as Shinra Saburō, was a late-Heian warrior, the third son of Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and younger brother of Yoshiie. He served in the Later Three Years' War, after which he was made governor of Kai Province and settled there.

He later fought his nephew Yoshikuni over land, and after Yoshiie's death was suspected of plotting the murder of Yoshitada. His son Yoshikiyo took the name Takeda, making Yoshimitsu ancestor of the Takeda clan; tradition also credits him with founding Daitō-ryū jūjutsu.

源义光（1045—1127），又名新罗三郎，是平安时代后期的武将，源赖义第三子、源义家之弟。他参加了后三年之役，因功出任甲斐守并在当地定居。

他后来曾与侄子源义国争地；义家死后，被疑策划暗杀源义忠。其子源义清改姓武田，源义光由此成为武田氏之祖；相传他还创立了大东流合气柔术。

en:
Minamoto no Yoshinari (1067–1133), first named Yoshishige, was a late-Heian warrior and the eldest son of Minamoto no Yoshimitsu, the effective founder of the Satake clan, though he never used that surname himself.

In 1106 he and his father fought their cousin Minamoto no Yoshikuni in the Kantō region. In 1109 his brother-in-law Kashima Saburō assassinated Minamoto no Yoshitada, head of the Kawachi Genji, drawing his line into the succession feud. He supported his father until his death from illness in 1133, leaving a son, Satake no Masayoshi.

en:
Minamoto no Yoshitomo (1123–1160) was the sixth head of the Kawachi Genji and father of Yoritomo, Noriyori and Yoshitsune. Sent east as a youth, he built ties with Kantō warrior houses and became governor of Shimotsuke.

In the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 he fought for Emperor Go-Shirakawa against his own father Tameyoshi. Three years later he joined Fujiwara no Nobuyori in the Heiji Disturbance, was defeated by Taira no Kiyomori, and was murdered by a treacherous retainer while fleeing through Owari in 1160.

en:
Suwabe no Sukenaga was an early Kamakura warrior of the line that later took the name Mitoya, a clan claiming Seiwa Genji descent from Shinano Province.

He fought for the Kamakura shogunate in the Jōkyū War of 1221 and was rewarded that same year with the jitō stewardship of Mitoya-gō in Iishi District, Izumo Province, where he then settled. His descendants made Mitoya their base and adopted the place as their family name.

en:
Miura Moritoki was a Kamakura shogunate gokenin of the Sahara branch of the Miura clan of Sagami Province. His mother had first been married to the regent Hōjō Yasutoki, so he stood close to Yasutoki's grandson Hōjō Tokiyori.

In the Hōji Conflict of 1247 he sided with Tokiyori against the Miura main family of Miura Yasumura; after its fall he was made Miura no suke and inherited the head house, founding the Sagami Miura line. After Tokiyori's death he took Buddhist vows in 1263 as Jōren.

三浦盛时是镰仓幕府御家人，出身相模国三浦氏的佐原支流。其母先嫁执权北条泰时，因此他与泰时之孙北条时赖关系亲近。

1247年宝治合战时，他站在北条时赖一边，与三浦泰村的宗家为敌；宗家覆灭后，他被任命为三浦介，继承宗家，开创相模三浦氏。1263年时赖死后，他出家为僧，法号净莲。

en:
Miura Takamichi was a Nanbokuchō-period warrior, head of the Sagami Miura clan and Muromachi shogunate shugo of Sagami Province. He fought beside his father Takatsugu at Aonogahara in 1338 and succeeded him in 1339, afterwards serving Ashikaga Yoshiakira. Made Sagami shugo by 1351, he backed Uesugi Noriaki during the Kannō Disturbance, lost the post, and in 1352 joined Nitta Yoshioki's attack on Kamakura, briefly occupying the city.

Later pardoned, he recovered his Miura lands in 1362 and was reappointed shugo in 1364. He yielded the headship to his son Takatsura and died between 1367 and 1376.

zh:
三浦高通是南北朝时代武将，相模三浦氏当主、室町幕府相模守护。1338年他随父高继参加青野原之战，1339年继任家督，出仕足利义诠。1351年前他受任相模守护，观应之扰乱中依附上杉宪显，不久被解职，1352年又随新田义兴等攻打镰仓，一度攻占该城。

en:
Miura Takatsugu (died 1339) was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Nanbokuchō periods and head of the Sagami Miura clan. The son of Miura Tokitsugu, he probably received the character 高 in his name from Hōjō Takatoki. During the 1335 Nakasendai Rebellion his father joined Hōjō Tokiyuki and was executed, while Takatsugu sided with Emperor Go-Daigo and was confirmed as family head.

He later joined Ashikaga Takauji, headed the Muromachi shogunate's Board of Retainers, and fought at Aonogahara in 1338 against Kitabatake Akiie. He died the following year.

三浦高继（1339年卒）是镰仓末期至南北朝时代的武将，相模三浦氏当主。他是三浦时继之子，名中“高”字一般认为得自北条高时的偏讳。1335年中先代之乱中，其父时继追随北条时行，败后被斩；高继始终站在后醍醐天皇一方，得承家督。

en:
Miura Takatsura (died between 1402 and 1407) was a Muromachi-period warrior, head of the Sagami Miura clan and Muromachi shogunate shugo of Sagami Province, with the title Miura-no-suke. The son of Takamichi, he founded the temple Enichizan Tōshōji in Kazusa Province.

He served as Sagami shugo from 1377 to 1402 and became a Buddhist monk between 1395 and 1400. He handed the headship and the title Miura-no-suke to Takamitsu sometime from 1402 to 1407 and died soon afterwards.

en:
Miura Tametsugu was a late-Heian warrior of Sagami province, head of the Miura house and son of Miura Tamemichi, later regarded as the clan's real founder. He followed Minamoto no Yoshiie in the Later Three Years' War of 1083 to 1087 and won distinction there.

A war chronicle recounts that when the young Kamakura Kagemasa was shot in the eye, Tametsugu first trod on his face to pull out the arrow; when Kagemasa angrily resisted, he knelt to remove it instead. His son Yoshitsugu succeeded him.

Miura Tokitsugu was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts era and head of the Sagami Miura clan with the title Miura no suke, succeeding his father Miura Tokiaki.

In 1331 he fought for the shogunate against Emperor Go-Daigo at the siege of Kasagi. In 1335 he joined Hōjō Tokiyuki's Nakasendai Rebellion against the Kenmu government; after Ashikaga Takauji retook Kamakura, Tokitsugu fled by sea to Atsuta in Owari Province, was captured and sent to Kyoto and beheaded, his head exposed.

Miura Yasumura (1184?–1247) was head of the Miura clan and the second son of Yoshimura. In the Jōkyū Disturbance of 1221 he distinguished himself in the shogunate army; Hōjō Yasutoki, his sponsor, gave him the character 'yasu' and a daughter in marriage.

他后来担任将军宗尊亲王的随兵，1264年护卫亲王迁入小町的新邸。1290年十一月，他捕获并斩首北条时辅的遗子，此人曾策划政变并试图寻求赖盛的支持。

en:
Miura Yoshiaki (1092–1180) was lord of Kinugasa Castle in Sagami Province and head of the Miura clan. As Miura-no-suke he followed Minamoto no Yoshitomo in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 and the Heiji Disturbance of 1160, and later contacted the exiled Yoritomo.

When Yoritomo rose in 1180, he sent his son Yoshizumi with the clan host while staying, aged 89, to defend Kinugasa Castle against Hatakeyama Shigetada. After letting his kinsmen escape to Awa, he was killed when the castle fell.

zh:
三浦义明（1092—1180）是相模国衣笠城城主、三浦氏当主。他自称三浦介，曾随源义朝参加1156年保元之乱与1160年平治之乱，后来仍与流放中的源赖朝保持往来。

1180年赖朝举兵时，他派儿子义澄率族人前往会合，自己以八十九岁高龄留守衣笠城，抵御畠山重忠的进攻。他让族人逃往安房国，自己则在城破时战死。

en:
Miura Yoshimura (1168–1239) was head of the Miura clan and one of the most powerful gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate. After Yoritomo's death in 1199 he helped bring down Kajiwara Kagetoki, took part in destroying Hatakeyama Shigetada in 1205 and fought for the shogunate in the Jōkyū Disturbance of 1221.

He joined the Council of State under Hōjō Yasutoki in 1225 and in 1232 signed the Goseibai Shikimoku. He died suddenly late in 1239, the shogunate's ranking councillor after the Hōjō.

三浦义村（1168—1239）是三浦氏当主、镰仓幕府最有权势的御家人之一。1199年源赖朝死后，他参与扳倒梶原景时，1205年参与攻灭畠山重忠，1221年承久之乱时又为幕府而战。

1225年他出任北条泰时麾下的评定众，1232年在《御成败式目》上署名，1239年末骤然病亡，时为幕府中地位仅次于北条氏的宿老。

en:
Miura Yoshizumi (1127–1200), son of Miura Yoshiaki and head of the Miura clan, was a leading gokenin of the early Kamakura shogunate. In 1180 he led the Miura host to join Minamoto no Yoritomo but arrived too late for Ishibashiyama; after repulsing Hatakeyama Shigetada at Yuigahama he fled to Awa while his father fell at Kinugasa.

He fought at Ichinotani, Dannoura and in the Ōshū campaign, and in 1199 joined the thirteen-man council under shōgun Yoriie. He died in 1200, days after Kajiwara Kagetoki's overthrow.

zh:
三浦义澄（1127—1200）是三浦义明之子、三浦氏当主，镰仓幕府初期的有力御家人。1180年他率三浦一族投奔源赖朝，却未能赶上石桥山之战；在由比浜击退畠山重忠后逃往安房国，父亲义明则战死在衣笠城。

此后他随军参加一之谷之战、坛之浦之战和奥州合战，1199年位列辅佐将军源赖家的十三人合议制。1200年梶原景时败死后数日，他随之去世。

en:
Mizawa Tamenaga, also called Tamenaka, founded the Izumo branch of the Mizawa clan. After a kinsman was granted the Mizawa manor in Nita district as jitō for service in the Jōkyū War of 1221, Tamenaga arrived there in 1302.

He grew powerful mining iron sand, running tatara furnaces and opening new fields, and in 1305 built Mizawa Castle on Mount Kamokura commanding Nita and the Shimane peninsula, then moved the family from Shinano and took the name Mizawa.

zh:
三泽为长（一作为仲）是三泽氏出云宗家的开创者。其亲族在1221年承久之乱中立功，以新补地头身份获封出云国仁多郡三泽庄；1302年，为长来到当地。

他靠开采砂铁、经营踏鞴制铁和开垦山野壮大势力，1305年在可俯瞰仁多郡与岛根半岛的鸭仓山修筑三泽城，随后将家族自信浓迁居于此，改称三泽姓。

The Mizawa served the Yamana family, shugo of Izumo. In 1391 Tametada followed Yamana Mitsuyuki when the shugo joined the Meitoku War against the Muromachi shogunate, and fell in the campaign.

en:
Shiba Kaneyori, also called Mogami Kaneyori, was the second son of the Oshu governor Shiba Iekane. In 1336 he fought the Southern Court general Kitabatake Akiie.

In 1356 he entered Yamagata in Mogami district as self-styled inspector of Dewa and built Yamagata Castle in 1357. Around 1373 the Muromachi shogunate granted him the yakata title, after which he took the name Mogami from his domain. In 1375 his son Naoie succeeded him; he died in 1379, founder of the Mogami clan.

斯波兼赖（亦称最上兼赖）是奥州探题斯波家兼的次子。1336年，他与南朝将领北畠显家交战。

1356年，他自称出羽按察使进入最上郡山形，并于1357年修筑山形城。约1373年获室町幕府准许使用“屋形”号，随后以领地最上郡改姓最上氏。1375年家督由嫡子直家继任，他于1379年去世，被尊为最上氏之祖。

en:
Momonoi Moriyoshi was a Northern Court commander in the Nanboku-chō wars. In 1336 he was posted to Bitchū and Bingo to check Nitta Yoshisada's westward advance, and he held office as shugo of Tajima from 1336 to 1338.

In 1338 he took part in the assault on the Southern Court stronghold of Shinmeiji Castle in Tajima, whose temple-fortress defenders were driven out. He may also have served as shugo of Noto around 1349 to 1351.

桃井盛义是日本南北朝时代的北朝方武将。1336年，他被部署到备中、备后，以阻击新田义贞西进；1336至1338年间他担任但马守护。

1338年，北朝军总攻南朝在但马的据点进美寺城时盛义参与此战，南朝守军最终被逐出这座寺院城塞。约1349至1351年间，他可能还担任过能登守护。

en:
Momonoi Tadakazu was a military commander of the early Nanboku-chō period, the son of Momonoi Tadatsune, shugo of Etchu Province. In 1362 he took up arms in Etchu for the Southern Court, fortifying Mount Isurugi against the Muromachi bakufu's forces in Noto.

In 1370 his father sent him to Nagasawa, where he was defeated and killed by the army of Shiba Yoshimasa, shugo of Etchu, at the Battle of Nagasawa.

en:
Momonoi Tadanobu was a Nanboku-chō general and a son of Momonoi Sadayori, younger brother of Tadatsune. In 1338 he fought Southern Court forces at Kanegasaki Castle in Echizen. In the Kannō Disturbance he followed Ashikaga Tadayoshi, fighting Takauji's partisans in Noto in 1350.

After Tadayoshi's death he served the Southern Court under Ashikaga Tadafuyu, then submitted to the Muromachi bakufu in 1367 and briefly became shugo of Etchū. By 1372 he was living in Kyoto; his death date is unknown.

en:
Momonoi Tadatsune was a Northern Court general of the Nanboku-chō wars. In 1338 he fought at Aonogahara and with his brother Tadanobu blocked Kitabatake Akiie from entering Kyoto at Hannyazaka. He became shugo of Wakasa, Iga and then Etchū in 1344.

In the Kannō Disturbance he sided with Ashikaga Tadayoshi, and in 1355 backed Ashikaga Tadafuyu and briefly occupied Kyoto. He submitted in 1367 but rebelled, routed at Nagasawa in 1370 where his son Tadakazu fell, and disappeared in 1371.

He submitted in 1367 but rebelled, routed at Nagasawa in 1370 where his son Tadakazu fell, and disappeared in 1371.
zh:
桃井直常是日本南北朝时代的北朝方武将。1338年他参加青野原之战，又与弟弟直信在般若坂合力阻击北畠显家，阻止其进入京都。他历任若狭、伊贺守护，1344年转任越中守护。

观应之乱中他追随足利直义对抗足利尊氏，1355年拥立足利直冬，一度占领京都。1367年归顺后他再度举兵，1370年在长泽之战大败，儿子直和战死，1371年后下落不明。

en:
Momonoi Yoshisuke (died 1221), also called Ashikaga Yoshisuke, was an early-Kamakura warrior commander and the second son of Ashikaga Yoshikane. He served the Kamakura shogunate.

He built Momonoi Castle in Momonoi manor, Gunma district, Kōzuke Province, and took the name Momonoi, becoming the ancestor of the clan. In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he fought for the shogunate against the court and was killed on 3 July at the battle of the Uji River, leaving a posthumous son, Yoshitane.

en:
Momonoi Yoshitane (fl. thirteenth century), also recorded as Ashikaga Yoshitane, was a gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate and the posthumous son of Momonoi Yoshisuke. After his father fell in the Jōkyū War in 1221, he was enfeoffed with the family estate at Momonoi in Kōzuke Province, settled there and adopted Momonoi as his surname.

First known as Ashikaga Shirō, he later styled himself Momonoi Ōmi-no-kami and held junior fifth rank, lower grade. Genealogies name his sons as Yoriuji and Yorinao.

en:
Emperor Monmu (683–707), personal name Karu, was the 42nd emperor of Japan and ruled from 697 to 707. Son of Crown Prince Kusakabe and the future Empress Genmei and grandson of Emperor Tenmu, he was enthroned at fourteen when Empress Jitō abdicated.

In 701 he proclaimed the Taihō era name, and the Taihō Code, Japan's first Ritsuryō code, was enacted in 701 and 702. He died in 707 at twenty-five, leaving the throne to his mother because his son Prince Obito was still young; Obito later became Emperor Shōmu.

文武天皇（683—707），名珂瑠，是日本第42代天皇，697年至707年在位。他是草壁皇子与后来的元明天皇之子、天武天皇之孙，697年因持统天皇禅让而十四岁即位。

701年他下诏启用大宝年号，701至702年施行日本第一部律令法典《大宝律令》。707年他以二十五岁之龄去世，因子首亲王年幼，皇位由母亲元明继承；首亲王后来即位为圣武天皇。

en:
Emperor Montoku (827–858) was the 55th emperor of Japan, reigning from 850 to 858. The eldest son of Emperor Ninmyō, he was made crown prince during the Jōwa Incident of 842 and succeeded his father in 850.

Later that year Fujiwara no Yoshifusa secured the appointment of his own infant grandson, Prince Korehito, as crown prince ahead of Montoku's eldest son, marking the rising power of the Fujiwara regents. In poor health throughout his reign, Montoku died suddenly in 858 at the age of thirty-two.

文德天皇（827—858）是日本第55代天皇，850年至858年在位。他是仁明天皇长子，842年承和之变中被立为皇太子，850年继位。

同年晚些时候，藤原良房将自己尚在襁褓的外孙惟仁亲王推上皇太子之位，排在文德长子之前，标志着藤原摄关势力的崛起。文德天皇在位期间一直体弱，858年突然病逝，时年32岁。

en:
Mōri Chikahira (died 1375) was a Nanboku-chō warrior and steward of Yoshida-no-shō in Aki Province. He first fought for the Southern Court with his father Sadachika, then submitted through his grandfather Tokichika and moved to Aki. As his son Motoharu had already inherited the clan headship, Chikahira built Kusakazu Castle and founded a branch house.

In the Kannō Disturbance of 1350 he joined the anti-bakufu side, and while Motoharu fought in Kyushu he attacked his son's lands, repulsing the Aki shugo's siege.

毛利亲衡（？—1375年）是南北朝时代武将，任安艺国吉田庄地头。他起初随父亲贞亲为南朝效力，后来经祖父时亲调停归顺，举族迁往安艺。由于嫡子元春已经继承毛利氏总领之位，亲衡修筑日下津城另立一家。

en:
Mōri Motoharu (1323–?) was a lord of Aki Province from the Nanboku-chō into the Muromachi period and steward of Yoshida-no-shō. He served Ashikaga Takauji: first named Morochika after Kō no Moroyasu, renamed himself Motoharu when the Kō fell in 1351. In 1341, aged nineteen, he succeeded his great-grandfather Tokichika as clan head, known as Lord Kōriyama.

He fought for the Northern Court in Kyushu while his father raided Aki. After his heir Hirofusa fell in 1385, he secured the succession of his grandson Mitsufusa.

en:
Mōri Sadachika (died 1351) was a warrior of the Mōri clan of Ōe descent, active from the late Kamakura period into the Nanboku-chō wars. The son of Mōri Tokichika, he likely received the character sada in his name from the regent Hōjō Sadatoki.

Mōri Suemitsu (1202–1247), fourth son of Ōe no Hiromoto, took the name Mōri from his Sagami estate, founding the Mōri clan. A Kamakura gokenin, he served Shōgun Minamoto no Sanetomo and in the Jōkyū War of 1221 fought under Hōjō Yasutoki, winning jitō posts at Yoshida manor in Aki and Sahashi in Echigo.

In the 1247 Hōji War he sided with his wife's Miura kin, was beaten by Hōjō Tokiyori, and killed himself at Kamakura's Hokkedō with his sons; only Tsunemitsu's line survived.

zh:
毛利季光（1202—1247）是大江广元第四子，以相模国的领地取“毛利”为姓，被视为毛利氏之祖。他身为镰仓幕府御家人，侍奉将军源实朝；1221年承久之乱中随北条泰时作战立功，获封安艺国吉田庄和越后国佐桥庄的地头职。

1247年宝治合战时，他因妻子出身三浦一族而加入三浦一方，被北条时赖击败，与诸子在镰仓法华堂自尽，唯有儿子经光一支存续。

en:
Mōri Tokichika (c. 1250 – 1341) was a Kamakura-period gokenin and the fourth son of Mōri Tsunemitsu, inheriting from him in 1270 the jitō stewardship of Yoshida manor in Aki and founding the Aki Mōri line.

After the shogunate's fall in 1333, he saved his house: his son Sadachika and grandson Chikahira joined the Southern Court, but in 1336 Tokichika arranged their submission to Ashikaga Takauji in Aki. In 1337 he passed Yoshida manor to his great-grandson Motoharu, ancestor of the later Mōri lords.

毛利时亲（约1250—1341年）是镰仓时代的御家人，毛利经光第四子。1270年，他从父亲手中继承安艺国吉田庄的地头职，开创安艺毛利氏一脉。

1333年镰仓幕府灭亡后，他保全了家族：儿子贞亲和孙子亲衡投奔南朝，时亲却在1336年斡旋二人归降足利尊氏。1337年，他把吉田庄让给曾孙元春，日后的毛利大名即出自元春一脉。

en:
Mōri Tsunemitsu was a Kamakura gokenin and the fourth son of Mōri Suemitsu, his name granted by the shōgun or regent; he later took monk's vows as Jakubutsu.

During the Hōji War of 1247 he was in Echigo and escaped the ruin that killed his father and brothers: the Sagami estate was lost, but through the Nagai family's intercession he kept the jitō posts of Sahashi in Echigo and Yoshida in Aki. He later passed Yoshida to his fourth son Tokichika, ancestor of the warlord Mōri Motonari.

en:
Prince Morisada (1179–1223), a son of Emperor Takakura, was carried west by the fleeing Taira in 1183 with the young Emperor Antoku and returned to Kyoto after their fall in 1185. He married and in 1212 took Buddhist vows as Gyōjo.

After the Jōkyū War of 1221, the Kamakura shogunate exiled Go-Toba and put Morisada's son Toyohito on the throne as Go-Horikawa. Morisada was exceptionally made retired emperor, ruled in cloister until his death, and was posthumously called Go-Takakura-in.

zh:
守贞亲王（1179—1223）是高仓天皇之子，1183年平家逃离京都时，他随年幼的安德天皇一同被带往西国，1185年平家灭亡后被送还京都。他娶妻后于1212年出家，法号行助。

1221年承久之乱后，镰仓幕府流放后鸟羽上皇，迎立守贞之子茂仁王为后堀河天皇。守贞被破例尊为太上天皇，以上皇身份实行院政直至去世，死后追号后高仓院。

en:
Prince Moriyoshi (1308–1335), known as the Ōtōnomiya, was a son of Emperor Go-Daigo. Sent into Buddhist orders young, he became head of the Tendai sect, then returned to secular life and led the imperial armies that overthrew the Kamakura shogunate in the Genkō War of 1333.

Under the Kenmu Restoration he was appointed Sei-i Taishōgun. His hostility to Ashikaga Takauji cost him his office and freedom: confined at Kamakura, he was killed there on 12 August 1335 by order of Ashikaga Tadayoshi.

护良亲王（1308—1335），通称大塔宫，是后醍醐天皇之子。他幼年出家，曾任天台座主，后来还俗，在1333年元弘之乱中统领倒幕官军，攻灭镰仓幕府。

建武新政时他被任命为征夷大将军，因敌视足利尊氏而遭解职并幽禁于镰仓。1335年8月12日，他被足利直义下令杀害。

en:
First known as Prince Kōen, Munakata no Kiyōuji was by tradition a son of Emperor Uda and the founder of the hereditary priestly line of Munakata Taisha in Chikuzen Province. In 898 he became the adopted son of Minamoto no Kiyohiro, received the Minamoto name, and rose to middle counselor.

In 914, after the former Munakata head left the shrine lands, Kiyōuji was appointed its priest, adopted the Munakata name, and served until 938. His son Ujio succeeded him.

en:
Munakata no Nagauji was the son of the daiguji Ujinari, who in 1251 placed the still-youthful Nagauji in the head priesthood of Munakata Taisha while guarding the shrine's affairs himself. From around 1273 Nagauji directed the shrine in name and fact.

When the Mongols invaded Kyushu, the Kamakura shogunate reinstated him as daiguji in 1279 for coastal defense, and after the 1281 Kōan campaign he was granted five chō of Kanzaki manor in Hizen Province.

en:
Munakata Ujikuni, a son of Ujisane, was a Kamakura gokenin and daiguji of Munakata Taisha in Chikuzen Province. During the Genpei War he held Shiroyama Castle and ruled the central Munakata lands.

He first became daiguji in 1189 and returned to the office in 1213. In 1222 the Kamakura shogunate confirmed his rule over the shrine domain, and in 1232 he resigned after granting the office to Ujitsune.

en:
Munakata no Ujinari was a son of the daiguji Ujitsune, adopted by his uncle Ujikuni, who passed him the head priesthood of Munakata Taisha in 1231. The traditional list names him daiguji in 1250, and in 1251 he transferred the office to his son Nagauji but stayed on as guardian.

For decades he settled shrine-land suits before the shogunate, enlarging the domains. Ordained as the monk Jōei, he issued a further transfer document in 1273 and was still living in 1274.

zh:
宗像氏业是大宫司氏经之子，被伯父氏国收为养子，氏国于1231年把宗像大社大宫司之职传给他。传统世系表列其为1250年的大宫司；1251年他把职务传给儿子长氏，自己则继续以监护人身份掌权。

此后数十年间，他在镰仓幕府处理社领诉讼，扩大社领。出家后法名净惠，1273年再下让状，1274年仍在世。

en:
Munakata no Ujio was the second hereditary high priest of Munakata Taisha in Chikuzen Province, said to be a son of the line's founder, Munakata no Kiyōuji. He held office from 939 to 963.

During the Tengyō War, when the pirate Fujiwara no Sumitomo rebelled against the Heian court, Ujio fought the rebels in Kyushu and killed a younger brother of Sumitomo. In 964 he was followed in the priesthood by Ujiyo, generally counted as his son.

en:
Munakata Ujisane was daiguji of Munakata Taisha in Chikuzen Province, holding the office five times between 1160 and 1188. A son of daiguji Ujinobu, he married a daughter of the Ō family, Hakata traders.

In 1187 Minamoto no Yoritomo confirmed his rule over those lands and made him a gokenin, turning the shrine house into a warrior house. He died on 27 November 1189, leaving sons Ujitada and Ujikuni.

en:
Munakata no Ujitada was a son of Ujizane, daiguji of Munakata Taisha in Chikuzen Province. He married a daughter of the Zhang family, Song merchants in Hakata, tying the house to Kyushu's China trade.

His daughter married Mutō Sukeyori, founder of the Mutō warrior house, while his son Ujinaka briefly served as the shrine's daiguji in 1198. In 1220 his wife adopted Mutō Tameyori and passed him three villages, prompting a long lawsuit.

en:
Munakata Ujitoshi was a head of the Munakata clan of Chikuzen, the maritime warrior house that monopolized the high-priesthood of Munakata Taisha, whose clan held the jitō office of Ishida estate on Iki from 1344.

In 1365 the Muromachi bakufu appointed Ujitoshi shugo of Iki Province, an office he held for some years after 1365 as a member of the Isshiki faction. His son Ujiyori succeeded him as both Iki shugo and high priest.

Munakata Ujiyori was the son of Munakata Ujitoshi, head of the Chikuzen house that supplied the hereditary high priests of Munakata Taisha. In 1369 he held the post of shugo of Iki Province, succeeding his father, and he also inherited the family's hereditary high-priesthood.

In 1391 he made over the headship of the main Munakata family to his younger brother Ujishige and moved east to Niwa District in Owari Province, adjoining the Isshiki shugo's domains, taking Ujishige's son Shigekatsu with him.

en:
Prince Muneyoshi (Munenaga, 1311–1385) was a son of Emperor Go-Daigo. He entered Myōhō-in in 1325 and became Tendai zasu in 1330, but was exiled to Sanuki after the Genkō War and later fought for the Southern Court.

In 1338 he sailed north with Kitabatake Chikafusa and was wrecked in Tōtōmi, and from 1344 held Ōgawara in Shinano for thirty years, earning the name Shinano no Miya. Appointed seii taishōgun in 1352, he led Southern armies and compiled Shin'yō Wakashū, completed in 1381.

zh:
宗良亲王（1311—1385）是后醍醐天皇之子。1325年入妙法院，1330年任天台座主；元弘之变后被流放赞岐，后来为南朝征战。

1338年，他随北畠亲房北上，途中座礁漂流至远江；1344年起以信浓大河原为据点达三十年，人称“信浓宫”。1352年他被任命为征夷大将军，统领南朝军队；晚年编订和歌集《新叶和歌集》，于1381年完成。

en:
Emperor Murakami (926–967), personal name Nariakira, reigned as Japan's 62nd emperor from 946 to 967. The fourteenth son of Emperor Daigo, he was named crown prince in 944 and succeeded on his brother Suzaku's abdication. Fujiwara no Tadahira remained regent until 949, after which Murakami ruled personally; his rule was remembered as the Tenryaku age of good government.

In 951 he ordered the Gosen Wakashū compiled. A skilled flautist and koto player, he died in 967, and his sons became Emperors Reizei and En'yū.

zh:
村上天皇（926—967），名成明，是日本第62代天皇，946年至967年在位。他是醍醐天皇第十四子，944年被立为太子，在兄长朱雀天皇退位后继位。藤原忠平担任摄政至949年，此后村上亲理政务，治世被后世誉为天历之治。

951年他下令编纂《后撰和歌集》。村上擅长吹笛与弹筝，967年去世，两个儿子后来成为冷泉天皇与圆融天皇。

en:
Mutō Sukeyori (1160–1228) was an early Kamakura shogunate warrior and the founder of the Shōni clan. He first served under Taira no Tomomori but surrendered to Minamoto no Yoritomo after the Battle of Ichinotani in 1184, and fought in the Ōshū campaign of 1189.

Sent to Kyūshū as Chinzei commissioner in the 1190s, he became governor of five Kyūshū provinces. In 1226 he became the first retainer to hold a junior post at Dazaifu; his son Sukeyoshi inherited the office and took the name Shōni.

1190年代他被派往九州，任镇西奉行，成为九州五国的守护。1226年，他成为首位以御家人身份出任大宰少贰者；该职由儿子资能继承并世袭，资能遂以少贰为姓。

en:
Mutō Yorihira was a warrior and gokenin of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods. Like his father Kondō Kageyori, he served in the imperial mushadokoro and lived in Musashi Province as mokudai deputy of Taira no Tomomori. During the Jishō-Juei War that began in 1180 he submitted to Minamoto no Yoritomo and became a Kamakura vassal.

His son Ujihira's descendants took the name Daihōji, while those of Sukeyori, whom he treated as a son, took the name Shōni.

en:
Nagai Munehide (1265–1327) was a Kamakura-period gokenin, son of Nagai Tokihide. At his coming of age he took a character from shikken Hōjō Tokimune. In 1282 he joined the hikitsuke court, but the Shimotsuki incident of 1285 drove him from office as a kinsman of the Adachi.

He returned after the Heizenmon disturbance of 1293, headed the appeals office and sat on Sadatoki's new shisō council, and went to Kyoto as a bakufu envoy in 1294. He led the hikitsuke from 1298 to 1309, took the monk's name Dōyū, and died in 1327.

1293年平禅门之乱后他复归，出任越诉头人，并进入贞时新设的执奏任职，1294年作为幕府使者上京。1298年他升任引付头人，任职至1309年；出家后称道雄，于1327年去世。

en:
Nagai Sadahide (c. 1278–1308) was a late Kamakura politician and warrior, son of Nagai Munehide and of a daughter of Hōjō Sanetoki. At his coming of age he received a character from the ninth shikken, Hōjō Sadatoki. In 1294 he was made a kurōdo.

In 1306 he pilgrimaged to Tsurugaoka Hachiman and the Izu and Hakone shrines as deputy for the shōgun Prince Hisaaki. He kept company with his cousin Hōjō Sadaaki and joined his cultural activities. He died in 1308 aged about thirty.

zh:
长井贞秀（约1278—1308）是镰仓时代后期的政治家与武将，长井宗秀与北条实时之女所生之子。元服时他从第九代执权北条贞时名中领受偏讳，1294年任藏人。

1306年，他作为将军久明亲王的代官，参拜鹤冈八幡宫及伊豆、箱根二所权现。他与母方表亲北条贞显交游，参与文化活动，于1308年去世，终年约30岁。

en:
Nagai Sadashige (1272–1331) was a late Kamakura gokenin and head of the Nagai clan's Kyoto cadet line, the Rokuhara hyōjōshū house founded by his grandfather. The son of Nagai Yorishige, he took a character of his name from the ninth shikken, Hōjō Sadatoki, at his coming of age.

He served in Kyoto as a Rokuhara hyōjōshū and inherited the family post of shugo of Bingo. He died in 1331, said to be aged sixty.

长井贞重（1272—1331）是镰仓时代后期御家人，长井氏京都旁支——由祖父开创的六波罗评定众家——的当主。他是长井赖重之子，元服时从第九代执权北条贞时名中领受偏讳。

他在京都担任六波罗评定众，世袭备后国守护，于1331年去世，享年60岁。

en:
Sadayori Nagai was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts era, the fourth head of the Nagai house of Bingo province. He served the Kamakura shogunate, then after the Kenmu Restoration of 1333 followed Ashikaga Takauji, acquiring manor stewardships in several provinces alongside his Bingo lands.

When the Kannō Disturbance threw Bingo into disorder after 1351, he sent reinforcements to the provincial shugo. In 1363 he fought Ashikaga Tadafuyu's party at Miyauchi in Bingo and was killed.

zh:
长井贞赖是镰仓末期至南北朝时代的武将，备后国长井氏第四代当主。他初仕镰仓幕府，1333年建武新政后追随足利尊氏，除备后的本领外，还获得数国庄园的地头职。

1351年观应之乱波及备后，他出兵支援备后守护。1363年，他在备后宫内与足利直冬一党交战，战死沙场。

en:
Takafuyu Nagai (1314–1347), also called Uma no suke, headed the main line of the Nagai, descendants of Oe no Hiromoto. His first name used a character from the regent Hojo Takatoki, and by the later 1320s he succeeded Nagai Munehide as steward of Akana manor in Mino.

When the shogunate fell in 1333 he dropped Takatoki's character, took the name Takafuyu, and joined the Kenmu Court of Miscellaneous Claims. He later served Ashikaga Takauji and died in 1347, succeeded by Ujimoto.

长井举冬（1314—1347），通称右马助，是大江广元后裔长井氏嫡流的当主。他初名高冬，名字中的“高”字得自执权北条高时；1320年代后期，他继长井宗秀之后任美浓国茜部庄正地头。

1333年镰仓幕府灭亡后，他弃用高时下赐的偏讳，改名举冬，出任建武新政杂诉决断所成员，此后追随足利尊氏，1347年去世，由氏元继位。

en: Takahiro Nagai was the eldest son of Nagai Sadashige, head of the Kyoto-based Nagai house that staffed the Rokuhara council and held the hereditary shugo post of Bingo. From 1349 to 1351 Takahiro served as shugo of Nagato province at the western end of Honshu, during the years of the Kannō Disturbance between Ashikaga Takauji and Tadayoshi.

en:
Nagai Tokihide (dates unknown, active 1247–1284), also called Ōe no Tokihide, was a Kamakura gokenin, son of Nagai Yasuhide and heir of the main line. The Azuma Kagami first names him in 1247 as Nagai Tarō, a guard at the Tsurugaoka Hachiman festival. In 1254 he joined the hikitsuke board and became a hyōjōshū in 1265.

He went to Kyoto repeatedly as the bakufu's envoy. In 1277 he carried a ceremonial cup as guardian at Hōjō Sadatoki's coming of age; after Tokimune's death in 1284 he took the tonsure as Saiki.

长井时秀（生卒年不详，活跃于1247—1284年），又称大江时秀，是镰仓幕府御家人，长井泰秀之子、嫡流继承人。《吾妻镜》于1247年首次提到他，以“长井太郎”之名担任鹤冈八幡宫放生会的随兵。1254年他就任引付众，1265年任评定众。

他多次作为幕府使者前往京都。1277年北条贞时元服时他担任持杯的后见役；1284年北条时宗去世后他出家，法号西规。

en:
Nagai Tokihiro was an early Kamakura gokenin, the second son of Ōe no Hiromoto, the shogunate's first Mandokoro chief. Holding the Nagai manor in Okitama district, Dewa province, he took its name and founded the Nagai clan. As a kurodo he attended the shōgun Sanetomo and witnessed his assassination at Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine in 1219.

After his brother Chikahiro's fall in the 1221 Jōkyū War and Hiromoto's death in 1225, he headed the Ōe house and is credited with building Yonezawa Castle in 1238. He died in 1241.

长井时广是镰仓幕府前期的御家人，幕府初代政所别当大江广元的次子。他领有出羽国置赐郡长井庄，遂以庄园为姓，成为长井氏之祖。他曾任藏人，随侍将军源实朝，1219年实朝在鹤冈八幡宫拜贺时被公晓暗杀，时广也在场。

兄长大江亲广在1221年承久之乱中失势、广元又于1225年去世后，他继任大江氏总领，相传1238年修筑了米泽城。他于1241年去世。

en:
Nagai Yasuhide (1212–1254), also called Ōe Yasuhide, was a Kamakura gokenin, the legitimate heir of Nagai Tokihiro and grandson of Ōe no Hiromoto. At his coming of age he received a character from the regent Hōjō Yasutoki's name. He held junior fifth rank by 1229 and became Kai no Kami in 1238.

After his father's death in 1241, Yasuhide joined the Hyōjōshū council. In the Hōji conflict of 1247 he backed Hōjō Tokiyori, securing the Nagai house's place in bakufu politics. He died in 1254, leaving a son, Tokihide.

长井泰秀（1212—1254），又称大江泰秀，镰仓幕府御家人，长井时广的嫡子、大江广元之孙。元服时获执权北条泰时赐以偏讳，取名泰秀。他晋升迅速，1229年已叙从五位下，1238年任甲斐守。

en:
Nagai Yasushige (dates unknown, alive in 1264) was a Kamakura-period gokenin, a son of Nagai Tokihiro and grandson of Ōe no Hiromoto. At his coming of age he took a character from Hōjō Yasutoki. While his elder brother Yasuhide's line kept the Dewa lands, Yasushige's branch settled in Kyoto under the Rokuhara Tandai.

In 1252 he became shugo of Suō and accompanied shōgun Prince Munetaka to Kamakura, later holding Bizen and Bingo as shugo.

长井泰重（生卒年不详，1264年仍在世）是镰仓时代的御家人，长井时广之子、大江广元之孙。元服时他从北条泰时名中领受偏讳，取名泰重。兄长泰秀的嫡流领有家族在出羽的领地，泰重这一支则定居京都，在六波罗探题麾下任职。

1252年他就任周防国守护，随新将军宗尊亲王前往镰仓，此后又出任备前、备后国守护。

Nagai Yorishige (dates unknown, alive in 1286) was a Kamakura-period gokenin, son of Nagai Yasushige and father of Nagai Sadashige. At his coming of age he took a character from the fifth shikken, Hōjō Tokiyori. He continued his family's Kyoto branch as a Rokuhara hyōjōshū and inherited the post of shugo of Bingo.

In 1282 he was exiled to Echigo after a forceful appeal by Kōfuku-ji, but the sentence was soon withdrawn, and records of 1286 show him back as Bingo shugo.

en:
Nagano Tanemori was a head of the Buzen Nagano, a local warrior clan of Kiku District in Buzen on northern Kyushu, and held the title of Buzen-no-kami with junior fifth rank.

Local Buzen gazetteers credit his day with building a ring of clan castles, including Ōmitsudake, Komitsudake and Shii-no-jō, which became strongholds of the Nagano kindred. The family death register records that he died in 1286 at age seventy.

Nagano Yasumori was, as Buzen gazetteers record, the sixth son of Taira no Tokimori. In 1157 he was appointed governor of Buzen, built a castle at Nagano in Kiku District, and took the place name as his family name, founding the Buzen Nagano clan.

He held the title Shuri-no-daibu with junior fourth rank, and the family death register records his death in 1178 and his Buddhist name Sūzan Hakuei. His descendants held the district as local lords for some four hundred years.

en: Naganuma Hidenao headed the main line of the Naganuma warriors during Japan's Nanboku-chō wars. When the clan could no longer keep its home manor of Naganuma in Shimotsuke Province, he moved the main house to its Nagae manor in Mutsu Province, also called the Minamiyama manor. The move split the clan into the Mutsu Naganuma and Shimotsuke Naganuma branches.

en:
Naganuma Munehide was a Japanese warrior of the late Kamakura and Nanboku-chō periods, whose father Naganuma Muneyasu held the Nagae manor in Mutsu Province. In 1299 the Kamakura shogunate confirmed him in that manor and his father's other lands under Muneyasu's deed of transfer.

In 1310 he built the Naganuma Minami-Furudate residence, and in 1312 he granted the jitō office of Naruhara village to Munezane. When the imperial schism opened in the 1330s, he took the side of the Northern Court.

en:
Naganuma Munemasa (1162–1240) was an early Kamakura-period warrior and gokenin, the second son of Oyama Masamitsu and founder of the Naganuma clan. He joined Minamoto no Yoritomo in 1180, campaigned against the Taira and the Northern Fujiwara of Ōshū, and received the Minamiaizu lands in 1189.

He supported the Hōjō and fought in the Jōkyū War of 1221, afterwards becoming shugo of Settsu and Awaji. In 1230 he passed the headship to his son Tokimune.

en:
Naganuma Muneyasu was a Kamakura-period warrior, gokenin and waka poet, the son of Naganuma Tokimune. In 1245 he guarded Prince Munetaka at the Hōjō-e festival of Tsurugaoka Hachimangū.

As shugo of Awaji he was ordered by the shogunate in 1258 to suppress akutō bands, and in 1277 he joined the Rokuhara hyōjōshū council in Kyoto. As a poet he had eight poems included in imperial anthologies such as the Shoku-Shūi Wakashū.

en:
Nagaya (684–729) was the most powerful imperial prince of the early Nara court. The eldest son of Prince Takechi and a grandson of both Emperors Tenji and Tenmu, he became grand councillor in 718.

After Fujiwara no Fuhito's death in 720, Nagaya dominated the court as minister of the left. In 729 Fuhito's four sons accused him of treason and forced him to kill himself; his wife Princess Kibi and several of his children perished with him in the Nagaya Incident.

zh:
长屋王（684—729）是奈良时代前期最有权势的皇族。他是高市皇子长子，兼具天智、天武两天皇的血统，718年拜为大纳言。

720年藤原不比等去世后，他以左大臣之尊总揽朝政。729年，不比等的四个儿子以谋反罪名逼迫他自尽，妻子吉备内亲王与几名子女同时遇难，史称“长屋王之变”。

en:
Nakahara no Munefusa was a late-Heian court official and the recorded founder of the Buzen Utsunomiya clan. A younger son of the Utsunomiya founder Fujiwara no Sōen, he served Empress Fujiwara no Shōshi, becoming senior secretary of her chūgū office at her enthronement in 1118.

After she took the nun-empress title in 1124 he became deputy secretary of her Taikenmon'in household, and many surviving documents from that office were drafted by him. Genealogies name Utsunomiya no Nobufusa as his son.

中原宗房是平安时代后期的朝廷官员，被奉为丰前宇都宫氏之祖。他是宇都宫氏始祖藤原宗圆的次子，出仕中宫藤原璋子，1118年璋子立后时出任中宫大属。

1124年璋子受院号称待贤门院后，他改任其院厅的主典代，该院厅留存的文书多出自他的手笔。各家系图把宇都宫信房记作他的儿子。

en:
Nakamura no Iechika was a late-Heian palace official of the Fujiwara Hokke Yamakage line, serving as an otoneri guard in the capital. He was the son of Nakamura no Suetaka, who as governor of Shimotsuke renamed Haga District Nakamura, and father of Nakamura no Mitsutaka, whose son Date Tomomune founded the Date clan in 1189.

One genealogy records that after his daughter's husband Kanno Masamitsu died, Iechika adopted their son Masamichi, who later became priest of Yanagawa Hachiman Shrine.

中村家周是平安时代后期的朝廷官人，出自藤原北家山荫流，在京都任大舍人。他是中村季孝之子；季孝任下野守时将芳贺郡改称中村。家周也是中村光隆之父，光隆之子伊达朝宗于1189年受封伊达郡，开创伊达氏。

据一部神主系谱，家周之女嫁给菅野政光，政光死后他收养外孙菅野正道，正道后来出任梁川八幡宫神主。

en:
Nakamura no Mitsutaka was a late-Heian court official, son of Nakamura no Iechika, serving as a hikurodo secretary to the retired empress Taikenmon'in. He married a daughter of Minamoto no Tameyoshi.

His son Date Tomomune joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's gokenin after 1180, fought in the Oshu War of 1189, and was enfeoffed with the Date district of Mutsu, founding the Date clan. Tradition makes Mitsutaka's granddaughter Daishin no Tsubone a concubine of Yoritomo and mother of the monk Jogyo.

中村光隆是平安时代后期官人，中村家周之子，为待贤门院的非藏人。他娶源为义之女为妻。

其子伊达朝宗在1180年后成为源赖朝的御家人，参加1189年的奥州合战，因功受封陆奥国伊达郡，开创伊达氏。相传光隆的孙女大进局为源赖朝侧室，生下僧人贞晓。

en:
Nakamura no Munehira was a warrior official of Sagami Province who took his name from Nakamura village in Yurugi District. In 1144 he followed Minamoto no Yoshitomo in the Ōba estate dispute and turned his own lands into the Nakamura manor as steward.

His sons and grandsons, including Dohi no Sanehira, formed the Nakamura warrior party, and in 1180 they joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's rising. In 1186 he distributed rice to the poor of Sagami on Yoritomo's orders.

zh:
中村宗平是相模国余绫郡中村乡的在厅官人，以地名为苗字。1144年源义朝侵攻大庭御厨时，他已作为义朝的属下见载，并将自领寄进，建成中村庄、自任庄官。

他的子孙中有土肥实平等人，结成号称“中村党”的武士团，于1180年随源赖朝举兵。1186年他又奉赖朝之命向相模的贫民施米。

en:
Nakamura no Sanemune was a late-Heian court official of the Fujiwara Hokke Yamakage line, son of Fujiwara no Sadato. In 1100 he was appointed governor of Mutsu, and in 1107 he led Emperor Horikawa's memorial rites.

As vice-governor of Hitachi from 1111 he built Isa Castle in Isa manor and, through the scholar Oe no Masafusa, won relief from an extraordinary tax. In 1113 he crushed the Yokoyama revolt in Musashi, then settled at Nakamura and took that clan name.

zh:
中村实宗是平安时代后期的朝廷官员，出自藤原北家山荫流，为藤原定任之子。1100年他就任陆奥守，1107年堀河天皇驾崩时担任法会使者。

1111年起任常陆介，在伊佐庄修筑伊佐城，并通过学者大江匡房为领地争取免除一次临时征税。1113年，他追讨平定武藏国的横山党之乱，此后移居中村之地，以中村为氏，是中村氏与伊佐氏的始祖。

en:
Nakamura no Suetaka was a late-Heian courtier, the son of Nakamura no Sanemune, who took the Nakamura clan name in 1113. He held junior fourth rank and served as chamberlain and governor of Shimotsuke, first living at Yamao in Hitachi's Isa manor.

As governor of Shimotsuke he settled in Haga District and, tradition says, renamed the place Nakamura after his own clan. After his term he retired to Shimodate and was known as the Shimodate chamberlain.

中村季孝是平安时代后期官人，其父中村实宗于1113年以中村为氏。季孝官至从四位下，历任侍从、下野守，起初住在常陆国伊佐庄的山尾。

出任下野守后他定居芳贺郡，相传以自己的氏名将当地改称中村。任满后他退居下馆，人称下馆侍从。

en:
Nakanoin Michikata (1189–1239) was an early Kamakura-period court noble and the fifth son of Minamoto no Michichika. He became head of the Kurōdo-dokoro in 1211 and joined the kugyō the following year. After the Jōkyū War of 1221 he was suspended from court.

Afterwards he supported his half-sister Shōmeimon-in and her grandson Prince Kunihito, the future Emperor Go-Saga. Promoted to chūnagon in 1227 and dainagon in 1238, he founded the Nakanoin house, wrote on court ceremonial, and left ten poems in imperial anthologies.

中院通方（1189—1239）是镰仓时代前期的公卿，源通亲的第五子，中院家之祖。他于1211年任藏人头，次年跻身公卿。1221年承久之乱后受到处分，停职闭门。

乱后他辅佐异父姐承明门院及其孙邦仁王，即后来的后嵯峨天皇。他于1227年任中纳言，1238年升大纳言，著有宫廷仪轨著作，并有十首作品收入敕撰和歌集。

en:
Nanbu Masanaga was a Southern Court warrior, the fourth son of Nanbu Masayuki. In 1333 he fought in Nitta Yoshisada's Kamakura campaign and received lands at Shichinohe in Mutsu, helped Kitabatake Akiie root out Hōjō remnants and held Nejō Castle.

After his brother Moroyuki fell at Ishizu in 1338 he inherited the family and repeatedly refused Ashikaga surrender calls. In 1341 he routed the Hienuki and received sword and armor from Emperor Go-Murakami. He died in 1360, leaving Hachinohe to his grandson Nobumitsu.

In 1333 he fought in #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_nitta_yoshisada').GetID],X #L Nitta Yoshisada#!#!'s Kamakura campaign and received lands at Shichinohe in Mutsu, helped #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_kitabatake_akiie').GetID],X #L Kitabatake Akiie#!#! root out Hōjō remnants and held Nejō Castle.

After his brother Moroyuki fell at Ishizu in 1338 he inherited the family and repeatedly refused Ashikaga surrender calls. In 1341 he routed the Hienuki and received sword and armor from #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_go_murakami_tenno').GetID],X #L Emperor Go-Murakami#!#!. He died in 1360, leaving Hachinohe to his grandson Nobumitsu.
zh:
南部政长是南朝武将，南部政行第四子。1333年，他参加新田义贞的镰仓攻略之战，受封陆奥七户乡的领地。他协助北畠显家肃清北条残党，后来镇守根城。

1338年其兄师行在石津战死后，他继承家督，屡次拒绝足利方的劝降。1341年他重创稗贯氏，并获后村上天皇赐予太刀与铠甲。1360年他去世，将八户乡让给孙子南部信光。

en:
Nanbu Masayuki, also called Jirō Yukinaga, was a mid-Kamakura warrior and the second son of Nanbu Tokizane, third head of the Sannohe Nanbu clan. Later genealogies name him ancestor of the Higashi clan.

They record that he married into the Kudō clan, while Nanbu family documents make his wife a daughter of Nanbu Sanetsugu. His sons were Tokinaga, Moroyuki, Masanaga and Sukeyuki, who later disputed the landed legacy of their grandfather Tokizane.

en:
Nanbu Masayuki (1328–1388) was the twelfth head of the Sannohe Nanbu clan of Mutsu province, succeeding his father Nobunaga, the eleventh head. A weak lord, he saw kinsmen usurp his estates. After the Kamakura shogunate fell he at first sided with the Southern Court, then dominant in Oshu under Kitabatake Akiie.

One account says that in 1346 he accepted Ashikaga Takauji's overtures and joined the Northern Court, fighting Southern Court forces in Oshu to expand his power. He died in 1388 aged sixty-one, and his son Moroyuki succeeded.

南部政行（1328—1388）是陆奥三户南部氏的第12代当主，继父亲、第11代当主南部信长之后继位。他掌家无力，领地遭到同族侵占。镰仓幕府灭亡后，因北畠显家经略奥州，他起初依附南朝。

另有一说称，1346年他接受足利尊氏的策反，转投北朝，与奥州的南朝势力交战以扩张势力。他于1388年去世，终年61岁，其子南部守行继位。

en:
Nanbu Mitsuyuki (1165–1236?) was a Kamakura-period warrior and the founder of the Nanbu clan. The third son of Kagami Tōmitsu of the Seiwa Genji, he fought for Minamoto no Yoritomo at Ishibashiyama in 1180 and was enfeoffed at the Nanbu lands in Kai, from which he took his name.

He accompanied Yoritomo to Kyoto in 1190. His six sons founded the clan's six main branches, and he was posthumously awarded Junior Third Rank.

en:
Nanbu Moroyuki was a Kamakura–Southern Court warrior, fourth head of the Hekii (Nejō) Nanbu branch and a son of Nanbu Masayuki. In 1333 he fought in Nitta Yoshisada's Kamakura campaign, then followed Kitabatake Akiie north to Mutsu, where he built Nejō Castle in Nukanobu, served as district governor and helped crush Hōjō remnants.

In 1338 he marched on Kyoto with Akiie, winning at Aonogahara in Mino before both fell to Kō no Moronao at Ishizu in Izumi that fifth month.

en:
Nanbu Munetsugu was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Nanboku-chō era, son of Nanbu Nagatsugu, head of the Hakii Nanbu branch in Kai. The Taiheiki shows him, styled Governor of Tōtōmi, campaigning for Ashikaga Takauji with his younger brother, notably at Shijōnawate in 1348 with Kō no Moronao, where Kusunoki Masatsura fell.

After Shijōnawate the chronicle writes his name as Minami. One theory equates him with the Muromachi councillor Minami Munetsugu, who died in 1371.

南部宗继是镰仓末期至南北朝时代的武将，为甲斐国波木井南部氏首领南部长继之子。《太平记》载其自称南部远江守，与弟弟一同追随足利尊氏转战，1348年在高师直军中参加四条畷之战，楠木正行在该役败死。

四条畷之战后，《太平记》将其姓氏写作“南”；有异说认为他就是1371年去世的室町幕府重臣南宗继。

en:
Nanbu Munetsune (1246–1283), childhood name Hikosaburō, was a mid-Kamakura warrior and the fifth head of the Sannohe Nanbu clan, Tokizane's third son. His brother Masamitsu, the fourth head, had no heir and chose Yoshiyuki as successor; when Yoshiyuki returned to Kai against his wishes, Munetsune inherited the headship.

Under him the clan declined and abandoned its Kyoto guard service and Kamakura attendance. He died in 1283 aged 38.

en:
Nanbu Nagatsugu was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Southern Court period and the third head of the Hekii, later Nejō, Nanbu branch. In 1327 the shogunate sent him to Mutsu to help crush the Andō revolt. In 1330 he went to Kyoto and served Prince Morinaga under Kusunoki Masashige.

After the prince was killed in 1335, he took Buddhist orders as Hōtatsu and backed Morinaga's son Prince Okiyo. He is thought to have fallen fighting the turncoat Akamatsu Norisuke in 1352.

en:
Nanbu Nobumasa was a Southern Court warrior of the Nanboku-chō period, the son of Nanbu Masanaga and sixth head of the Nejō Nanbu. In the twelfth month of 1335 he accompanied Kitabatake Akiie's march on Kyoto as his uncle Moroyuki's deputy and fought with distinction, and in 1345 Akinobu recommended him to a guards post at the Yoshino court.

He died before succeeding his father, and his son Nobumitsu became the next head. A later warrior chronicle makes him fall against Kō no Moronao at the battle of Shijōnawate in 1348.

南部信政是南北朝时代的南朝武将，南部政长之子，被列为根城南部氏第六代当主。1335年12月，他代伯父师行随从北畠显家上洛，在各处战斗中立功；1345年，经北畠显信推举，他出任吉野朝廷的右近藏人。
