en:
Nanbu Nobuyuki, also called Rokurō or Suketoki and later titled Satsuma no Kami, was a Southern Court warrior and a son of Nanbu Yoshiyuki. In 1333 he joined his brothers on the imperial side, and in 1335 he marched west under Kitabatake Akiie. In early 1338 he attended the Yoshino court and was named Satsuma no Kami.

In 1360 he was enfeoffed at Kuroishi and Medani in Tsugaru, and in 1363 he dedicated a bronze gong with a Southern Court date to Tendai-ji.

zh:
南部信行，又名六郎、祐时，官称萨摩守，是南朝武将，南部义行之子。1333年，他与兄长们一同投身勤王；1335年他随北畠显家西上，1338年初谒见吉野行宫，被任命为萨摩守。

en:
Nanbu Sanemitsu (born 1181) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and the second head of the Nanbu clan, succeeding as the second son of its founder Mitsuyuki. In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he joined Hōjō Yasutoki's army and fought at the Uji River.

The Azuma Kagami records him guarding Shogun Fujiwara no Yoritsune on his 1238 visit to Kyoto, and in 1252 attending the new shogun Prince Munetaka at Tsurugaoka Hachiman shrine together with his heir Tokizane.

南部实光（1181年生）是镰仓中期御家人、南部氏第二代当主，为始祖光行次子。1221年承久之乱时，他加入北条泰时的军队，在宇治川作战。

《吾妻镜》记载，1238年将军藤原赖经上洛时他担任随兵；1252年他又与嫡子时实一同供奉新任将军宗尊亲王参诣鹤冈八幡宫。

en:
Nanbu Sanenaga (1222–1297) was a mid-Kamakura gokenin and the third son of Nanbu Mitsuyuki, enfeoffed with the Hakiri valley in Kai as its jitō. In 1238 he and his elder brother Sanemitsu escorted Shogun Yoritsune to Kyoto.

Around 1269 he became a leading patron of the monk Nichiren, and in 1274 welcomed the pardoned exile back to Hakiri and built his Minobu retreat. In 1281 he founded Kuon-ji and took vows as Nichien. His eldest son Sanetsugu's line became the Hachinohe Nanbu.

南部实长（1222—1297）是镰仓时代中期的御家人、南部光行的第三子，受封甲斐国波木井乡并担任地头。1238年，他与兄长实光一同随将军赖经上洛。

约1269年，他皈依僧人日莲，成为其重要檀越；1274年将遇赦归来的日莲迎入波木井，并在身延山为其建造草庵。1281年，他舍建久远寺并出家，号日圆。长子实继的后裔成为八户南部氏。

en:
Nanbu Sanetsugu (c. 1250–1332) was the late-Kamakura second head of the Hakiri Nanbu clan, succeeding his father Sanenaga. In 1282 he escorted the frail Nichiren from Minobu to Ikegami, where he died.

In 1331, already over seventy, he joined the Genkō War for Emperor Go-Daigo and held Akasaka Castle. Captured when it fell, he was beheaded at Kyoto's Rokujō-gawara in the twelfth month of 1332, the first of the rebels executed. His son Nagatsugu succeeded him.

南部实继（约1250—1332）是镰仓时代后期波木井南部氏第二代当主，继承其父实长的家业。1282年，他护送衰老的日莲自身延山前往池上，日莲在当地圆寂。

1331年元弘之变时，年逾七旬的实继投身后醍醐天皇一方，据守赤坂城。城池陷落后他被俘，于1332年十二月在京都六条河原被斩首，是同批受刑者中最先就义之人。家督由其子长继继承。

en:
Nanbu Shigetoki (1299–1333), the clan's tenth head by its genealogies, was a late-Kamakura warrior and, by family tradition, the second son of Nanbu Yoshiyuki. Born to a Hōjō mother, he won Regent Hōjō Takatoki's trust at Kamakura and in 1329 took junior fifth rank as Right Stables captain.

In 1333 he fought for the shogunate at Akasaka, Yoshino and Rokuhara. After the Hōjō defeat at Bubaigawara and the clan suicide at Tōshō-ji, he broke out to Fujisawa and killed himself at Shōjōkō-ji.

南部茂时（1299—1333）是镰仓时代后期的武将，南部氏谱系称其为第十代当主，据家族传承为南部义行的次子。因母亲出身北条氏，他在镰仓得到执权北条高时的信任，1329年叙任从五位右马头。

元弘之乱中他站在幕府一方，1333年先后参战赤坂城、吉野城并救援六波罗。北条军在分倍河原战败、一族在东胜寺自尽后，他突围至藤泽，在清净光寺切腹自尽。

en:
Nanbu Tameshige, also called Nakayuki, was a Southern Court warrior of the Nanboku-chō wars, said by one tradition to be a son of Nanbu Yoshiyuki. In 1322 he helped storm Fujisaki Castle and subdue the rebel Andō Takitoyo. He marched west with Kitabatake Akiie in 1335 and again in 1337, and after the 1338 victory at Aonogahara was received with Akiie at the Yoshino court, where he was appointed Sakon no Shōgen.

He then guarded Kazuno in the far north, earning Kitabatake Akinobu's praise for a victory there in 1345, and died in 1346.

en:
Nanbu Tokinaga was a warrior of the Kamakura–Southern Court period, legitimate son and heir of Nanbu Masayuki. As clan head he fought a long land lawsuit against his cousin Takeyuki and half-brother Sukeyuki, who used forged documents and the backing of the Hōjō's Nagasaki vassals.

In 1333 he joined Emperor Go-Daigo with his brothers, fighting under Nitta Yoshisada in the storming of Kamakura; the Kenmu regime appointed him Kai no Kami. When Ashikaga Takauji rebelled he served the Southern Court with Yoshisada, and after the 1336 defeat at Minatogawa he vanished from the records.

The Azuma Kagami records that in 1252 father and son served together as attendants when the new shogun, Prince Munetaka, worshipped at Tsurugaoka Hachimangū in [ShowLocationName('kamakura')].

His sons included Masamitsu, who succeeded as fourth head, Munetsune and Masayuki. In later years his grandsons fought over his landed legacy.
zh:
南部时实是甲斐国三户南部氏第三代当主、第二代当主南部实光的嫡子。《吾妻镜》记载，1252年新任将军宗尊亲王参拜镰仓鹤冈八幡宫时，他与父亲一同担任供奉人。

他的儿子有政光、宗经、政行等，其中政光继任第四代当主。多年以后，他的诸孙曾围绕其遗留的领地发生争执。

en:
Nanbu Yoshimoto was a warrior of the late Kamakura period and the first head of the Kai branch of the Nanbu clan. The fifth son of Nanbu Tokizane, third head of the main Nanbu line, he was enfeoffed by his father with the Nanbu-no-shō estate in Kai Province and established his own house there.

During the Genkō War of 1333, when Nitta Yoshisada's rising overthrew the Hōjō regime, Yoshimoto returned to Kai. His heir Yoshiyuki succeeded him as second head of the Kai Nanbu.

The fifth son of #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_nanbu_tokizane').GetID],X #L Nanbu Tokizane#!#!, third head of the main Nanbu line, he was enfeoffed by his father with the Nanbu-no-shō estate in Kai Province and established his own house there.

zh:
南部义元是镰仓时代后期的武将，甲斐南部氏初代当主。他是南部氏宗家第三代当主南部时实的第五子，受父亲分封甲斐国南部庄，在当地开创家门。

1333年元弘之乱中，新田义贞举兵推翻北条政权，义元于是返回甲斐。嫡子义行继他之后担任甲斐南部氏第二代当主。

en:
Nanbu Yoshiyuki was a warrior of the late Kamakura period and the second head of the Kai Nanbu branch, based at Nambu-no-shō in Kai Province. The legitimate son of branch founder Nanbu Yoshimoto, he was chosen as successor by Nanbu Masamitsu, fourth head of the main Nanbu line, but returned to Kai against that decision.

In 1333 he marched with the Hōjō army sent to stop Nitta Yoshisada's advance on Kamakura and fought at Bubaigawara in Musashi, where the Hōjō forces were routed, opening the way for the fall of the Kamakura shogunate.

zh:
南部义行是镰仓时代后期的武将，甲斐南部氏第二代当主，本据在甲斐国南部庄。他是初代当主南部义元的嫡男，曾被宗家第四代当主南部政光定为继承人，却违背其安排返回甲斐。

1333年，他随北条军出征，在武藏国分倍河原迎战进攻镰仓的新田义贞军，北条军全线溃败，镰仓幕府随后灭亡。

en:
Prince Nariyoshi (1326–1338 or 1344) was a son of Emperor Go-Daigo by Ano Renshi, younger brother of Prince Tsuneyoshi. In 1334 he was made head of the Kamakura shogun office and sent east with Ashikaga Tadayoshi to govern Kantō.

He returned to Kyoto during the Nakasendai War of 1335 and was briefly appointed seii taishōgun. In 1336 Takauji named him crown prince under his Northern Court puppet Emperor Kōmyō, then deposed him.

The Taiheiki says he was poisoned together with Tsuneyoshi in 1338, though a contemporary diary records a former crown prince dying in 1344, which may instead refer to him.

zh:
成良亲王（1326—1338或1344）是后醍醐天皇与阿野廉子之子，恒良亲王的同母弟。1334年，他被任命为镰仓将军府将军，由足利直义奉送东下镰仓，负责治理关东。

1335年中先代之乱时他回到京都，一度被任命为征夷大将军。1336年足利尊氏把他立为北朝傀儡光明天皇的皇太子，随后又将他废黜。

《太平记》说他1338年与恒良一同被毒杀；但另有日记载1344年有一位前皇太子去世，也可能就是他。

en:
Nasu no Mitsusuke was a Kamakura-period warrior and gokenin, the fifth head of the Nasu clan of Shimotsuke and a son of Yorisuke. In 1193 he received estates in Shimotsuke from Shogun Minamoto no Yoritomo and served as host when Yoritomo held his grand hunt at Nasu.

The Azuma Kagami names him as Nasu Tarō Mitsusuke around the time of the hunt. In 1199 he founded the temple Tenshōji within his domains.

《吾妻镜》在卷狩前后以“那须太郎光助”之名记载他。1199年，他在领地内创建天性寺。

en:
Nasu no Sukefuji (died 1355) was the ninth head of the Nasu clan of Shimotsuke Province, succeeding his father Suketada. During the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts he took the Northern Court side, and in the Kannō Disturbance from 1349 he campaigned for Ashikaga Takauji.

In 1355 he was killed fighting Ashikaga Tadafuyu, together with his younger brother Ashino Sukekata. His son Sukesuyo succeeded him as family head.

en:
Nasu no Sukemura was a Kamakura-period warrior and the sixth head of the Nasu clan of Shimotsuke, son of Mitsusuke. He embraced Pure Land nenbutsu, became a disciple of the monk Shinran under the clerical name Shinganbō Kyōnen, and in 1223 founded Jigan-ji.

Genealogies credit him with a life of seventy-eight years. A modern theory holds instead that he never held the headship, which passed to his uncle Sukenaga's Iōno line and was recovered only under his son Sukeie.

en:
Nasu no Suketaka was a late Heian-period warrior and, in clan tradition, the first head of the Nasu of Shimotsuke, son of Sudō Munesuke. When Minamoto no Yoritomo rose against the Taira in 1180, only two of his sons, Tametaka and Yoichi, joined the Minamoto; the other nine sided with the Taira.

His sons founded the Nasu branch houses, among them Fukuhara and Senbon. After Yoichi, his fifth son Sukeyuki succeeded as head of the clan.

那须资隆是平安时代后期的武士，按那须氏系图为下野国那须氏初代当主，须藤宗资之子、那须与一之父。1180年源赖朝举兵反抗平氏时，他众多儿子中只有为隆和与一投奔源氏，其余九子都依附平氏。

诸子分别成为福原氏、千本氏等那须支族之祖。与一之后，五男资之继任当主。

en:
Nasu no Sukeyuki was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods and the third head of the Nasu clan of Shimotsuke, the fifth son of its founder Suketaka. In the Genpei War of 1180 he at first backed the Taira, but later submitted to the Minamoto and received lands from Yoichi.

When Yoichi took monastic vows without an heir, Sukeyuki succeeded him. With no available son of his own, he married his daughter to Yorisuke and made him the next clan head.

en:
Nasu no Yoichi (c. 1169–c. 1189) was a warrior of the Nasu clan of Shimotsuke, famed through the war tale Heike Monogatari. He fought under Minamoto no Yoshitsune at the Battle of Yashima in 1185 and rode into the sea to shoot down the fan target on a Taira warship, earning manors in five provinces from Yoritomo.

Though the eleventh son, he succeeded after nine of his brothers joined the Taira. He is said to have pardoned and enfeoffed his brothers.

zh:
那须与一（约1169—约1189）是下野国那须氏武将，因军记物语《平家物语》中“扇靶”的故事闻名。1185年屋岛之战中，他随源义经作战，策马入海一箭射落平氏战船上升起的扇靶，因此被源赖朝赐予五国庄园。

他虽是第十一子，但因九位兄长投靠平氏而继承家督。相传他后来赦免流亡各地的兄长并分给领地。

en:
Nasu no Yorisuke was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods and the fourth head of the Nasu clan of Shimotsuke. Genealogies make him a son of the Kamakura gokenin Utsunomiya no Tomotsuna, adopted as heir by the third head Sukeyuki; the character yori in his name was granted by his sponsor Minamoto no Yoritomo.

If the genealogical order is correct, his tenure was short: at Yoritomo's Nasu hunt in 1193, his son Mitsusuke had already succeeded. Another son, Sukenaga, founded the Iōno branch house.

zh:
那须赖资是平安末期至镰仓初期的武将、下野国那须氏第四代当主。系图多称他是镰仓幕府御家人宇都宫朝纲之子，被三代当主资之收为养子、立为继承人；其名中的“赖”字，相传来自源赖朝赐予的偏讳。

若系图所载继承顺序无误，他在任时间可能很短：1193年源赖朝到那须卷狩时，其子光资已经继任当主。另一子资长是伊王野氏的始祖。

en:
Nawa Akioki, son of Nawa Motonaga, was a Southern Court warrior of the Northern and Southern Courts era. After Nawa Nagatoshi and his heir Yoshitaka were killed fighting Ashikaga Takauji and the clan broke, Akioki was adopted as Yoshitaka's heir and withdrew to Higo Province under Kikuchi Takemitsu.

He settled at Yatsushiro and held Furumoto Castle, and with the Kikuchi formed the core of the Southern Court cause in Kyushu, taking Ashikita district from the Sagara. He resisted the Kyushu tandai Imagawa Ryōshun until 1391, when Furumoto was besieged and he surrendered, his lands confirmed.

zh:
名和显兴是南北朝时代的南朝方武将，名和基长之子。名和长年与其嫡子义高在和足利尊氏的交战中战死后，名和一族没落，显兴作为义高的养子继承家督，投奔菊池武光，南下肥后国。

他在八代定居，以古麓城为据点，与菊池氏同为南朝在九州的核心力量，并从相良氏手中夺取苇北郡。他长期抵抗九州探题今川了俊，至1391年古麓城被围后出降，所领得到安堵。

en:
Nawa Motonaga, second son of Nawa Nagatoshi, was a warrior across the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts years. In 1333, after Emperor Go-Daigo escaped his exile on Oki, Motonaga and his clan welcomed the emperor at Mount Senjō in Hōki Province and rose against the Kamakura shogunate, defeating its punitive commander Enya Takasada in battle.

He was known as Magosaburō and titled Saemon-no-jō, and took the Buddhist name Shin'a. He is said to have later entered religion on Mount Kōya.

名和基长是镰仓时代后期至南北朝时代的武士，名和长年的次子。1333年后醍醐天皇逃出隐岐的流放地后，基长与一族在伯耆国船上山迎驾，举兵反抗镰仓幕府，并在交战中击败幕府追讨军将领盐冶高贞。

en:
Nawa Nagatoshi (c. 1250 – 7 August 1336) was head of the wealthy Nawa shipping clan of Hōki Province. In 1333, when Emperor Go-Daigo escaped exile on Oki, Nagatoshi welcomed him to Mount Senjō and fought the Kamakura shogunate's forces there. Under the Kenmu Restoration he was made governor of Hōki and ranked among the emperor's closest generals, the Three Trees and One Grass.

He opposed Ashikaga Takauji. After the imperial defeat at Minatogawa, he was killed fighting Takauji's troops in Kyoto on 7 August 1336.

名和长年（约1250—1336年8月7日）是伯耆国经营海运的名和氏当主。1333年后醍醐天皇从隐岐配所逃出，长年将天皇迎至船上山，并在此迎战镰仓幕府军队。建武新政时他被任命为伯耆守，位列天皇最亲信的“三木一草”。

他与足利尊氏对立。1336年宫方在凑川战败后，他于8月7日在京都与尊氏军队作战时战死。

en:
Nawa Yoshitaka (1302–1338) was a warrior of the Northern and Southern Courts period and the eldest son of Nawa Nagatoshi, lord of Nawa in Hōki Province. He fought beside his father at Mount Senjō in 1333 helping Emperor Go-Daigo escape exile on Oki, and entered Kyoto with the imperial army.

Under the Kenmu government he served in the Mushadokoro and in 1334 received the stewardship of Yatsushiro manor in Higo. When Ashikaga Takauji rebelled he served under Kitabatake Akiie and fell at the Battle of Sakaiura on 10 June 1338.

en:
Niiro Sanehisa was a Nanboku-chō-period warrior and the second head of the Niiro family, Shimazu retainers in Hyūga, and son of its founder Niiro Tokihisa. In 1357, after the Southern Court partisan Nirei Yorichika killed himself at Matsuo Castle in Shibushi, Sanehisa occupied it and, together with Shimazu Ujihisa, repelled an invasion by Hatakeyama Naoaki, afterwards helping Ujihisa administer Ōsumi Province.

In 1379 he led the left wing under Ujihisa at the Battle of Minohara against the Kyūshū deputy Imagawa Ryōshun, using the Tsuki-ikki formation to defeat a larger army; the formation became a standard Shimazu tactic.

zh:
新纳实久是日本南北朝时代的武将，日向岛津氏的家臣、新纳氏第二代当主，为初代当主新纳时久之子。1357年，在志布志松尾城举兵的南朝方武将榆井赖仲自刃之后，实久进驻该城，与岛津氏久合力击退畠山直显的进攻，此后协助氏久经营大隅国。

1379年蓑原之战中，氏久与九州探题今川了俊交战，实久在氏久指挥下统领左翼，以“月一揆”阵势击破兵力占优的今川军；这一阵势后来成为岛津家的基本战术。

en:
Niiro Tokihisa was a Nanboku-chō-period warrior and the first head of the Niiro family, the fourth son of Shimazu Tadamune, head of the Shimazu of Satsuma. In 1335 he was made jitō of Niiro-in in Koyu district, Hyūga province, entered Takajō and took the name Niiro.

In the war between Emperor Go-Daigo and Ashikaga Takauji he followed the main Shimazu house onto Takauji's side. In 1349 he joined the faction of Takauji's brother Tadayoshi and received Kuni-in in Hyūga, but in 1350 Takajō fell to Hatakeyama Naoaki's attack and he moved his base to Kuni-in.

新纳时久是日本南北朝时代的武将，新纳氏初代当主，为萨摩岛津氏第四代当主岛津忠宗的第四子。1335年，他被任命为日向国儿汤郡新纳院的地头，进入高城，遂以新纳为氏。

后醍醐天皇与足利尊氏交兵时，他随岛津本家站在尊氏一方。1349年，他转投尊氏之弟足利直义一派，受领日向的救仁院；但1350年高城在畠山直显的攻打下陷落，他把据点移往救仁院。

en:
Nijō (1143–1165) was the eldest son of Emperor Go-Shirakawa, who abdicated in 1158 and kept ruling as cloistered emperor; the Heiji Disturbance of 1159–1160 opened his reign. He relied on Taira no Kiyomori, whom he made commander of the capital police.

In 1161 he foiled a plot to name the infant Norihito crown prince, purged his father's aides and ruled directly, continuing Shinzei's reforms. Gravely ill in 1165, he named his son Nobuhito heir, abdicated, and died weeks later at twenty-two.

二条天皇（1143—1165）是后白河天皇的长子，1158年父亲让位后以上皇身份继续执政，1159至1160年的平治之乱发生在他在位初年。他依靠平清盛巩固权力，任命清盛为检非违使别当，掌管京城治安。

1161年，他挫败立襁褓中的宪仁亲王为太子的图谋，罢免后白河上皇的近臣，亲自执政，延续信西的改革。1165年他病重，立儿子顺仁亲王为太子并让位，数周后去世，年仅二十二岁。

en:
Nikaidō Sadafuji (1267–1335) was a Kamakura gokenin, Administrative Board steward and shugo of Kai Province, the son of Nikaidō Yukifuji. In Kai he invited Musō Soseki to restore Jōkyōji in 1305 and found Erin-ji in 1330.

In 1331 he went to Kyoto to press Emperor Go-Daigo's abdication and joined the siege of Chihaya Castle, and in 1332 he served as steward. Pardoned after the shogunate fell, he joined the Kenmu regime but was executed in 1335 for Saionji Kinmune's Hōjō-restoration plot.

1331年他作为使者上洛敦促后醍醐天皇让位，并参加攻打千早城；1332年担任政所执事。镰仓幕府灭亡后他一度获赦，加入建武政权，却因卷入西园寺公宗复兴北条氏的阴谋，于1335年被处死。

Nikaidō Sadahira (1291–1332) was a late Kamakura gokenin and head steward of the shogunate's Administrative Board, the son of Nikaidō Yukisada. He took Buddhist vows in 1326, styling himself Gyōe, and in 1329 succeeded his late father as steward.

He held the post only briefly, dying in 1332 at the age of 42. His son Yukinao later served the Muromachi shogunate in the same office.

en:
Nikaidō Tokitsuna (born c. 1280) was a samurai administrator of the late Kamakura and Nanbokuchō eras, the son of Nikaidō Moritsuna. He first served on the Kamakura shogunate's Council of State, then took Buddhist vows in 1311 under the name Gyōin.

In 1333 the Kenmu Restoration named him the first head of the Administrative Board of the Kamakura governor's office, and the Muromachi shogunate reappointed him to that post four times between 1346 and 1350. During the Kannō Disturbance he sided with Ashikaga Tadayoshi.

en:
Nikaidō Yoritsuna (1239–1283) was a Kamakura gokenin and head steward of the shogunate's Administrative Board. The second son of Nikaidō Yukitsuna, he became heir after his elder brother died young. He joined the Board of Adjudicants in 1275, and in 1278 went to Izu to suppress a rising by monks of the Izu Gongen shrine.

He succeeded his father as steward in 1281 and joined the Council of State in 1282, but died in 1283 aged 45; his uncle Yukitada succeeded him.

Nikaidō Yukiari (1220–1292), second son of Nikaidō Yukiyoshi, was a Kamakura shogunate samurai. He became a police commissioner by 1258, but served chiefly in Kamakura as a close attendant to the three successive shoguns sent from Kyoto.

A skilled mounted archer, he joined the Board of Adjudication in 1265 and the Council of State in 1270, taking Buddhist vows the same year. Named confirmations commissioner in 1272, he died in 1292.

Nikaidō Yukifuji (1246–1302) was a warrior of the Nikaidō house's Oki branch who rose to head steward of the shogunate's Administrative Board. After joining the Board of Adjudicants in 1282, he was made steward in 1293 in place of the dismissed Nikaidō Yukisada.

en:
Nikaidō Yukimasa (c. 1140 – after 1219) was a court official and chief civilian administrator of the early Kamakura shogunate, ancestor of the Nikaidō house. Entering Yoritomo's service around 1184, he served in the new records office under Ōe no Hiromoto.

In 1191 he became deputy head of the Mandokoro, rising to co-head in 1193, and in 1199 he was named among the thirteen councilors governing after Yoritomo's death. His signatures vanish from documents under Sanetomo, and his death date is unrecorded.

en:
Nikaidō Yukimitsu (1164–1219), son of Nikaidō Yukimasa, was a Kamakura shogunate vassal who became chief steward of the Administrative Board under Hōjō Yoshitoki. A trusted aide to the nun-shogun Hōjō Masako, he directed the shogunate's administration and its dealings with the Kyoto court.

en:
Nikaidō Yukimori (1181–1253) was a Kamakura shogunate vassal and the son of Nikaidō Yukimitsu. After his father's death in 1219 the stewardship of the Administrative Board passed to his cousin Iga Mitsumune; when Mitsumune was exiled in the Iga incident of 1224, Yukimori succeeded to the post.

He took Buddhist vows in 1225 but kept his office rather than retire. He remained chief steward until he died in 1253, founding a line that held the stewardship hereditarily after him.

Nikaidō Yukimura (1155–1238), son of Nikaidō Yukimasa, was a samurai official of the early Kamakura shogunate. In 1213 he held military command on the Hōjō side in the Wada War and received the Ōi estate in Sagami Province.

Named governor of Oki in 1218, he took Buddhist vows after Shogun Sanetomo was slain at Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine the next year. Joining the Council of State in 1225, he died in 1238 in Ise Province.

en:
Nikaidō Yukinao (died 2 July 1348), originally named Takahira, was a Nanbokuchō-era samurai, the son of Nikaidō Sadahira. In 1340 he succeeded Nikaidō Yukitomo as head of the Administrative Board, the Muromachi shogunate's chief civil office.

en:
Nikaidō Yukisada (1269–1329) was a late Kamakura gokenin who twice served as head steward of the shogunate's Administrative Board. He succeeded his grandfather Yukitada in 1290 at age 22. In 1293 Hōjō Sadatoki killed Taira no Yoritsuna and overturned his appointments; Yukisada was dismissed and replaced by Nikaidō Yukifuji.

Restored after Yukifuji's death in 1302, he held the post until he died. Regarded as one of the compilers of the Azuma Kagami, he died in 1329 aged 61 and was succeeded by his son Sadahira.

Nikaidō Yukitada (1221–1290), a son of Nikaidō Yukimori, was a veteran councillor of the Kamakura shogunate. He took Buddhist vows in 1256 and later sat on the Council of State.

After his brother Yukitsuna died in 1281, the stewardship passed to Yukitsuna's son Yoritsuna, who died within two years; the sixty-three-year-old Yukitada then took the post himself. His son Yukimune died before him, and Yukitada died in 1290.

Nikaidō Yukitomo (died 1353) was a bureaucratic samurai of the late Kamakura and Nanbokuchō eras, the son of Nikaidō Sadatsuna. He first served the Hōjō regent Takatoki, but took Buddhist vows in 1326 as Gyōchin.

The Muromachi shogunate named him head of the Administrative Board three times, in 1335, 1338 and 1352. In the Kannō Disturbance he first backed Ashikaga Tadayoshi, then surrendered to Takauji. He died in 1353 after falling from his horse while accompanying Takauji to Kyoto.

en:
Emperor Ninmyō (810–850) was the 54th emperor of Japan, reigning from 833 to 850, and the first emperor born in Heian-kyō. The second son of Emperor Saga, he was named crown prince in 823 and succeeded his uncle Emperor Junna in 833.

Tang-style rites and Chinese poetry flourished at his court, and a last embassy to Tang China sailed in 838–839. After the Jōwa Incident of 842, the crown prince was deposed and his son Prince Michiyasu made crown prince. Chronically ill, Ninmyō abdicated in 850 and died two days later.

zh:
仁明天皇（810—850）是日本第54代天皇，833年至850年在位，也是第一位在平安京出生的天皇。他是嵯峨天皇次子，823年被立为皇太子，833年继叔父淳和天皇即位。

在位期间唐风礼仪与汉诗鼎盛，838年至839年还派出了最后一批遣唐使。842年承和之变后，皇太子被废，仁明之子道康被立为太子。仁明天皇体弱多病，850年退位，两天后去世。

en:
Nitsuki Sanekuni was a Kamakura-period warrior of Seiwa Genji stock, the eldest son of Hirosawa Yoshizane and grandson of Ashikaga Yoshikiyo.

After Ashikaga Yoshiuji was appointed shugo of Mikawa Province for his service in the Jōkyū War of 1221, Sanekuni moved into Niki village in Nukata district and styled himself Niki Tarō, becoming the founder of the Nitsuki house. His younger brother Yoshisue founded the Hosokawa house, and both houses served the Ashikaga main line as hereditary retainers.

1221年承久之乱后，足利宗家的足利义氏凭军功就任三河守护，实国遂迁往三河国额田郡仁木乡居住，自称仁木太郎，成为仁木氏之祖。其弟义季开创细川氏；两家同为足利嫡流的谱代被官。

en:
Niki Yoriaki (1299–1359) was a senior general and steward to Ashikaga Takauji, founder of the Muromachi shogunate. Son of Niki Yoshikatsu, he was born in Mikawa and followed Takauji from 1333, holding Tanba against the Southern Court when Takauji fled to Kyūshū. He rejoined him after Minatogawa in 1336, helped retake Kyoto from Nitta Yoshisada, and fought at Kanegasaki and Shijōnawate.

In the Kannō Disturbance he backed Takauji and became steward in 1351, holding several governorships as the office grew into the kanrei post. He took vows after Takauji's death in 1358 and died in Kyoto in 1359.

仁木赖章（1299—1359）是室町幕府初代将军足利尊氏麾下的重臣与执事。他生于三河国，为仁木义胜之子，1333年起追随尊氏；尊氏败走九州时，他固守丹波国抵御南朝追兵。1336年凑川之战后他与尊氏会合，协助从新田义贞手中夺回京都，又转战金崎城与四条畷。

观应之扰乱中他始终支持尊氏，1351年被任命为执事，身兼数国守护，其职务后来演变为管领。1358年尊氏去世后他出家，1359年在京都去世。

Niki Yorikatsu (active 1353–1365) was a warrior of the Niki clan, an Ashikaga kinsman house from Mikawa Province. He served the Muromachi shogunate as military governor of Tango from 1353 to 1360 and of Tajima from 1361 to 1365.

The Taiheiki records an attack by Southern Court forces on Ara Castle in Tajima, where Yorikatsu is thought to have held out with the castle lord Ara Jūrōzaemon.

en:
Niki Yoshinaga (c. 1300–1376) was a Muromachi-era general, younger brother of Niki Yoriaki, son of Niki Yoshikatsu of Mikawa. He served Ashikaga Tadayoshi in Kamakura, fled the Hōjō rising of 1335, then fought for Takauji at Tatara Beach in Kyūshū and stayed to subdue the Kikuchi.

He governed Ise, Iga and other provinces, and the brothers once held nine between them. After Yoriaki died in 1359 his arrogance isolated him; attacked by Hosokawa Kiyouji's coalition, he failed to seize the shōgun Yoshiakira, fled to Ise, and surrendered to the Southern Court in 1361. Later pardoned and returned to the shogunate, he died in 1376.

en:
Nitsuki Yoshitaka (died 1336) was a Nanboku-chō warrior from a cadet line of the Nitsuki clan, the Mikawa offshoot of the Ashikaga. In April 1336 a Southern Court army from Tōtōmi under Nitta Samanosuke invaded Mikawa; Yoshitaka, his son Mijirō Yoshinaga and others defeated it at Kira-no-shō and Hō District and cleared the province.

That September the Ashikaga forces invaded Tōtōmi, and on the thirteenth day Yoshitaka was killed by the Tenryū River while pursuing the Nitta army.

仁木义高（？—1336）是日本南北朝时代的武将，出身仁木氏庶流，仁木氏为足利氏在三河国的分支。1336年4月，新田左马助率领远江国的南朝军攻入三河，义高与儿子弥二郎义长等迎战，在吉良庄和宝饭郡连败敌军，将其逐出三河。

同年9月，足利氏攻入远江，13日义高在追击新田军时战死于天龙川畔。

en:
Nitta Masauji (1208–1271) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and gokenin, the fifth head of the Nitta main house and eldest son of Nitta Masayoshi. After his father's unauthorized tonsure in 1244, real power over the Nitta passed to collaterals Serada Yoshisue and Iwamatsu Tokikane.

Masauji recovered his position when Yoshisue's son Serada Yoriuji was exiled to Sado Island. A maternal grandson of Ashikaga Yoshiuji, he took the character uji of his name from an Ashikaga patron, beginning a Nitta naming custom. He died in 1271.

新田政氏（1208—1271）是镰仓时代中期的武将、御家人，新田氏本宗家第五代当主，新田政义的长子。1244年父亲擅自出家失势后，新田氏的实权落入世良田义季与岩松时兼等庶家手中。

义季之子世良田赖氏被流放佐渡岛后，政氏借机恢复地位。他是足利义氏的外孙，名字中的“氏”字得自足利氏当主的偏讳，此后新田历代当主沿袭此例。1271年去世。

en:
Nitta Masayoshi (c. 1187–1257) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and the fourth head of the Nitta main house, succeeding his father Yoshifusa at the age of thirteen under family guardianship. He married a daughter of Ashikaga Yoshiuji.

In 1244, while on guard duty in Kyoto, he sought court office without Kamakura's leave, then took the tonsure and withdrew to Nitta Manor, refusing to serve the shogunate. He lost part of his lands and the sōryō headship, founded Enpuku-ji temple, and died in 1257 aged seventy-one.

新田政义（约1187—1257）是镰仓时代中期的武将、新田氏本宗家第四代当主，13岁时在亲族后见之下继承父亲义房。他娶了权势御家人足利义氏之女。

1244年在京都担任大番役期间，他未经镰仓许可便谋求朝廷任官，事后又擅自出家回到新田庄，拒不出仕幕府。他被没收部分所领与总领职，隐居并创建圆福寺，1257年以71岁去世。

en:
Nitta Motouji (1253–1324) was a Kamakura warrior and gokenin, the sixth head of the Nitta main house. Although he was the fifth son of Nitta Masauji, he became clan head at nineteen over his elder brothers, possibly because his mother was a daughter of Akahashi Hidetoki of the Hōjō family.

In a dispute over rice fields he backed his kinsman Ōdate Muneyuji against Iwamatsu Tsunekane and his sons, but the Kamakura shogunate ruled in his rivals' favour. He died in 1324 aged seventy-two and was buried at Enpuku-ji; Nitta Yoshisada was his grandson.

新田基氏（1253—1324）是镰仓时代的武将、御家人，新田氏本宗家第六代当主。他虽为新田政氏的第五子，却在19岁时越过诸位兄长继任当主，有说法认为其生母出自北条氏赤桥流，即赤桥秀时之女。

在一场围绕水田的纷争中，他支持同族大馆宗氏，与岩松经兼及其儿子们对抗，镰仓幕府却作出有利于对手的裁决。1324年他以72岁去世，葬于圆福寺；新田义贞是他的孙子。

en:
Nitta Tomouji (1274–1318) was a Kamakura gokenin and the seventh head of the Nitta main house, the eldest son of Nitta Motouji and father of the celebrated Nitta Yoshisada. A 1314 document from Chōraku-ji names him Tomokane, showing he later changed his name to Tomouji while the Nitta lived under strong Ashikaga influence.

About 1313 he summoned his kinsmen the Asaya brothers, notorious bandits in southern Hitachi, to Nitta Manor and favoured them with lands and his sister's hand. He died of illness in 1318 at forty-five, before his father, leaving the young Yoshisada as his heir.

en:
Nitta Yoshiaki (c. 1318–1337), the eldest son of Nitta Yoshisada, joined his father's rising that overthrew the Kamakura shogunate in 1333. Under the Kenmu government of 1334 he was named governor of Echigo.

After Ashikaga Takauji turned against the restoration, he followed his father north, and in the tenth month of 1336 entered Kanegasaki Castle in Echizen guarding the imperial princes Tsunenaga and Takanaga. Besieged for half a year by Shiba Takatsune's forces, he fired the castle and killed himself with Prince Takanaga when it fell in 1337, aged twenty.

en:
Nitta Yoshifusa (1162–1195), also called Nitta Kurōdo, was a Kamakura-period warrior and the third head of the Nitta main line. The only son of Nitta Yoshikane, he served the imperial consort Jōsaimon-in at court in his youth.

He died in 1195 at the age of thirty-four, before his father, leaving his young son Masayoshi to inherit the Nitta estates in Kōzuke Province. The boy's grandfather and great-grandfather, Yoshikane and Yoshishige, acted as his guardians.

en:
Nitta Yoshikane (1139–c. 1206), an early Kamakura warrior and gokenin, was the second head of the Nitta main line and the second son of Nitta Yoshishige. He served Empress Kōka-mon'in as a court secretary before joining Minamoto no Yoritomo with his father, after an early bid for independence failed.

As a Kamakura vassal he took part in the 1189 Ōshū campaign but won no distinction. His heir Yoshifusa died young, so Yoshikane helped guard his grandson Masayoshi's succession; documents show he lived until at least 1205.

Nitta Yoshimune (c. 1331–1368) was the third son of Nitta Yoshisada and a Southern Court commander in the Nanbokuchō Wars. After his father fell in 1338 he was raised in hiding in Echigo as the clan's heir.

In 1352 he and his brother Yoshioki rose against Ashikaga Takauji, fought in Musashi and briefly retook Kamakura before defeat drove him back to Echigo. A later rising collapsed when Yoshioki was murdered, and in 1368 Yoshimune fell in the Musashi revolt.

In 1352 he and his brother Yoshioki rose against #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_ashikaga_takauji').GetID],X #L Ashikaga Takauji#!#!, fought in Musashi and briefly retook [ShowLocationName('kamakura')] before defeat drove him back to Echigo. zh:
新田义宗（约1331—1368）是新田义贞第三子，南北朝时代的南朝方武将。1338年父亲战死后，他在越后被新田一族藏匿抚养，被视为嫡子。

1352年，他与兄长义兴举兵对抗足利尊氏，在武藏交战，一度夺回镰仓，战败后退回越后。后来再起，义兴却被谋杀，计划落空；1368年义宗在武藏的起义中战败身死。

en:
Nitta Yoshioki (c. 1331–1358), the second son of Nitta Yoshisada, rose in Kōzuke in 1337 and joined Kitabatake Akiie's northern army; at Yoshino, Emperor Go-Daigo gave him his adult name. In 1352, during the Kannō Disturbance, he raised troops for Prince Muneyoshi and briefly seized Kamakura.

In 1358 he was murdered at the Yaguchi ferry by men sent by the Kamakura kubō Ashikaga Motouji, aged twenty-eight. The Taiheiki made his vengeful ghost famous, and he was later worshipped as Nitta Daimyōjin.

zh:
新田义兴（约1331—1358）是新田义贞的次子。1337年他在上野举兵，加入北畠显家的奥州军，后在吉野谒见后醍醐天皇，由天皇赐名。1352年观应之扰乱期间，他奉宗良亲王举兵，一度攻占镰仓。

1358年他在矢口渡口被镰仓公方足利基氏派来的人谋杀，年仅二十八岁。《太平记》渲染他的怨灵复仇，后来他被奉为新田大明神。

en:
Nitta Yoshisada (1301–1338) was lord of Nitta Manor in Kōzuke and the general who brought down the Kamakura shogunate. He became clan head in 1318. In 1333, after killing a Hōjō tax collector, he rose at Go-Daigo's call with 150 horsemen.

Beaten at Bubaigawara on 15 May, he won there the next day. The Taiheiki says at Inamuragasaki he threw his gold-mounted sword into the sea and the tide drew back. On 22 May Takatoki killed himself. Sent against Ashikaga Takauji in 1335, he was beaten back and lost at Minatogawa in 1336.

He then escorted two princes to Echizen. Besieged at Kanegasaki until the garrison ate horses, it fell in March 1337; his son and a prince killed themselves. In August 1338 he met Shiba's troops at Fujishima and fell; the Taiheiki says an arrow struck his forehead and he slew himself. His head was paraded through Kyoto.

zh:
新田义贞（1301—1338）是上野国新田庄领主，也是灭亡镰仓幕府的将领。1318年他继任新田氏当主。1333年，他杀死一名北条家税使，随后响应后醍醐的号召，率150名骑兵起兵。

5月15日他在分倍河原战败，次日在同地获胜。据《太平记》记载，他在稻村崎把镶金的太刀投入海中，潮水随即退去。5月22日，高时自杀。1335年他受命讨伐足利尊氏，被击退，1336年在凑川之战中再败。

他随后护送两位亲王前往越前。金崎城被围至守军以马为食，1337年3月城陷，其子与一位亲王自尽。1338年8月，他在藤岛遇上斯波军，坠马而亡；据《太平记》记载，一支箭射中他的额头，他自刎而死。他的首级被送到京都游街示众。

en:
Minamoto no Yoshishige (1114–1202), later called Nitta Yoshishige, was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods and the founder of the Nitta clan. Eldest son of Minamoto no Yoshikuni and grandson of Yoshiie, he opened the Nitta Manor in Kōzuke Province, securing its charter in 1157, and defeated Chichibu and Ashikaga forces after forcing a crossing of the Watarase River.

In 1180 he held aloof from Yoritomo's uprising before submitting late, and remained an uneasy Kamakura vassal. Tonsured as Jōsei, he died at Nitta in 1202.

zh:
源义重（1114—1202），后称新田义重，是平安时代后期至镰仓时代初期的武将、新田氏的始祖。他是源义国的长子、名将源义家之孙，以上野国新田庄为据点，1157年成功为新田庄立券，并在强渡渡良濑川的合战中击败秩父氏与藤姓足利氏。

1180年源赖朝起兵时，他先持观望态度，迟迟才归顺，在镰仓政权中始终处境微妙。他出家后法号上西，1202年于新田庄去世。

en:
Chikazane, also called Oda Chikazane, was a Shinto official of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods, claimed ancestor of the Oda clan. The Oda genealogy calls him a son of Taira no Sukemori, hidden in Ōmi when the Taira fell in 1185, but modern scholars regard this as a later fabrication.

In 1233 he became head priest of the Tsurugi Shrine at Oda-no-shō in Echizen, and took Buddhist vows in 1258 as Kakusei. His death is dated to either 1260 or 1290. He was the father of Oda no Chikamoto.

亲真又称织田亲真，是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期的神官，被织田氏奉为始祖。织田家系图称他是平资盛之子，1185年平家灭亡时被藏匿于近江，现代学者认为此说系后世假托。

1233年，他出任越前国织田庄剑神社神主，1258年出家，法号觉盛（一作觉性）。他的卒年有1260年和1290年两说。其子为织田亲基。

Oda Suehiro was a Japanese bushi of the Nanboku-chō to Muromachi periods, recorded in the early Oda clan genealogies as a son of Oda Yukihiro. He used the common name Saburō and held the style Tarō Hyōe-no-jō.

The genealogies name his sons Oda Hirosada and Oda Motozane, and Oda Norihiro, after whom one Oda lineage branch is named, is also said to have been his son.

Oda Yukihiro was a Japanese bushi of the late Kamakura to Muromachi periods and an early documented figure of the Oda clan, which arose at Oda-no-shō in Nyū District of Echizen Province. Genealogies make him the son of Oda Chikayuki and give him the style Tarō Hyōe-no-jō.

en:
Ogasawara Ienaga was a Kamakura warrior and the second head of the Iwami Ogasawara, son of the line's founder Nagachika. When his father died in 1313, he inherited the Kawamoto and Mura estates in Ōchi district, Iwami Province, and moved there from Awa with his heir Nagatane.

Father and son developed the two estates for about twenty years. Tradition holds that Ienaga died in battle in the wars that brought down the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, and he was succeeded by Nagatane.

Ogasawara Ienaga was a Kamakura warrior and the second head of the Iwami Ogasawara, son of the line's founder Nagachika. When his father died in 1313, he inherited the Kawamoto and Mura estates in [ShowLocationName('oochi')] district, Iwami Province, and moved there from [ShowLocationName('awa_shikoku')] with his heir Nagatane.

Father and son developed the two estates for about twenty years. Tradition holds that Ienaga died in battle in the wars that brought down the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, and he was succeeded by Nagatane.
zh:
小笠原家长是镰仓时代的武士、石见小笠原氏第二代当主，该氏始祖小笠原长亲之子。1313年父亲去世后，他继承石见国邑智郡的河本乡与村之乡，与嫡子长胤一起从阿波国移居村之乡。

父子二人在此后约二十年间经营这两处庄园。相传他在1333年镰仓幕府灭亡前后的战乱中战死，死后由长胤继任家督。

en:
Ogasawara Masanaga (1319–1365) was a Northern Court general and head of the Shinano Ogasawara, Sadamune's son. He fought under Ashikaga Takauji, and in 1345 his father transferred to him the Shinano shugo post and its core estates.

During the Kannō Disturbance he went over to Ashikaga Tadayoshi in 1351, but soon returned to Takauji and was reinstated as shugo. He led Takauji's vanguard into Tōtōmi and in 1355 helped crush Prince Muneyoshi's rising at Kikyōgahara. He died in 1365, leaving the military treatise Gunjutsu Heiyōki.

zh:
小笠原政长（1319—1365）是北朝方武将、信浓小笠原氏当主，小笠原贞宗之子。他随足利尊氏转战各地，1345年父亲将信浓守护职及一族主要领地让给他，由他继承家督。

观应之扰乱中，他于1351年转投足利直义一方，后回归尊氏麾下，恢复守护之职。他曾率尊氏军先锋出兵远江，1355年在桔梗原参与镇压宗良亲王的举兵。1365年去世，终年47岁，著有兵书《军术兵用记》。

en:
Ogasawara Munenaga (1273–1330) was a late-Kamakura warrior, head of the Ogasawara clan and father of Sadamune, the future shugo of Shinano. Born at Matsuo in Shinano, he came of age in 1284 and in 1296 received from his father Nagauji the transmission of the Ogasawara school's mounted-archery teachings.

In 1307 he appears as Ogasawara Magojirō in the service roster of Engaku-ji in Kamakura. He took Buddhist vows in 1323 and died in 1330, aged 59.

小笠原宗长（1273—1330）是镰仓时代后期的武将、小笠原氏当主，即后来的信浓守护小笠原贞宗之父。他生于信浓国松尾，1284年元服，1296年从父亲长氏处受传小笠原流弓术。

1307年，镰仓圆觉寺“每月四日大斋番文”中出现“小笠原孙次郎”之名，即为宗长。1323年他出家，1330年去世，享年59岁。

en:
Ogasawara Nagachika, also called Awa no Matatarō, was a Kamakura warrior and a son of Ogasawara Nagafusa, shugo of Awa Province. For his service in the Kōan campaign against the second Mongol invasion in 1281, he was granted the Mura estate in Ōchi district, Iwami Province, where he settled and founded the Iwami Ogasawara line.

He married a daughter of the local lord Masuda Kanetoki. He was charged with guarding the unsettled Iwami coast after the invasion.

小笠原长亲，通称阿波又太郎，是镰仓时代的武将，阿波国守护小笠原长房之子。1281年弘安之役，即元朝第二次入侵日本时，他立有军功，受封石见国邑智郡村之乡，遂移居该地，成为石见小笠原氏的始祖。

他娶当地有力国人益田氏当主益田兼时之女为妻。弘安之役后他负责警备局势不稳的石见国沿海。

en:
Ogasawara Nagafusa (1213–1276) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and gokenin, ancestor of the Awa Ogasawara line. The second son of Ogasawara Nagatsune, he took over as shugo of Awa Province after the Jōkyū War of 1221, when his elder brother Nagatada, appointed to the post, chose to return to Shinano.

In 1267, on the shogunate's orders, he destroyed Taira no Moritaka and was rewarded with over twenty-six thousand chō of land in the Mima and Miyoshi districts. He ruled Awa from Iwakura Castle, and his descendants held the Awa shugo post until the fall of Kamakura.

zh:
小笠原长房（1213—1276）是镰仓时代中期的武将、御家人，阿波小笠原氏之祖。他是小笠原长经的次子，1221年承久之乱后，被任为阿波守护的兄长小笠原长忠希望返回信浓，长房遂接任阿波守护。

1267年，他奉幕府之命讨杀平盛隆，受赐美马郡与三好郡二万六千余町的土地，以岩仓城为据点统治阿波。他的子孙世代担任阿波守护，直至镰仓幕府灭亡。

en:
Ogasawara Nagakiyo (1162–1242) was a Kai Province warrior, the second son of Kagami Tōmitsu of the Kai Genji, who held the Ogasawara estate and became the first head of the Ogasawara clan, traditionally the ancestor of Ogasawara-ryū archery and etiquette. In 1180 he joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's rising, fighting at Ichinotani in 1184 and taking part in the Fuji hunt of 1193.

In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he commanded the Tōsandō army against the court and was made shugo of Awa Province. He died in Shinano in 1242, aged eighty-one.

en:
Ogasawara Nagamasa was a Kamakura-period warrior and gokenin who succeeded his father Nagatada as head of the Ogasawara clan. Modern research holds that, far from ruling the family's Shinano lands, he may have held only an estate in Koma district, Kai Province, while the Tomono line controlled the Shinano holdings.

Appointed a councilor of the Rokuhara tandai, he appears to have been based in Kyoto. When the Tomono were destroyed in the Shimotsuki Incident of 1285, the clan's headship passed to his son Nagauji, ancestor of the later Shinano shugo house.

en:
Ogasawara Nagatada (1202–1264) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and gokenin, the third head of the Ogasawara clan, succeeding his father Nagatsune; he was also called Matsuo Nagatada after his seat at Matsuo in Shinano's Ina district.

In Nagatada's day the clan's standing in Shinano belonged to the Tomono main line, while his elder brother Nagamura fled after backing the Miura in the Hōji War of 1247. His son Nagamasa succeeded him, and Nagamasa's son Nagauji later recovered the family headship.

小笠原长忠（1202—1264）是镰仓时代中期信浓国的武将、镰仓幕府御家人、小笠原氏第三代当主，继父亲长经之后继任；因居住在信浓国伊那郡的松尾，又称松尾长忠。

长忠的时代，小笠原氏在信浓的地位由嫡家伴野氏把持；兄长小笠原长村在1247年宝治合战中支持三浦氏，兵败后逃亡。长忠死后由其子长政继任，长政之子长氏后来恢复了小笠原氏的当主之位。

en:
Ogasawara Nagatane was the third head of the Iwami Ogasawara, a warrior clan based at Kawamoto in Ōchi district, Iwami province. When his father Ienaga fell in battle in 1333, he took over the family lands.

In 1335 he supported the Southern Court against Ashikaga Takauji, but in 1336 he switched to the Northern side, and with his son Nagauji defeated the Kusunoki forces at Mikusu. He later built Yunoyu Castle as his seat and died in 1346.

en:
Ogasawara Nagatsune (1179–1247) was a Kamakura-period warrior and second head of the Ogasawara clan, son of Nagakiyo. He attended the second shogun Minamoto no Yoriie as a mounted archer.

In the Hiki purge of 1203 he was imprisoned and left Kamakura. After the Jōkyū War of 1221 he became jitō of a manor in Awa Province and is recorded as Awa shugo by 1223. Ordained a monk, he led a yabusame rite at Kyoto's New Hie Shrine in 1247 and died aged 69.

小笠原长经（1179—1247）是镰仓时代前期的武将、小笠原氏第二代当主，小笠原长清之子。后来他担任二代将军源赖家的近习，以流镝马射手侍奉。

en:
Ogasawara Nagauji was a Kamakura-period warrior who recovered the Ogasawara clan's headship for his line. The son of Nagamasa and great-grandson of Nagatsune, he became sōryō in 1285, when the Tomono collateral house was destroyed in the Shimotsuki Incident and its head was killed.

In 1296 he transmitted the Ogasawara-school mounted-archery teachings to his son Munenaga, whose son Sadamune later became shugo of Shinano.

zh:
小笠原长氏是镰仓时代的武将，为长政之子、长经曾孙。1285年霜月骚动中，执掌小笠原氏惣领职的庶流伴野氏当主被杀，伴野氏没落，长氏遂接掌小笠原氏惣领之位，使该职回到长经一脉。

1296年，他向其子宗长传授小笠原流弓术；宗长之子贞宗后来成为信浓守护。

en:
Ogasawara Nagauji was the fourth head of the Iwami Ogasawara, based at Yunoyu Castle in Iwami Province, and son of the third head Nagatane. In 1336 he joined his father, now with the Northern Court, in defeating Kusunoki forces at Mikusu, and the two built Yunoyu Castle around 1340. He succeeded as head in 1346.

In 1350 he helped Kō no Moroyasu storm Aoyagi Castle and kill Saba Aritsura. Ashikaga Tadafuyu briefly drove him from the castle in 1354. He died in 1383, followed by his son Nagayoshi.

zh:
小笠原长氏是以石见国温汤城为据点的国人、石见小笠原氏第四代当主，第三代当主长胤之子。1336年，他随改投北朝的父亲在三久须击败南朝方楠木氏，约1340年父子筑成温汤城。1346年父亲死后，他继任家督。

1350年，他与高师泰一同攻破佐波顕连的青杉城并将其讨死。1354年足利直冬来攻，他一度退出温汤城。1383年去世，由嫡子长义继任。

en:
Ogasawara Sadamune (1292–1347) was head of the Shinano Ogasawara clan and shugo of Shinano. He first served the Kamakura shogunate, fighting at Akasaka in 1331, but switched sides with Ashikaga Takauji in 1333 and was made shugo after Kamakura fell. In 1336 he helped defeat Nitta Yoshisada in Ōmi and cut Southern Court supply lines on Lake Biwa.

Inheriting his family's archery tradition, he taught kyūjutsu and yabusame to Takauji and Go-Daigo, shaped the Ogasawara school and wrote on mounted archery. He died in Kyoto in 1347.

zh:
小笠原贞宗（1292年4月30日—1347年7月5日）是信浓小笠原氏当主、信浓守护。他初仕镰仓幕府，1331年曾在赤坂城与后醍醐天皇方军队作战；1333年随足利尊氏倒幕，镰仓陷落后被任命为信浓守护。1336年，他在近江击败新田义贞，并封锁琵琶湖切断南朝粮道。

他继承家传弓术，向尊氏与后醍醐天皇教授弓术与流镝马，奠定小笠原流，还著有骑射论书，1347年在京都去世。

en:
Ogasawara Sadanaga was a warrior of the Ogasawara clan of Shinano Province in the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts period, a son of Ogasawara Munenaga. The Kansei Choshu Shokafu calls him the younger brother of Sadamune.

Older genealogies instead name him either the eldest son or an adopted heir of his grandfather Nagauji. He lived in Shinano, and his son Takanaga carried on the family.

Oguni Masamitsu was the head of the main line of the Oguni, a warrior clan of Kariwa District in Echigo Province, and fought for the Southern Court in the Northern and Southern Courts wars.

In 1335 he built Kanbarazu Castle on Mount Kanbachi as a base for loyalist commanders in lower Echigo. In 1341 Masamitsu and his allies came under attack from Northern Court forces there.

en:
Oguni Yoritsugu was an early-Kamakura warrior and gokenin, founder of the Oguni clan based at Oguni in Kariwa district, Echigo. In 1212 he was summoned as the first archer at Shogun Sanetomo's yumi-hajime ceremony.

Having brought no bow, he used an Araki bow given him for the occasion and showed such strength and skill that the shogun granted him the jitō post of the Inazu manor in Echizen.

小国赖连（一作赖继）是镰仓时代前期的武将、御家人，是以越后国刈羽郡小国保为据点的小国氏家祖。1212年正月，他被召为将军源实朝弓始仪式的第一射手。

当日他未带弓，便使用赐予的荒木弓射箭，凭刚力与出众弓术令实朝叹赏，获赐越前国稻津保的地头职，事见《吾妻镜》。

en:
Prince Okiyoshi (born c. 1326) was a Southern Court prince, a grandson of Emperor Go-Daigo by Prince Moriyoshi and a Kitabatake mother. Soon after Go-Murakami's accession he was appointed seii taishōgun, or palace general. In 1341 he went east to join Kitabatake Chikafusa at Oda Castle, holding Daihō and Oyama in turn until the strongholds fell in 1343.

In the west he campaigned with the Akamatsu in Harima and Tamba, but in 1360 he rebelled against the Southern Court: he burned the residence at Anō in Yoshino, was defeated and vanished from the records.

兴良亲王（约1326年生）是南朝皇族，后醍醐天皇之孙、护良亲王之子，母亲出自北畠家。后村上天皇即位不久，他被任命为征夷大将军，人称“宫将军”。1341年他东下常陆，投奔据守小田城的北畠亲房，先后转移到大宝城、小山城，1343年宫方据点陷落后西走。

回到西国后，他在播磨、丹波随赤松氏转战；但1360年举兵背叛南朝，火烧吉野贺名生行宫，兵败后下落不明。

en:
Ōe no Hiromoto (1148–1225), a Kyoto court noble, was a chief architect of the Kamakura shogunate. Summoned east by Minamoto no Yoritomo in 1184, he became the first bettō of the Kumonjo and, in 1191, of the Mandokoro.

In 1185 he urged Yoritomo to appoint jitō stewards and shugo governors. After Yoritomo's death he backed Hōjō Masako and in the Jōkyū War of 1221 pressed a march on Kyoto. His son Suemitsu founded the Mōri clan.

zh:
大江广元（1148—1225）出身京都公卿，是镰仓幕府制度的主要缔造者之一。1184年他被源赖朝召往东国，同年就任公文所首任别当，1191年又成为政所首代别当。

1185年，他建议赖朝在各国设置地头与守护。赖朝死后，他支持北条政子；1221年承久之乱中，他力主主动进兵京都。其子季光开创了毛利氏。

en:
Ōgimachisanjō Hideko (1311–1353) was a court woman of the Northern and Southern Courts period, the daughter of Inner Minister Kinhide. She long served the cloistered Emperor Kōgon and received junior third rank in 1337.

She bore Kōgon two sons who both took the throne, Emperors Sukō and Go-Kōgon. Falling ill in 1352, she received the honorary rank of empress and the cloister title Yōrokumon-in, and died early in 1353, aged forty-two.

正亲町三条秀子（1311—1353）是南北朝时代的宫廷女性，内大臣公秀之女。她长期侍奉光严上皇，1337年叙从三位。

她为光严生下两个后来都登基的儿子——崇光天皇与后光严天皇。1352年她卧病后，受封准三宫、院号阳禄门院，于次年初薨去，享年四十二岁。

en:
Kinhide Ōgimachisanjō (1285–1363) was a court noble of the late Kamakura period, the son of Provisional Major Councillor Sanemi. Ranked Senior Second Rank and known as the Hachijō Minister, he rose from his first ennoblement in 1286 to provisional major councillor in 1321, later serving as inspector and viceroy of Dazaifu.

In 1352 the Northern Court named him inner minister; he took Buddhist vows and resigned the next year. Through his daughter Hideko he was the maternal grandfather of Emperors Sukō and Go-Kōgon.

Ōgimachisanjō Kintsura (1238–1313) was a Kamakura-period court noble, the eldest son of Councilor Sanekage. After his father's early death he was adopted by the Minister of the Left.

He rose to Provisional Middle Counselor in 1286, surpassing his father's highest office, and was promoted to Provisional Major Counselor in 1300. He resigned the next year, took Buddhist vows in 1303 as Kūen, and died in 1313 aged seventy-eight.

He also used the names Saga and Saikō, and founded the Ōgimachisanjō house, a branch of the Sanjō family. He died in 1237.

Ōgimachisanjō Sanemi (1264–after 1317) was a Kamakura-period court noble, the third son of Kintsura and fourth head of the family, who served the Daikakuji imperial line. He rose to Middle Counselor before being forced to resign, and in 1316 was made Provisional Major Counselor.

Ōhira Kuninobu was an early Kamakura-period warrior, the son of Kondō Kunihira, who served the Minamoto in the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 and was made shugo of Sanuki Province.

Kuninobu moved to Tosa Province and became jitō of the Takaoka and Hasuike manors in Takaoka District, taking the name Ōhira and making Hasuike Castle his seat. He thus founded the Tosa Ōhira clan, which ruled the district until 1566.

Ōida Tsunetaka was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Northern and Southern Courts period, from a branch of the Nitta clan settled at Ōida in Uonuma District, Echigo Province.

When Nitta Yoshisada rose against the Hōjō at Nitta-no-shō in Kōzuke in 1333, Tsunetaka led his Echigo kinsmen to join him. In the Battle of Kamakura he broke through the Keshōzaka pass and helped overthrow Hōjō Takatoki, bringing down the Kamakura shogunate.

Ōida Ujitsune was a Southern Court warrior from a Nitta branch clan settled at Ōida in Echigo's Uonuma District and the son of Ōida Tsunetaka. In 1333 he and his father joined Nitta Yoshisada's rising and fought at the Battle of Kamakura against Hōjō Takatoki. He served Yoshisada across the country, holding Fukuyama in Bitchū against Ashikaga Takauji before defeat by Tadayoshi.

He followed Yoshisada to Hokuriku and, after his lord's death, protected Nitta Yoshimune, thrice battling the Ichikawa of Shinano and campaigning through Hokuriku and Musashi.

en:
Ōida Yoshitsugu was a Kamakura-period warrior, the second son of Satomi Yoshinari of Kōzuke Province. He was granted a holding at Ōidagō in Hataki Manor, Uonuma District in Echigo Province, which he and his son Ujitsugu held.

The branch house they founded took the name Ōida, and with houses such as the Toriyama and Tanaka it formed the Echigo Nitta league, whose horsemen joined Nitta Yoshisada's rising against the Hōjō in 1333.

en:
Ōkura Nagasada was the tenth head of the Ōkura clan, hereditary district officials who ruled part of Hita District in Bungo Province. Around 1299 he began building Gakurinji in Hita and gave thirteen years to the work.

Under an edict of Emperor Go-Daigo it became an imperial prayer temple. His son Nagatoshi, the eleventh head, continued his father's work and completed the temple halls in 1342.

en:
Ōkura Nagasue (1056–1104?) was a lord of the Ōkura clan, local magnates of Hita District in Bungo Province, and the first of the clan to enter recorded history. A champion wrestler, he fought at the sumai no sechie bouts in Kyoto.

Hita district records credit him with ten appearances without a single defeat. In 1104, returning from the capital, he fell ill and died at Ōoi Manor.

en:
Ōsaki Tadamochi (1327–1383) was a Nanboku-chō warrior, the first head of the Ōsaki clan and eldest son of Shiba Iekane. In 1352, as his father's Wakasa deputy, he led Wakasa troops to aid Ashikaga Yoshiakira in Kyoto. When Iekane became Ōshū kanrei in 1354, Tadamochi followed him into Mutsu and succeeded to the post in 1356.

Around 1366 he took the surname Ōsaki, after an ancestral estate in Shimōsa. In 1367 he joined Shogun Yoshiakira's campaign against the rebel Kira Haruie. He died in 1383.

zh:
大崎直持（1327—1383）是南北朝时代的武将、奥州管领，大崎氏初代当主，斯波家兼的嫡长子。1352年，他以父亲的若狭国守护代身份率若狭军上洛，支援足利义诠。1354年父亲就任奥州管领后，他随军进入陆奥，1356年父亲死后接任该职。

约1366年，他以下总国先祖的领地大崎为号，改称大崎氏。1367年，他参与将军足利义诠讨伐谋叛者吉良治家的军事行动。1383年去世。

约1366年，他以下总国先祖的领地大崎为号，改称大崎氏。1367年，他参与将军足利义诠讨伐谋叛者吉良治家的军事行动。1383年去世。

en:
Ōtomo Chikahide (c. 1195–1248) was the second head of the Ōtomo clan of Bungo and a gokenin of the Kamakura shogunate. Working with his younger brother, he consolidated the clan's hold on its Kyūshū domains.

In 1236 he retired and passed the headship to his son Yoriyasu. He served the sesshō shōgun Fujiwara no Yoritsune and accompanied him to Kyoto in 1238, and died in 1248.

zh:
大友亲秀（约1195—1248）是镰仓时代前期御家人，大友氏第二代当主。他与弟弟协力处理国政，巩固大友氏在九州的领地根基。

1236年，他把家督之位让给儿子赖泰后隐居。他侍奉摄家将军藤原赖经，并于1238年随赖经上洛，1248年去世。

Ōtomo Chikatoki (c. 1236–1295) was the fourth head of the Ōtomo clan of Bungo and the third son of Yoriyasu. He took the headship after his father retired, but died before him in 1295.

The succession passed to his younger brother, or possibly his son, Sadachika. His sons founded the Nyūta and Nozu branch houses, and his daughter married Shimazu Sadahisa.

en:
Ōtomo Sadachika (1246–1311) was the fifth head of the Ōtomo clan of Bungo, most likely the second son of Yoriyasu. When Chikatoki died in 1295, he succeeded to the headship on the retired elder's order.

The character sada in his name was presumably granted by Hōjō Regent Sadatoki, who in 1305 ordered him to establish Manju-ji temple in Bungo; he founded it in 1306. He died in 1311 aged sixty-six, and his younger brother Sadamune succeeded him.

大友贞亲（1246—1311）是丰后大友氏第五代当主，从年龄推断更可能是赖泰的次子。1295年亲时去世后，他奉隐居的长辈之命继承家督。

en:
Ōtomo Sadamune (c. 1265 – 9 January 1334) was the sixth head of the Ōtomo clan of Bungo. He succeeded his brother Sadachika in 1311 and served the Chinzei tandai Hōjō Hidetoki.

In March 1333 he refused to join Kikuchi Taketoki's rising and helped crush it. Two months later, after the Rokuhara headquarters fell, he switched sides and destroyed Hidetoki, earning the shugo post of Bungo. He died suddenly in Kyoto that December, leaving the headship to his son Ujiyasu.

大友贞宗（约1265—1334年1月9日）是丰后大友氏第六代当主。1311年兄长贞亲死后他继为当主，出仕镇西探题北条英时。

1333年3月菊池武时举兵，邀他同反，他拒绝参与，并协助击败击杀武时。同年5月六波罗探题陷落后，他倒戈攻灭英时，因此受封丰后守护。同年十二月他在京都突然去世，家督由儿子氏泰继承。

en:
Ōtomo Sadayori was a warrior of the late Kamakura and Nanbokuchō eras, the illegitimate eldest son of Ōtomo Sadamune, sixth head of the Bungo Ōtomo. Excluded from the succession when Sadamune made his younger brother Ujiyasu heir in 1333, he broke from the main house after their father's death in 1334. In 1336 he fought on the Southern Court side against Ashikaga Takauji at Tatarahama.

Reconciled with Ujiyasu, he rejoined the Northern Court in 1345 and received pardon and confirmation of his lands, but later rebelled again and took his own life under Northern Court attack.

zh:
大友贞顺是镰仓末期至南北朝时代的武将，为丰后国大友氏第六代当主大友贞宗的庶长子。1333年贞宗绕过年长的贞顺，把家督传给其弟氏泰；1334年父亲死后，贞顺脱离宗家。1336年多多良滨之战中，他站在南朝方与足利尊氏作战。

1345年他与氏泰和解、归附北朝，获尊氏赦免并安堵所领；但此后再度反叛，最终在北朝方进攻下自尽。

en:
Ōtomo Ujitoki (c. 1325–1368), childhood name Miyamatsumaru, was eighth head of the Ōtomo clan and a Nanbokuchō shugo daimyō, seventh son of Ōtomo Sadamune. With his brother Ujiyasu he was a nominal son of Ashikaga Takauji, receiving the Genji surname and the character uji. In 1348 he took the headship and Bungo shugo post from Ujiyasu, later gaining Buzen, Higo and Chikugo.

He briefly joined the Southern Court, then fought for the North, and in 1359 was defeated by Kikuchi Takemitsu at the Chikugo River. He ceded his lands to his heir Ujitsugu in 1364 and died of illness in 1368.

大友氏时（约1325—1368），幼名宫松丸，是南北朝时代的守护大名、大友氏第八代当主，大友贞宗第七子。他与兄长氏泰同被足利尊氏收为犹子，获赐源姓与“氏”字。1348年，他从氏泰手中继承家督与丰后守护职，后来又补任丰前、肥后、筑后守护。

他一度归降南朝，不久复归北朝，1359年在筑后川之战中被菊池武光大败。1364年他把所领让给嫡子氏继，1368年病死。

en:
Ōtomo Ujiyasu (c. 1321–1362) was the seventh head of the Ōtomo clan of Bungo Province. In 1333 his father Sadamune passed him the headship before marching against the Hōjō, and Ujiyasu succeeded on his father's death that year.

When Ashikaga Takauji fled to Kyushu in 1336, Ujiyasu helped him regain power; Takauji made him a nominal son and granted the character uji, and the Muromachi bakufu named him shugo of four provinces. He died in 1362, succeeded by his brother Ujitoki.

en:
Ōtomo Yoriyasu (1222–1300) was the third head of the Ōtomo clan. He inherited in 1236 and changed his name from Yasunao after receiving a character from Regent Hōjō Tokiyori. As the Mongol threat grew, the shogunate made him eastern Chinzei magistrate, and he moved to Bungo in 1272 for Kyūshū's defense.

He helped repel the Yuan invasions at Torikaigata in 1274 and at Shikanoshima in 1281. He died in Sagami in 1300, aged seventy-nine, having settled the clan in Bungo.

en:
Ōtomo Yoshinao (29 January 1172 – 20 December 1223), born Kondō Ichihōshimaru, was a gokenin of the early Kamakura shogunate and the founder of the Ōtomo clan. Adopted by Nakahara no Chikayoshi, he became a close favourite of Shogun Minamoto no Yoritomo.

He fought in the Ōshū campaign of 1189 and shielded Yoritomo during the Soga brothers' revenge in 1193. In 1196 he was made shugo of Buzen and Bungo, carrying the Ōtomo name into Kyūshū. He died in Kyoto in 1223.

Ōuchi Hiromori was a Suō warrior and the seventeenth head of the Ōuchi clan, then still named Tatara. Exiled in 1177 for the Shishigatani conspiracy and pardoned in 1178, he came to dominate the provincial office as Ōuchisuke.

In the Genpei War he gave Minamoto no Noriyori's army Suō as a base against the Taira. After 1185 he was the province's strongest man; in 1191 he was accused of blocking Tōdai-ji rebuild timber, but the bakufu dismissed the suit.

Hironari Ōuchi was a warrior of Suō Province and the 19th head of the Ōuchi clan, succeeding his father Mitsumori. His years continued the family's rise.

en:
Hirosada Ōuchi was a provincial official of Suō Province and the fourth head of the Ōuchi line there, succeeding his father Hironari. Where earlier heads had kept the Kamakura shogunate at arm's length, he acted much like a shogunal vassal and helped build the Kan'in palace.

A devout Buddhist, he founded Daishō-ji in 1266. During the second Mongol invasion of 1281 he advanced into Buzen Province by shogunal order, and he died in 1286.

en:
Ōuchi Hiroyo (c. 1326–1380) was the ninth head of the Ōuchi clan and a Nanbokuchō shugo daimyō, son of Ōuchi Hiroyuki. In 1351 he submitted to the Southern Court and was named Suō shugo; after his father's death in 1352 he fought the Washizu and brought their faction under his authority, taking Nagato as shugo in 1358.

In 1360 he moved the clan seat to Yamaguchi, laying out a town modeled on Kyoto that became the base of later Ōuchi culture. He submitted to the Muromachi bakufu in 1363, added Iwami in 1366, and died in 1380.

Ōuchi Hiroyuki (c. 1305–1352) was the eighth head of the Ōuchi clan of Suō Province in the late Kamakura period. He inherited in 1320 and marched to Kyoto on Hōjō Takatoki's orders in the Genkō War of 1332, after which the Kenmu regime gave the clan's Suō shugo post to his uncle Washizu Nagahiro.

Hiroyuki joined Ashikaga Takauji in 1335 and in 1350 marched against Nagahiro with his son Hiroyo. He submitted to the Southern Court in 1351, when Hiroyo was made Suō shugo, and died in 1352 with the feud unresolved.

Mitsumori Ōuchi was the 18th head of the Ōuchi clan of Suō Province, succeeding his father Hiromori. He styled himself Ōuchinosuke, and from his day the clan heads took the title Suō no gon-no-suke.

In 1206 he founded the temple Zuiun-ji at Shiraishi in Yamaguchi, the family's first foothold in the Yamaguchi basin where the Ōuchi would later centre their power. After his death the headship passed to his son Hironari.

en:
Prince Oshisaka no Hikohito no Ōe, eldest son of Emperor Bidatsu by Princess Hirohime, unusually carried no Soga blood among Emperor Kinmei's descendants, making him the leading non-Soga prince. He held an independent base through the Osakabe group at Mimata Palace, far from the capital.

After Emperor Yōmei's death in 587 he was a succession candidate, but Soga-backed princes prevailed and he vanishes from the chronicles, perhaps killed around 600. His sons included the future Emperor Jomei and Prince Chinu, ancestors of later emperors.

After #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_youmei_tenno').GetID],X #L Emperor Yōmei#!#!'s death in 587 he was a succession candidate, but Soga-backed princes prevailed and he vanishes from the chronicles, perhaps killed around 600. His sons included the future #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_jomei_tenno').GetID],X #L Emperor Jomei#!#! and #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_chinu_no_ookimi').GetID],X #L Prince Chinu#!#!, ancestors of later emperors.
zh:
押坂彦人大兄皇子是敏达天皇与广姬所生的长子。他在钦明天皇的子孙中罕见地没有苏我氏血统，是非苏我系皇族中最有实力的皇子。他以忍坂部为独立经济基础，据点设在远离都城的水派宫。

587年用明天皇死后，他被视为皇位继承人选，但苏我系皇子得势，他从此在史籍中销声匿迹，约600年前后或遭暗杀而死。他的儿子包括后来的舒明天皇和茅渟王，后世皇室均出自其血脉。

en:
Oyama Hidetomo (?–1335), first named Takatomo, was a late Kamakura commander, eighth head of the Shimotsuke Oyama clan and lord of Oyama Castle. He first served the Hōjō, fighting at the 1331 sieges of Kasagi and Shimo-Akasaka in the Genkō War.

In 1333 he defected to Nitta Yoshisada and helped overthrow the Kamakura shogunate, after which Emperor Go-Daigo made him governor of Shimotsuke. In 1335 he met Hōjō Tokiyuki's Nakasendai Rebellion at Fuchū in Musashi and was killed in the defeat.

zh:
小山秀朝（？—1335），初名高朝，是镰仓末期武将，下野小山氏第八代当主、小山城城主。他起初从属北条氏，1331年元弘之乱中参加了笠置城与下赤坂城的攻城战。

1333年新田义贞举兵进攻镰仓，他倒戈响应，参与攻灭镰仓幕府，事后被后醍醐天皇任命为下野守。1335年北条时行发动中先代之乱，他在武藏国府中迎战，兵败战死。

en:
Masamitsu Oyama was a late Heian to early Kamakura warrior and founder of the Oyama clan, whose estates around the Shimotsuke capital made him leader of its largest warrior band. Born into Musashi's Ōta house, he was first called Ōta Masamitsu and moved to the Oyama estate around 1150.

When Minamoto no Yoritomo rose in 1180, Masamitsu's wife Samukawa, Yoritomo's wet nurse, pledged his warriors to him; he and his sons served Yoritomo as gokenin. He died before 1199.

zh:
小山政光是平安时代末期至镰仓时代初期的武将、御家人，小山氏的始祖。他在下野国府周边拥有大片领地，统领国内最大的武士团。政光出身武藏太田家，初名太田政光，约1150年（久安六年）移居下野小山庄，开创小山氏。

1180年（治承四年）源赖朝举兵时，政光之妻、赖朝的乳母寒河尼将全族武士投效赖朝；此后政光与诸子成为赖朝的御家人。他于1199年以前去世。

en:
Nagamura Oyama was a mid-Kamakura warrior and the fourth head of the Oyama, leading lords of Shimotsuke. Skilled with the bow, he first appears in the Azuma Kagami in 1228 as a yabusame archer. His father Tomonaga died young, and in 1230 his grandfather Tomomasa passed the headship to him.

In 1250 he petitioned the shogunate after the hereditary office of Shimotsuke no ōsuke was reassigned following a complaint by Ise shrine officials; the council ordered its return. He also held the Harima shugo post and died in 1269.

小山长村是镰仓时代中期武将、幕府御家人，下野有力豪族小山氏的第四代当主。长村擅长弓矢，《吾妻镜》1228年（安贞二年）已记载他担任流镝马射手。父亲朝长早逝，1230年（宽喜二年）祖父朝政将家督与所领官职传给他。

1250年（建长二年），下野大介一职在伊势神宫杂掌的控诉下被改授他人，经长村申诉，幕府评定判令返还；他还担任播磨守护。1269年（文永六年）长村去世。

en:
Oyama Sadatomo (1282–1330) was a late Kamakura commander and shogunal gokenin, seventh head of the powerful Oyama clan of Shimotsuke and lord of Oyama Castle. He received the character sada in his name from the regent Hōjō Sadatoki.

In 1323 he donated a hundred kanmon in cash at the thirteenth-anniversary memorial for Sadatoki. The Jōraku-ki records that he died in 1330 aged forty-nine, and his son Hidetomo succeeded him.

en:
Tomomasa Oyama was the second head of the Oyama clan and a leading early Kamakura gokenin, serving Minamoto no Yoritomo from 1180. In 1183 he feigned alliance with Shida Yoshihiro and ambushed him at Nogi-no-miya in Shimotsuke; wounded, he still routed the rebel with his brother.

He fought the Taira under Minamoto no Noriyori, including Dan-no-ura in 1185, and joined the Ōshū campaign of 1189. He held the Shimotsuke and Harima shugo posts, took the tonsure in 1234 and died in 1238 aged 84.

小山朝政是小山氏第二代当主、镰仓早期的有力御家人，1180年（治承四年）起便追随源赖朝。1183年（寿永二年），他假装加入志田义广一方，在下野野木宫设伏；虽负伤，仍与弟弟合力将叛军击溃。

en:
Tomonaga Oyama was a Kamakura-period warrior, shugo of Shimotsuke and castellan of Oyama Castle, the legitimate heir of Tomomasa. Originally named Masayoshi, he first appears in 1193 as a yabusame archer at Tsurugaoka.

In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he served as a general of the Tōsandō army, helping defeat court forces at the Ōido crossing before entering Kyōto, and afterwards beheaded Hamuro Muneyuki in Suruga by shogunal order. He succeeded to the family headship and died in 1229 aged 42, before his father.

小山朝长是镰仓时代武将，官至下野守护、小山城城主，为朝政的嫡子。他初名政义，1193年（建久四年）曾作为流镝马射手在鹤冈登场。

1221年（承久三年）承久之乱中，他担任东山道大将，在大井户渡口击败京方军队，随后进入京都；乱后奉命在骏河国将叶室宗行斩首。其后他继承家督，1229年（宽喜元年）先于父亲去世，年仅42岁。

en:
Oyama Tomosato (died 1346), childhood name Jōkenmaru and first called Tomouji, was the ninth head of the Oyama warrior house of Shimotsuke Province. In 1335 his father Hidetomo was killed in the Nakasendai Rebellion, and Tomosato inherited the family domains and shugo post as a child under a guardian.

In 1337 Kitabatake Akiie's Southern Court army seized Oyama Castle and captured him, but Yūki Munehiro interceded to spare his life. Around 1340 he was reportedly at war with his Northern Court-aligned brother Ujimasa, and died suddenly in May 1346 without children, so Ujimasa succeeded him.

小山朝郷（？—1346），幼名常犬丸，初名朝氏，是下野国小山武家的第九代当主。1335年中先代之乱中，父亲小山秀朝战死，朝郷幼年在监护人辅佐下继承家族领地与守护职。

1337年，南朝将领北畠显家的军队攻陷小山城将他俘虏，因结城宗广进言而保住性命。约1340年据传他与投靠北朝的弟弟氏政交战，1346年5月突然去世，没有子嗣，由氏政继位。

en:
Oyama Ujimasa (1329–1355) was a warrior of the Northern and Southern Courts period and shugo of Shimotsuke Province. His father Hidetomo was killed in the Nakasendai Rebellion of 1335, and the headship passed to his elder brother Tomosato; when Tomosato died without an heir in 1346, Ujimasa inherited the family domains and shugo post.

He joined Ashikaga Takauji against Ashikaga Tadayoshi, fighting at Sattamine Pass in 1351 and Fuefuki Pass in 1352, then campaigned around Kyoto until his death in 1355, aged twenty-seven.

小山氏政（1329—1355）是日本南北朝时代的武将，任下野国守护。1335年中先代之乱中，父亲小山秀朝战死，家督由兄长小山朝郷继承；1346年朝郷无嗣而终，氏政遂继承家族领地与守护之职。

他随足利尊氏讨伐足利直义，参加1351年的萨埵峠之战和1352年的笛吹峠之战，此后在京都周边转战，于1355年去世，年二十七岁。

en:
Emperor Reizei (950–1011), personal name Norihira, was Japan's 63rd emperor, reigning from 967 to 969. The second son of Emperor Murakami, he was made crown prince in infancy through the Fujiwara brothers Morosuke and Saneyori.

He grew up mentally ill, so at his accession at eighteen Fujiwara no Saneyori ruled as regent. In 969 the Anna Incident brought down Minamoto no Takaakira, and Reizei abdicated the same year. He lived forty-four years in retirement, dying in 1011; his sons became Emperors Kazan and Sanjō.

zh:
冷泉天皇（950—1011），名宪平，是日本第63代天皇，967年至969年在位。他是村上天皇的第二子，因藤原师辅、实赖兄弟之力，在襁褓中即被立为太子。

他成年后患有精神疾病，因此十八岁即位时由藤原实赖以摄政身份主政。969年安和事件扳倒源高明，冷泉也于同年退位。退位后他又度过了四十四年，1011年去世；他的儿子后来成为花山天皇与三条天皇。

en:
Rokkaku Tokinobu (1306–1346) was head of the Rokkaku, the main Sasaki line, and shugo of Ōmi Province. He succeeded his father Yoritsuna in 1311 and came of age in 1314. In the Genkō War of 1331 he fought for the Kamakura shogunate, and in 1333 submitted to the imperial court, serving in the Kenmu government.

After following Ashikaga Takauji, he lost the Ōmi shugo post to Sasaki Dōyo of the Kyōgoku branch, took vows, passed headship to his son Ujiyori, and died in 1346.

六角时信（1306—1346）是佐佐木氏嫡流六角氏的第三代当主、近江国守护。1311年父亲赖纲死后继承家督，1314年元服。1331年元弘之乱中他站在镰仓幕府一方作战，1333年归降朝廷，在建武政权杂诉决断所任职。

en:
Rokkaku Ujiyori (1326–1370) was a Nanboku-chō warlord and shugo of Ōmi Province, the fourth head of the Rokkaku. He succeeded his father Tokinobu as family head and Ōmi shugo around 1335 while still a child and was overshadowed by Sasaki Dōyo of the Kyōgoku branch, whose daughter he married.

In 1338 he helped check Kitabatake Akiie's Southern Court army on the Ōmi–Mino border. During the Kannō Disturbance he switched to the Tadayoshi faction, took vows and resigned as shugo in 1351; he returned as Ōmi shugo in 1354, founded Eigen-ji in 1361, and died in 1370.

en:
Sasaki Yasutsuna, also called Rokkaku Yasutsuna (1213–1276), was a Kamakura gokenin and Ōmi shugo, founder of the Sasaki Rokkaku branch; the name came from his Kyoto residence at Rokkaku-Higashinotōin. Third son of Sasaki Nobutsuna, he sat on the Rokuhara council.

Favoured by Shogun Kujō Yoritsune, he drew Hōjō suspicion and lost Ōmi estates in a 1243 feud with his brother. He later passed the headship to his son Yoritsuna, took the tonsure and died in 1276.

因受将军九条赖经宠爱而遭北条氏忌惮，1243年与兄长争夺领地时，近江领地被没收。后来他把家督让给儿子赖纲，出家，于1276年去世。

en:
Sasaki Yoritsuna, also called Rokkaku Yoritsuna (1242–1311), was a Kamakura gokenin, Ōmi shugo and second head of the Rokkaku house. In 1250 he came of age at Hōjō Tokiyori's residence, taking yori from his name, and served as governor of Bitchū.

He joined the Rokuhara council in 1277 and extended his powers, even taxing Chikubushima shrine lands. A 1307 territorial quarrel with Kōfuku-ji monks led to his Owari exile in 1308, and he died there in 1311.

Rokujō (1164–1176), the infant son of Emperor Nijō, was named crown prince before his first birthday and enthroned in 1165 at eight months old, when his dying father abdicated. His grandfather, retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa, ruled throughout.

In 1168 the Taira pressed for his removal, and Go-Shirakawa deposed him for his uncle Takakura. He died of dysentery in 1176 at the age of eleven, leaving neither consort nor children.

en:
Imperial Prince Sadasumi (873–916), also called Prince Momozono, was the sixth son of Emperor Seiwa. Invested as prince in 873, he held senior posts under Emperor Uda, as titular governor of Kazusa and Kōzuke and head of two ministries, his rank never passing the fourth grade.

He died in 916. His son Minamoto no Tsunemoto founded the Seiwa Genji, from whom the Kamakura, Ashikaga and Tokugawa houses claimed descent.

en:
Emperor Saga (786–842) was Japan's 52nd emperor, reigning 809–823. A son of Emperor Kanmu, he succeeded his brother Heizei and in 810 defeated the retired emperor's bid to reclaim the throne in the Kusuko Incident. He founded the kurōdo-dokoro and kebiishi police.

His peaceful reign saw Tang-style culture flower: he was one of the early Heian age's three great calligraphers, and from 814 gave many children the surname Minamoto, originating the Saga Genji. He abdicated in 823 for Emperor Junna.

嵯峨天皇（786—842）是日本第52代天皇，809—823年在位。他是桓武天皇之子，继兄长平城天皇即位，810年在药子之变中挫败上皇复位的企图。他设立藏人所与检非违使。

其治世太平，唐风文化兴盛，他本人被列为平安初期“三笔”之一；814年起他将众多皇子皇女赐姓源氏，是为嵯峨源氏之祖。823年他让位于淳和天皇。

Ōe no Chikahiro was a Kamakura-period gokenin, the eldest son of Ōe no Hiromoto, first head of the shogunate's Mandokoro. In 1192 he inherited the jitō post of Sagae manor in Dewa province, seed of the Sagae clan, and married a daughter of Hōjō Yoshitoki.

In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he sided with Retired Emperor Go-Toba and disappeared after the defeat at Uji. He is said to have retired to Sagae manor, where he died on 17 January 1242.

en:
Ōe no Hirotoki was a Kamakura-period gokenin, a son of Ōe no Chikahiro and grandson of Ōe no Hiromoto. Although his father had backed the losing court side in the Jōkyū War of 1221, Hirotoki entered shogunate service through his elder brother Sukefusa's war record.

After his brother Takamoto, who held Sagae manor, died young in 1254, Hirotoki succeeded to the Dewa estate, though its northern portion passed to the Hōjō. He stayed in Kamakura and governed Sagae through a deputy, and was succeeded by his eldest son Masahiro.

en:
Ōe no Masahiro was a Kamakura-period gokenin and the fourth head of the Sagae line, great-grandson of Ōe no Hiromoto and son of Ōe no Hirotoki. On his father's death in 1262 he succeeded to Sagae manor in Dewa, but like him remained in Kamakura, administering the estate through a deputy.

en:
Sagae Motomasa, also recorded as Ōe no Motomasa (died 1359), was a Nanbokuchō commander and head of the Sagae branch of the Ōe clan in Dewa Province, and a fifth-generation descendant of Ōe no Hiromoto. He succeeded his father in 1322.

Siding with the Southern Court, he marched on Kyoto with Kitabatake Akiie in 1335 and helped rout Ashikaga Takauji at Teshimagawara in Settsu in 1336, driving him to Kyushu. By 1351 he had recovered the Kita-Sagae manor seized by the Hōjō, and in 1359 he fell fighting Shiba Kaneyori.

Sagae Mototaka, also called Ōe no Mototaka, was a Kamakura-period gokenin and the fifth head of the Sagae house of Dewa Province. In 1277 he succeeded his father Ōe no Masahiro.

After the Shimotsuki Disturbance of 1285 killed several of his Ōe kinsmen, he withdrew to Sagae manor to escape Hōjō pressure and rebuilt the burned Jion-ji temple. He died in 1322 and was succeeded by his eldest son Motomasa.

en:
Sagae Tokishige, also recorded as Ōe no Tokishige (died 1373), was the seventh head of the Sagae Ōe clan in Dewa Province. Succeeding his father Motomasa after he fell fighting Shiba Kaneyori in 1359, he posted his sons and kinsmen in new forts across Sagae manor.

At the battle of Urushigawa in 1368 his heir Shigenobu led the clan against Shiba Kaneyori and was crushingly defeated, with sixty-one clansmen killing themselves. Tokishige kept the main manor but lost Kita-Sagae, and died in 1373, bidding his surviving fourth son Tokiuji to make peace with the Northern Court.

en:
Sagara Nagauji (died c. 1355), fourth head of the Sagara clan in Higo Province, Kyushu, succeeded his father Yoritoshi in 1287. In 1326 he took vows as Rendō and passed the headship to his son Yorihiro, yet kept real authority.

In 1333 he sent three sons to join Prince Takayoshi's anti-Hōjō rising, helping destroy the Chinzei tandai at Dazaifu. In 1338 he received the northern Hitoyoshi lands, which he gave to his grandson Sadayori, and later mediated peace among warring kinsmen; he died around 1355, outliving his son.

Sagara Nagayori (1177–1254) was a Kamakura vassal and the first Sagara lord of Hitoyoshi in Higo. Born at Sagara manor in Tōtōmi, he was sent to Kyushu by Yoritomo in 1198, destroyed the Yaze and seized Hitoyoshi Castle.

His vanguard service at the Battle of Futamatagawa in 1205 won him the jitō post of Hitoyoshi manor. He died at Hitoyoshi in 1254 and was succeeded by his son Yorichika.

Sagara Sadayori (died 1372) was the sixth head of the Sagara clan in Higo Province and a Northern Court commander in the Nanbokuchō wars. In 1335 he and his grandfather Nagauji submitted to the Shōni of Kyushu, and from 1336 he fought the Southern Court partisan Taraki Tsuneyori in Kuma.

In 1338 a land grant from Nagauji made him lord of Hitoyoshi. He rejected Prince Kanenaga's overtures in 1346 and campaigned in Hyūga, then retired as the monk Keia about 1370 and died in 1372, several retainers dying after him.

en:
Sagara Yorihiro (died c. 1338) was the fifth head of the Sagara clan in Higo Province. In 1326 his father Nagauji passed him the headship, and the Kamakura shogunate appointed him jitō of the Hitoyoshi manor, though Nagauji kept real influence.

In 1333 he joined Nitta Yoshisada's attack on Kamakura, then marched to Kyushu to serve Prince Takayoshi under the Shōni, winning court confirmation of the clan's Higo and Buzen lands. In 1336 he raided Ashikaga Takauji's estate in Hyūga; he had yielded the Kuma lands to Sadayori and died around 1338.

相良赖广（？—约1338）是肥后国相良氏第五代当主。1326年父亲长氏把家督让给他，镰仓幕府承认他对人吉庄的地头职，但长氏作为后见人仍握有实权。

en:
Sagara Yorikage was steward of Sagara manor in Tōtōmi Province when Minamoto no Yoritomo rose against the Taira in 1180, and he fought on the Taira side until their fall in 1185. His lands were confiscated, but repeated apologies won his pardon.

In 1193 he received Taragi manor in Kuma district, Higo, and went down to Kyushu; in 1197 Yoritomo confirmed the estate as his holding.

en:
Sagara Yoritoshi was the third Sagara lord of Hitoyoshi and a younger son of Nagayori. He took the headship when his brother Yorichika stepped aside.

During the second Mongol invasion in 1281, though already old, he led Sagara troops under Kikuchi Takefusa at Hakata, capturing enemy soldiers driven onto Mount Goryū by the typhoon and beheading them on the beach. He was rewarded with Ashikita district and yielded the headship to his son Nagauji in 1287, dying around 1311.

en:
Sahara Mitsumori was a Kamakura-period warrior, the fourth son of Sahara Moritsura. He inherited the headship of the Sahara house, a Miura offshoot which had held Aizu since his grandfather Sahara Yoshitsura received it after the Ōshū campaign of 1189.

When the main Miura house was destroyed in the Hōji Conflict of 1247, Mitsumori and his brothers fought for the Hōjō and survived. A branch of the Sahara in Aizu took the name Ashina, from which the later Ashina lords descended.

en:
Sahara Moritsura was a warrior of the early Kamakura period and the second son of Sahara Yoshitsura. He married Yabe-zenni, formerly wife of Hōjō Yasutoki, and in 1221 fought for the shogunate in the Jōkyū War.

While in Kyoto in 1226 he rioted drunkenly as far as Uji, wounding people, which earned him the nickname Aku-Tōtōmi-no-kami, the wicked governor of Tōtōmi. In disgrace he wandered the provinces until he was killed trying to force his way into Kyoto in 1233.

Sahara Yoshitsura was a warrior of the late Heian and early Kamakura periods, youngest son of the Sagami magnate Miura Yoshiaki; he took the name Sahara from his castle southeast of the Miura seat at Kinugasa. In 1180 he joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's uprising and became a founding gokenin.

He fought under Minamoto no Yoshitsune at Ichinotani, where the Heike Monogatari makes him the first rider to charge down the Hiyodorigoe descent. He was shugo of Izumi from 1196 until his death around 1203.

en:
Fujiwara no Sadamasa was a mid-Heian warrior of the Fujiwara Toshihito line and a son of Bungo no kami Fujiwara no Shigemitsu. In 985 he joined the Takiguchi palace guard.

In 989 he and his cousin Fujiwara no Tamenobu shot dead Mikuni Yukimasa, a strongman of Echizen Province, at Awataguchi in Kyoto; the court sent Kebiishi police to arrest him, but in vain. His son Masashige's descendants took the name Katō and served the Kawachi Minamoto.

en:
Samukawa no Ama (1138–1228) was a daughter of Hatta Munetsuna and a wet nurse of Minamoto no Yoritomo. She became the second wife of the Shimotsuke warrior chieftain Oyama Masamitsu and the mother of Yūki Tomomitsu.

In 1180 she brought her fourteen-year-old son to Yoritomo's camp at Sumida; Yoritomo personally presided over his coming-of-age, and the Oyama warrior band joined the rising. In 1187 Yoritomo made her land steward of Samukawa District in Shimotsuke.

1180年源赖朝举兵时，她携十四岁的朝光前往隅田宿谒见赖朝，赖朝亲自为朝光主持元服，小山氏武士团就此加入赖朝阵营。1187年，赖朝任命她为下野国寒川郡的地头。

en:
Sanjō Kiminori (1103–1160) was a late-Heian court noble, son of Sanjō Saneyuki and second head of the Sanjō house. Through his cousin Bifukumon'in he won the cloistered Emperor Toba's trust. In 1155 he joined the council that placed Go-Shirakawa on the throne, and in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 served him, becoming minister of the centre in 1157.

During the Heiji Disturbance he helped Emperor Nijō flee the palace to Taira no Kiyomori at Rokuhara. He died of dysentery in 1160, before his father.

zh:

平治之乱中，他设计让二条天皇脱出内里，行幸平清盛所在的六波罗。1160年他因赤痢急逝，死在父亲之前。

en:
Sanjō Sanefusa (1147–1225) was a late-Heian to early-Kamakura court noble and poet, the third son of Sanjō Kiminori and third head of the Sanjō house. He joined the senior nobility at junior third rank in 1160, aged fourteen, and after Minamoto no Yoritomo's court reforms became a gisō councillor.

He became minister of the right in 1189 and minister of the left in 1190, resigned through illness in 1196 and took Buddhist vows as Seikū.

en:
Sanjō Saneyuki (1080–1162) was a late-Heian court noble and the second son of Fujiwara no Kinzane. As half-brother of Taikenmon'in he served the retired Emperor Sutoku and rose with backing from Fujiwara no Yorinaga, becoming minister of the right in 1149 and junior first-rank grand minister in 1150.

After Yorinaga's disgrace in 1155 he parted from the Sutoku faction and escaped the Hōgen Disturbance. He retired in 1157, took Buddhist vows as Renkaku in 1160, and founded the Sanjō house.

en:
Emperor Sanjō (976–1017), personal name Okisada, was the second son of Emperor Reizei and the sixty-seventh sovereign of Japan. Named crown prince in 986, he only took the throne in 1011, and his relations with Fujiwara no Michinaga soon grew strained.

Having lost his sight, Sanjō abdicated in 1016 on condition that his eldest son Atsuakira become crown prince. He took Buddhist vows in 1017 and died months later; that year Atsuakira withdrew from the succession under Michinaga's pressure.

三条天皇（976—1017）名居贞，是冷泉天皇的次子、日本第六十七代天皇。986年他被立为皇太子，直到1011年才即位，此后与藤原道长的关系日渐紧张。

1016年三条天皇因双目失明，以长子敦明亲王立为皇太子为条件退位。1017年他出家，数月后去世；同年敦明在道长的压力下辞去储位。
