en:
Sasaki no Hideyoshi (1112–1184) was lord of Sasaki Manor in Gamō District, Ōmi Province, and father of the four Sasaki brothers who served Minamoto no Yoritomo. He fought under Minamoto no Yoshitomo in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 and the Heiji Disturbance of 1159; after the defeat he sheltered for twenty years in Sagami.

In 1180 he sent his son Sadatsuna to warn Yoritomo of a planned attack and committed his sons to his rising. In 1184 he fell fighting Taira remnants at Kaminomura.

Minamoto no Nariyori (976–1003) was a mid-Heian noble of the Uda Genji line, the eldest son of the councillor Minamoto no Sukenori. The Sonpi Bunmyaku gives him junior fifth rank and posts in the imperial guards.

Genealogies relate that he settled on the Sasaki Manor in Gamō District, Ōmi Province, and was the ancestor after whom the Sasaki clan named itself, although modern scholars note this identification is debated. Skilled with bow and horse, he died in 1003, aged only twenty-eight.

en:
Sasaki no Nobutsuna (c. 1181–1242), fourth son of Sasaki no Sadatsuna, was a Kamakura gokenin and head of the Sasaki clan. In the Jōkyū War of 1221 his Uji River crossing was held up; after calling for reinforcements, he crossed with Hōjō Tokiuji and broke the court forces. He received the ancestral Sasaki estates in Ōmi, while his elder brother Hirotsuna, who sided with the retired emperor, was executed.

He served as Ōmi no kami. After his death his four sons divided Ōmi and founded the Ōhara, Takashima, Rokkaku and Kyōgoku houses.

zh:
佐佐木信纲（约1181—1242）是佐佐木定纲的四男，镰仓幕府御家人，后成为佐佐木氏总领。1221年承久之乱中，他参加宇治川之战，渡河受阻后请求援军，与北条时氏共同渡河击破京方军队。乱后他受赐近江的佐佐木氏祖传领地，而追随上皇的长兄广纲被斩首。

此后他历任近江守。他去世后，四个儿子瓜分近江，分别开创大原氏、高岛氏、六角氏与京极氏。

en:
Sasaki no Sadatsuna (1142–1205), eldest son of Sasaki no Hideyoshi, was a leading general of the early Kamakura shogunate. He served Minamoto no Yoritomo, joined his 1180 rising and fought at Ishibashiyama; after the Genpei War he became shugo of Ōmi and three other provinces.

In 1191 a clash with Enryakuji monks caused his exile to Satsuma; he was pardoned in 1193. He took vows on his deathbed in 1205 and died two days later, aged sixty-four.

en:
Sasaki no Tsunekata was an eleventh-century Uda Genji warrior in Ōmi Province, after whom the Sasaki clan is named. Genealogies make him the eldest son of Sasaki no Yoshitsune and record him as the first to settle at Kowaki in the Sasaki Manor of Gamō District, serving as steward and priest of Sasaki-no-miya Shrine.

He held Junior Fifth Rank and the office of Hyōgo-no-suke. His grandson Sasaki no Hideyoshi, born in 1112, fought in the Hōgen and Heiji disturbances.

en:
Sasaki no Yoshikiyo (c. 1160–c. 1248), fifth son of Sasaki no Hideyoshi, was a Kamakura gokenin and ancestor of the Izumo Genji. He fought for the Taira against Minamoto no Yoritomo at Ishibashiyama in 1180 before changing sides after Fujigawa and serving the shogunate.

en:
Satake Hideyoshi (1151–1226) was the third head of the Satake clan of Hitachi. In 1180 he held Kinsaja Castle against Minamoto no Yoritomo; after the castle fell through his uncle Satake Yoshisue's treachery, he fled and succeeded his father in 1183. He resisted until 1189, when he submitted and fought in the Ōshū campaign.

The fan-on-white-banner emblem Yoritomo ordered became the Satake crest. In the Jōkyū War of 1221 he sent his son Yoshishige for the bakufu. He died in 1226.

en:
Satake Moroyoshi was a Nanboku-chō warrior, the seventh son of the Hitachi shugo Satake Sadayoshi by a concubine. He joined Ashikaga Tadayoshi's army with his half-brother Yoshiatsu when the Ashikaga marched on Kyōto, then followed Takauji to Kyushu and fought at Tatarahama and Minatogawa in 1336.

While Yoshiatsu returned to govern Hitachi, Moroyoshi remained Takauji's close retainer, and in 1349 backed Kō no Moronao against Tadayoshi. A renga poet anthologized in the Tsukubashū, he received the Yamauchi lands in Kuji district from Takauji and founded the Yamauchi Satake and Kuniyasu clans.

en:
Satake Nagayoshi (1207–1272) was the fifth head of the Satake clan of Hitachi and eldest son of Yoshishige. He held the office of Hitachi no suke and served as Satake bettō. In 1252 he was assigned to attend the shogun Prince Munetaka's visit to Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine, though the ceremony was canceled.

In 1267 he founded Yōun-ji for his grandmother's memorial, and in 1269 he restored the family temple Satake-dera. He died in 1272.

en:
Satake Sadayoshi (1287–1352) was the eighth head of the Satake clan of Hitachi Province and took one character of his name from Hōjō Sadatoki. In 1331 he became shugo of Hitachi and fought for the Kamakura bakufu at the siege of Mount Kasagi, but was won over by Ashikaga Takauji and joined the imperial side.

In 1335 Takauji confirmed him as shugo of Hitachi, an office that became hereditary in the clan, and he occupied Satake-tate, the later Ōta Castle. He died in 1352 and was succeeded by his son Yoshiatsu.

佐竹贞义（1287—1352）是常陆国佐竹氏第八代当主，元服时取北条贞时名字中的一字为名。1331年他被补任为常陆国守护，作为幕府军参加笠置山攻城战，后经足利尊氏策反而倒向讨幕一方。

1335年足利尊氏承认他的常陆守护之职，此后该职由佐竹氏世袭；同年他进驻佐竹楯，即后来的太田城。1352年贞义去世，由嫡子义笃继任家督。

en:
Satake Takayoshi (1118–1183) was the second head of the Satake clan of Hitachi Province. A grandson of Fujiwara no Kiyohira, he moved his base from Masasaka to Ōta Castle and extended rule over seven inland districts of northern Hitachi. After 1159 he served Taira no Kiyomori.

When Minamoto no Yoritomo rose in 1180, the Satake opposed him: heir Yoshimasa was murdered and Kinsaja Castle, where Hideyoshi took refuge, was stormed, and most Satake lands were seized. He died in 1183 and his son Hideyoshi succeeded.

佐竹隆义（1118—1183）是常陆国佐竹氏第二代当主，藤原清衡的外孙。他把本据从马坂城移到太田城，将佐竹氏的支配扩展到北常陆的奥七郡。1159年后他侍奉平清盛。

1180年源赖朝举兵，佐竹氏与之敌对：嫡子义政被谋杀，秀义退守的金砂城被攻破，大部分领地被没收。1183年他去世，秀义继任家督。

en:
Satake Yoshiatsu (1311–1362) was the ninth head of the Satake clan of Hitachi Province and Sadayoshi's second son; he inherited because his elder brother was an illegitimate monk. When the Nanboku-chō war began he sided with Ashikaga Takauji, was appointed shugo of Hitachi, and after returning east led the Northern Court faction there.

In Kyōto from 1354 to 1357, he headed the Muromachi bakufu's Samurai-dokoro. In his last years he took Zen vows as Shunzan Jōki and founded Seion-ji in Naka district, and he died in 1362.

佐竹义笃（1311—1362）是常陆国佐竹氏第九代当主，贞义的次子；因长兄为庶子、已出家为僧，由他继承家督。南北朝战乱爆发后，他追随足利尊氏，被任命为常陆守护，归国后成为常陆国内北朝势力的核心。

en:
Satake Yoshishige (1186–1252) was the fourth head of the Satake clan of Hitachi. With his father Hideyoshi he fought for the bakufu in the Jōkyū War of 1221 and took heads at the Uji River. He succeeded around 1226 and was appointed Hitachi no suke in 1245, restoring its former shodaibu rank.

He also established the cadet Nukata, Okada and Okabe houses for his sons. He died in 1252 and his son Nagayoshi succeeded him.

en:
Satake Yoshitane (1227–1278) was the sixth head of the Satake clan of Hitachi, succeeding his father Nagayoshi in 1272. He served as Sanuki no kami and Hitachi no suke. He married a daughter of the Iwasaki of Iwaki district in Mutsu.

He used the marriage to extend Satake influence into southern Mutsu, where his sons founded cadet branches. In 1276 he founded the Rinzai temple Shōgin-ji. He died in 1278 and his son Yukiyoshi succeeded him.

He founded the Shōhō-in subtemple at the family mortuary temple Shōraku-ji and endowed it with lands, and Emperor Fushimi granted it an imperial plaque. He died in 1305 and his son Sadayoshi succeeded him.

en:
Satomi Yoshinari (1157–1234) was a Kamakura warrior based at Satomigō, son of Satomi Yoshitoshi. When Minamoto no Yoritomo rose in 1180, Yoshinari slipped out of Kyoto by pretending to rejoin his grandfather against him and hastened to Kamakura, earning Yoritomo's favor.

In 1195 he rode as second archer in the yabusame ceremony, and in 1204 became Iga no kami. He lost office after his patron Hiraga Tomomasa was killed in 1205 and died in 1234; the Azuma Kagami called him Yoritomo's cherished man.

Emperor Seiwa (850–881), personal name Korehito, was the 56th emperor of Japan, reigning from 858 to 876. The fourth son of Emperor Montoku, he was made crown prince through the influence of his maternal grandfather Fujiwara no Yoshifusa and ascended at nine, leaving Yoshifusa to rule as sesshō, the first Fujiwara regent.

Seiwa abdicated in 876 in favour of his young son Emperor Yōzei, took Buddhist vows in 878, and died in 881. His descendants led the Seiwa Genji warrior line.

zh:
清和天皇（850—881），名惟仁，是日本第56代天皇，858年至876年在位。他是文德天皇第四子，因外祖父藤原良房的影响被立为太子，九岁即位，朝政由良房以摄政身份执掌，这是藤原氏首次担任摄政。

876年清和让位于年幼的儿子阳成天皇，878年出家，881年去世。他的后裔是武士家族清和源氏的始祖。

en:
Senka (467–539), the 28th emperor of Japan in traditional order, was the second son of Emperor Keitai and the full younger brother of Emperor Ankan. He took the throne in 536 after Ankan's death and ruled a little over three years; his reign marks the close of the Kofun period on the eve of the Asuka period.

His empress was Tachibana no Nakatsu, a daughter of Emperor Ninken. Their daughter Ishi-hime became empress to his half-brother and successor, Emperor Kinmei.

宣化天皇（467—539）是日本传统世系中的第28代天皇，继体天皇的次子，安闲天皇的同母弟。536年安闲天皇死后即位，在位仅三年余，其统治时期标志着古坟时代结束、飞鸟时代前夜。

皇后橘仲皇女是仁贤天皇之女。两人所生的石姬皇女后来成为他的异母弟、继位者钦明天皇的皇后。

en:
Shiba Iekane (1308–1356) was son of Shiba Muneuji and younger half-brother of Shiba Takatsune. He joined Ashikaga Takauji's uprising against the Kamakura shogunate in 1333 and was made shugo of Wakasa in 1336, fighting Southern Court general Nitta Yoshisada in Hokuriku, whom he helped destroy in 1338.

During the Kannō disturbance he sided with Takauji against his own brother. In 1354 he was appointed kanrei of Ōshū, where he defeated rival generals, made the office hereditary in his clan, and founded the Ōsaki and Mogami lines; he died there in 1356.

斯波家兼（1308—1356）是斯波宗氏之子、斯波高经的异母弟。1333年，他随足利尊氏举兵推翻镰仓幕府，1336年被任命为若狭守护，在北陆与南朝大将新田义贞作战，并于1338年攻灭新田。

en:
Shiba Ienaga (1321–1338) was the eldest son of Shiba Takatsune and fought for Ashikaga Takauji from boyhood. In 1335 he was named commander-in-chief of Ōshū, holding the front against Kitabatake Akiie's Southern Court Mutsu government from Takamizushiro castle in Shiwa.

He then served as Kantō steward at Kamakura, assisting the young Ashikaga Yoshiakira and eroding Akiie's authority among the warriors of the north. In December 1337 he tried to stop Akiie's army before Kamakura and was killed at the battle of Sugimoto castle, aged seventeen.

en:
Ieuji was the eldest son of the Kamakura gokenin Ashikaga no Yasuuji. He apparently lost his place as heir after his father married a Tokusō Hōjō wife, yet became Nakatsukasa-dayū in 1253 and in 1261 Kebiishi and Saemon-dayū, styled Hangan-daibu.

He became Owari no kami in 1265, guarded the young clan head Ietoki and acted as de facto sōryō until c. 1269, and died as the monk Ren'a. Enfeoffed with Shiba district in Mutsu, he founded the future Shiba line; his son was Muneie.

en:
Muneie (dates unknown) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and second head of the Shiba (Owari-Ashikaga) house, succeeding his father Ieuji. He served the shogunate as an independent gokenin, taking the ‘Mune’ of his name from Hōjō Tokimune. He held Junior Fifth Rank with the post of Sakon no shōgen, and was known as Owari Saburō; tradition makes him the first Shiba by name.

He survived the 1285 Shimotsuki purge, losing many lands, and was still active in the Kagen disturbance of 1305. His son was Muneuji.

en:
Shiba Muneuji (c. 1250–1312) was the third head of the Shiba, the Owari branch of the Ashikaga clan, and father of generals Shiba Takatsune and Shiba Iekane. The eldest son of Shiba Muneie, he was known as Matasaburō and held the title Owari no Kami. In 1309 he submitted documents under shogunate questioning, evidence he had succeeded.

He was a waka poet whose verses entered the imperial anthology Shoku-Goshūi Wakashū. A Mount Kōya gorintō dated the twelfth month of 1312 likely records his death.

en:

en:

1360年，幕府任命他为九州探题；但1362年10月，他的军队在长者原合战中被怀良亲王的南朝军击溃，逃往周防。他返回京都，1367年出家，法号道荣，隐居嵯峨。

en:
Shiba Ujiyori was the third son of Shiba Takatsune and a Northern Court commander who was made shugo of Wakasa. He married a daughter of Sasaki Dōnyū, the strongest man in the Muromachi bakufu.

After his eldest brother Ienaga fell in battle in 1338 and Ujitsune was disgraced after his Kyūshū campaign of 1362, many backed Ujiyori for the vacant office of kanrei, but Takatsune favored his younger sons and passed him over. Disillusioned, Ujiyori took Buddhist vows and withdrew to Ōmi province.

长兄家长于1338年战死，次兄氏经在1362年九州之役后失脚，室町幕府管领出缺时，众人曾推举氏赖继任；但父亲高经偏爱幼子而加以排斥。氏赖心灰意冷，不久出家，隐居近江。

Shigenoi Sanekuni (1140–1183), also called Fujiwara no Sanekuni, was a court noble and poet at the end of the Heian period and the second son of Sanjō Kiminori. He received his first court rank in 1147 and became a councillor in 1160.

He eventually reached senior second rank and provisional major counsellor, styled the Sanjō Major Counsellor. He founded the Shigenoi house, a branch of the Sanjō family, and died early in 1183, soon after his mother.

en:
Shijō Arisuke was a Southern Court noble in the Nanboku-chō wars, a son of the Dainagon Shijō Takasuke. Appointed governor of Iyo Province, he traveled to his province in 1337 and, based at Uwa Manor, led Southern Court forces in the local fighting.

He crossed to Kutsuna Island to take command in battle and worked with the Kutsuna clan to extend Southern Court control over Iyo.

en:
Shijō Fusana (1229–1288) was a Kamakura-period court noble, the fifth head of the Shijō house and eldest son of Shijō Takachika. He received his first rank in 1237 and reached junior third rank in 1249.

After rising to senior second rank in 1257 he waited more than twenty years without a substantive post, only becoming councillor in 1279. Dismissed in 1282 for missing the New Year ceremony, he was soon reinstated, served as grand councillor in 1285 before retiring, and died in 1288.

en:
Shijō Takaaki (1243–after 1277) was a Kamakura-period court noble, the second son of Shijō Takachika and head of the Zenshōji cloister, known as the Zenshōji Grand Councillor. He rose to senior second rank as provisional grand councillor. In 1276 his father returned to the post of grand councillor and Takaaki resigned; the next year he took Buddhist orders, said to be over his bitter estrangement from Takachika.

Nothing is recorded of him after 1277. His line, continued through Takazane, Takasuke and Takatoshi, served the Southern Court and later died out.

en:
Shijō Takachika (1202–1279) was a Kamakura-period court noble and waka poet, the fourth head of the Shijō house and the second son of Shijō Takahira. He rose through court office to become grand councillor in 1250. When Emperor Shijō died in 1242, the Kamakura shogunate placed Prince Kunihito on the throne as Emperor Go-Saga at Takachika's residence, where his wife had nursed the prince.

He resigned in 1260 but returned as grand councillor in 1276 after quarrelling with his heir Takaaki, and died in 1279.

Fujiwara no Takafusa (1148–1209), also called Shijō Takafusa, was a late Heian and early Kamakura court noble and second head of the Shijō house. Eldest son of Fujiwara no Takasue, he married a daughter of Taira no Kiyomori and held several provincial and palace posts.

He reached senior second rank in 1199 and provisional grand councillor in 1204. He took the tonsure in 1206 as Jakue and died in 1209.

en:
Shijō Takahira (1172–1255), or Fujiwara no Takahira, was a Kamakura-period court noble and the third head of the Shijō house. The eldest son of Fujiwara no Takafusa, he was Taira no Kiyomori's maternal grandson.

He married a sister of Shogun Minamoto no Sanetomo's wife and kept rising after the Taira fell, becoming councillor in 1202 and provisional grand councillor in 1219. His house rose with Emperor Go-Horikawa's accession in 1221. He took the tonsure in 1227 and died in 1255.

他还担任家族菩提寺善胜寺的长者，晚年出家，法名宗怡。

en:
Fujiwara no Takasue (1127–1185) was a late Heian court noble, eldest son of Chūnagon Fujiwara no Ienari. Ranked in 1133 at age seven, he entered the kugyō in 1158.

He bound his family to the Taira by marrying his heir Takafusa to a daughter of Kiyomori, rose to Gon-Dainagon in 1168 and ran Retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa's office. In the 1179 coup Kiyomori made him Dazai gon-no-sochi. He took vows in 1182, died in 1185, and founded the Shijō house.

藤原隆季（1127—1185）是平安时代后期的公卿，中纳言藤原家成的长子。他1133年七岁叙爵，1158年进入公卿之列。

他与平氏联姻，让嫡子隆房迎娶清盛之女，1168年升任权大纳言，执掌后白河院的院厅事务。1179年治承政变中，清盛任命他为大宰权帅。1182年他出家，1185年去世，是四条家之祖。

en:
Shijō Takasuke (1292–1352) was a noble and pillar of the Southern Court in the Nanbokuchō wars. Close to Emperor Go-Daigo, he became Kebiishi bettō in 1330. In the Genkō War of 1331 he followed the emperor to Mount Kasagi, escaped its fall by taking vows, and backed Prince Morinaga until the Hōjō fell in 1333.

From 1339 he ran Southern Court administration. Named Dainagon in 1350, he probably received Junior First Rank around 1351. He was killed in 1352 covering Emperor Go-Murakami's retreat from Otokoyama against Akamatsu troops, and was posthumously made Sadaijin in 1356.

zh:
四条隆资（1292—1352）是镰仓后期至南北朝时代的公卿，南朝的柱石之臣。他早年即追随后醍醐天皇，1330年任检非违使别当。1331年元弘之乱中，他随天皇退守笠置山，城破后剃发脱身，暗中支持护良亲王，直到1333年北条氏灭亡。

1339年起，他主持南朝政务。1350年任大纳言，约1351年叙从一位。1352年男山八幡之战，他在掩护后村上天皇从男山撤退时迎战赤松军而死，1356年被追赠左大臣。

en:
Shijō Takatoshi was a Southern Court noble during the Nanboku-chō wars, the son of the Dainagon Shijō Takasuke. When his father fell in 1352, he succeeded as family head, and in 1372 he was appointed Naidaijin. A war-party leader, he repeatedly commanded Southern Court armies attacking Kyoto.

In 1369, after Kusunoki Masanori defected, he stormed Tōjō Castle on Emperor Chōkei's order. In 1373 he died fighting in the rear guard during the retreat from the Amanosan Kongō-ji. His poetry appears in the Shin'yō Wakashū anthology.

四条隆俊是日本南北朝时代的南朝公卿，为大纳言四条隆资之子。1352年其父战死后他继任家督，1372年就任内大臣。作为主战派核心人物，他多次担任南朝军总大将进攻京都。

1369年楠木正仪投降北朝后，他奉长庆天皇之命攻打东条城。1373年天野山金刚寺遭幕府军进攻，他在撤退时担任殿军，力战而死。其和歌收录于《新叶和歌集》。

en:
Emperor Shijō (1231–1242), the 87th emperor of Japan, came to the throne in 1232 at barely two and was left an infant sovereign by his father Emperor Go-Horikawa's death in 1234. His maternal grandfather Kujō Michiie then ran court affairs under the Kamakura shogunate.

A mischievous boy, he died at ten after slipping on talcum powder he had scattered in a palace corridor to make attendants fall, leaving the succession in dispute.

四条天皇（1231—1242）是日本第87代天皇。1232年父亲后堀河天皇退位，年仅两岁的他继位，1234年父皇去世，他成了幼主，此后由外祖父九条道家在镰仓幕府之下主持政务。

他生性顽皮，1242年在宫中走廊撒下滑石粉想让近侍滑倒，自己却失足摔伤，十岁便夭折，死后皇位继承再起争端。

en:
Prince Shiki (c. 668–716) was the seventh son of Emperor Tenji and an imperial prince of the late Asuka period. In 679 he joined the princes at Yoshino in swearing unity before Emperor Tenmu, the Yoshino Covenant.

Keeping clear of succession struggles, he devoted himself to waka poetry, and an elegy on his death is preserved in the Man'yōshū. He rose to the second imperial rank and died in 716. When his sixth son, Prince Shirakabe, ascended as Emperor Kōnin in 770, Shiki was posthumously honored as Emperor Kasuga.

zh:
志贵皇子（约668—716）是飞鸟时代末期的皇族，天智天皇第七子。679年，他与众皇子在吉野向天武天皇盟誓团结，史称“吉野盟约”。

他远离皇位之争，潜心和歌，《万叶集》中留有为其去世所作的挽歌。他位阶升至二品，于716年去世。770年，其第六子白壁王即位为光仁天皇，他被追尊为春日宫御宇天皇。

en:
Shimazu Hisatsune (1225–1284) was the third head of the Shimazu clan and a Kamakura vassal. In 1265 he succeeded his father Tadatoki and went to Kamakura.

In 1275 he returned to Kyushu against the Mongol invasions and was posted to defend Chikuzen; in the 1281 Kōan invasion he led the Shimazu army with distinction, a feat pictured in the Mongol Invasion scrolls. He died in 1284 at Hakozaki, aged sixty, succeeded by his son Tadamune.

岛津久经（1225—1284）是岛津氏第三代当主、镰仓幕府御家人。1265年，他从父亲忠时手中接过家督，前往镰仓。

en:
Shimazu Morohisa (1325–1376) was a commander of the Northern and Southern Courts period and the sixth head of the Shimazu clan of Satsuma. Third son of the fifth head Sadahisa, he fought for Ashikaga Takauji and was made steward of estates in Satsuma and Hizen.

In 1363, after an elder brother's early death, he succeeded as clan head and shugo of Satsuma, founding the Sōshū branch while his brother Ujihisa took Ōsumi. In 1375 he broke with Imagawa Ryōshun over the murder of Shōni Fuyusuke, and died the following year.

岛津师久（1325—1376）是日本南北朝时代的武将，萨摩岛津氏第六代家督，也是总州家的初代当主。他是第五代当主岛津贞久的第三子，追随足利尊氏立下战功，被任命为萨摩、肥前的地头。

1363年次兄宗久早逝，他继承家督与萨摩守护职，大隅守护则由弟弟氏久继承。1375年水岛之变中今川了俊暗杀少贰冬资，师久激愤之下与了俊对立，次年去世。

en:
Shimazu Munehisa (1322–1340) was a Nanboku-chō-period warrior and the legitimate second son of the fifth Shimazu head, Shimazu Sadahisa. In 1338 he fought alongside his father in Kō no Moronao's army against the Southern Court general Kitabatake Akiie and won distinction.

He was the leading candidate to succeed as head of the Shimazu, but in 1340, aged nineteen, he died after falling from his horse while travelling in Satsuma. His early death opened the succession dispute that split the family into the Sōshū and Ōshū houses.

en:
Shimazu Sadahisa (1269–1363) was fifth head of the Shimazu and shugo of Satsuma, Ōsumi and Hyūga. He succeeded his father Tadamune as shugo of Satsuma in 1318, and in 1333, answering Ashikaga Takauji's call against the Kamakura shogunate, he helped destroy the Chinzei deputy Hōjō Hidetoki, gaining Ōsumi and Hyūga as reward.

He aided Takauji at Tatara beach in 1336 and then spent decades fighting Southern Court forces in Kyūshū, at one point submitting to them during the Kannō disturbance. In 1363 he divided Satsuma and Ōsumi between his sons Morohisa and Ujihisa and died aged ninety-five.

zh:
岛津贞久（1269—1363）是岛津氏第五代当主，萨摩、大隅、日向三国的守护。1318年他继父亲忠宗之后就任萨摩守护；1333年响应足利尊氏推翻镰仓幕府的举兵，参与攻灭镇西探题北条英时，因功获任大隅、日向两国守护。

1336年他在多多良滨之战中援助尊氏，此后数十年在南九州与南朝势力苦战，观应之扰乱期间还曾一度归降南朝。1363年他把萨摩与大隅分别让给儿子师久和氏久，以九十五岁高龄去世。

en:
Shimazu Tadahisa (died 1227), born Koremune no Tadahisa, was a Kamakura shogunate vassal and founder of the Shimazu clan. In 1185, on Minamoto no Yoritomo's recommendation, he became a deputy administrator of the Shimazu estate in southern Kyushu, later taking his name from the estate.

He became shugo of Satsuma and Ōsumi in 1197. Implicated in the Hiki purge of 1203, he lost his governorships but recovered Satsuma after backing the Hōjō in the 1213 Wada conflict. He died at Kamakura in 1227.

zh:
岛津忠久（卒于1227年），原名惟宗忠久，是镰仓幕府御家人、岛津氏的始祖。1185年，经源赖朝推荐，他出任九州南部岛津庄的下司，后来以岛津为氏。

1197年他出任萨摩和大隅守护。1203年比企之变中他受牵连被没收守护之职；1213年和田合战时他站在北条一方，得以恢复萨摩职位。1227年，他在镰仓去世。

en:
Shimazu Tadamune (1251–1325) was the fourth head of the Shimazu clan and a Kamakura shogunate vassal. He fought beside his father Hisatsune in Kyushu during the Mongol invasions and succeeded as clan head in 1284.

He later served under the Kyushu deputy Hōjō Sanemasa. In 1317 he was made steward of estates in Hyūga and Hizen, which he parcelled out among his sons; these grants founded several Shimazu branch houses. He died in 1325 and was succeeded by Sadahisa.

岛津忠宗（1251—1325）是岛津氏第四代当主、镰仓幕府御家人。元军来袭时，他在九州随父亲久经作战立功，1284年继承家督。

他曾在镇西探题北条实政手下任职。1317年，他被任命为日向、肥前等地庄园的地头，并把领地分给诸子，由此产生多家岛津分家。1325年他去世，由贞久继任。

en:
Shimazu Tadatoki (1202–1272) was the second head of the Shimazu clan and a Kamakura shogunate vassal. He fought with distinction in the shogunate army in the Jōkyū War of 1221.

Succeeding his father Tadahisa in 1227, he stayed in Kamakura rather than governing Satsuma in person, rose among the shogun's inner vassals, and received stewardships in several provinces. In 1265 he passed the clan leadership to his heir Hisatsune, and died in 1272, aged seventy-one.

en:
Shimazu Ujihisa (1328–1387) was a Northern and Southern Courts commander and the fourth son of the Shimazu head Sadahisa. In 1352 his father gave him military command over Ōsumi, where he fought the local Hatakeyama governor, briefly joining the Southern Court in 1356 before returning to the Ashikaga side and becoming Ōsumi shugo in 1363.

He expanded into Hyūga and traded with Ming China. Enraged by Imagawa Ryōshun's murder of Shōni Fuyusuke in 1375, he repeatedly rebelled and submitted, defeating Ryōshun's cousin at Minohara in 1379. He died in 1387.

zh:
岛津氏久（1328—1387）是日本南北朝时代的武将，岛津氏第五代当主贞久的第四子。1352年父亲将大隅的军事指挥权交给他，他在大隅与当地畠山氏交战，1356年一度转投南朝，后又归顺足利一方，1363年就任大隅守护。

他向日向扩张势力，并与明朝开展贸易。1375年今川了俊谋杀少贰冬资，氏久愤而反复叛服，于1379年在蓑原之战击败了俊的从兄弟今川满范，1387年去世。

en:
Emperor Shirakawa (1053–1129), personal name Sadahito, was the 72nd emperor of Japan and the founder of cloistered rule. The son of Emperor Go-Sanjō, he reigned from 1073, seeking to rule directly and keep the Fujiwara regent houses in check; in 1077 he founded Hosshō-ji temple.

In 1087 he abdicated in favour of his young son Horikawa, and for the next 43 years directed government from his retirement palace. Ordained a monk in 1096, he kept power until his death in 1129.

白河天皇（1053—1129），名贞仁，日本第72代天皇，院政制度的开创者。他是后三条天皇之子，1073年即位，力图亲政、抑制藤原摄关家；1077年发愿修建法胜寺。

1087年，他让位于幼子堀河天皇，在此后43年间退居白河院执掌朝政。1096年他出家受戒，仍紧握大权，直到1129年去世。

en:
Shō Iehiro, also called Kodama no Iehiro, was a late-Heian warrior and fourth head of the main house of the Kodama band, the largest of Musashi Province's seven great warrior parties.

Son of Kodama Ieyuki, he settled at Kurisaki, now Honjō in Saitama Prefecture. He replaced the name Kodama with Shō and built Kurisaki Hall. He was an ancestor of the Honjō clan.

作为儿玉家行之子，他定居于栗崎（今埼玉县本庄市）。他改儿玉氏为庄氏，并修筑栗崎馆。他是本庄氏之祖。

en:
Shō Ienaga, known as Tarō, was a late-Heian and early-Kamakura warrior and fifth head of the Kodama band's main house in Musashi, succeeding his father Iehiro. In 1175 he led the Kodama party in a clash over the Takayama manor.

At the Battle of Ichinotani in 1184 he killed Taira no Tomoaki and captured the Taira commander Taira no Shigehira, but his eldest son Yoriie fell. Rewarded with the jitō post of Kusanagi manor in Bitchū, he built Sarukake Castle there and founded the Bitchū Shō line.

en:
Shō Ietsugu, known as Saburō, was an early-Kamakura warrior of the Kodama band in Musashi, the third son of Shō Ienaga. After his elder brother Yoriie, the sixth head, fell at the Battle of Ichinotani in 1184, Ietsugu was made Yoriie's adopted heir and became the seventh head.

He later went west to take up the Kusanagi jitō post in Bitchū, settled there, and became ancestor of the Bitchū Shō. The Azuma Kagami mentions him once, in 1250, serving in Kyoto.

en:
Shō Sukefusa, known as Saemon Shirō, was a warrior of the late Kamakura period from Oda District in Bitchū Province and castellan of Kōyama and Takayama castles. He is thought to have been a son of Shō Aritsugu, and from his day the Bitchū Shō took 'suke' as their generational character.

During the Genkō War he served the shogunate under Hōjō Nakatoki, the Echigo governor; in 1333 he fled east with Nakatoki's kin after the Rokuhara tandai fell, reached Banba, and died with them at Renge-ji.

庄资房，通称左卫门四郎，是镰仓末期备中国小田郡的武将，幸山城与高山城的城主。他相传为庄有次之子，从他这一代起，备中庄氏以“资”字为通字。

元弘之乱中，他追随幕府方的越后守北条仲时；1333年六波罗探题陷落后，他随仲时一族向东败退，至番场莲华寺时，与之一同忠死。

元弘之乱中，他追随幕府方的越后守北条仲时；1333年六波罗探题陷落后，他随仲时一族向东败退，至番场莲华寺时，与之一同忠死。

en:
Shō Sukemasa, known as Saemon, was a warrior of Oda District in Bitchū Province from the end of the Kamakura period. A son of Shō Sukefusa, he was adopted by his elder brother Sukeuji and entered the main line as lord of Sarukake Castle.

Genealogies record that he served the Southern Court under Kitabatake Akiyoshi and repeatedly fought Kō no Moronao, steward of Ashikaga Takauji, earning a letter of commendation in 1353. His son Shō Sukeaki succeeded him.

zh:
庄资政，通称左卫门，是镰仓末期至南北朝时代备中国小田郡的武将，庄资房之子。他被兄长庄资氏收为养子，由此进入嫡流，成为猿挂城主。

据家谱记载，他追随南朝的北畠显能，与足利尊氏的执事高师直屡次交战，1353年因军功获赐感状。其子庄资昭继嗣。

en:
Shō Sukeuji, known as Shichirō, was a warrior of Oda District in Bitchū Province at the end of the Kamakura period. His father Shō Sukefusa died fighting for the Hōjō in 1333 during the Genkō War, and Sukeuji succeeded him as second lord of Takayama Castle, also called Kōyama Castle.

He then took service with Emperor Go-Daigo on the Southern Court side in the Nanboku-chō wars, and adopted his younger brother Sukemasa, who became lord of Sarukake Castle.

庄资氏，通称七郎，是镰仓时代末期备中国小田郡的武将，高山城（又称幸山城）第二代城主。1333年元弘之乱中，父亲庄资房随北条仲时作战而死，资氏继任城主。

随后他投奔后醍醐天皇，在南北朝动乱中为南朝效力。他收弟弟庄资政为养子，资政后来成为猿挂城主。

en:
Shō Tomotsugu, also called Honjō Tomotsugu, was a Kamakura-period warrior, the legitimate son of Shō Ietsugu and possibly the second of the Bitchū Shō line; his birthplace is uncertain. In 1238 the Azuma Kagami names him among the vanguard guards who escorted the fourth shogun, Fujiwara no Yoritsune, into Kyoto.

He did not inherit the Kodama main-house lands, settling instead at Ōtaki in Chichibu District while his uncle Tokiie took the main line. He was the father of Aritsugu.

庄朝次，亦称本庄朝次，是镰仓时代的武士，庄家次的嫡子，可能是备中庄氏第二代，出生地不详。1238年，《吾妻镜》记载他作为先锋随兵护卫第四代将军藤原赖经入洛。

他没有继承儿玉党本宗家的领地，而是移居秩父郡的大泷，本宗家由叔父时家继承。其子为有次。

en:
Shō Yoriie, known as Kotarō, was a late-Heian warrior from Kurisaki in Musashi, seat of the Kodama band. The legitimate son of Shō Ienaga, he was the sixth head of the Kodama main house.

In 1184 he followed Minamoto no Noriyori against the Taira and was killed at the Battle of Ichinotani. He left no heir, so the headship passed to his younger brother Ietsugu, and his young widow Myōsei founded Yūsō-ji near his grave in 1202.

庄赖家，通称小太郎，是平安时代末期武藏国栗崎（儿玉党本据）的年轻武将。他是庄家长的嫡子，为儿玉党本宗家第六代当主。

1184年，他追随源范赖讨伐平家，在一之谷之战中奋战而死。他身后无嗣，家督由弟弟家次继承；年轻的夫人妙清于1202年在其墓旁建立宥庄寺。

en:
Emperor Shōmu (701–756), the 45th emperor of Japan, reigned from 724 to 749. A devout Buddhist, he ordered provincial monasteries and nunneries in 741 and in 743 commissioned Tōdai-ji's sixteen-metre Vairocana Buddha in Nara.

His rule saw the Fujiwara no Hirotsugu rebellion of 740, after which he moved the capital to Kuni-kyō. He made the Fujiwara-born Kōmyō the first empress from outside the imperial family, then abdicated in 749 for his daughter Kōken, took Buddhist vows, and attended the Buddha's consecration in 752.

zh:
圣武天皇（701—756）是日本第45代天皇，724年至749年在位。他笃信佛教，741年下令在各国建立国分寺与国分尼寺，743年发愿铸造奈良东大寺高约十六米的卢舍那大佛。

在位期间发生740年的藤原广嗣之乱，乱后迁都恭仁京。他立藤原氏出身的光明子为皇后，是首位非皇族出身的皇后；749年让位于女儿孝谦，出家为僧，并于752年出席大佛开眼供养法会。

en:
Shōni Fuyusuke was a Kyushu warrior of the Nanboku-chō wars, the second son of Shōni Yorihisa and eighth head of the clan. After his brother Tadasuke fell in 1359 and their father retired in 1361, he succeeded as clan head and fought the Southern Court alongside the Ōtomo and Shimazu.

In 1371 he welcomed the new Kyushu deputy Imagawa Sadayo, and in 1372 helped retake Dazaifu. In 1375, after reluctantly joining Sadayo's campaign at Mizushima, he was cut down at a welcoming banquet on Sadayo's orders in the Mizushima Incident. His brother Yorizumi succeeded him.

zh:
少贰冬资是日本南北朝时代的九州武将，为少贰赖尚的次子、少贰氏第八代当主。1359年兄长直资战死后，父亲又于1361年隐居，他遂继承家督，联合大友氏、岛津氏与南朝作战。

1371年他迎接新任九州探题今川贞世（了俊），并于1372年协助其收复大宰府。1375年他勉强前往水岛参加贞世的军阵，却在欢迎宴会上被贞世下令斩杀，史称水岛之变。家督由弟弟赖澄继承。

en:
Shōni Moritsune (1254–1308) was a mid-Kamakura commander and the fourth head of the Shōni clan, thought to have been the eldest son of Shōni Tsunesuke. He inherited the shugo posts of Chikuzen, Tsushima and Iki, while the clan's other provinces passed into Hōjō hands.

In 1297 the shogunate posted the first Chinzei tandai to Hakata, tightening Hōjō rule over Kyushu as Moritsune prepared against a third Mongol invasion. He died in Kamakura in 1308.

zh:
少贰盛经（1254—1308）是镰仓时代中期的武将、九州少贰氏第四代当主，一般认为是少贰经资的长子。他继承了父亲的筑前、对马、壹岐守护之职，而少贰氏的其他领国守护则落入北条之手。

1297年，镰仓幕府向博多派出首任镇西探题，在盛经防备蒙古第三次来袭的同时，北条氏对九州的控制日益加强。1308年，盛经在镰仓去世。

en:
Shōni Sadatsune (1272–1336) was a commander of the late Kamakura and Nanboku-chō eras and the fifth head of the Shōni clan. In 1333 he helped the Chinzei tandai defeat Kikuchi Taketoki's revolt, then defected to Ashikaga Takauji after the Rokuhara tandai fell, forcing the Chinzei tandai to kill himself.

He joined Takauji's revolt in 1335; in 1336, with his son Yorihisa away leading the main army, he was attacked by Kikuchi Taketoshi at Uchiyama Castle and took his own life.

少贰贞经（1272—1336）是镰仓时代后期至南北朝时代的武将、少贰氏第五代当主。1333年菊池武时举兵时，他起初协助镇西探题将其击败；六波罗探题陷落后便倒向足利尊氏，迫使镇西探题自尽。

en:
Shōni Sukeyoshi (1198–1281) was a Kamakura-period warrior and the second head of the Shōni clan, the first to take the Shōni name. As the shogunate's Chinzei commissioner over northern Kyūshū, he received envoys from the Mongol Yuan in 1268.

He took Buddhist orders before the first Mongol invasion of 1274 and passed family leadership to his son Tsunesuke, yet still led Kyūshū's forces against the invaders. In 1281 he fought at Iki Island and helped drive the Mongols out, dying soon afterwards from his wounds at eighty-four.

zh:
少贰资能（1198—1281）是镰仓时代武将、少贰氏第二代当主，也是家族中最先以少贰为姓者。作为幕府的镇西奉行，他在北九州势力极大，1268年曾负责接待元朝使者。

1274年文永之役前夕他出家，将家督让给长子经资，但仍以高龄出任九州总指挥官迎战元军。1281年弘安之役，他在壹岐岛之战中奋力将元军逐出，却因战伤不久后去世，享年84岁。

en:
Shōni Tadasuke was a Kyushu warrior of the Nanboku-chō wars, the eldest son of Shōni Yorihisa and seventh head of the clan. By 1350 his father had transferred to him the hereditary title of Dazai Shōni, and the character 'tada' in his name was granted by Ashikaga Tadafuyu, husband of his sister.

He led the Shōni under his father, and in 1359 fell at the Battle of Chikugogawa, also called Ōbara, against Kikuchi Takemitsu's Southern Court army. His brother Fuyusuke succeeded him as clan head.

By 1350 his father had transferred to him the hereditary title of Dazai Shōni, and the character 'tada' in his name was granted by #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_ashikaga_tadafuyu').GetID],X #L Ashikaga Tadafuyu#!#!, husband of his sister.

He led the Shōni under his father, and in 1359 fell at the Battle of Chikugogawa, also called Ōbara, against #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_kikuchi_takemitsu').GetID],X #L Kikuchi Takemitsu#!#!'s Southern Court army. His brother Fuyusuke succeeded him as clan head.
zh:
少贰直资是日本南北朝时代的九州武将，为少贰赖尚的长子、少贰氏第七代当主。约1350年，父亲将世代相传的大宰少贰名号让给他，名字中的‘直’字则得自其姐妹之夫足利直冬的偏讳。

他随父亲领兵征战，1359年在筑后川之战（又称大保原之战）中对阵菊池武光的南朝军，战死沙场。家督由弟弟冬资继承。

en:
Shōni Tsunesuke (1229–1292) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and the third Shōni head, succeeding his father Sukeyoshi. In Kyūshū he organised the anti-Mongol coastal defences, including the Hakata stone wall, and inherited the family headship in 1275.

At the 1281 Battle of Iki Island he fought wounded and drove off the Mongols, but lost his son Suketoki. Ordained in 1284, he sided against his brother in the Shimotsuki conflict of 1285, and the Shōni were stripped of several governorships. He died in 1292 and was succeeded by Moritsune.

zh:
少贰经资（1229—1292）是镰仓时代中期的武将、少贰氏第三代当主，继承父亲资能。他在九州负责整备抵御蒙古的沿海防御，统括博多石垒的修筑，1275年继承家督。

1281年壹岐岛之战，他带伤奋战、击退元军，却失去了儿子资时。1284年出家；1285年霜月骚乱中与弟弟兵戎相向，少贰氏随后被剥夺数国守护职。1292年去世，家督由盛经继承。

en:
Shōni Yorihisa (1294–1372) was sixth head of the Shōni house of Kyushu. In 1333 he joined the Genkō War and helped his father Sadatsune destroy the Hōjō deputy at Hakata. He fought beside Ashikaga Takauji at Tatarahama in 1336 and Minatogawa, receiving several provincial shugo posts in return.

In 1349 he backed Ashikaga Tadafuyu, marrying him to his daughter, and later joined the Southern Court's Prince Kanenaga against the Isshiki. Defeated by Kikuchi Takemitsu at the Chikugogawa in 1359 and driven from Dazaifu in 1361, he retired to Kyoto in 1367 and died in 1372.

zh:
少贰赖尚（1294—1372）是九州武家少贰氏第六代当主。1333年他参加元弘之乱，随父亲少贰贞经攻灭博多的北条氏镇西探题。他追随足利尊氏，在1336年的多多良滨之战和凑川之战中作战，受封数国守护职。

1349年他扶植逃到九州的足利直冬并招其为婿，后又与南朝的怀良亲王结盟对抗一色氏。1359年他在筑后川之战败于菊池武光，1361年被逐出大宰府，1367年隐居上京，1372年在京都去世。

en:
Soga no Iname (c. 506–570) led the Soga clan and became the first verifiable Ōomi, or great minister, in 536, serving Emperor Kinmei. He strengthened his house by marrying two daughters, Kitashihime and Oanegimi, to Kinmei; their children included Emperor Yōmei, Emperor Sushun and Empress Suiko.

After Buddhism reached the Yamato court from Baekje in 552, he became its leading patron and built a temple, drawing the hostility of the Mononobe and Nakatomi clans. He died in 570, and his son Soga no Umako inherited his power.

zh:
苏我稻目（约506—570）是苏我氏首领，536年成为日本史上第一位可考的大臣，侍奉钦明天皇。他把坚盐媛、小姊君两个女儿嫁给钦明天皇，所生子女中包括用明天皇、崇峻天皇和推古天皇。

552年佛教自百济传入大和朝廷后，他成为最主要的崇佛者并建寺，由此招致物部氏与中臣氏的敌视。他于570年去世，其子苏我马子继承了他的权势。

en:
Soga no Kitashihime was a daughter of the Soga clan leader Soga no Iname and a consort of Emperor Kinmei. She bore him seven sons and six daughters, among them Emperor Yōmei and Princess Nukatabe, who reigned as Empress Suiko, Japan's first empress regnant.

After her death she received the title kōtaifujin, and in 612 a grand state funeral re-interred her beside Emperor Kinmei in his Hinokuma tumulus, a ceremony that displayed the Soga clan's power.

Soga no Oane no Kimi was a daughter of the Soga clan leader Soga no Iname and a sister of Soga no Umako. She followed her sister Kitashihime into the palace as a consort of Emperor Kinmei and bore him five children.

They included Prince Hatsusebe, who reigned as Emperor Sushun from 587 until his assassination in 592, and Princess Anahobe no Hashihito, wife of Emperor Yōmei and mother of Prince Shōtoku.

en:
Sō Moriakira was a Kamakura-period warrior and deputy steward (jitō-dai) of Tsushima, the eldest son of Sō Sukekuni. In 1274 his father was killed opposing the Mongol landing at Sasuura in the Bun'ei campaign; Moriakira escaped because he was serving at Dazaifu, and succeeded him as the Sō family's head on the island.

He fought the Mongols once more when they returned in force during the Kōan campaign of 1281. His common name was Umatarō.

en:
Sō Morikuni was the fourth head of the Sō clan, the warrior family that ruled Tsushima Island, succeeding his father Moriaki. He received a character for his name from the Shōni of northern Kyushu, his suzerains.

After the Muromachi shogunate was founded in 1336, he acknowledged its authority and governed Tsushima as the Shōni's deputy through the Northern and Southern Courts wars. His son Tsuneshige succeeded him as head of the clan.

Sō Morinao was a warrior of the Northern and Southern Courts period and the eldest son of Sō Morikuni. Born in Chikuzen, he lost a struggle for the family headship to Tsuneshige, Morikuni's designated heir.

While Tsuneshige joined the Northern Court, Morinao served Kikuchi Takemitsu on the Southern Court's side. He fought the forces of Imagawa Ryōshun, the shogunate's commissioner in Kyushu, and was killed in battle in 1372.

en:
Sō Shigehisa was a legendary Kamakura-period warrior whom the Sō clan of Tsushima called its founder. Tradition makes him a son of Taira no Tomomune.

In 1245, after Abiru Kuninobu of Tsushima defied orders from Dazaifu, Shigehisa defeated him and was appointed deputy steward (jitō-dai) of the island, the foundation of the Sō family's rule there. His grave is shown at Kifurugoba Shrine.

In 1245, after Abiru Kuninobu of Tsushima defied orders from Dazaifu, Shigehisa defeated him and was appointed deputy steward (jitō-dai) of the island, the foundation of the Sō family's rule there. His grave is shown at Kifurugoba Shrine.
zh:
宗重尚是传说中的镰仓时代武将，被对马宗氏尊为始祖。相传他是平知宗之子。

1245年，对马的阿比留国信违抗大宰府之命，重尚将其讨伐，并因功被任为对马地头代，这成为宗氏统治对马的根基。木武古婆神社存有相传为他的坟墓。

en:
Sō Sukekuni (1207–1274) was a mid-Kamakura warrior and deputy steward of Tsushima for the Shōni family. He is counted the second Sō head on the island.

In the Bun'ei campaign a Mongol fleet said to number four hundred and fifty ships landed at Sasuura on 4 November 1274. Sukekuni rode through the night with only eighty-odd horsemen, and next morning sent an interpreter to question the invaders, who opened fire; his men formed ranks to fight.

The Hachiman Gudōkun recounts that he fell with his sons and his men in the Mongol invasions' first battle. He is enshrined at Komodahama Shrine.

zh:
宗助国（1207—1274）是镰仓时代中期武将，任对马国地头代，代少贰氏管理对马。他被视为对马宗氏第二代当主。

文永之役时，据称四百五十艘船只的元丽联军于1274年11月4日在佐须浦登陆，助国仅率八十余骑连夜穿山驰赴战场。次日清晨，他派通译前去问询，来军随即射箭，助国等人列阵应战。

据《八幡愚童训》记载，他与儿子及郎党一同战死，这是蒙古袭日的首场战斗。他被祭祀于小茂田浜神社。

en:
Sō Tsuneshige, also called Sōkei, was the fifth head of the Sō clan of Tsushima and a son of Morikuni. He received a character for his name from Shōni Sadatsune of northern Kyushu, to whom the Sō were vassals.

In 1349 he made his younger brother Yoritsugu his deputy on the island and moved him to Nii village. After the Shōni ceased issuing orders on Tsushima around 1362, he turned the Sō holdings there into a domain of their own. Sumishige succeeded him.

zh:
宗经茂，一称宗庆，是对马宗氏第五代当主，宗盛国之子。他从宗氏的主君、北九州的少贰贞经处接受偏讳。

1349年他任命弟弟宗赖次为对马的代理，让其移住仁位村。1362年以后少贰氏不再向对马下发文书，经茂开始将宗氏在岛上的领地经营为独立领国。宗澄茂后来继他之后成为当主。

en:
Sō Yoritsugu, better known as Nii Shūkō, was a commander of the Northern and Southern Courts period and a younger son of the Tsushima lord Sō Morikuni. In 1349 his elder brother Tsuneshige made him deputy governor of Tsushima, and he moved from Dazaifu to Nakamura in Nii village on the island.

He banned reckless mountain logging and in 1362 set the crop tax at two bu five rin, working to stabilize the island's government. After his death islanders enshrined him at the Jinushi shrine.

zh:
宗赖次，通常以仁位宗香之名著称，是日本南北朝时代的武将，对马领主宗盛国之子。1349年，兄长宗经茂任命他为对马守护代，他遂从大宰府迁往岛上的仁位村中村。

他禁止滥伐山林，并于1362年将田租定为二分五厘，致力于安定民政。死后岛民感念其功绩，在地主社祭祀他。

en:
Sōma Chikatane (dates unknown) was the seventh head of the Mutsu Sōma clan and lord of Odaka Castle, who accompanied his father Shigetane in the clan's migration from Shimōsa to Mutsu. He inherited the headship in 1335 and fought for Ashikaga Takauji against the Kenmu regime, seeing action at Hakone and Takenoshita.

While he campaigned as far as Kyushu, his father fell at Kamakura and Odaka fell to the Southern Court. Returning north, he rallied the clan survivors, defeated Kitabatake Akiie, and retook the old domains. He appears to have retired as a monk in 1358.

相马亲胤（生没年不详）是陆奥相马氏第七代当主、小高城城主，在父亲重胤一代随一族从下总迁往陆奥。1335年他继承家督，追随足利尊氏反抗建武政权，在箱根、竹之下等地作战。

他转战至九州期间，父亲在镰仓战死，小高城被南朝攻陷；亲胤返回陆奥后聚拢残党，击败北畠显家，收复旧领。据推测他于1358年出家隐居。

en:
Sōma Morotane was a Kamakura-period warrior of the Sōma clan, a Chiba branch house, and the fifth head of the line later called the Mutsu Sōma. A son of Sōma Tanemura by a later wife, he claimed after Tanemura's death that the will named him heir over his half-brother Sōma Ujiuji.

The headship was confirmed to Ujiuji and Morotane remained without rank or office. In the Shōō era (1288–1293) he ceded his lands to his son Sōma Shigetane; he had died by the Einin era.

相马师胤是镰仓时代武将，出自千叶氏庶流相马氏，被列为日后陆奥相马氏一脉的第五代当主。他是相马胤村后妻所生之子，父亲去世后声称胤村遗命立自己为继承人，与异母兄相马胤氏对立。

最终家督由胤氏继承，师胤无位无官。正应年间（1288—1293），他将所领让给儿子相马重胤，至永仁年间已经去世。

en:
Sōma Morotsune (1139?–1205) was a son of Chiba Tsunetane and the first head of the Sōma house. With his father he joined Minamoto no Yoritomo's rising of 1180 and campaigned under Yoritomo's brother Noriyori; his service in the 1189 Ōshū campaign is said to have earned him a banner of Hachiman Daibosatsu from Yoritomo.

When Tsunetane died in 1201 he took Buddhist orders and passed leadership to his son Yoshitane. He is said to have died seated at his Kamakura mansion in 1205 while chanting the nenbutsu.

相马师常（1139？—1205）是千叶常胤之子、相马氏初代当主。他与父亲一同参加源赖朝1180年的举兵，隶属赖朝之弟源范赖的军队转战各地；相传他在1189年奥州合战时立功，获赖朝赐予“八幡大菩萨”旗帜。

1201年父亲常胤去世后他出家为僧，把家督让给儿子义胤。相传他于1205年在镰仓的相马邸端坐念佛而终。

en:
Sōma Shigetane was the sixth head of the Mutsu Sōma line and its effective founder in Mutsu. Repeatedly worsted in land disputes with the main Sōma line, in 1323 he led eighty-odd mounted followers north to Namekata District, where he built Odaka Castle and extended his holdings along the Ota River.

After the Kamakura shogunate fell in 1333 he joined the Kenmu Restoration, then sided with Ashikaga Takauji. He died in 1336 defending Kamakura against Kitabatake Akiie's Southern Court army.

相马重胤是陆奥相马氏一脉的第六代当主，也是该氏在陆奥的实际开创者。他与相马氏嫡流因领地屡次相争、渐处下风，遂于1323年率八十余骑北上进入陆奥国行方郡，修筑小高城，沿太田川扩张势力。

1333年镰仓幕府灭亡后，他先归附建武新政，后转投足利尊氏。1336年，他在镰仓抵御南朝方北畠显家的进攻时战死。

en:
Sōma Yoshitane was the second head of the Sōma clan and a Kamakura shogunate vassal, succeeding his father Morotsune in 1201. In 1205, although related to Hatakeyama Shigetada by marriage, he took Hōjō Yoshitoki's side and helped destroy him, receiving the stewardship of Takagi in Mutsu as his reward.

During the Jōkyū War of 1221 he and his son Tanetsuna fought for the shogunate at the Uji River and at Seta Bridge in Ōmi.

en:
Sue Hiromasa was the second head of the Sue, a warrior clan of Suō Province that served the Ōuchi as hereditary retainers. The son of the clan founder Sue Hirokata, he held the Tonda estate in Tsuno District before a war in 1352, and built a fortified residence called Hirajō there.

He founded Shōeiji, whose grounds were ringed with earthen ramparts and a moat, and placed outlying forts on the nearby hills. He also founded Shōgo-ji in Sue village, where his grave remains.

en:
Sue Hironaga was the third head of the Sue clan of Suō Province and the son of Sue Hiromasa. In 1399 he followed Ōuchi Yoshihiro in the Ōei Rebellion against the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. Hironaga urged Yoshihiro to return to Suō and try again, but Yoshihiro fought on and was killed.

Hironaga later supported Ōuchi Moriharu in the succession struggle, and in 1401 the Ōuchi appointed him shugodai, deputy military governor of Nagato Province. He was killed campaigning at Inodake in Buzen Province. His cousin Morinaga succeeded him as head of the Sue.

en:
Suiko (554–628), Japan's first recognised empress, was a daughter of Emperor Kinmei and Soga no Kitashihime, and from 576 empress to her half-brother Emperor Bidatsu. After Soga no Umako had Emperor Sushun murdered in 592, she was enthroned in 593.

She named her nephew Shōtoku regent, and their rule promoted Buddhism with the Flourishing Three Treasures Edict of 594, opened relations with Sui China in 600, and introduced the Seventeen-Article Constitution. In 624 she rejected Umako's bid for the Kazuraki district; she died in 628.

zh:
推古天皇（554—628）是日本第一位得到广泛承认的女帝，为钦明天皇与苏我坚盐媛之女，576年成为异母兄敏达天皇的皇后。592年苏我马子弑杀崇峻天皇后，她于593年被拥上皇位。

她立侄儿圣德太子为摄政，在位期间以594年的《兴隆三宝诏》弘扬佛教，600年与中国隋朝建立关系，并推行《十七条宪法》。624年，她断然拒绝马子索要葛城县封地的请求；628年去世。

en:
Sukō (1334–1398), personal name Okihito, was the third emperor of the Northern Court in Kyoto and the eldest son of Emperor Kōgon. He became crown prince and ascended in 1348 after Emperor Kōmyō abdicated, while Kōgon directed affairs as cloistered emperor.

In 1351 Ashikaga Takauji made peace with the Southern Court and forced Sukō from the throne. In 1352 Southern troops carried him off to Yoshino with Kōgon and Kōmyō; he returned to Kyoto in 1357. His great-grandson became Emperor Go-Hanazono in 1428.

en:
Sushun (c. 553–592), the 32nd emperor of Japan, was a son of Emperor Kinmei who ascended in 587 as Prince Hatsusebe. His reign was dominated by the minister Soga no Umako.

Resenting this, Sushun planned to do away with Umako, but the minister struck first: in 592 he sent an agent who murdered the emperor. He is the only Japanese sovereign whose assassination by a subject the official chronicles record outright. The throne then passed to his half-sister, Empress Suiko.

en:
Emperor Sutoku (1119–1164) was the 75th emperor of Japan, a son of Emperor Toba by Fujiwara no Tamako. Put on the throne at three in 1123, he was a figurehead under Shirakawa and then Toba, who in 1141 forced him to abdicate for his younger brother Konoe.

After Toba's death he rose in the Hōgen Rebellion of 1156, was defeated by Go-Shirakawa's forces, and died in 1164 in exile in Sanuki Province. He was later counted among Japan's three vengeful spirits and enshrined at Shiramine Shrine.

en:
Suwa Morishige was a mid-Kamakura warrior and a miuchibito of the Hōjō tokusō. First appearing in the Azuma Kagami in 1230, he kept a residence inside Hōjō Yasutoki's compound from 1236 and handled dealings with the court. After ordination he was known as Renbutsu.

As spokesman for the tokusō's housemen he calmed the warriors gathering at Kamakura on the eve of the Hōji War of 1247 and was praised by Hōjō Tokiyori for matchless service. He died around the fourth month of 1267.

en:
Suwa Naoyori was the name taken by Suwa Upper Shrine high priest Yoritsugu after he received a character from Ashikaga Tadayoshi. In the Kannō Disturbance of 1350 to 1352 he led Tadayoshi's faction in Shinano, and in 1351 captured Suzawa Castle, where Kō no Morofuyu killed himself.

After Tadayoshi's fall he served Prince Munenaga of the Southern Court and fought at Musashino in 1352, but returned to the Muromachi shogunate by 1359. Ordained as Fukan, he remained the Suwa clan's elder statesman until his death around 1395.

en:
Suwa Tokitsugu was high priest of the Upper Shrine of Suwa and the legitimate heir of Suwa Yorishige. He likely fought for the shogunate at the 1331 siege of Akasaka Castle, and after the shogunate's fall joined his father in sheltering Hōjō Tokiyuki.

In the second month of 1335 he passed the high-priesthood to his seven-year-old son Yoritsugu, and that summer father and son rose in the Nakasendai War and briefly held Kamakura. Defeated by Ashikaga Takauji, Tokitsugu killed himself on 6 September 1335.

en:
Suwa Yorishige was high priest of the Upper Shrine of Suwa in Shinano and leader of the Suwa Shrine warrior league. After the Kamakura shogunate fell in 1333, he sheltered the orphaned Hōjō Tokiyuki.

In the seventh month of 1335 he and his son Tokitsugu raised Tokiyuki in the Nakasendai War, routing Ashikaga Tadayoshi and taking Kamakura. Ashikaga Takauji marched east and crushed the rising, and on 6 September 1335 Yorishige killed himself in Kamakura, letting Tokiyuki escape.

en:
Suwa Yoritsugu (1329–c. 1395) was the ōhōri, high priest of the Upper Shrine of Suwa in Shinano Province, and the son of Suwa Tokitsugu. His father and grandfather died backing Hōjō Tokiyuki in the Nakasendai Rebellion of 1335, so he inherited the priesthood as a child.

In 1347 he petitioned the Muromachi shogunate for the rank of Shinano-no-kami and joined Ashikaga Tadayoshi's faction, rivalling the Ogasawara clan for mastery of Shinano. He later took the names Naoyori and then Yorihiro.

en:
Emperor Suzaku (923–952), personal name Yutaakira, was Japan's 61st emperor, reigning from 930 to 946. The eleventh son of Emperor Daigo, he ascended at eight under the regency of his uncle Fujiwara no Tadahira.

His reign saw the Shōhei–Tengyō rebellions: Taira no Masakado's revolt was crushed in 940 and Fujiwara no Sumitomo's western rising in 941. Sickly and heirless, Suzaku abdicated to his brother Emperor Murakami in 946, took vows, and died in 952.

zh:
朱雀天皇（923—952），名宽明，是日本第61代天皇，930年至946年在位。他是醍醐天皇第十一子，八岁即位，舅父藤原忠平以摄政身份掌权。

在位期间爆发承平、天庆年间的叛乱：平将门起兵，940年被讨平；藤原纯友在西方的叛乱于941年被镇压。朱雀体弱无嗣，946年让位于弟村上天皇，随后出家，952年去世。

en:
Taira no Kiyomori (1118–1181) succeeded his father Tadamori as head of the Taira in 1153. In 1156 he crushed the Hōgen Rebellion, then defeated Minamoto no Yoshitomo in the 1160 Heiji Disturbance, leaving the Taira supreme in Kyoto.

In 1167 he became the first warrior appointed daijō-daijin. He married a daughter to Emperor Takakura, seized power in a 1179 coup, and placed his grandson Antoku on the throne in 1180 as the Genpei War began. He died in 1181.

Taira no Korehira was a mid-Heian warrior, the fourth son of Taira no Sadamori, who built a power base in Ise Province and founded the Ise Taira line, from which Taira no Kiyomori later sprang.

en:
Taira no Kunika (872–935) was the eldest son of Taira no Takamochi and, through his son Sadamori, the ancestor of the Hitachi and Ise Taira lines. In 898 he went east with his father and settled at Ishida in Hitachi, west of Mount Tsukuba.

Marrying a daughter of Minamoto no Mamoru, he succeeded to his father-in-law's post and extended the family's local power. In 935 his nephew Taira no Masakado burned the Ishida hall and killed Kunika, the first bloodshed of the Tengyō War.

en:
Taira no Masahira was a mid-Heian warrior of the Ise Taira and the fifth son of Taira no Masanori, the clan's head. Based in Ise, in 1075 he backed a monk's forced seizure of the Tado Jingū-ji estates, later ruled invalid by the court.

In Kyoto he served Fujiwara no Morozane, and in 1079 helped defend the capital against Enryaku-ji warrior monks. Appointed governor of Dewa in 1099, he vanishes from the records afterward; his son Masamori laid the groundwork for the Taira rise.

en:
Taira no Masamori was a late-Heian warrior and head of the Ise Taira, son of Taira no Masahira and grandfather of Taira no Kiyomori. He rose under Retired Emperor Shirakawa as a palace guard.

In 1108 he crushed Minamoto no Yoshichika's rebellion in Izumo and received Tajima as his reward, though contemporaries doubted he had killed the famed rebel. He suppressed pirates in 1114 and a rebel magnate in Hizen in 1119, spreading Taira power across the western seas, and died around 1121.

en:
Taira no Masanori was a mid-Heian warrior, the eldest son (by another account, the second) of Taira no Korehira, under whom the Ise Taira consolidated their power. He expanded the family's holdings in Ise and rose through provincial posts to the junior fourth rank.

His son Masahira's line led to Taira no Kiyomori, while another son, Suehira, founded the house that later served as stewards of the Muromachi shogunate. Masanori was dead by 1067.

en:
Taira no Masatsune was a mid-Heian warrior of the Kanmu Taira line and founder of Musashi's Chichibu clan, born to Taira no Tadayori and Haruhime, daughter of Taira no Masakado. In 1023 he led troops against Musashi's assistant governor, who had defied an imperial order, and defeated him at Toshima.

He was rewarded with lands in several provinces. He took no part in his brother Taira no Tadatsune's 1028 revolt and kept his lands; based in Chichibu, he is said to have fallen in the Earlier Nine Years' War aged fifty-one.

en:

He held an estate at Kamakura, and after marrying his daughter to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi made over his lands and retainers to the groom. She bore Yoriyoshi sons including Minamoto no Yoshiie, and the Hōjō and Kumagai clans claimed descent from him.

en:
Taira no Sadamori (died 989) was a warrior of the Kammu Taira line and the legitimate son of Taira no Kunika. In 935 his father was killed in the rising of their cousin Taira no Masakado. Sadamori fought Masakado for years, once fleeing to the capital after defeat in Shinano, and in 940 joined Fujiwara no Hidesato to kill him at Kojima.

Rewarded, he later became Chinjufu shōgun and governor of Mutsu, and was called the Taira General. His son Korehira founded the Ise Taira branch.

en:
Taira no Shigemori (1138–1179) was the eldest son of Taira no Kiyomori. He fought beside his father in the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 and the Heiji Disturbance of 1159, rising to become inner minister. Known as the Komatsu minister from his Rokuhara mansion, he was the Taira leader closest to Cloistered Emperor Go-Shirakawa.

He struggled to mediate between the cloistered emperor and his father, then died of illness in 1179, aged forty-two; his brother Munemori inherited the clan's leadership.

en:
Taira no Shigemori was a mid-Heian warrior, the second son of Taira no Kunika and younger brother of Taira no Sadamori. He fought beside Sadamori to suppress Taira no Masakado's revolt of 939–940 and won fame, but got little reward and was left resentful.

Appointed daijō, senior secretary of Hitachi, he became known as Daijō Shigemori, founder of the Hitachi Taira. In 986 he dedicated six hundred scrolls of the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra to Enryaku-ji, an offering his rivals obstructed in Musashi.

zh:
平繁盛是平安时代中期的武将，平国香的次子、平贞盛之弟。他随兄长贞盛参与平定939—940年的平将门之乱，以武勇闻名，却所得恩赏甚少，心怀不满。

他受任常陆大掾，被称为“大掾繁盛”，是常陆平氏事实上的始祖。986年，他将六百卷《大般若经》奉献延历寺，途经武藏国时遭到仇敌阻挠。

en:
Taira no Sukemori (1161–1185) was the second son of Taira no Shigemori and a grandson of Kiyomori. In 1170 his quarrel with the retinue of Regent Matsudono Motofusa, the carriage incident, led to an armed revenge attack on the regent's men and stalled his court career.

A gifted poet whose verses appear in imperial anthologies and a favourite of Retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa, he later fought in the Genpei War. Routed at Mikusa-yama in 1184, he drowned himself after the Taira defeat at Dannoura in 1185, aged twenty-five.

平资盛（1161—1185）是平重盛次子、平清盛之孙。1170年他与摄政松殿基房的随从争执，引发武士袭击车队的报复，即“殿下乘合事件”，他的升迁也由此停滞。

资盛擅长和歌，作品收入敕撰和歌集，深受后白河法皇宠爱，后参加源平合战。他1184年在三草山遭击溃，1185年坛之浦平家败亡后投水自尽，年二十五岁。

en:
Taira no Tadamasa (died 1156) was an Ise Taira warrior, younger brother of Tadamori and uncle of Taira no Kiyomori. He first served Retired Emperor Shirakawa, and in 1119 was appointed guardian of Prince Akihito, the future Emperor Sutoku.

Dismissed by Retired Emperor Toba in 1133, he became a retainer of Fujiwara no Yorinaga. In the Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 he fought for Retired Emperor Sutoku, holding the Shirakawa palace; defeated, he fled to Ise, surrendered to Kiyomori and was executed at Rokuhara.

zh:
平忠正（？—1156）是平安时代末期的伊势平氏武将，忠盛之弟、平清盛的叔父。他仕于白河法皇，1119年被任命为显仁亲王（后来的崇德天皇）的御监。

1133年遭鸟羽上皇勘当后，他成为藤原赖长的家人。1156年保元之乱中他据守白河北殿，支持崇德上皇，兵败后逃往伊势，向侄儿清盛投降，终在六波罗被清盛处死。

en:
Taira no Tadamitsu was a mid-Heian warrior and landowner of the eastern provinces, a son of Taira no Yoshifumi and younger brother of Taira no Tadayori. Adopted as heir by his eldest brother Tadasuke, who died young, he inherited Tadasuke's estates.

After Taira no Masakado's revolt the brothers feuded with Taira no Shigemori; in 986 Tadamitsu helped block his sutra dedication to Enryaku-ji, and the court once issued pursuit orders against them. His son Taira no Tadamichi was counted an ancestor of the Miura clan.

zh:
平忠光是平安时代中期的武将、东国豪族，平良文之子、平忠赖之弟。他被早逝的长兄忠辅收为养子，继承了其领地。

平将门之乱后，忠赖、忠光兄弟与平繁盛长期对立；986年，忠光参与阻挠繁盛向延历寺奉纳经书，朝廷一度对他们发出追讨官符。其子平忠通被视为三浦氏之祖。

en:
Taira no Tadamori (1096–1153) was head of the Taira clan and father of Taira no Kiyomori. Serving retired emperors Shirakawa and Toba as a palace guardsman, he became the first samurai admitted to court. From 1129 he campaigned against pirates and confronted the warrior monks of Nara and Mount Hiei.

He governed several provinces, grew rich from trade with Song China, and built Kyoto's Rengeō-in, home of the Sanjūsangen-dō hall. His power and wealth laid the foundations of Taira rule.

zh:
平忠盛（1096—1153）是平安时代后期的武将、伊势平氏首领，也是平清盛之父。他仕于白河、鸟羽两位上皇，以北面武士身份成为首位获准升殿的武士。1129年起，他追讨海贼，并与奈良和比叡山的僧兵对抗。

他历任多国国司，借对宋朝贸易积累巨资，又在京都建造莲华王院，即三十三间堂所在。他的武力与财力为日后的平氏政权奠定了基础。

en:
Taira no Tadatsune (c. 975–1031) was a warrior chieftain of the Bōsō peninsula, son of Taira no Tadayori and maternal grandson of Taira no Masakado. Heir to great eastern estates and titled Kazusa no suke, he defied officials and withheld taxes.

In 1028 he burned the Awa headquarters and killed its governor in open revolt. He resisted the court's punitive army until 1031, when his forces were spent; he took vows and surrendered to Minamoto no Yorinobu, dying in Mino on the way to the capital.

en:
Taira no Tadayori (930–1019) was a mid-Heian warrior of the Kammu Taira, a son of Taira no Yoshifumi and cousin of Taira no Masakado. Styled Muraoka Jirō, he served as assistant governor of Musashi Province.

In 986 he and his younger brother obstructed Taira no Shigemori's dedication of six hundred sutra scrolls to Enryaku-ji, branding Shigemori, who had helped destroy Masakado, their enemy. He died early in 1019. His son Taira no Tadatsune later led a major rising in the east.

en:
Taira no Takamochi (839–911), born Prince Takamochi, was a great-grandson of Emperor Kanmu. In 889, by order of Emperor Uda, he received the surname Taira and left the imperial family, becoming vice-governor of Kazusa.

Unlike absentee officials, he took up his post with his sons, built a residence in Kazusa in 898, and stayed in the east after his term. Through local marriages and new rice lands, he built up the warrior bands on which the Kanmu Taira clans were founded.

平高望（839—911），原称高望王，是桓武天皇的曾孙。889年，他奉宇多天皇敕命获赐平朝臣姓、降为臣籍，出任上总介。

与许多遥任的国司不同，他带着儿子们赴任，898年在上总国营造居所，任满后留居东国。他与当地豪族联姻、开垦荒地，培植起武士团，奠定了桓武平氏的根基。

en:
Taira no Taketsune, also called Chichibu no Taketsune, was the second son of Taira no Masatsune of the Chichibu Taira. Toshima clan tradition names him as the founder of the Toshima line.

He followed Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Minamoto no Yoshiie on their Ōshū campaigns and fell in either the Earlier Nine Years' War of 1051–1062 or the Later Three Years' War of 1083–1087. His son was Taira no Tsuneie.

平武常又称秩父武常，是秩父平氏平将恒的次男。按照丰岛氏的谱系传说，他是丰岛氏的始祖。

en:
Taira no Tomomori (1152–1185) was a son of Taira no Kiyomori and one of the Taira's foremost Genpei War generals. He beat the Minamoto at the Uji River in 1180 and the Yahagi River in 1181, and won at Mizushima in 1183.

After Taira reverses at Kurikara and Ichinotani, where his eldest son was killed, he held Hikoshima. At Dannoura in 1185, he strapped an anchor to himself and leapt into the sea rather than be captured.

en:
Taira no Tomomune (1184–1255) was a son of Taira no Tomomori, born while the Taira fled the capital during the Genpei War. After the clan's destruction at Dannoura in 1185, he was sheltered in Kyūshū by Mutō Sukeyori and became his adopted son.

In 1200 he was appointed dazai daikan at Dazaifu. He also used the names Koremune Tomomune and Sō Tomomune, and died there in 1255. The Sō lords of Tsushima claimed him as their ancestor.

en:
Taira no Tsunekane (1045–1126) was a warrior and the first head of the Chiba clan. The son of Taira no Tsunenaga, he is said to have taken the title Chiba Daisuke from the Chiba estate in Shimōsa, which gave the clan its name.

Chronicles record him fighting beside his father in the Later Three Years' War of 1083–1087. His third son Tsuneshige, adopted by his younger brother Tsuneharu, inherited both the Chiba name and the headship of the Bōsō Taira, a succession that later split the clan.

平常兼（1045—1126）是平安时代武将、千叶氏初代当主。他是平常长之子，相传因下总国千叶乡而号称“千叶大介”，千叶氏由此得名。

据记载，他在1083—1087年的后三年之役中随父出征，立下战功。三男常重被弟弟常晴收为养子，同时继承千叶之名与房总平氏的惣领地位，这一安排日后成为一族抗争的根源。

en:
Taira no Tsunemasa (1010–1076) was a mid-Heian warrior of the Bandō Taira and a son of Taira no Tadatsune. After his father's revolt of 1028 and surrender in 1031, Tsunemasa and his younger brother escorted him toward the capital; Tadatsune died of illness in Mino and the brothers were pardoned.

Back in Shimōsa, he styled himself Chiba no suke, and Chiba genealogies count him as the first head of the Chiba clan. He was the father of Taira no Tsunenaga.

Taira no Tsunenaga (1024–1108) was a Heian warrior, son of Taira no Tsunemasa, who fought for Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Minamoto no Yoshiie in the Earlier Nine Years' and Later Three Years' wars.

en:
Taira no Yoshifumi (886–953), fifth son of Taira no Takamochi, was born in Kyoto. He did not go east with his father in 898, but in 923 Emperor Daigo sent him to suppress bandits in Sagami, and he settled in the Kantō.

In 939 he was made chinjufu general, and the next year brought the capital the first report of Taira no Masakado's defeat and death. Known as Muraoka Gorō after his stronghold, he is regarded as ancestor of the eight Taira clans of Bandō.

en:
Takakura (1161–1181), son of retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa, took the throne in 1168 after Emperor Rokujō was deposed. Real power rested with his father through cloistered rule and, after 1172, with his father-in-law Taira no Kiyomori, whose daughter Tokuko became empress.

Their son Tokuhito was born in 1178 and named heir within weeks. Pressed by the Taira, he abdicated in March 1180 for the year-old Tokuhito, the future Emperor Antoku. He briefly joined the court at Fukuhara and died in January 1181, aged nineteen.

Pressed by the Taira, he abdicated in March 1180 for the year-old Tokuhito, the future #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_antoku_tenno').GetID],X #L Emperor Antoku#!#!. He briefly joined the court at Fukuhara and died in January 1181, aged nineteen.
zh:
高仓天皇（1161—1181）是后白河上皇之子，1168年六条天皇被废后被扶上皇位。实权先由父亲以院政掌握，1172年他娶平清盛之女德子为皇后，岳父清盛也把持朝政。

1178年德子生下言仁亲王，出生仅数周即被立为太子。在平家压力下，高仓于1180年3月让位给一岁的言仁，即后来的安德天皇。他曾随朝廷短暂迁往福原京，1181年1月去世，年仅十九岁。

en:
Sasaki Takanobu, also called Takashima Takanobu, was an early Kamakura-period warrior of Ōmi and the second son of Sasaki Nobutsuna, head of the Sasaki clan. As jitō of Tanaka village in Takashima district he founded the Takashima clan.

In 1235 a dispute with the Hiyoshi Shrine escalated when his deputy killed a shrine monk; Enryakuji monks marched on Kyoto with portable shrines, and the court exiled Takanobu to Bungo Province. His descendants and the unrelated Yamazaki clan became known as the Seven Heads of Takashima.

佐佐木高信，又称高岛高信，是镰仓时代前期近江国武士，佐佐木氏惣领佐佐木信纲的次子。他担任高岛郡田中乡的地头，成为高岛氏之祖。

1235年，他与日吉社发生争端，其地头代杀死社中僧人；延历寺僧众抬神舆进入京都强诉，朝廷将高信流放丰后国。他的后裔与另系的山崎氏合称高岛七头。

en:
Takashina no Mineo was an early Heian aristocrat, the son of Prince Iwami and great-grandson of the minister Prince Nagaya. In 844 he received the Takashina surname and left imperial status, later governing Iyo and Higo. In 868 he became head of the Department of Divinities.

Later genealogies trace the Kō clan back to him. Tradition also says he took in a boy born to Ariwara no Narihira and the Ise priestess Princess Yasuko, making the boy the adopted son of his own son Shigenori; the boy was called Moronao.

Takashina no Moronao was an early Heian noble and a son of Takashina no Shigenori, governor of Shimotsuke. He served as Middle Captain of the Right.

en:
Takashina no Naritō (965–1010) was a mid-Heian noble, son of Takashina no Toshitada. He governed Etchū and served Crown Prince Okisada, later Emperor Sanjō, rising to Provisional Director of the Crown Prince's Quarters.

In 1004 his work on the Rajōmon relocation earned him Tanba again, and in 1005 he was put in charge of the Buraku-in hall. He resigned ill in 1010 and died in the fourth month, aged forty-six. As steward to Regent Fujiwara no Michinaga he was called without equal.

1004年，他因罗城门移建之功被重任为丹波守；1005年又奉命负责丰乐院营造。1010年他因病辞官，四月去世，享年四十六岁。作为藤原道长的家司，他被评为当世无双。

Takashina no Shigenori was an early Heian noble and a son of the Jingi-haku Takashina no Mineo. In 883, holding the post of Shikibu-shōjō, he was appointed reception envoy for the embassy from Balhae and oversaw its reception in the capital.

He later served as governor of Shimotsuke Province. Genealogies name him as the father of Takashina no Moronao, whom a famous tradition linked with the poet Ariwara no Narihira.

Takashina no Yoshiomi (898–980) was a mid-Heian noble, the son of Takashina no Moronao. In 939 the court sent him, then a Lesser Lieutenant of the Left Gate Guards, to verify Minamoto no Tsunemoto's report of Taira no Masakado's eastern revolt; he and his colleagues refused and were dismissed in 940.

Pardoned in 941, he held civil and guard posts and rose to Minister of the Imperial Household. Deeply devout, he took vows in summer 980 and died in the seventh month.

Taira no Koremoto was a mid-Heian warrior and founder of the Hitachi Taira. A nephew adopted by Taira no Sadamori, he was posted to Hitachi after Sadamori's victory in the Jōhei-Tengyō War. Settling at Take in Tsukuba District, he styled himself Take-gon-no-daibu and built the clan's power.

The Konjaku Monogatari records his feud with Taira no Tadatsune before 1016, and during Tadatsune's revolt he led three thousand cavalry under Minamoto no Yorinobu.

《今昔物语集》记载，1016年以前他便与#TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_taira_tadatsune').GetID],X #L 平忠常#!#!争利结怨；忠常之乱时，他率三千骑兵跟随#TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_minamoto_yorinobu').GetID],X #L 源赖信#!#!作战。

en:
Taira no Shigemoto, also called Take no Shigemoto, was a powerful Hitachi Taira lord in the late Heian period. From Take Castle, inherited from his grandfather Koremoto and father Tamemoto, he led the clan as Take-gon-no-daibu.

In 1106 he joined Minamoto no Yoshimitsu in repelling Yoshikuni's invasion of Hitachi; the court then ordered his arrest, but his local power held. His sons divided his lands into houses including the Yoshida and Makabe.

zh:
平重干，一称多气重干，是平安时代后期常陆平氏的有力领主。他继承祖父维干与父亲为干的基业，以多气城为据点，自称多气权大夫。

1106年，源义国攻入常陆，重干与源义光合力迎击，击退义国的军队；朝廷随后下令拘拿他，他却保住了在常陆的地盘。他的儿子们分割所领，派生出吉田、真壁等武士家族。

en:
Prince Takechi (c. 654–696), eldest son of Emperor Tenmu, escaped the Ōmi court in the Jinshin War of 672, joined his father in Iga and commanded at Fuwa in Mino, where blocking the highway helped win Tenmu the throne.

Under Empress Jitō he became Daijō-daijin, the highest subject in the land. He died suddenly in 696 amid rumours of assassination. His son was Prince Nagaya, and three of his love poems survive in the Man'yōshū.

zh:
高市皇子（约654—696）是天武天皇的长子。672年壬申之乱中，他逃出近江大津京，在伊贺与举兵的父亲会合，并受命在美浓国不破总领军事、封锁要道，为天武天皇取胜立下大功。

持统天皇即位后，他出任太政大臣，位居百官之首。696年他突然去世，有遇刺之说。其子为长屋王；《万叶集》中存有他的三首恋歌。

en:
Takeda Masatsuna was a mid-Kamakura-period warrior of the Takeda clan and a miuchibito, a direct vassal of the Hojo tokuso family. The Azuma Kagami records him as an archer at shogunate ceremonies, including preparing the target for Hojo Tokimune's kasagake in 1261.

In 1263 he was among the seven vassals attending Hojo Tokiyori on his deathbed. While his elder brother Nobutoki moved to Aki as shugo, Masatsuna kept the family base at Isawa in Kai and became ancestor of the Isawa Takeda line.

zh:
武田政纲是镰仓时代中期的武田氏武将、北条得宗家的御内人。《吾妻镜》记载他在幕府仪式中担任射手，1261年曾为北条时宗的笠悬准备靶子。

1263年北条时赖临终时，他是在侧侍奉的七名被官之一。其兄武田信时出任安艺守护后移居安艺，政纲则留在甲斐，以石和为本据，开创石和流武田氏。

en:
Takeda Masayoshi (c. 1300–1343) headed the Ishikawa branch of the Kai Genji Takeda and is the only attested governor of Kai in the late Kamakura period. In 1331 he led Kai troops for the shogunate against Emperor Go-Daigo, fighting at Mount Kasagi and Akasaka Castle.

After the shogunate fell he joined the Kenmu government, then followed Ashikaga Takauji and invaded Shinano's Suwa District in 1336. He later went over to the Southern Court and was killed by a shogunal governor-deputy in 1343.

zh:
武田政义（约1300—1343）是甲斐源氏石和流武田氏的当主，镰仓末期唯一可确认的甲斐守护。1331年后醍醐天皇举兵时，他率甲斐军为镰仓幕府出征，参与笠置山与赤坂城之战。

镰仓幕府灭亡后，他加入建武新政，随后追随足利尊氏，于1336年攻入信浓国诹访郡；后来转投南朝，1343年在幕府方守护代的进攻下战死。

en:
Takeda Nobumasa (1196–1265) was the third Takeda clan head, heir of Nobumitsu. At his coming of age in 1204, Regent Hojo Tokimasa capped him and gave him the character masa. As a young man he was exiled to Aki on a false charge but later pardoned.

He fought beside his father for the Kamakura shogunate in the Jokyu War of 1221 and succeeded as clan head when Nobumitsu became a monk. He died in 1265 and was succeeded by his son Nobutoki.

en:
Takeda Nobumitsu (1162–1248), fifth son of Nobuyoshi, was the second Takeda clan head and a master of bow and horse, one of the Four Heavenly Kings of archery. In 1180 he joined his father's rising and captured the Taira-appointed Suruga deputy at the Battle of Hatta.

In the Jokyu War of 1221 he commanded the shogunate's Tosando army, entered Kyoto, and executed the courtier Fujiwara no Mitsuchika. Made shugo of Aki, he became a monk in 1239, passed the clan to Nobumasa, and died in 1248 aged about 87.

武田信光（1162—1248）是武田信义第五子、武田氏第二代家督，精于弓马，为弓马四天王之一。1180年他随父起兵，在钵田之战擒获平家任命的骏河目代。

1221年承久之乱中，他受镰仓幕府之命担任东山道军大将，率军攻入京都，处死公卿藤原光亲，战后受封安艺国守护。1239年他出家，将家督让给儿子信政，1248年去世，享年约87岁。

en:
Takeda Nobumune (1269–1330) was the sixth head of the Takeda clan, son of Tokitsuna. At his coming of age at Kamakura in 1277, Regent Hojo Tokimune capped him and gave him the character mune, and he served the shogunate as a trusted gokenin.

He recovered the office of shugo of Aki Province for the main Takeda line and is credited with founding Kanayama Castle there. He became a monk in 1320 under the name Koa and died in 1330.

en:
Takeda Nobunari (d. 1394) was the eighth head of the Takeda and the eldest son of Takeda Nobutake. From 1339 he acted as shugo-dai in Kai. During the Kannō Disturbance he mustered Kai warriors for the battles of Hakone and Takeshita in 1351 and the Musashino campaign of 1352.

After Nobutake died in 1359 he took the family headship and the Kai governorship, while his brother Ujinobu held Aki. He remained head of the clan until his death in 1394.

en:
Takeda Nobutake (1292–1362) was the seventh head of the Kai Genji Takeda and governor of Aki Province. He campaigned for the Kamakura shogunate during the Genkō War of 1332, then answered Ashikaga Takauji's summons against the Kenmu government, storming Yano Castle in 1335 and fighting loyalist forces in the Kinai.

During the Kannō Disturbance he served as governor of Kai and entered the province. His sons Nobunari and Ujinobu founded the Kai and Aki Takeda lines.
en_rich:
Takeda Nobutake (1292–1362) was the seventh head of the Kai Genji Takeda and governor of Aki Province. He campaigned for the Kamakura shogunate during the Genkō War of 1332, then answered #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_ashikaga_takauji').GetID],X #L Ashikaga Takauji#!#!'s summons against the Kenmu government, storming Yano Castle in 1335 and fighting loyalist forces in the Kinai.

During the Kannō Disturbance he served as governor of Kai and entered the province. His sons Nobunari and Ujinobu founded the Kai and Aki Takeda lines.
zh:
武田信武（1292—1362）是甲斐源氏武田氏第七代当主、安艺国守护。1332年元弘之乱时他作为镰仓幕府一方出征，其后响应足利尊氏举兵，1335年攻落矢野城，又在畿内与朝廷一方作战。

观应之乱中他担任甲斐守护并进入甲斐。其子信成、氏信分别开创甲斐武田氏与安艺武田氏。

en:
Takeda Nobutoki (1220–1289) was the fourth Takeda clan head, heir of Nobumasa and ancestor of the line that later held the Kai shugo office. At his coming of age in 1229, Regent Hojo Yasutoki capped him and gave him the character toki.

In 1269 he was sent west with Kamakura vassals against the Mongol threat, probably serving as shugo of Aki. He became a monk in 1279 as Kokai, died in 1289, and was succeeded by his son Tokitsuna.

zh:
武田信时（1220—1289）是武田氏第四代家督、武田信政的嫡子，也是后来世代担任甲斐守护的信时流武田氏之祖。1229年元服时，由执权北条泰时担任乌帽子亲，获赐“时”字。

1269年，为防备蒙古袭来，他奉命率御家人前往西国，一般认为他当时在任安艺守护。1279年他出家，法号光海，1289年去世，由其子武田时纲继任。

en:
Takeda Nobuyoshi (1128–1186) was a Kai Genji warrior, the second son of Minamoto no Kiyomitsu and first head of the Takeda clan. He came of age at Takeda Hachiman shrine in 1140 and took the Takeda name.

In 1180 he answered Prince Mochihito's call against the Taira, led Kai Genji troops into Suruga, and joined Minamoto no Yoritomo to win the Battle of Fujikawa. After Yoritomo had his son Ichijo Tadayori killed in 1184, Nobuyoshi died in 1186.

武田信义（1128—1186）是甲斐源氏武将、源清光的次子，也是武田氏初代家督。1140年，他在武田八幡宫元服，取武田为姓。

1180年，他响应以仁王讨伐平家的令旨起兵，率甲斐源氏攻入骏河，与源赖朝会合，在富士川之战击败平家军。1184年，其子一条忠赖在镰仓遇害，信义最终于1186年去世。

en:
Takeda Tokitsuna (1245–1307) was the fifth Takeda clan head, son of Nobutoki. At his coming of age in 1253 Regent Hojo Tokiyori capped him and gave him the character toki, and he succeeded as clan head in 1289.

His headship was largely nominal: his uncle Masatsuna's Isawa branch, allied with the Hojo, held real power in Kai and a Hojo kinsman held the Aki shugo post. He became a monk in 1300 as Kojun and died in 1307. His son Nobumune later recovered the Aki shugo office.

武田时纲（1245—1307）是武田氏第五代家督、武田信时之子。1253年元服时，由执权北条时赖担任乌帽子亲，获赐“时”字，1289年父亲去世后继承家督。

en:
Takeda Ujinobu (1312–1380) was a son of Takeda Nobutake and founder of the Aki Takeda line. During the Kannō Disturbance his father sent him into Aki, where with the Kikkawa he routed Ashikaga Tadafuyu's followers at Saijō and Yoshida.

Succeeding as governor of Aki around 1359, he was removed by the shogunate in 1368 for failing to check the Ōuchi, made partial governor of Satō district in 1378, and retired the next year. His son Nobuari succeeded him.

en:
Takō Munetomo was a mid-Kamakura-period gokenin and the seventh son of Utsunomiya Yoritsuna of Shimotsuke. In 1238 he accompanied the shogun Fujiwara no Yoritsune on his progress to Kyoto and Rokuhara, and he appears frequently in the Azuma Kagami.

In 1248 he built Takō Castle and founded the Takō clan. He held the post of governor of Iwami Province by 1258 and died in 1292 aged seventy-three.

en:
Taku no Munenao was an early Kamakura-period warrior and head of the Taku house of Hizen Province in northern Kyushu, a family that traced its descent from the Tsukui. The Taku had long been based at their mansion in Minami-Taku.

Around 1193 Munenao built Kajimine Castle on the mountain above Taku, together with outer forts and a new residence. Also known as Taku Castle, it served as the seat of the Taku lords for more than 350 years.

en:
Emperor Tenji (626–672), formerly Naka no Ōe, was Japan's 38th sovereign. In 645 he and Nakatomi no Kamatari killed Soga no Iruka in the Isshi incident, and as crown prince he drove the Taika reforms. His Paekche relief armies were crushed by Tang China at Baekgang in 663.

He issued the Ōmi-ryō code, moved the court to Ōtsu, and was enthroned in 668, granting Kamatari the surname Fujiwara the next year. When he died in 672 his brother Prince Ōama defeated his son Prince Ōtomo in the Jinshin War.

zh:
天智天皇（626—672）又称中大兄皇子，是日本第38代天皇。645年，他与中臣镰足发动乙巳之变诛杀苏我入鹿，又以皇太子身份主导大化改新。他派军援助百济复国，663年在白江口之战中被唐朝大军击败。

他制定《近江令》，迁都大津，668年正式即位，次年赐镰足藤原之姓。672年他去世后，弟弟大海人皇子在壬申之乱中击败其子大友皇子。

en:
Emperor Tenmu (c. 631–686), born Prince Ōama, was Japan's 40th sovereign. In 671 he renounced the succession and became a monk at Yoshino Palace. In 672 he overthrew his nephew Prince Ōtomo in the Jinshin War after fleeing Yoshino and raising the eastern provinces.

Enthroned in 673, he built a Tang-style centralised state, began the chronicles later the Nihon Shoki, and probably first used the title tennō. He died in 686; his consort succeeded him as Empress Jitō.

Emperor Tenmu (c. 631–686), born Prince Ōama, was Japan's 40th sovereign. In 671 he renounced the succession and became a monk at Yoshino Palace. In 672 he overthrew his nephew Prince Ōtomo in the Jinshin War after fleeing [ShowLocationName('yoshino')] and raising the eastern provinces.

Enthroned in 673, he built a Tang-style centralised state, began the chronicles later the Nihon Shoki, and probably first used the title tennō. He died in 686; his consort succeeded him as #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('jap_jitou_tenno').GetID],X #L Empress Jitō#!#!.
zh:
天武天皇（约631—686）名大海人皇子，是日本第40代天皇。671年他辞让继承权，到吉野宫出家。672年，他逃出吉野、召集东方诸国兵马，在壬申之乱中推翻侄子大友皇子。

673年即位后，他效仿唐朝建立中央集权国家，下令编纂后来成为《日本书纪》的史书，并可能是首位使用“天皇”称号的统治者。686年他去世，皇后继位为持统天皇。

en:
Emperor Toba (1103–1156) was the 74th emperor of Japan. Raised by his grandfather, the cloistered Emperor Shirakawa, he was placed on the throne at four in 1107 and forced to abdicate in 1123 in favour of his son Sutoku, and only took power on Shirakawa's death in 1129.

As cloistered sovereign he dominated the reigns of Sutoku, Konoe and Go-Shirakawa for 28 years. Ordained in 1142, he died in 1156; the ensuing succession feud became the Hōgen Rebellion.

zh:
鸟羽天皇（1103—1156）是日本第74代天皇。他由祖父白河法皇抚养，1107年4岁登基，1123年又在白河法皇主持下被迫让位于皇子崇德天皇，直到1129年白河法皇去世后才亲自执掌院政。

此后他左右崇德、近卫、后白河三代天皇的朝务实权达28年。1142年他受戒出家，1156年去世后，随即爆发的皇位之争便是保元之乱。

en:
Toda Yoshiyasu was a Kamakura-period gokenin, the fourth son of Sasaki no Yasukiyo and ancestor of the Sasaki-line Toda clan. Around 1278, when his brother Yoriyasu succeeded to the Izumo shugo post and took the Enya name, Yoshiyasu received the Toda Manor in Ou District of Izumo and adopted the surname Toda.

He made his seat at Gassan-Toda Castle, built by his grandfather Sasaki no Yoshikiyo. He held the titles of saemon-no-jō and daibu hōgan.

富田义泰是镰仓时代的御家人，佐佐木泰清的四男，佐佐木流富田氏之祖。1278年前后，其兄赖泰继任出云守护、另立盐冶氏，义泰也分得出云国意宇郡富田庄，遂以富田为姓。

他以祖父佐佐木义清所筑的月山富田城为居城，官居左卫门尉、大夫判官。

en:
Togashi no Iekuni was a Heian-period warrior of Kaga province, the son of Saitō no Sōsuke of a warrior house that claimed descent from the general Fujiwara no Toshihito.

Genealogies of the Togashi record that Iekuni held Togashi village in Kaga and was the first of his line to take the place name as his surname, calling himself Togashi Iekuni. He is therefore counted as the clan's founder and first head, and his son Nobuie succeeded him.
