索尔姆斯-利希伯爵赖因哈德（1491—1562）是德意志将领与军事工程师，生于利希城堡。青年时他参加了1534年围攻明斯特再洗礼派政权的战役。

他主持改造哈瑙的城防，1539至1542年间为巴伐利亚的英戈尔施塔特要塞修筑棱堡；他在那里察觉住所不安全，及时让家人搬离，房屋随后坍塌。1544年在皇帝查理五世的对法战争中，他指挥了对圣迪济耶的炮击与坑道作业。他于1546年成为帝国陆军元帅，后任帝国顾问，1562年在利希去世。

en:
Joan of Rethel (died 1328) was the only daughter of Count Hugh IV of Rethel and Isabella of Grandpré, and succeeded her father as countess of Rethel in 1285. In 1290 she married Louis I of Nevers, son of Count Robert III of Flanders, and the marriage was notoriously quarrelsome.

She was also countess of Nevers until Louis's death in 1322. Her children were Joan, who married John of Montfort in 1329, and Louis of Crécy, later count of Flanders and Rethel. Joan ruled Rethel until her death in 1328.

勒泰勒的让娜（1328年卒）是勒泰勒伯爵于格四世与格朗普雷的伊莎贝拉的独生女，1285年继承父位成为勒泰勒女伯爵。1290年她嫁给佛兰德伯爵罗贝尔三世之子、讷韦尔伯爵路易一世，这段婚姻以争吵不断闻名。

她在1322年路易去世前还身兼讷韦尔伯爵夫人。她的子女：女儿让娜于1329年嫁给蒙福尔的让，儿子路易·德·克雷西后来成为佛兰德与勒泰勒伯爵。让娜统治勒泰勒直至1328年去世。

en:
Giberto III da Correggio, called ‘Il Difensore’, was an Italian noble, son of Guido II da Correggio. In 1303 he reconciled Parma's feuding families and recalled its exiles, except the Rossi, and the people acclaimed him lord and defender of the city.

Victories over the Rossi and Este won him the castles of Campagnola and Fabbrico. He attended Emperor Henry VII at Milan in 1311 but later joined the Guelphs, and in 1314 he made peace with the Rossi and married their daughter Maddalena.

In 1316 a revolt led by the Rossi and some of Giberto's relatives drove him from Parma. He died at Castelnovo di Sotto in 1326.

吉贝尔托三世·达·科雷焦，绰号‘守护者’，是意大利贵族，圭多二世·达·科雷焦之子。1303年，他调解帕尔马世代仇杀的各家族并召回流亡者，但罗西家族除外；他被民众拥戴为该城的领主与守护者。

他凭借对罗西家族和埃斯特家族的连番胜仗，取得坎帕尼奥拉和法布里科城堡。1311年他在米兰伴随皇帝亨利七世，后来却转而与圭尔夫派合作；1314年他与罗西家族议和，娶其女马达莱娜。

1316年，罗西家族与他的部分亲族领导的叛乱将他逐出帕尔马，他于1326年在卡斯泰尔诺沃迪索托去世。

en:
Niccolò da Fogliano (c. 1260, fourteenth century) was an Italian condottiere and lord of Reggio nell'Emilia, the son of Ugolino of the Guelph da Fogliano family. He led the faction called the Parte di Sopra against the rival Parte di Sotto, backed by the Canossa, and in 1287 seized places including Carpineti.

After sharing the city's signoria with Obizzo III d'Este, he went over to the Ghibellines. In 1329 Emperor Louis the Bavarian named him imperial vicar, making him lord of Reggio, and he accompanied the emperor as far as Trento on his return to Germany.

尼科洛·达·福利亚诺（约1260年生，14世纪去世）是意大利佣兵首领、雷焦艾米利亚领主，出身圭尔夫派的达·福利亚诺家族，为乌戈利诺之子。他统领家族中名为‘上派’的派系，对抗卡诺萨家族支持的敌对派系‘下派’，于1287年夺取包括卡尔皮内蒂在内的若干据点。

en:
Louis III, Count of Rieneck (c. 1236 – 1289/1291), was the eldest son of Count Louis of Rieneck (died 1243) and Adelaide of Henneberg. In 1243 Rothenfels Castle on the Main passed to him through his wife Udelhilt, heiress of Albert II of Grumbach, adding lands that nearly doubled Rieneck's territory.

From 1257 his Rothenfels line bore a standing swan on its helmet, proclaiming descent from the Swan Knight Lohengrin. His children included counts Thomas and Louis V, and Elizabeth, married in 1272 to Ulrich I of Hanau.

en:
Louis V, Count of Rieneck-Rothenfels (c. 1256 – 3 July 1333), was a son of Count Louis III of Rieneck and Udelhilt of Grumbach. In 1296 he signed an inheritance treaty with his brother-in-law Ulrich I of Hanau. Under Louis the county was partitioned: he kept Lauda, Partenstein and Gemünden, while his cousins received Lohr and Grünsfeld.

In 1329 he made his daughter Udelhilt sole heiress. When he died on 3 July 1333 without an adult son, Mainz and Würzburg rejected her claim and the county of Rieneck lost much of its land.

Friedrich von Pernstein (c. 1270–1340), a Moravian nobleman and Franciscan, was Archbishop of Riga from 1304. His episcopate was consumed by war with the Teutonic Order, which built Dünamünde castle to blockade the city.

He negotiated with Grand Duke Gediminas of Lithuania over conversion, helping to bring the Order's expulsion from Lithuania, and Riga's citizens backed him against the knights.

In 1330 the Order laid the foundations of Riga Castle and took control. Of his 37 years as archbishop, Friedrich spent fewer than five in Riga, living mostly at the papal court in Avignon, where he amassed a library and died in 1340.

弗里德里希·冯·佩恩施泰因（约1270—1340），摩拉维亚贵族、方济各会会士，1304年起任里加大主教。他的主教任上始终与条顿骑士团交战：骑士团修建迪纳明德城堡封锁里加。

他曾与立陶宛大公格迪米纳斯谈判其皈依事宜，促成骑士团被逐出立陶宛，里加市民也支持他对抗骑士。

1330年，骑士团为里加城堡奠基并控制了城市。任大主教37年间，他在里加停留不足五年，大部分时间住在阿维尼翁教廷，在那里搜罗了大量藏书，1340年去世。

en:
Sen no Rikyū (1522–1591), born in the merchant city of Sakai, was the Japanese tea master who shaped the tea ceremony more than any other. Trained under Kitamuki Dōchin and Takeno Jō'ō, he became tea master to Oda Nobunaga in 1579 and later the tea confidant of Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

In 1585 the emperor bestowed on him the title Rikyū Koji, and in 1587 he led Hideyoshi's Grand Kitano Tea Ceremony. He perfected wabi-cha, the way of rustic simplicity, designing the two-mat Tai-an tearoom and Raku tea bowls with the tile-maker Chōjirō. In 1591 Hideyoshi ordered him to kill himself at the Jurakudai palace in Kyoto.

zh:
千利休（1522—1591）生于商埠堺，是对日本茶道影响最深的茶道宗师。他师从北向道陈，又随武野绍鸥学茶，1579年成为织田信长的茶头，后来成为丰臣秀吉倚重的茶人。

1585年他获天皇赐号“利休居士”，1587年主持秀吉发起的北野大茶汤。他确立了讲求枯淡简素的侘茶，设计出两叠大小的茶室“待庵”，并与瓦匠长次郎合作创制乐烧茶碗。1591年，秀吉命他在京都聚乐第的邸内切腹自尽。

en:
Ferrantino Malatesta (1258–1353) was a condottiero of the Rimini Malatesta, son of Malatestino I, in the years when the family was carving a lordship out of the papal March. In 1304 he joined Pandolfo I in seizing Pesaro by force and also took Fano and other cities, though in 1306 they lost every city to a papal legate.

On Pandolfo's death in 1326 he became defender of Rimini. Banned by the papal legate in 1330, he won the city back in 1333.

Two years later Malatesta III lured him to Pesaro and imprisoned him at Gradara, while Malatesta IV had himself proclaimed lord of Rimini; Ferrantino was moved to Fossombrone, where his son and grandson were killed. Freed in 1336, he lived in Urbino, returned to Rimini in 1351 and died there in 1353.

费兰提诺一世·马拉泰斯塔（1258—1353）是里米尼马拉泰斯塔家族的佣兵首领，马拉泰斯蒂诺一世之子，生活在这个家族于教皇国的马尔凯地区开辟领地的年代。1304年，他与潘多尔夫一世合力强取佩萨罗，又攻占法诺等城市，但1306年败给教皇使节，丢掉了全部城市。

1326年潘多尔夫死后，他成为里米尼守护者。1330年他被教皇使节放逐，1333年夺回里米尼。

两年后，马拉泰斯塔三世将他诱至佩萨罗，囚禁于格拉达拉，马拉泰斯塔四世则自立为里米尼领主；费兰提诺被转押福松布罗内，他的儿子和孙子在那里被杀。他于1336年获释，居住在乌尔比诺，1351年返回里米尼，1353年在该地去世。

en:
Galeotto I Malatesta (1299–1385), born in Rimini, was the younger son of Pandolfo I and brother of Malatesta III Guastafamiglia. Captured at Ferrara in 1333 and soon freed, he fought beside Ferrantino against the papal legate, then imprisoned Ferrantino when he plotted against him and declared himself lord of Rimini; Emperor Louis IV also made him lord of Fano.

After a pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 1349 he served Naples. When Cardinal Albornoz came to restore papal authority, Rodolfo II defeated Galeotto and forced the family to become papal vicars.

In 1373 he beat Bernabò Visconti at Montichiari as commander of the papal army. He gathered the whole family lordship in Romagna, taking Cesena in 1376 and Senigallia in 1383; he died at Cesena in 1385, and his sons carried on the wars.

加莱奥托一世·马拉泰斯塔（1299—1385）生于里米尼，是潘多尔福一世的幼子、马拉泰斯塔三世（古斯塔法米利亚）之弟。1333年他在费拉拉被俘，旋即获释，随后与费兰蒂诺并肩对抗教皇特使；费兰蒂诺图谋对付他时，他把对方囚禁，宣布自己为里米尼领主，皇帝路德维希四世又将法诺封给他。

1349年他前往圣地朝圣，随后为那不勒斯效力。枢机主教阿尔沃诺斯为恢复教皇权威而来，罗多尔福二世击败加莱奥托，迫使其家族成为教皇代理人。

1373年他以教皇军队统帅的身份在蒙蒂基亚里击败贝尔纳博·维斯孔蒂。他把家族在罗马涅的领地收归一人之手，1376年攻取切塞纳，1383年夺取塞尼加利亚，1385年卒于切塞纳，战事由儿子们接续。

en:
Giovanni Malatesta, later numbered Giovanni III (c. 1300–1375), was a Romagnol condottiero of the Riminese Malatesta and a cousin of the lords of Rimini and Pesaro. Knighted in 1324, he campaigned with Ferrantino Malatesta against Urbino, but the host was routed and he escaped. In 1326 he was suspected of backing his uncle Ramberto's attempted seizure of Rimini and, though cleared, kept away from the city.

He later supported Malatesta II Guastafamiglia against their cousins. In 1344 Filippo Gonzaga captured him. In 1348 he served Queen Joanna of Naples against Louis of Hungary and was taken at Aversa, and later held Ascoli against Cardinal Albornoz.

Reconciled with the Church, he fought for the papacy from 1356, and the peace of 1363 lifted his excommunication. He died in 1375, leaving ten children by his wife Violante della Faggiola.
en_rich:
Giovanni Malatesta, later numbered Giovanni III (c. 1300–1375), was a Romagnol condottiero of the Riminese Malatesta and a cousin of the lords of Rimini and [ShowLocationName('pesaro')]. Knighted in 1324, he campaigned with #TOOLTIP:CHARACTER,[GetCharacter('rim_ferrantino_malatesta').GetID],X #L Ferrantino Malatesta#!#! against [ShowLocationName('urbino')], but the host was routed and he escaped. In 1326 he was suspected of backing his uncle Ramberto's attempted seizure of Rimini and, though cleared, kept away from the city.

He later supported Malatesta II Guastafamiglia against their cousins. In 1344 Filippo Gonzaga captured him. In 1348 he served Queen Joanna of Naples against Louis of [GetCountry('HUN').GetName] and was taken at Aversa, and later held Ascoli against Cardinal Albornoz.

Reconciled with the Church, he fought for the papacy from 1356, and the peace of 1363 lifted his excommunication. He died in 1375, leaving ten children by his wife Violante della Faggiola.

乔瓦尼·马拉泰斯塔，后世称乔瓦尼三世（约1300—1375），是出身里米尼马拉泰斯塔家族的罗马涅雇佣军首领，里米尼与佩萨罗诸位领主的堂亲。1324年他受封骑士，随费兰提诺出征乌尔比诺，兵败脱身。1326年他涉嫌支持叔父兰贝托夺取里米尼，洗清嫌疑后仍远离该城。

后来他支持马拉泰斯塔二世·瓜斯塔法米利亚对抗堂亲。1344年他被菲利波·贡扎加俘虏。1348年他投奔那不勒斯女王乔万娜一世，对匈牙利国王拉约什作战，在阿韦尔萨被俘；后又守卫阿斯科利，抵御阿尔沃诺斯枢机主教。

与教会和解后，他自1356年起为教皇征战，1363年和约解除其绝罚。他1375年去世，与妻子维奥兰特·德拉·法焦拉生有十个子女。

en:
Giovanni di Malatesta (1185–1221) was an Italian noble of the Malatesta house. Orphaned young, he built a position for his family in Rimini, where he sat on the General Council from 1206. After his brother's death he became guardian of his nephew Malatesta della Penna.

In March 1216 the two were granted Rimini citizenship and a town house under an agreement with the commune, which gave them protection and tax immunity; in return they owed military service. Giovanni died in 1221, and his place passed to his nephew.

乔瓦尼·迪·马拉泰斯塔（1185—1221）是马拉泰斯塔家族的意大利贵族。他幼年丧父，在里米尼为家族谋得地位，1206年起进入大议事会。兄弟去世后，他成为侄子马拉泰斯塔·德拉·彭纳的监护人。

1216年3月，叔侄二人根据与公社的协议获得里米尼公民权和城内宅邸，公社给予保护与免税；作为交换，他们须服兵役。乔瓦尼于1221年去世，其地位由侄子继承。

en:
Malatesta da Verucchio, the Mastin Vecchio (1212–1312), was the condottiero who made his family lords of Rimini. Ghibelline podestà of the city in 1239, he switched to the Guelphs after Frederick II's defeat at Parma in 1248 and became Romagna's leading Guelph captain. Around 1263 he married Margherita Paltenieri, a papal legate's niece, strengthening his new alliances.

In 1295 he expelled Rimini's Ghibellines, executed their leader Montagna di Parcitadi and made himself lord. Dante names him with his son Malatestino in the Inferno, and he died in Rimini in 1312, almost a centenarian.

韦鲁基奥的马拉泰斯塔，绰号‘老马斯廷’（1212—1312），是使马拉泰斯塔家族成为里米尼统治者的佣兵首领。1239年他任里米尼的吉伯林派波德斯塔，1248年腓特烈二世在帕尔马战败后转投圭尔夫派，成为罗马涅最重要的圭尔夫派将领。约1263年，他迎娶教皇使节的侄女玛格丽塔·帕尔泰尼耶里，巩固了新联盟。

1295年，他驱逐里米尼的吉伯林派、处死其首领蒙塔尼亚·迪·帕尔奇塔迪，自立为里米尼领主。但丁在《神曲·地狱篇》中把他与其子马拉泰斯蒂诺一同提及。他于1312年在里米尼去世，年近百岁。

en:
Malatesta I Malatesta, called della Penna (Pennabilli, 1183 – Rimini, November 1248), was an Italian condottiero, the first of his house to govern Rimini. Orphaned young, he was raised by his uncle Giovanni, and in March 1216 both were admitted to Rimini citizenship with tax immunity and full jurisdiction over their lands.

As podestà of Pistoia in 1228 he fought Florence at Vairano, where he was captured, and was excommunicated for opposing a papal legate. A supporter of Emperor Frederick II, he was podestà of Rimini in 1239 and 1247.

马拉泰斯塔一世·马拉泰斯塔，绰号‘德拉·彭纳’（1183年生于彭纳比利，1248年11月卒于里米尼），是意大利佣兵首领，也是其家族中最早统治里米尼者。他幼年丧父，由叔父乔瓦尼抚养，1216年3月叔侄二人一同成为里米尼公民，获得免税特权和对自有领地的完全管辖权。

1228年他任皮斯托亚波德斯塔，在瓦伊拉诺之战中对抗佛罗伦萨，兵败被俘，又因对抗教皇使节而被处以绝罚。他是皇帝腓特烈二世的支持者，1239年和1247年两度出任里米尼波德斯塔。

en:
Malatesta III Malatesta (c. 1299–1364), called Guastafamiglia, ‘the Ruiner of the Family’, was known for the massacres of his campaigns. Eldest son of Pandolfo I, lord of Rimini, Pesaro and Fano, he lost the succession in 1326 to his father's nephew Ferrantino and received only Pesaro.

Captured by the Este at Ferrara in 1333, he was freed with his brother Galeotto to fight the papal troops; the two first restored Ferrantino, then imprisoned him at Gradara and took Rimini. Ferrantino was freed in 1336 and long war followed. In 1342 a peace with the pope confirmed Malatesta in Rimini.

When the pope fled to Avignon he turned Ghibelline as imperial vicar, but Cardinal Albornoz's army took his cities. He submitted, kept most of his lands as papal vicar, and in 1363 retired, leaving Rimini to Galeotto.

马拉泰斯塔三世·马拉泰斯塔（约1299—1364）绰号“古斯塔法米利亚”，意为“毁家者”，他的战事以屠杀闻名。他是里米尼、佩萨罗和法诺领主潘多尔福一世的长子，1326年领主之位被父亲的侄子费兰蒂诺继承，他只得到佩萨罗。

1333年他在费拉拉被埃斯特家族俘获，与弟弟加莱奥托获释后转而对抗教皇军队；二人先扶费兰蒂诺复位，随即将他囚禁在格拉达拉，独占里米尼。1336年费兰蒂诺获释，双方长期交战。1342年与教皇议和，他的里米尼领地得到确认。

教皇逃往阿维尼翁后，他倒向吉伯林派任帝国代理人，但阿尔沃诺斯的军队夺取了他的城市。他屈服后以教皇代理人名义保住大部领地，1363年退位，把里米尼交给加莱奥托。

en:
Malatestino I Malatesta, called dell'Occhio (Rimini, c. 1254 – 14 October 1317), was an Italian condottiero and lord of Rimini, the third son of Malatesta da Verucchio. His nickname came from the loss of an eye. Expelled in 1288, he returned in 1290 and led the family's wars against Romagna's Ghibellines, becoming podestà of Rimini in 1301.

On his father's death in 1312 he took Rimini, granting his other lands to his nephew Uberto and half-brother Pandolfo. Dante, in the Inferno, brands him a tyrant and the murderer of the two best men of Fano, drowned in weighted sacks.

en:
Malatestino Novello Malatesta (died 1335) was a condottiero, son of Ferrantino Malatesta and his lieutenant at Cesena. Knighted in 1324, he defeated Claudio before Cesena, and in 1325 the Bolognese made him captain-general against Passerino dei Bonacolsi, who captured him at Zappolino.

He later fell into his cousin Ramberto's trap at Santarcangelo but was freed by the townspeople, and in 1333 was captured again at Borgo San Silvestro. After helping his father retake Rimini he was betrayed to Malatesta III, and probably murdered at Fossombrone in 1335.

马拉泰斯蒂诺·诺韦洛·马拉泰斯塔（1335年卒）是雇佣兵首领，费兰提诺·马拉泰斯塔之子，在切塞纳担任父亲的副手。1324年他受封骑士，在切塞纳城下击败克劳迪奥；1325年博洛尼亚人推举他为总司令抵御帕塞里诺·代·博纳科尔西，他在扎波利诺战败被俘。

他后来落入堂兄兰贝托的圈套、被囚于圣阿尔坎杰洛城堡，为当地市民所救；1333年又在圣西尔韦斯特罗堡被俘。他随父亲收复里米尼后遭到出卖，被交给马拉泰斯塔三世，1335年可能在福松布罗内遇害。

en:
Pandolfo I Malatesta (died 1326) was an Italian condottiero and lord of Rimini, a son of Malatesta da Verucchio. He conquered Pesaro, seized Senigallia, and in 1306 took and sacked Fano before the townspeople drove him out. He recovered Pesaro in 1312 but became its lord only in 1320.

In 1313 he entered Fano by stealth, murdered leading citizens and had their bodies thrown from the palace windows, ruling as a tyrant until a popular revolt expelled him. In 1317 he succeeded his brother Malatestino as lord of Rimini.

In 1322 he made peace with San Marino. He had his nephew Uberto killed in 1324 and died two years later, succeeded by Ferrantino.

潘多尔福一世·马拉泰斯塔（？—1326）是意大利佣兵首领、里米尼领主，韦鲁基奥的马拉泰斯塔之子。他攻占佩萨罗，又夺取塞尼加利亚，1306年攻陷并洗劫法诺，随后被城中居民逐出。1312年他夺回佩萨罗，直到1320年才成为该城领主。

1313年，他潜入法诺，杀害城中显贵并将尸体从宫殿窗口抛出，以暴君姿态统治，终被起义民众赶走。1317年他继兄长马拉泰斯蒂诺之后成为里米尼领主。

1322年他与圣马力诺议和。1324年他命人杀死侄子乌贝托，两年后去世，由费兰提诺继位。

en:
Pandolfo II Malatesta (1325–January 1373), eldest son of Malatesta III Guastafamiglia, became podestà of Pesaro in 1347, held it for life and founded the Malatesta line there. He served Galeazzo II Visconti as cavalry captain.

Galeazzo trusted him, but his co-ruler Bernabò hated him enough to have him bound and ordered beheaded, until Galeazzo saved him and sent him home to Pesaro. In 1358 Florence made him captain of war, and he drove the mercenary companies from its lands without bloodshed.

In 1363–1364 he led Florence's troops against Pisa while angling for lordship of the city; Florence refused, he let the enemy ravage its countryside, and he was dismissed. He spent his last years governing Pesaro, a friend of Petrarch, who had sent him a manuscript of the Rerum vulgarium fragmenta.

潘多尔福二世·马拉泰斯塔（1325—1373年1月）是马拉泰斯塔三世（古斯塔法米利亚）的长子，1347年任佩萨罗最高行政官，终身执掌该城，开创了马拉泰斯塔家族的佩萨罗支系。他曾任加莱亚佐二世·维斯孔蒂的骑兵统领。

加莱亚佐信任他，共治者贝尔纳博却恨他入骨，把他捆起来并下令斩首，幸得加莱亚佐相救，将他送回佩萨罗。1358年佛罗伦萨任他为战争统帅，他不流血地将雇佣兵团伙赶出其领地。

1363至1364年他率佛罗伦萨军队对抗比萨，同时图谋该城统治权；遭拒后任由敌军蹂躏乡间，终被解职。晚年他治理佩萨罗，与彼特拉克交好，诗人曾赠他《歌集》的手抄本。

en:
Polentesia da Polenta was the daughter of Guido Novello da Polenta, lord of Ravenna, and Caterina Malabocca of Bagnacavallo. She married the condottiero Malatestino Novello Malatesta, son of Ferrantino Malatesta of Rimini.

On 9 July 1326 her husband was seized through treachery by their cousin Ramberto I Malatesta and locked in the castle of Sant'Arcangelo. Polentesia placed herself at the head of a column of women who marched through Rimini demanding his release, and only laid down her arms when false news of his murder arrived. Her daughter Anna married Ubertino da Carrara, lord of Padua, in 1340.

波伦泰夏·达·波伦塔是拉韦纳领主圭多·诺韦洛·达·波伦塔与巴尼亚卡瓦洛的卡泰丽娜·马拉博卡之女，嫁给里米尼的费兰提诺·马拉泰斯塔之子、雇佣军首领马拉泰斯蒂诺·诺韦洛·马拉泰斯塔。

en:
Ramberto Malatesta (died 28 January 1330) was the youngest son of Gianciotto Malatesta. In 1323 his cousin Uberto drew him into a plot to murder their uncle Pandolfo I; Ramberto pretended to join and killed Uberto at a banquet. At the family partition of 1326 he received no lands, while Malatesta III took Pesaro and Ferrantino Rimini.

He tried to seize his relatives at a banquet, but Polentesia, wife of Malatestino Novello, organised Rimini's defence. Driven from Rimini, he reconciled with Malatesta in January 1327, yet in 1328 persuaded his brother Guido to attack the city. On 28 January 1330 Malatestino Novello slew him at Poggio Berni castle.

兰贝托·马拉泰斯塔（1330年1月28日卒）是詹乔托·马拉泰斯塔的幼子。1323年，堂兄乌贝托拉拢他密谋杀害叔父潘多尔福一世，兰贝托假意应承，在宴席上亲手杀死乌贝托。1326年家族分封时他一无所获，马拉泰斯塔三世得到佩萨罗、费兰蒂诺得到里米尼。

他设宴企图拘捕同族，马拉泰斯蒂诺·诺韦洛的妻子波伦泰西亚则组织里米尼的防御。他被逐后，1327年1月与马拉泰斯塔和解，却在1328年说服兄弟圭多进攻该城。1330年1月28日，马拉泰斯蒂诺·诺韦洛在波焦贝尔尼城堡将他杀死。

en:
Samaritana Malatesta (died 1347) was the daughter of Ferrantino Malatesta, lord of Rimini, and Belluccia Baligani of Jesi. In 1314 she married Count Tolberto III da Camino of Ceneda. Widowed in 1317, she guarded her two young children, Beatrice and Biaquino VII, and ruled the castles of Portobuffolé, Camino, Motta and Cessalto.

In 1326 she held them against Guecellone VIII da Camino with Venetian support. After her son Biaquino VII was killed in 1337, she lost her lands and retired to Rimini, where she died in 1347.

萨马里塔纳·马拉泰斯塔（？—1347）是里米尼领主费兰提诺·马拉泰斯塔与耶西的贝尔卢恰·巴利加尼之女。1314年，她嫁给切内达伯爵托尔贝托三世·达·卡米诺。1317年丈夫去世后，她监护两名年幼的子女贝阿特丽切和比亚奎诺七世，统辖波尔托布福莱、卡米诺、莫塔和切萨尔托等城堡。

Taddea da Rimini (c. 1267–1362) was an Italian noblewoman and, by her marriage to Pandolfo I Malatesta, lady consort of Rimini and Pesaro until his death in 1326.

She was the mother of Malatesta Guastafamiglia (1299–1364), lord of Pesaro and Rimini; Galeotto I (1300–1385), the condottiero; and Caterina, who married Luigi I Gonzaga of Mantua and died around 1340. Taddea died in Rimini in 1362.

en:
Malatesta Ungaro (June 1327 – 17 July 1372) was born Galeotto Malatesta, a younger son of Malatesta Guastafamiglia, lord of Pesaro and Rimini, and Costanza Ondedei. He took the name Ungaro after King Louis I of Hungary knighted him in December 1347. He married Costanza d'Este, daughter of Obizzo III of Ferrara, in 1363.

As a papal commander under Cardinal Gil de Albornoz he fought the Ordelaffi and Manfredi, and on 16 April 1363 he heavily defeated Bernabò Visconti. He helped Pope Urban V return to Rome in 1367 and died at Rimini in 1372.

马拉泰斯塔·翁加罗（1327年6月—1372年7月17日）原名加莱奥托·马拉泰斯塔，是佩萨罗与里米尼领主马拉泰斯塔·瓜斯塔法米利亚与科斯坦扎·翁代代伊较年幼的儿子。1347年12月匈牙利国王拉约什一世封他为骑士后，他改名“翁加罗”。1363年，他娶费拉拉侯爵奥比佐三世之女科斯坦扎·德埃斯特为妻。

作为枢机主教希尔·德·阿尔沃诺斯麾下的教廷将领，他征战奥尔德拉菲家族和曼弗雷迪家族，并于1363年4月16日重创贝尔纳博·维斯孔蒂。1367年他协助教宗乌尔班五世返回罗马，1372年在里米尼去世。

en:
Bardic tradition calls Chokrana a prince of the Parmar dynasty of Ujjain who ruled Junaraj, the old capital of Rajpipla. Having no son of his own, he summoned to his court his sister's younger son Samarsinhji, a Gohil boy.

Samarsinhji's father Mokhadaji had held Ghogha and the island of Piram until Muhammad bin Tughluq's troops killed him in 1347. Samarsinhji took the name Arjunsinhji, succeeded Chokrana and became the founder of the Gohil ruling line of Rajpipla State.

en:
Rodrigo Borgia (1431–1503), born near Valencia, was the Spanish cardinal who became Pope Alexander VI, the most notorious Renaissance pope. Made cardinal in 1456 when his uncle became Pope Callixtus III, he was vice-chancellor of the Church from the next year for 35 years. He openly acknowledged his mistresses' children, among them Cesare and Lucrezia.

Elected pope in August 1492, he was soon accused of buying votes. His bull Inter caetera of 1493 divided the New World between Spain and Portugal and became the basis of the Treaty of Tordesillas. His son Cesare was made archbishop of Valencia at seventeen and cardinal at eighteen.

When Charles VIII of France invaded Naples, the French entered Rome in 1494 until a Holy League drove them out in 1495; Borgia then moved against the Orsini to advance Cesare. He died in August 1503, and his surname became a byword for nepotism.

罗德里戈·波吉亚（1431—1503）生于瓦伦西亚附近，后成为教宗亚历山大六世，是文艺复兴最声名狼藉的教宗。1456年舅父任教宗加里斯都三世后擢他为枢机，次年他任副秘书长，在任三十五年。他公开承认情妇所生子女，包括切萨雷与卢克蕾齐娅。

1492年8月当选教宗，随即被指控买票。1493年他颁布诏书《在其他事务之中》，将新大陆分给西班牙和葡萄牙，成为《托尔德西拉斯条约》的基础。儿子切萨雷十七岁任瓦伦西亚大主教、十八岁任枢机。

法王查理八世进军那不勒斯时，法军1494年进入罗马，1495年神圣同盟将其逐出；他随后打击奥尔西尼家族、为切萨雷铺路。1503年8月去世，其姓氏成了任人唯亲的代名词。

en:
Euphemia de Ross (c. 1329–c. 1389) was a daughter of Hugh, Earl of Ross, and sister of Earl William. She first married John Randolph, 3rd Earl of Moray, who was killed at Neville's Cross in 1346, leaving her large widow's estates including Badenoch.

Before May 1355 she married Robert Stewart, nephew and heir of David II. When he became Robert II in 1371 she was queen, but her coronation at Scone was delayed to 1372–1373, possibly in part because of disputes over her sons' succession rights. Her son David gained Strathearn and Caithness. She died around 1389 and was buried at Dunfermline Abbey.

尤菲米娅·德·罗斯（约1329—约1389）是罗斯伯爵休之女、威廉伯爵的妹妹。她先嫁第三代马里伯爵约翰·兰道夫，后者1346年战死于内维尔十字，留给她包括巴德诺赫在内的大片寡妇领地。

en:
Hugh, probably Gaelic Aodh, was Mormaer of Ross from 1323 until his death. The eldest son of Earl William II and Euphemia de Berkeley, he became a favourite of King Robert I and married the king's sister Maud Bruce in Orkney; after her death he married Margaret de Graham in 1329.

His daughter Euphemia took as her second husband the future King Robert II. Hugh was killed beside many Scottish nobles at the Battle of Halidon Hill on 19 July 1333, and was succeeded by his son William.

en:
Maud Bruce, also called Matilda, was a Scottish noblewoman, daughter of Robert de Brus, Lord of Annandale, and sister of King Robert I. In 1306 she was seized by the Earl of Ross's men and handed to the English as a prisoner; after her release her brother married her to Hugh, the earl's son, to seal the reconciliation of the two houses.

Her children included William, later Earl of Ross, and Marjory, wife of the Earl of Strathearn. She died before November 1329 and was buried at Dunfermline Abbey.

en:
William, 5th Earl of Ross (died 1372), was the son of Earl Hugh and Matilda Bruce, Robert the Bruce's sister, and first cousin of David II. His father fell at Halidon Hill in 1333; William returned from Norway in 1336 to take up the earldom.

In 1339 he forced the English garrison out of Perth by draining its moat. In 1346 he killed his vassal Ronald MacRuari at Elcho Priory and withdrew before Neville's Cross.

He joined the Highland lords' revolt of 1366 and died in 1372. He left the earldom to his daughter Euphemia.

en:
John II (died 1251), of the House of Pierrepont, was count of Roucy and lord of Pierrepont, son of Robert of Pierrepont and Eustachie of Roucy. Recognized as heir in 1211, he probably fought at Bouvines in 1214 and stayed loyal to the crown during the barons' revolt against Blanche of Castile.

In 1227 he gained Sissonne from the rebel Enguerrand III of Coucy. He was killed in 1251 fighting for Charles of Anjou in the Flemish succession dispute, leaving a son, John III, by his wife Marie of Dammartin.

en:
John IV (born between 1260 and 1269, died 1302), of the House of Pierrepont, was count of Roucy and lord of Pierrepont, succeeding his father John III in 1282 or 1285. By his wife Jeanne of Dreux, countess of Braine, he also held Braine and Rochefort.

In 1302 he joined the war against Flanders, falling in battle near Mons-en-Pévèle. He left three children, John V, Marie and Béatrix.

en:
John V de Pierrepont (c. 1300–1346) was Count of Roucy, Braine and Rochefort, succeeding his father John IV and inheriting Braine through his mother Jeanne de Dreux.

In 1320 he went as a French royal envoy to Flanders to mediate between Count Robert III and his son Louis of Nevers. In October 1339 he served in Philip VI's army facing Edward III at Buironfosse near Saint-Quentin, the first standoff of the Hundred Years' War.

He was killed at Crécy on 26 August 1346. With his wife Marguerite de Bommiers he left sons Robert II, Simon and Hugues.

Jeanne de Pierrepont, lady of Blazon and Chemillé, was a daughter of Count John V of Roucy, who was killed at Crécy in 1346, and Marguerite de Beaumez. On 26 January 1341 she married in Paris Charles I de Montmorency, a royal councillor who became Marshal of France in 1343 and fought at Crécy.

Their children were Jean, who died young in 1352, and three daughters, Marguerite, Jeanne and Marie. She died on 10 January 1361.

en:
Robert II de Pierrepont (died 1364) succeeded his father John V as Count of Roucy and Braine after Crécy in 1346. He was royal lieutenant in Vermandois and governor of Burgundy, and in 1356 ceded Braine to his younger brother Simon.

Captured at Poitiers in 1356, he paid a heavy ransom. In December 1358 the English took the castle of Roucy with him and his family inside; they were ransomed and the castle was retaken the following July. He died in 1364, leaving one daughter, Isabelle.

罗贝尔二世·德·皮埃尔蓬（?—1364）在1346年克雷西之战后继承父亲约翰五世，成为鲁西和布赖讷伯爵。他曾任驻韦芒杜瓦代理官和勃艮第总督，1356年把布赖讷让给弟弟西蒙。

同年他在普瓦捷之战被俘，付出巨额赎金。1358年12月，英军攻占鲁西城堡，将他与家人一同俘虏；一家人支付赎金后，城堡于次年7月收复。1364年他去世，只留下女儿伊莎贝尔。

en:
Simon de Pierrepont (c. 1325–18 February 1392), count of Braine, was the youngest of the five sons of Count John V of Roucy and Marguerite de Beaumetz. When his father was killed at Crécy in 1346, Simon inherited Braine with its attached lordships.

In 1381 his childless niece Isabelle sold the county of Roucy to Louis of Anjou, the French king's brother. Louis died in September 1384, and Simon, by then the eldest of the house, contested the sale by claiming the right of lineage redemption.

The Parlement ruled for him, and by a treaty of 1385 he compensated Louis's heirs and took Roucy back, uniting it with Braine. He died at Bois-lez-Roucy, leaving by Marie de Châtillon a son, Hugh II, who succeeded him.

西蒙·德·皮埃尔蓬（约1325—1392年2月18日）是布赖讷伯爵，鲁西伯爵让五世与玛格丽特·德·博梅五个儿子中最小的一个。1346年父亲在克雷西战役中阵亡，他继承了布赖讷及其附属领地。

1381年，他没有子嗣的侄女伊莎贝尔把鲁西伯国卖给法王之弟安茹的路易。1384年9月路易去世，此时西蒙已是家族中最年长者，他援引亲属回赎权对这笔交易提出异议。

高等法院判他胜诉，1385年的条约规定，他补偿路易的继承人，收回鲁西，与布赖讷合为一体。他卒于布瓦莱鲁西，与玛丽·德·沙蒂永生子于格二世，由其继位。

en:
Andrei Fedorovich (1328/1331–1409), only son of Prince Fyodor Vasilievich, inherited the Usretinsky half of Rostov in 1331 and ruled as a loyal ally of Moscow. In 1360 his uncle Konstantin Vasilievich obtained a Tatar yarlyk for all Rostov and drove him out; four years later a Moscow host sent by Dmitry Donskoy restored him.

He served Dmitry in campaigns against Tver and fought on the right wing at Kulikovo in 1380. In 1408 he fled Edigu's raid, which burned Rostov, and died in 1409 after taking the monastic name Afanasy.

安德烈·费奥多罗维奇（1328/1331—1409）是费奥多尔·瓦西里耶维奇王公的独子，1331年承袭罗斯托夫的乌斯列滕斯基一侧，作为莫斯科的忠实战友统治。1360年，他的叔父康斯坦丁·瓦西里耶维奇取得金帐汗统辖整个罗斯托夫的诰封，将他驱逐；四年后，德米特里·顿斯科伊派来的莫斯科大军助他恢复领地。

en:
Boris Vasilkovich (1231-1277) was prince of Rostov from his father Vasilko's death fighting the Mongols in 1238; he kept Rostov while his younger brother Gleb received Beloozero, with their mother Maria ruling during their minority. In 1244 he travelled to Batu Khan and received his patent (yarlyk), the first of his eight visits to the Golden Horde.

A loyal ally of Alexander Nevsky, he accompanied Mongol census-takers to Novgorod in 1258. In 1277 he joined Mengu-Timur's campaign against the Alans, fell ill and died on 16 September, leaving sons Dmitry and Konstantin.

en:
Boris Vladimirovich (died 24 July 1015), baptized Roman, was a son of Vladimir the Great of Kyiv and prince of Rostov from about 1010. In 1015, while campaigning against the Pechenegs, he learned of his father's death and his half-brother Sviatopolk's seizure of Kyiv. Refusing to march on the throne, he kept only his own retinue.

On 24 July Sviatopolk's men wounded him in his tent and killed him as they carried him away. With his brother Gleb he became one of the first saints canonized in Kievan Rus, and was buried at Vyshgorod.

en:
Dmitry Borisovich (1253-1294), eldest son of Boris Vasilkovich of Rostov, brought his father's body home from the Golden Horde in 1277 and in 1278 took Rostov jointly with his brother Konstantin. In 1279 he seized Beloozero from his cousin and in 1281 drove Konstantin out; a khan-ordered partition in 1286 gave him Uglich, and in 1288 he swapped back to Rostov.

He marched against Tver with Grand Prince Dmitry Aleksandrovich and in 1293 joined the destructive Dyuden campaign. On his death in 1294 he left a son, Alexander, and a daughter Anna, later the saint Anna of Kashin.

Fyodor Vasilievich (1311–1331) was a son of Vasily Konstantinovich of Rostov. In 1320, after the death of their cousin Yuri Alexandrovich, he and his brother Konstantin divided the Rostov principality, Fyodor taking the Sretensk side and ruling as prince of Rostov-Sretensk.

In 1326 he married Maria Fyodorovna. He died on 28 March 1331, leaving a single son, Andrei, who succeeded him.

en:
Gleb Vasilkovich (1237-1278), younger son of Vasilko Konstantinovich, became the first prince of Beloozero after his father was captured and killed following the defeat at the Sit River in 1238, while his brother Boris held Rostov. A close ally of Alexander Nevsky, in 1257 he married a daughter or kinswoman of Sartak Khan, baptized Feodora.

In 1277-78 he joined Mengu-Timur's campaign against the Alans; when Boris died on campaign he succeeded to Rostov, but died on 13 December 1278 after a week's illness. His son Mikhail inherited Beloozero.

Konstantin Borisovich (1255-1307), younger son of Boris Vasilkovich of Rostov, went to the Golden Horde with his father in 1277 and, when Boris died there, served on Mengu-Timur's Alan campaign with his uncle Gleb, returning in 1278 to share Rostov with his brother Dmitry.

Driven out by Dmitry in 1281 and reconciled soon after, he received Rostov in the khan's partition of 1286, then exchanged it for Uglich about 1289. He regained Rostov on Dmitry's death in 1294, gave Uglich to his son Alexander and died at the Horde in 1307; in 1302 he had married a Tatar khan's daughter.

Konstantin Vasilievich (1312–1365), second son of Prince Vasily Konstantinovich of Rostov, became in 1320 the first prince of the Borisoglebsk half of divided Rostov. In 1328 he married Maria, daughter of Ivan Kalita of Moscow, and thereafter served Moscow as a subordinate prince.

In 1360 he obtained a Tatar yarlyk for all of Rostov, dispossessing his nephew Andrei Fedorovich, but Moscow-backed resistance drove him to Ustyug four years later. He returned to Rostov and died of the plague in 1365.

Yuri Alexandrovich (died 30 May 1320), also called Georgy, was son of Alexander Konstantinovich of Uglich. He succeeded his father in Uglich in 1307 while still a child, and in 1316 he also took Rostov after his uncle Vasily Konstantinovich's death, becoming the last prince to rule a united Rostov.

In 1318 a fierce Tatar envoy from the Golden Horde brought much suffering on the city. Yuri died in 1320 aged about seventeen, leaving no certain heir, and Rostov was divided between his cousins into two halves.

en:
Hasdai Crescas (c. 1340–1410/11) was a Jewish philosopher and legal scholar born in Barcelona who later served as crown rabbi of Aragon. His major work, Or Adonai (Light of the Lord), challenged the Aristotelian logic that dominated Jewish theology, arguing that faith and God's will could not be reduced to it.

His only son was killed in the massacre of 1391, after which he wrote his most famous works. His critique of Aristotle later shaped the thought of Baruch Spinoza.

en:
Sabbatai Zevi (1626–c. 1676) was a mystic and rabbi from Smyrna, born to a Romaniote Jewish family. In 1665 he declared himself the Jewish Messiah, and his movement spread through Jewish communities in Italy, Germany, the Netherlands and the Ottoman lands. He taught that sins would become righteous acts in the Messianic Age, and some followers deliberately broke Jewish law.

Arrested in Constantinople in 1666, he chose conversion to Islam over death, and about 300 follower families converted with him. He was later banished to Ulcinj, where he died in isolation.

Ferrand Martínez (fl. late 14th century) was a cleric of Seville cathedral and archdeacon of Écija. For years he preached against the Jews of Castile, and historians regard him as the prime mover of the 1391 massacres, which began in Seville and spread across the Iberian kingdoms.

The royal government imprisoned him in 1395. He was soon released, died shortly afterwards, and left his fortune to a hospital he had founded in Seville.

en:
Gracia Mendes Nasi (1510–1569) was a Portuguese Jewish merchant and philanthropist born in Lisbon to a converso family. On her husband Francisco Mendes's death in 1535 she inherited part of his fortune, and in 1542 took control of the Mendes banking and trading house. From 1549 she openly practised Judaism in Ferrara.

In 1553 she settled in Constantinople, where she ran escape networks for converso families fleeing the Inquisition. In 1558 Suleiman the Magnificent granted her a long-term lease of Tiberias, and she financed its rebuilding as a refuge for Jewish exiles.

Joseph Nasi (1524–1579) was a financier born to a Marrano family in Portugal who fled the Inquisition with his aunt Gracia Mendes Nasi. They reached the Ottoman capital in 1554, and his backing of Selim II against the rival Bayezid made him a leading diplomat.

He was appointed lord of Tiberias to resettle Jews there, but the project largely failed. Selim later made him Duke of Naxos. After Selim's death he lost influence, but he kept his titles.

Samuel Pallache (c. 1550–1616) was a Moroccan Jewish merchant who served the Saadi sultan Zidan Abu Maali as an envoy to the Dutch Republic. In 1608 he negotiated at The Hague with Prince Maurice of Nassau, and the 1610 Treaty of Friendship and Free Commerce was an early formal treaty between a European and a non-Christian state.

Maurice licensed him to privateer against Portuguese and Spanish shipping. Arrested in England in 1614 after taking a Portuguese ship, he was freed with Maurice's help and died at The Hague in 1616.

en:
Thomas Fairfax, 3rd Lord Fairfax of Cameron (1612–1671), known to his men as Black Tom, was an English Parliamentarian general. From 1642 he fought for Parliament under his father in the north and distinguished himself at Marston Moor in 1644.

In 1645 he took command of the newly formed New Model Army, which forced Charles I to surrender in 1646. In 1648 he subdued royalist insurgents in Kent before besieging Colchester.

He refused to join the king's trial and tried to prevent his execution. He resigned in 1650 and later backed George Monck's restoration of Charles II in 1660.

Dilawar Khan, who reigned as Amid Shah Daud Dilawar Shah, was an Afghan governor who founded the Malwa Sultanate. The Tughlaq court appointed him governor of Malwa at Dhar in 1392.

Following Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398, the fugitive Sultan Muhammad Shah sought shelter with him, and Dilawar offered him his kingdom and treasure. As Tughlaq authority collapsed, he had the Friday sermon read in his own name in 1401 and ruled Dhar as an independent sultan.

He warred unsuccessfully against Malik Sarwar of Jaunpur. He died in 1406 and was succeeded by his son Hoshang Shah.

1398年帖木儿洗劫德里后，出逃的苏丹穆罕默德沙前来避难，迪拉瓦尔将自己的国土与财宝供其使用。随着图格鲁克权威崩溃，他于1401年命人以自己的名义宣读周五布道，在达尔建立独立的苏丹国。

他与江布尔的马利克·萨尔瓦尔交战，却兵败撤退。他于1406年去世，其子胡尚格沙继位。

After their victory over the imperial army, Ismail stood down on 3 August 1347 in favour of Zafar Khan, who founded the Bahmani Sultanate as Ala-ud-din Bahman Shah. He was later poisoned by a local chieftain named Narayana.

en:
Malik Sarwar (died 1399), a eunuch of humble, possibly African origin, rose in the Delhi Sultanate from keeper of the royal jewels under Firuz Shah Tughlaq to wazir. He helped Muhammad Shah IV gain the throne and was later made governor of the eastern provinces.

In 1394 Sultan Mahmud Shah sent him east with an army and twenty elephants to crush a rebellion at Jaunpur. With Delhi collapsing, he ruled the eastern provinces in practical independence, struck coins and had the Friday sermon read in his own name. He founded the Sharqi dynasty of Jaunpur and was succeeded by his adopted heir Mubarak Shah.

en:
Muzaffar Shah I (1342–1411), born Zafar Khan, was a Tughlaq-appointed governor who founded the Gujarat Sultanate. In 1391 Delhi made him governor of Gujarat, and the next year he defeated and killed the rebel Farhat-ul-Mulk at Kamboi.

When Timur sacked Delhi in 1398 and the sultanate disintegrated, Zafar Khan ruled Gujarat on his own. His son Tatar Khan deposed him in 1403 but died the next year, when he regained power. He proclaimed himself Sultan Muzaffar Shah in 1407 and died in 1411, succeeded by his grandson Ahmad Shah I.

穆扎法尔沙一世（1342—1411）原名扎法尔汗，本是德里图格鲁克王朝任命的古吉拉特长官，后成为古吉拉特苏丹国的开创者。1391年德里朝廷任命他为古吉拉特长官，次年他在坎博伊之战击败并杀死叛乱的法尔哈特·穆勒克。

1398年帖木儿攻陷德里、苏丹国瓦解，扎法尔汗便独自统治古吉拉特。1403年其子塔塔尔汗将他废黜，塔塔尔汗次年死去，他重掌权力。1407年他自立为穆扎法尔沙，1411年去世，其孙艾哈迈德沙一世继位。

Ferdinand I (1380–1416), called Ferdinand of Antequera and the Just, was the younger son of John I of Castile and Eleanor of Aragon. From 1406 he was regent of Castile for his nephew John II, and in 1410 he took Antequera from Granada.

When his uncle Martin I of Aragon died without surviving legitimate offspring, the Compromise of Caspe chose Ferdinand king in 1412, making him the first Castilian ruler of the Crown of Aragon.

In 1416 he helped end the Western Schism by abandoning Antipope Benedict XIII. He died at Igualada on 2 April 1416.

斐迪南一世（1380—1416），又称安特克拉的斐迪南、“正义者”，是卡斯蒂利亚国王胡安一世与阿拉贡的埃莉诺所生的次子。1406年起他为侄子胡安二世摄政卡斯蒂利亚，1410年从格拉纳达手中夺取安特克拉。

他的舅父阿拉贡国王马丁一世去世时没有在世的合法子嗣，1412年卡斯佩妥协会议推举斐迪南为王，使他成为阿拉贡联合王国首位卡斯蒂利亚出身的统治者。

1416年他抛弃对立教宗本笃十三世，帮助结束西方教会大分裂。同年4月2日他卒于伊瓜拉达。

Joanot Martorell (c. 1410–1465) was a Valencian knight and writer, born in Valencia into a minor noble family from Gandia. Knighted by 1433, he spent long years in England, Portugal and Naples over his many chivalric disputes, and in 1454 joined Alfonso the Magnanimous at Naples.

In 1460 he began his Valencian romance Tirant lo Blanch. He died in Valencia in 1465, leaving the manuscript with his creditor Martí Joan de Galba, who had it printed there in 1490. Cervantes later praised the book in Don Quixote.

Abraham Cresques (1325–1387), whose Hebrew name was Elisha ben Abraham, was a Jewish cartographer of Palma on Majorca and a leading figure of the Majorcan cartographic school. He made his living as a master map-maker and builder of clocks, compasses and nautical instruments.

Together with his son Jehuda Cresques he drew the Catalan Atlas, conventionally dated 1375, a six-leaf world map on vellum counted among the finest medieval maps.

亚伯拉罕·克雷斯克斯（1325—1387），希伯来名为以利沙·本·亚伯拉罕，是马略卡岛帕尔马的犹太地图学家，也是马略卡地图学派的代表人物。他以绘制地图为业，兼造钟表、罗盘和航海仪器。

他与儿子耶胡达·克雷斯克斯合作绘制了通常系年于1375年的《加泰罗尼亚地图集》，这部绘在六张羊皮纸上的世界地图被视为中世纪最杰出的地图作品之一。

Francisco Herrera the Younger (1622–1685), el Mozo, was a Spanish painter and architect, born in Seville, the son of painter Francisco Herrera the Elder. He fled his father's violent temper for Rome, where he studied architecture and fresco and became known for his still lifes of fish.

He returned to Seville in 1656, helped found the Seville Academy and in 1660 served under Murillo as sub-director. From about 1661 he worked in Madrid, where Philip IV made him court painter and superintendent of royal buildings. He designed the rebuilding of the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar in Zaragoza, begun in 1681, and died in Madrid in 1685.

小弗朗西斯科·埃雷拉（埃尔·莫索，1622—1685）是西班牙画家、建筑师，生于塞维利亚，是画家老弗朗西斯科·埃雷拉之子。他因父亲脾气暴烈而逃往罗马，在那里研习建筑与湿壁画，并以鱼类静物画闻名。

Jerónimo Zurita (1512–1580) was a Spanish historian, born in Zaragoza, who founded the modern tradition of historical scholarship in Spain. He studied at Alcalá de Henares and entered public service through his father Miguel, a physician to Charles V.

In 1548 he was appointed the first official chronicler of the Kingdom of Aragon, and in 1566 Philip II made him secretary to the council of the Inquisition.

He resigned in 1571 to finish his Anales de la Corona de Aragón, printed between 1562 and 1580 after archival research in Aragon. He died at Zaragoza in November 1580.

Gualberto Fabricio de Vagad was an Aragonese Cistercian monk and the first chronicler of the Kingdom of Aragon, born in Zaragoza in the first third of the fifteenth century.

Commissioned by the deputies of Ferdinand II, who named him senior chronicler, he wrote the Crónica de Aragón in the vernacular, from the legendary kingdom of Sobrarbe to the death of Alfonso V in 1458. He consulted archives across the Crown of Aragon for his research.

In its prologues he argued for the preeminence of Aragon and the importance of Zaragoza. The work was printed in Zaragoza in 1499.

Juan de Lanuza y Urrea (1564–1591), called the Younger, was the last hereditary Justice of Aragon, succeeding his father in September 1591. He was at once caught up in the Alterations of Aragon, sparked by Philip II's attempt to seize the fugitive secretary Antonio Pérez through the Inquisition.

When royal troops marched on Zaragoza, Lanuza declared the invasion a violation of Aragon's fueros and led a makeshift force against them; his men scattered and he was captured. On 20 December 1591 Philip II had him beheaded without trial.

Juan Fernández de Heredia (c. 1310–1396) was an Aragonese knight, born at Munébrega. He joined the Knights Hospitaller in 1328 and in 1346 received the castellany of Amposta, fighting for Peter IV of Aragon at the victory of Epila in 1348.

Elected Grand Master in 1377, he led the Hospitallers' fruitless attempts to acquire the Principality of Achaea in Greece, and from Avignon commissioned Aragonese translations and historical works, among them the Chronicle of Morea. He died in 1396.

Giovanni Pontano (1426–1503) was an Italian humanist and poet, born at Cerreto in the Duchy of Spoleto. After his father was killed in a street brawl he grew up in Perugia and around 1448 settled in Naples, where he entered the chancery of Alfonso the Magnanimous.

He tutored the king's sons and served the Aragonese dynasty as political adviser and chancellor. From 1471 he led the Accademia Pontaniana, which took his name, and wrote Latin treatises such as De liberalitate. In 1495 he welcomed Charles VIII of France into Naples, and he died in Naples in 1503.

Constantine Phaulkon (1647–1688), born Konstantinos Gerakis on Cephalonia, was a Greek adventurer who became chief minister to King Narai of Siam. He left Cephalonia at thirteen for London, where his name became Falcon and then Phaulkon, and in 1669 joined the English East India Company.

In Siam from 1675, he mastered Siamese and entered Narai's court as an interpreter in 1681. He ran the royal treasury and steered Siam toward alliance with France. His power provoked the 1688 revolution: as Narai lay dying, Phetracha seized the court and had Phaulkon beheaded that June.

Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), born Johann Georg Turmair at Abensberg in Bavaria, was a Renaissance humanist historian and philologist. He studied at Ingolstadt, taking his master's degree in 1504, and in 1517 became Bavaria's first court historiographer.

Research in Bavarian monasteries fed his Latin Annals of the Dukes of Bavaria (1521), and he later wrote the German Bavarian Chronicle. Suspected of Protestant sympathies, he was briefly imprisoned in 1528 and died at Regensburg in 1534, honoured as the father of Bavarian historiography.

Jörg von Halsbach, also called Ganghofer (died 6 October 1488), was a late Gothic bricklayer and architect trained probably at Braunau or Wasserburg am Inn. First recorded in 1441 during reconstruction of the choir at Ettal Abbey, he later worked on the parish church at Polling, completed in 1450, but is most famous for Munich's Frauenkirche, begun in red brick in 1468 and raised within twenty years.

From 1470 he remodelled Munich's Old Town Hall in late Gothic style and in 1478 began the Kreuzkirche. He died in Munich in 1488 and was buried in the Frauenkirche.

Nur Qutb Alam was a Bengali Muslim scholar and Chishti Sufi of Hazrat Pandua, son and successor of the court scholar Alaul Haq. After the Hindu raja Ganesha seized power and persecuted Bengal's Muslims, Alam wrote to Sultan Ibrahim Sharqi of Jaunpur begging him to invade.

Ganesha and his wife offered their son Jadu to Alam for guidance; the boy became a Muslim and ruled as Sultan Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah. Alam also pioneered the Dobhashi idiom of Bengali literature. He died in 1415 or 1416 and was buried at Pandua beside his father.

Syed Sultan (c. 1550–1648) was a medieval Bengali Muslim poet, born at Habiganj in the Taraf region of greater Sylhet, into a family claiming royal descent. He devoted his verse to Islamic themes and championed the Bengali language against maulvis who despised the vernacular.

His masterpiece, the Nabibangsha of 1584, retells the lives of the prophets in Bengali epic verse and is one of the earliest Bengali adaptations of the Qisas al-Anbiya. In it he expressed his love for his mother tongue.

Khan Jahan Ali, also called Ulugh Khan, was a Muslim commander and saint who governed the Sundarbans region of Khalifatabad for the Bengal sultans. A noble under Delhi's Tughlaq sultans, he appears to have migrated to Bengal after Timur sacked the city in 1398 and was made governor.

Clearing the mangrove forests of the Ganges Delta, he laid out roads, bridges, tanks and hundreds of baked-brick mosques around his capital at Bagerhat; the great Sixty Dome Mosque was completed in 1459 and gave its name to the Khan Jahan style. He died in October 1459 and was buried beside one of his reservoirs.

John Amos Comenius (Jan Amos Komenský, 1592–1670) was a Czech theologian and pedagogue born in Moravia, the last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren. Ordained in 1616, he became a pastor four years later.

Religious war in 1621 cost him his property and writings; persecuted by the Habsburgs, he led the Brethren into exile in Poland in 1628. His Janua linguarum reserata of 1631 made him famous, and Didactica Magna laid out universal education.

He later settled in Amsterdam, where in 1658 he published Orbis Pictus, the first widely used illustrated textbook. He died there in November 1670, remembered as the Teacher of Nations.

1621年的宗教战争使他失去财产和著作；在哈布斯堡王朝的迫害下，1628年他带领兄弟会信徒流亡波兰。1631年出版的《语言入门》使他名扬欧洲，《大教学论》则系统阐述了普及教育。

他晚年定居阿姆斯特丹，1658年在那里出版第一部广泛使用的插图教科书《世界图解》。1670年11月他在阿姆斯特丹去世，被誉为“人类的导师”。

Jan Rokycana (c. 1396–1471) was a Hussite theologian born in Rokycany and the elected, though never papally confirmed, archbishop of the Utraquist church. He became vicar of Prague's Týn Church in 1427 and rector of Charles University in 1435.

At the 1441 Kutná Hora diet he helped establish the fundamentals of Hussite belief as the law of the land. After seeking recognition from Pope Nicholas V, he backed George of Poděbrady's election as king in 1458, though he later preached against him. He died in Prague in February 1471 and was buried in the Týn Church.

扬·罗基察纳（约1396—1471）生于罗基察尼，是胡斯派神学家、圣杯派教会选出的大主教，但始终未获教皇批准。他1427年任布拉格泰恩教堂代理神父，1435年任查理大学校长。

1441年，他在库特纳霍拉的邦国会议上协助把胡斯派基本信条定为国家法律。他向教皇尼古拉五世寻求承认后，于1458年支持波杰布拉德的伊日当选国王，后来却在布道中反对伊日。1471年2月他在布拉格去世，葬于泰恩教堂。

en:
Jiří Melantrich z Aventina (c. 1511–1580), born Jiří Černý Rožďalovický, was the leading Czech Renaissance printer and publisher. He opened his Prague workshop in the mid-1540s, and after Ferdinand I banned Czech Protestant literature in 1547 he joined a Catholic printer, whose workshop he later took over.

His Melantrich's Bible appeared from 1549 in five editions by 1577, and he also printed humanist and scholarly works. A Lutheran tolerant of Catholicism, he was ennobled with the title z Aventina in 1557, and after his death in 1580 his press passed to his partner Daniel Adam z Veleslavína.

伊日·梅兰特里赫·兹·阿文蒂纳（约1511—1580），原名伊日·切尔尼·罗日达洛维茨基，是文艺复兴时期捷克最重要的印刷商和出版家。他于1540年代中期在布拉格开办印刷坊，1547年斐迪南一世禁止捷克语新教书籍后，加入一位天主教印刷商的商号，后来接手其印刷坊。

《梅兰特里赫圣经》1549年首次刊行，到1577年共出五版；他还印制人文主义与学术著作。他身为路德宗信徒而包容天主教，1557年获封“兹·阿文蒂纳”贵族称号；1580年他去世后，印刷坊由合作者丹尼尔·亚当·兹·韦莱斯拉温接手。

en:
Kilian Ignaz Dientzenhofer (1689–1751) was a German-Bohemian Baroque architect, born in Prague, the most gifted of the Dientzenhofer family of architects. He left Bohemia around 1710, toured Germany, France and Italy and trained under Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt in Vienna, returning in 1716.

In Prague he built the Church of Saint John of Nepomuk at Hradčany (1720–1728), redesigned the Loreta in 1723 and completed the Church of Saint Nicholas in Malá Strana. He also rebuilt Broumov monastery and planned its surrounding group of village Baroque churches. He died in Prague in December 1751.

基利安·伊格纳茨·丁岑霍费尔（1689—1751）生于布拉格，是德意志裔波希米亚巴洛克建筑师，也是丁岑霍费尔建筑世家中最有才华的一员。他约1710年离开波希米亚，游历德意志、法兰西和意大利，在维也纳拜约翰·卢卡斯·冯·希尔德布兰特为师，1716年返回。

他在布拉格的作品包括城堡区的内波穆克圣约翰教堂（1720—1728）、1723年改建的洛雷托，以及由他完工的小城圣尼古拉教堂。他还重建了布劳莫夫修道院，并规划了周边一组乡村巴洛克教堂。1751年12月他在布拉格去世。

en:
Josef Dobrovský (1753–1829) was a Czech philologist and historian, born at Balassagyarmat in Hungary, and a founder of the Czech National Revival. Once a Jesuit novice, he studied theology in Prague after the order was dissolved in 1773.

In 1792 he travelled to Scandinavia and Russia in search of manuscripts scattered during the Thirty Years' War, and he helped found the Royal Czech Society of Sciences in Prague in 1784.

His History of the Czech Language and Literature (1792) and Czech grammar (1809) put the language on a scholarly footing, and his 1822 Old Church Slavonic grammar made him a founder of Slavic studies. He died at Brno in January 1829.

约瑟夫·多布罗夫斯基（1753—1829）生于匈牙利包洛绍焦尔毛特，是捷克语言学家、历史学家，捷克民族复兴的奠基人之一。他早年入耶稣会为初学修士，1773年该会解散后回到布拉格学习神学。

1792年他前往斯堪的纳维亚和俄国，寻找三十年战争中散失的手稿；他还在布拉格参与创立了捷克皇家科学学会（1784年）。

其《捷克语言与文学史》（1792年）和捷克语语法（1809年）为捷克语奠定了学术基础，1822年的古教会斯拉夫语语法更使他成为斯拉夫学的奠基人之一。1829年1月他在布尔诺去世。

en:
Benedikt Rejt (c. 1454–1536) was a Bohemian architect of German origin, summoned to Prague by King Vladislav II as a master builder. From 1485 he modernized Prague Castle's fortifications, adding the Daliborka and Mihulka towers.

His masterpiece, the Vladislav Hall of 1493–1502, was the largest vaulted hall without interior supports in Central Europe, and its broad Knights' Staircase let horsemen ride in for tournaments.

He also built St. Barbara's Church in Kutná Hora and St. Nicholas's Church in Louny. In 1518 he chaired a congress of architects and stonemasons at Annaberg in Saxony.

贝内迪克特·赖特（约1454—1536）是德意志血统的波希米亚建筑师，被国王弗拉迪斯拉夫二世召到布拉格任工匠师傅。他自1485年起改建布拉格城堡的防御工事，增建了达利博尔卡和米胡尔卡塔楼。

他的代表作是1493—1502年建成的弗拉迪斯拉夫大厅，为当时中欧最大的无内部支撑拱顶大厅；宽阔的骑士阶梯可让骑士骑马入场比武。

他还主持修建了库特纳霍拉的圣巴巴拉教堂和洛乌尼的圣尼古拉教堂。1518年，他在萨克森的安纳贝格主持建筑师与石匠大会。

en:
Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), born at Weil der Stadt, was a German astronomer and mathematician. He taught mathematics before moving to Prague in 1600 as Tycho Brahe's assistant; after Brahe's death in 1601 he inherited his observations and became imperial mathematician under Rudolf II.

In Astronomia nova (1609) he showed that Mars moves in an ellipse and formulated his first two laws of planetary motion, the third following in Harmonice Mundi (1619). Later based in Linz and then Sagan, he died at Regensburg in November 1630; his laws underpinned Newton's theory of universal gravitation.

约翰内斯·开普勒（1571—1630）生于魏尔代斯塔特，是德意志天文学家和数学家。他先教授数学，1600年到布拉格担任第谷·布拉赫的助手；1601年布拉赫去世后，他继承其观测资料，成为鲁道夫二世治下的皇家数学家。

他在1609年的《新天文学》中证明火星沿椭圆轨道运行，提出行星运动前两条定律，第三定律载于1619年的《世界的和谐》。他后来辗转林茨和萨甘，1630年11月在雷根斯堡去世；其行星运动定律为牛顿的万有引力理论奠定了基础。

en:
Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), born at Knutstorp in Danish Scania, was the greatest astronomer of the pre-telescopic age. His 1572 observations of a new star in De nova stella (1573) shattered the Aristotelian idea of an unchanging sky.

King Frederick II gave him the island of Hven, where from 1576 he built Uraniborg and gathered precise planetary data. He later worked at the underground observatory Stjerneborg.

Forced out by Christian IV in 1597, he became imperial astronomer in Prague under Rudolf II, where Johannes Kepler assisted him until his death in 1601. Kepler later used his data to develop the laws of planetary motion.

第谷·布拉赫（1546—1601）生于丹麦斯科讷的克努兹托普庄园，是望远镜发明前最伟大的天文学家。他在1572年观测到一颗新星，1573年在《论新星》中加以记述，打破了亚里士多德天界不变的学说。

丹麦国王腓特烈二世将汶岛赐给他，他自1576年起在岛上修建天堡，积累了精确的行星观测数据。他后来还在地下的星堡观测所工作。

1597年他被克里斯蒂安四世逐离丹麦，到布拉格出任鲁道夫二世的皇家天文学家，约翰内斯·开普勒担任他的助手，直到他1601年去世。开普勒后来利用他的数据提出行星运动定律。

en:
Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553) was a German astronomer and mathematician, born and died at Saalfeld in Saxony. Educated at Wittenberg, he became professor of higher mathematics there in 1536 through Philipp Melanchthon.

He praised Copernicus in a 1542 commentary while rejecting heliocentric cosmology on physical and theological grounds. Backed by Duke Albert of Prussia, he issued the Prutenic Tables in 1551, which recast Copernicus's calculations in a geocentric frame and replaced the old Alfonsine Tables; after his death they helped underpin the Gregorian reform of 1582.

伊拉斯谟·赖因霍尔德（1511—1553）是德意志天文学家与数学家，生于萨克森的萨尔费尔德，并卒于故乡。他在维滕贝格求学，1536年经菲利普·梅兰希通举荐任高等数学教授。

他在1542年的一部注疏中称赞哥白尼，却因物理学和神学理由拒绝日心宇宙观。在普鲁士公爵阿尔布雷希特资助下，他于1551年刊行《普鲁士星表》，把哥白尼的计算方法重新纳入地心体系，取代旧的《阿方索星表》；他去世后，该表成为1582年格列高利历改革的基础之一。

en:
Johann Crüger (1598–1662) was a German composer and hymn editor, born a Sorb innkeeper's son near Guben. After schooling and theological study at Wittenberg, he settled in Berlin in 1622, where for forty years he taught at the Gymnasium zum Grauen Kloster and served as cantor of the Nikolaikirche.

During the Thirty Years' War he survived plague that claimed his wife and five children in 1636. From 1643 he set hymns by Paul Gerhardt, and in 1647 he published the Praxis pietatis melica, the most influential Lutheran hymnal of the century. His tunes include Nun danket alle Gott. He died in Berlin.

约翰·克吕格尔（1598—1662）是德意志作曲家与圣诗集编者，索布人，生于古本附近一个客栈主家庭。他求学后在维滕贝格攻读神学，1622年定居柏林，此后四十年间在灰色修道院文理中学任教，并担任圣尼古拉教堂唱诗班指挥。

en:
Moses Mendelssohn (1729–1786) was a German-Jewish philosopher and a father of the Jewish Enlightenment, born in Dessau. Destined for the rabbinate, he followed his teacher to Berlin in 1743 and educated himself in languages and philosophy, becoming a silk merchant's partner and a Berlin writer.

In 1763 he won the Berlin Academy's essay prize, ahead of Kant; his Platonic dialogue Phaedo (1767) made him famous as the German Socrates. He defended religious liberty in Jerusalem (1783) and translated the Pentateuch into German. A lifelong friend of Lessing, he died in Berlin in 1786.

Johannes Agricola (1494–1566), born Johann Schneider at Eisleben, was a Protestant reformer and once a close friend of Martin Luther, as his secretary at the 1519 Leipzig disputation. He taught and preached before his recall in 1536, and defended the doctrine Luther branded antinomian: that Christians were no longer bound by the Mosaic law.

The quarrel drove him from Wittenberg to Berlin in 1540. Elector Joachim II made him court preacher, and he helped draft the Augsburg Interim of 1548, whose concessions to Catholic authority made him an outcast. He died of plague in Berlin.

Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814) was a German philosopher and founder of German idealism, born at Rammenau. The son of a ribbon weaver, he studied theology and immersed himself in Kant's writings.

He visited Kant at Königsberg in 1791 and won fame with Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation (1792), first mistaken for Kant's own work. He took a chair at Jena in 1794, but was dismissed over atheism in 1799 and moved to Berlin.

In occupied Berlin he delivered the Addresses to the German Nation (1807–1808), and in 1810 became the first rector of Berlin's new university. He died in 1814.

约翰·戈特利布·费希特（1762—1814）是德国哲学家、德国唯心主义的奠基人之一，生于拉梅瑙。他是织带工之子，曾攻读神学，并潜心研读康德的著作。

1791年他到柯尼斯堡拜访康德，随后以《试评一切天启》（1792）一举成名——该书最初还被读者当成康德的著作。1794年他出任耶拿大学教授，1799年因无神论之争被解职，迁居柏林。

在法军占领的柏林，他发表了《对德意志民族的演讲》（1807—1808），1810年成为柏林新建大学的首任校长。1814年他在当地去世。

Christoph Friedrich Nicolai (1733–1811) was a Berlin bookseller, critic and satirical novelist, the son of the founder of the Nicolaische Buchhandlung. After learning the bookselling trade in Frankfurt an der Oder from 1749, he returned to Berlin in 1752. With Lessing and Mendelssohn he edited the review journal Briefe, die neueste Literatur betreffend (1759–1765), followed by his own Allgemeine deutsche Bibliothek (1765–1792), the organ of the popular Enlightenment philosophers.

His novel The Joys of Young Werther (1775) parodied Goethe's Sorrows of Young Werther, giving its hero a happy ending. He died in Berlin in 1811.

Wilhelm von Humboldt (1767–1835) was a Prussian philosopher, linguist and diplomat, born at Potsdam. After serving as a Prussian diplomat in Rome, he was placed in charge of church and school affairs in 1809.

He overhauled Prussian education from primary schools through gymnasia to teacher training, seeing education as a means of realizing individual potential rather than preparing pupils for fixed social roles. In 1810 he founded the University of Berlin on the principle that teaching and research are inseparable, a model copied across Europe and beyond.

He later represented Prussia in London, while his philosophy of language helped found ethnolinguistics. He died at Tegel in 1835.

威廉·冯·洪堡（1767—1835）是普鲁士哲学家、语言学家、外交官，生于波茨坦。他曾任普鲁士驻罗马外交官，1809年受命主管宗教与教育事务。

他对从小学、中学到师资培训的普鲁士教育体系进行全面改革，认为教育应当帮助个人实现潜能，而非让学生适应固定的社会角色。1810年他创立柏林大学，以教学与研究相统一为原则，这一模式后为欧洲及其他地区的大学所效仿。

此后他在伦敦担任外交使节，其语言哲学研究为民族语言学奠定了基础。1835年他在泰格尔去世。

Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–1781) was a German dramatist and critic of the Enlightenment, born in Kamenz. After study in Leipzig and journalism in Berlin, he served in Breslau from 1760, where he wrote Laocoön. From 1767 he was the Hamburg National Theatre's critic, pioneering dramaturgy, and in 1770 became librarian at Wolfenbüttel.

His feud with Pastor Goeze in 1778 brought a ban, to which he replied with Nathan the Wise (1779), whose ring parable pleads for tolerance among Judaism, Christianity and Islam; its hero was modelled on his friend Moses Mendelssohn. He died in Brunswick in 1781.

Carl Gotthard Langhans (1732–1808) was a Prussian architect and a pioneer of Neoclassicism in Germany. Born in Landeshut, Silesia, he studied law at Halle before teaching himself architecture from Vitruvius and Winckelmann. He rebuilt Hatzfeld Palace between 1766 and 1774; the count also introduced him to the Berlin court, and from 1775 he headed Silesia's Prussian building authority.

In 1788 Frederick William II named him first director of the royal building commission in Berlin and charged him with the Brandenburg Gate, modelled on Athens's Propylaea and crowned by Schadow's quadriga. He died near Breslau in 1808.

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831), born in Stuttgart, was the culminating philosopher of German idealism. At the Tübingen seminary he roomed with the poet Hölderlin and the philosopher Schelling, and his thought was shaped by the French Revolution and the Napoleonic wars.

His Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) and Science of Logic (1812–1816) unfold a dialectic in which consciousness advances through contradiction toward self-knowing spirit, or Geist — humanity coming to know itself through a historical process of rational development.

Appointed to the philosophy chair at Berlin, he taught there until his death in 1831. His followers then split into Right and Left camps, the latter shaping the young Karl Marx.

格奥尔格·威廉·弗里德里希·黑格尔（1770—1831），生于斯图加特，是德国唯心主义哲学的集大成者。在图宾根神学院求学时，他与诗人荷尔德林、哲学家谢林同窗，法国大革命和拿破仑战争深刻塑造了他的思想。

1807年问世的《精神现象学》与1812至1816年出版的《逻辑学》以辩证法展开其体系：意识经由矛盾不断前进，最终达到自我认识的“精神”，即人类通过理性发展的历史进程认识自身。

Anna Dorothea Therbusch (1721–1782) was a leading Rococo portrait painter born Anna Dorothea Lisiewski in Berlin, daughter of portraitist Georg Lisiewski. She and her sister were celebrated as child prodigies, but after marrying an innkeeper in 1742 she abandoned painting for nearly twenty years, returning to her easel around 1760.

She worked for the Duke of Württemberg in Stuttgart, was elected to the Paris Académie Royale in 1767 with Denis Diderot's patronage, and returned to Berlin in 1768 as Frederick the Great's court portraitist, decorating Sanssouci and painting the Prussian royal family. She died there in 1782.

Christian Wolff (1679–1754) was a German rationalist philosopher, born in Breslau. Appointed professor of mathematics and natural philosophy at the University of Halle in 1706, he built a comprehensive system modelled on Leibniz, presenting every science in mathematical order. He wrote chiefly in German, making it a language of scholarly instruction.

His praise of Confucian ethics in a 1721 oration enraged the Pietist faculty, and in 1723 King Frederick William I expelled him from Prussia on pain of death. He taught at Marburg until 1740, when Frederick the Great recalled him to Halle.

Kurt Christoph von Schwerin (1684–1757) was a Prussian field marshal under Frederick the Great. After soldiering in Dutch and Mecklenburg ranks, he entered Prussian service in 1720, and in 1730 sat on the court martial that tried Crown Prince Frederick for desertion.

Promoted field marshal and count on Frederick's accession, he saved the campaign at Mollwitz in April 1741: he persuaded Frederick to leave the wavering field and converted it into the victory that secured Silesia.

He later took part in the siege and capture of Prague in 1744. On 6 May 1757, leading a regiment with its colours at Prague, he was killed by a cannonball.

库尔特·克里斯托夫·冯·施维林（1684—1757）是腓特烈大帝麾下的普鲁士陆军元帅。他早年先后在荷兰和梅克伦堡的军队中服役，1720年转入普鲁士效力，1730年作为军事法庭成员审判以逃亡罪名受审的王储腓特烈。

腓特烈即位后，他晋升元帅并受封伯爵；1741年4月的莫尔维茨会战中，他先劝腓特烈撤离胜负未卜的战场，随后把战局扭转为确保西里西亚到手的胜利。

1744年他参与围攻和占领布拉格。1757年5月6日，他在布拉格战役中高举团旗带队冲锋，被炮弹击中阵亡。

Andreas Schlüter (1659–1714) was a German Baroque sculptor and architect. After work for John III Sobieski's Wilanów Palace, he was invited to Berlin in 1694 as court sculptor to Elector Frederick III, and in 1696 toured Italy studying its masters.

Thereafter he decorated the Zeughaus armory with his dying warriors and, as court architect, reshaped the Berlin City Palace. He designed the Amber Room (1701–1709) and cast the equestrian statue of the Great Elector in 1708. In 1713 he joined Tsar Peter the Great in Saint Petersburg, where he died the next year.

Constantine Harmenopoulos (1320–c. 1385) was a Byzantine jurist of Armenian descent who served in Thessalonica as nomophylax and katholikos krites, one of the highest judgeships of the late empire.

His fame rests on the Hexabiblos, compiled in 1344–1345, a six-volume handbook gathering a wide range of Byzantine legal sources. After his death, it was widely adopted in the Ottoman Balkans.

Giovanni Giustiniani Longo (1418–1453) was a Genoese nobleman and mercenary captain from Chios's Giustiniani family. In January 1453 he sailed to Constantinople with seven hundred men to defend it against Sultan Mehmed II, and Emperor Constantine XI named him protostrator.

He cushioned the cannonade by packing breaches in the Theodosian Walls with rubble. He held the St. Romanus sector through the 55-day siege until gravely wounded in the final assault of 29 May. Evacuated to Chios, he died of his wounds on 1 June 1453.

George Sphrantzes (1401–c. 1478) was a Byzantine courtier and historian born in Constantinople. From 1418 he attended Emperor Manuel II and became a lifelong confidant of Constantine XI: he governed Glarentza in the Morea, negotiated Constantine's marriage to Caterina Gattilusio in 1440 and was made prefect of Mystras in 1446.

He witnessed the fall of Constantinople in 1453, was enslaved by the Ottomans and ransomed that September; in 1454 he went to Adrianople to ransom his wife.

After taking monastic vows in 1472 he wrote his Chronicle. This key eyewitness record of the empire's final decades ends in 1477.

Alexander Mavrocordatos the Exaporite (1641–1709) was a Greek physician and statesman of the Mavrocordatos family. Educated at Rome, Padua and Bologna, he earned a medical doctorate in 1664 with a treatise on blood circulation before entering Ottoman service. In 1673 he became Grand Dragoman of the Porte.

As chief Ottoman negotiator of the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 he received the title Keeper of Secrets and an imperial countship. His sons began the family's rule as hospodars of Moldavia and Wallachia. He died in 1709.

en:
Philotheos Skoufos (c. 1615/1625–1685) was a Greek painter, educator and clergyman, born at Chania on Crete. On Corfu he collaborated with painter Emmanuel Tzanes. Skoufos belonged to both the Cretan and Heptanese schools, blending their Byzantine icon tradition with Venetian painting, and was briefly attached to Venice's Greek church of San Giorgio dei Greci.

As a priest he officiated at the wedding of the painter Ioannis Moskos. He died on Zakynthos in 1685; his best-known works are the Stoning of Saint Stephen and the Virgin in the Temple.

Demetrios Kydones (1324–1398) was a Byzantine theologian, translator and statesman born in Thessalonica who served an unprecedented three terms as mesazon, the empire's chief minister, under John VI Kantakouzenos from 1347, John V Palaiologos from 1369 to 1383 and Manuel II. Learning Latin at John VI's request, he translated Thomas Aquinas' Summa contra Gentiles and Summa Theologica into Greek, introducing Latin scholasticism to Byzantine readers.

A Catholic by 1365, he sought reconciliation between the Eastern and Western churches to secure a military alliance. In 1369 he accompanied John V to Rome to seek papal support against the Ottoman Turks.

德米特里奥斯·基多尼斯（1324—1398）是塞萨洛尼基出身的拜占庭神学家、翻译家与政治家，曾史无前例三度出任帝国首席大臣“梅萨宗”，先后侍奉约翰六世·坎塔库泽努斯（1347年起）、约翰五世·巴列奥略（1369—1383年）与曼努埃尔二世。他应约翰六世之请学习拉丁语，把托马斯·阿奎那的《反异教大全》和《神学大全》译为希腊语，将拉丁经院哲学引入拜占庭读书界。

他在1365年前已皈依天主教，并争取东西教会和解以建立军事同盟。1369年他随约翰五世前往罗马，谋求教宗支持以对抗奥斯曼土耳其人。

Tomás de Torquemada (1420–1498) was a Castilian Dominican friar, born at Valladolid, who became confessor and closest advisor to Queen Isabella I and supported her marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469. After the Catholic Monarchs set up the Spanish Inquisition in 1478, Pope Sixtus IV made him an inquisitor in 1482 and first Grand Inquisitor in 1483.

He issued 28 articles guiding its tribunals and built a court network across Castile and Aragon. A driving force behind the Alhambra Decree of 1492 expelling Spain's Jews, he died at Ávila in 1498, his name a byword for persecution.

Francisco de Zurbarán (baptized 7 November 1598 – 27 August 1664) was a Spanish Baroque painter born at Fuente de Cantos in Extremadura. Sent to Seville to train in 1614, he made his name with twenty-one paintings for the monastery of San Pablo el Real, settled there in 1629, and around 1630 became painter to Philip IV.

In 1631 he painted the altarpiece of the Apotheosis of Saint Thomas Aquinas. Called the Spanish Caravaggio for his chiaroscuro, he painted monks, nuns and still lifes exported to Spanish America. He moved to Madrid in 1658 and died there in 1664.

Jerónimo de Ayanz y Beaumont (1553–1613) was a Navarrese soldier and inventor. A page to Philip II from 1567, he later fought in Tunisia, at Gembloux and in the Azores, winning the Order of Calatrava.

Appointed administrator of the crown mines in 1587, he oversaw mines in Spain and America and turned to technology. He tested an immersion suit before Philip III in 1602, designed mine ventilation systems, and in 1606 registered the first patent for a steam-powered machine, built to drain flooded mines. He died in Madrid in 1613.

en:
Diego de Huallpa was a Quechua Indian of sixteenth-century Upper Peru, credited with the accidental discovery of silver on the Cerro Rico at Potosí in 1545. Tradition says he lit a fire against the cold while looking for a lost llama and found silver in the ashes.

He sold the silver and told his companion Huanca. After a quarrel between them, the story reached the Spaniards at Porco, and the mountain became a great silver mine.

Huallpa won no reward; the legendary native leader Chaqui Catari cursed him for revealing the mountain. He later told Viceroy Toledo of a shrine on its slopes.

en:
Tomás Luis de Victoria (c. 1548–1611) was Spain's greatest Renaissance composer of sacred music. After his father's death, his uncle became his guardian. A choirboy at Ávila Cathedral, he went to Rome in 1565 with a grant from Philip II, absorbed Palestrina's polyphony and was ordained a priest in 1574.

His motets, masses and Holy Week Offices set Latin texts in expressive polyphony. In 1587 Philip II made him chaplain to the Dowager Empress María at Madrid's Descalzas Reales convent; after she died in 1603 he stayed on as organist. He died there in 1611.

Pedro Cieza de León (c. 1518–1554) was a Spanish conquistador and chronicler of Peru. Born in Llerena, he sailed for the Indies around 1536 and for years campaigned and travelled through Peru, recording Inca history and the geography of the Andes.

He returned to Seville in 1551, and in 1553 published the first part of his Crónica del Perú, describing the geography and customs of the Andes; its second part dealt with Inca rule. He died in 1554, leaving three parts unpublished, which appeared only centuries later.

Juan de Castellanos (1522–1607) was a Spanish soldier, chronicler and priest of the New Kingdom of Granada. Born in Alanís, he sailed to the Indies in the 1530s and fought across the Caribbean.

In 1555 he pursued an ecclesiastical career at Cartagena and was ordained a priest. From 1562 he was parish priest of Tunja, where he amassed a library and spent four decades in his ministry and writing.

His epic Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias is one of the longest poems in Spanish, a verse history of the conquest and the Muisca. He died at Tunja in 1607.

en:
Josefa Amar y Borbón (1749–1833) was a Spanish writer of the Enlightenment. Born at Saragossa, she moved to Madrid when her father became royal physician and was educated by royal preceptors, mastering Greek, Latin and Italian.

Married in 1764, she returned to Saragossa in 1772 and became the first woman admitted to the Aragonese Economic Society in 1782. In 1790 she joined the Medical Society of Barcelona.

Through essays and translations she defended women's equal capacity for learning and public office, and her Discourse on the Physical and Moral Education of Women appeared in 1790.

她通过论文和译作论证女性在学习和担任公职上具有同等能力，所著《论女性的身体与道德教育》于1790年出版。

en:
María de Zayas y Sotomayor (baptized 12 September 1590; died around 1661) was a Spanish Golden Age writer born in Madrid, the daughter of an infantry captain.

In 1637 she published in Zaragoza her first novella collection, Novelas amorosas y ejemplares, followed in 1647 by the starker Desengaños amorosos, whose heroines expose the wrongs women endured in their day; both collections are now read as early feminist fiction.

Admired by Lope de Vega, who dedicated poems to her, she was called the Sibyl of Madrid. She vanishes from the records after 1647.

en:
Francisca de Pedraza was an orphan from Alcalá de Henares, raised in a convent girls' college. In 1612 she married Jerónimo de Jaras, who beat her from their wedding night. She appealed to civil and ecclesiastical courts; early rulings ordered him to change his conduct, but she continued to seek a separation.

In 1624 the papal nuncio referred her case to the University of Alcalá's tribunal. Its rector granted her separation, the return of her dowry and a restraining order, one of the first such rulings for an abused wife in Spain.

Bartolomé de las Casas (1484–1566) was a Dominican friar who defended the indigenous peoples of Spanish America. He reached Hispaniola in 1502 and held an encomienda, but after the conquest of Cuba renounced it in 1514.

As Protector of the Indians from 1516 he lobbied the Crown, helped win the New Laws of 1542, and served as Bishop of Chiapas. His Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies denounced atrocities, and at the Valladolid debate of 1550 he refuted Sepúlveda's claim that Indians were natural slaves. He died in 1566.

Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda (1490–1573) was a Spanish humanist and theologian born in the province of Córdoba. After studying at Alcalá and Bologna, he translated works of Aristotle from Greek into Latin and served at the papal curia in Rome.

In 1529 he urged Charles V to unite Europe against the Turks. In Democrates (1535) he argued that a just war founded on natural law was compatible with Christianity.

He is chiefly remembered as the opponent of Bartolomé de las Casas at the Valladolid debate of 1550–1551, where he defended the Spanish conquest of the Indies and the subjugation of Native Americans.

Luisa de Medrano (1484–1527), born into a noble family at Atienza, was one of the puellae doctae, the learned girls of Renaissance Spain. At the court of Queen Isabella I, she studied history and humanist philosophy alongside the royal children. She taught Latin at the University of Salamanca, taking the chair once held by Antonio de Nebrija; on 16 November 1508 the rector recorded her reading in the chair of Canons.

The humanist Lucio Marineo Siculo praised her public lectures on Latin letters. Her poems and philosophical writings have not survived, and she died in 1527.

Zenón de Somodevilla, Marquess of Ensenada (1702–1781), entered the navy administration in 1720 and rose under Philip V's ministers. In 1736 he was made Marquess of Ensenada, and in 1743 Philip V named him minister of finance, war and the navy. He led Spain through the War of the Austrian Succession and from 1749 ordered the census known as the Catastro of Ensenada.

He strengthened royal control over the Church, promoted public works and sent students abroad. Ousted by court intrigue in 1754, he was briefly recalled under Charles III, exiled again in 1766, and died at Medina del Campo.

Juan de Mena (1411–1456) was a Castilian poet born at Córdoba and educated at Salamanca, who travelled in Italy before entering the court of King Juan II.

The king named him secretary of Latin letters and royal chronicler, though he chiefly wrote Dantean poetry that was full of classical myth.

His masterpiece, the Laberinto de Fortuna of 1444, uses three Wheels of Fortune to survey Castilian history, urging national unity and the Reconquista under Juan II. He held the post under Enrique IV and died at Torrelaguna in 1456, one of the century's three great Castilian poets.

Jorge Manrique (c. 1440–1479) was a Castilian nobleman and poet of the Manrique de Lara family and nephew of the poet Gómez Manrique. He fought for Isabella and Ferdinand against Juana la Beltraneja in the Castilian War of Succession.

After his father Rodrigo, Grand Master of the Order of Santiago, died in 1476, Jorge composed the Coplas por la muerte de su padre, an elegy on death as the equaliser of worldly glory and one of the classics of Spanish poetry. In April 1479 he was mortally wounded storming Garcimuñoz Castle, held by the Marquis of Villena.

In April 1479 he was mortally wounded storming Garcimuñoz Castle, held by the Marquis of [ShowLocationName('villena')].

霍赫·曼里奎（约1440—1479）是贵族、诗人，出身曼里克·德·拉腊家族，为诗人戈麦斯·曼里克之侄。他在继承战争中为伊莎贝拉与斐迪南作战，对抗胡安娜·拉·贝尔特兰内哈。

1476年他的父亲、圣地亚哥骑士团团长罗德里戈去世后，霍赫写下《祭父词》，以死亡抹平世间一切荣华为题，是西班牙语诗歌的千古名篇。1479年4月，他在攻打比列纳侯爵据守的加尔西穆尼奥斯城堡时伤重而死。

en:
Juan Bautista Muñoz (1745–1799) was a Spanish historian born at Museros near Valencia. A Dominican philosopher, he taught at Valencia University until Charles III made him cosmographer-major of the Indies in 1770. In 1779 the king charged him with writing an archive-based history of the Spanish Americas.

In Seville from 1784 he persuaded ministers to gather all overseas documents into one repository; the result was the Archive of the Indies in a former merchants' exchange. The first volume of his History of the New World appeared in 1793, and he died in Madrid six years later.

Ambrogio Spinola (1569–1630) was a Genoese nobleman who became the foremost general of Habsburg Spain. Entering Spanish service in 1602, he raised troops at his own expense and took Ostend in 1604, then commanded the Army of Flanders and seized a string of Rhine towns from Maurice of Nassau.

After the Twelve Years' Truce ended, he won his famous victory at Breda in 1625, later immortalized by Velázquez in The Surrender of Breda. Hampered by his rivalry with Olivares, he left Flanders in 1628 and died at the siege of Casale in September 1630.

安布罗焦·斯皮诺拉（1569—1630）是热那亚贵族，后成为哈布斯堡西班牙最杰出的统帅。1602年他投效西班牙，自费募兵，1604年攻克奥斯坦德，随后出任佛兰德军团司令，从拿骚的莫里斯手中夺取莱茵河畔一连串城镇。

十二年停战协定结束后，他于1625年赢得生平最著名的布雷达大捷，后来委拉斯开兹据此绘成《布雷达的投降》。因与奥利瓦雷斯相争而处处受制，他于1628年离开佛兰德，1630年9月死于卡萨莱围城战。

Fernán Sánchez de Valladolid was the first royal chronicler of Castile, active at the court of Alfonso XI from about 1325 to 1348. On the king's commission he compiled an ordered history of the realm from materials assembled under Alfonso X and Sancho IV, and is credited above all with the Crónica de Alfonso Onceno.

That work follows Alfonso XI from his troubled minority through his wars against Granada and the siege of Algeciras, depicting the nobles' misdeeds and presenting the king as a ruler who sought justice and fought steadfastly against the Moors. His chronicles became a principal source for the period.

费尔南·桑切斯·德·巴利亚多利德是卡斯蒂利亚第一位王室史官，约1325至1348年效力于阿方索十一世的宫廷。他奉国王之命，依据阿方索十世和桑乔四世时期整理的史料编写体系完整的王国史，最重要的著作是《阿方索十一世编年史》。

该书从阿方索十一世多舛的幼年写起，记述到他对格拉纳达的战争和阿尔赫西拉斯围城战，描绘国王年幼时贵族的恶行，把阿方索写成伸张正义、顽强对抗摩尔人的君主。他的编年史成为研究这一时期的主要史料。

Juan Ruiz (c. 1283–c. 1350), known as the Archpriest of Hita, was a Castilian cleric and poet, born in Alcalá de Henares and probably educated in Toledo. He wrote El Libro de buen amor, a mixture of fables, parodies, love adventures and comic autobiography, completed around 1343.

In his verse he says he was imprisoned on the order of the Archbishop of Toledo. He died around 1350, regarded as the greatest Castilian poet of his century.

Antonio de Nebrija (1444–1522) was the leading Spanish humanist of his age. Born at Lebrija and educated at Salamanca and Bologna, he held the first chair of grammar at Salamanca from 1476 and published a Latin textbook in 1481.

In 1492 he brought out the Gramática de la lengua castellana, the first printed grammar of any modern European language, telling Queen Isabella that language was the instrument of empire. His Spanish-Latin dictionary followed in 1495. Later, under Cisneros, he worked on the Complutensian Polyglot Bible, and he died at Alcalá de Henares in 1522.

Francisco de Enzinas (1518–1552) was a Spanish humanist and Protestant reformer, the first to translate the New Testament from Greek into Spanish. The son of a Burgos wool merchant, he studied at Louvain and at Wittenberg under Melanchthon.

His Spanish New Testament was printed at Antwerp in 1543, and he presented a copy to Emperor Charles V in Brussels. Weeks later the Inquisition arrested him and ordered almost the entire edition burned. He escaped in 1545 and fled to Wittenberg, later taught Greek in England, and died at Strasbourg in 1552.
